thales.sub: the man Aristotle nominated as the first philosopher
world: Miletus in the early sixth century was the richest Ionian city: a port at the mouth of the Maeander exporting worked wool, holding a share in the Greek trading station at Naucratis in Egypt, claiming colonies around the Black Sea. Inland lay Lydia, and beyond it the record-keeping bureaucracies of Mesopotamia. Such commerce put Babylonian eclipse tables and Egyptian land-measurement within a Milesian’s reach.

Politics pressed hard. Lydia under Alyattes and Croesus reduced the Ionian cities one by one, Miletus alone keeping a negotiated treaty; in 547 or 546 Cyrus took Sardis and his general Harpagus brought Ionia under Persia. Herodotus reports that Thales urged the Ionians to pool their government in one council at Teos, advice they refused. Lydia also struck the first coins around 600. None of that shaped his physics.
life: Almost every date comes from Apollodorus of Athens, a chronographer of the second century BCE who pegged a thinker’s prime to a datable event and counted back forty years. For Thales the peg was the eclipse, giving a birth around 624 and a death around 546. Every version of the Seven Sages includes him, and that canon was one of practical shrewdness rather than of philosophy.

Whether he wrote at all was disputed in antiquity, and Diogenes Laertius records both opinions without settling them. Nothing survives under his name. Everything passes through Aristotle, who is himself repeating what is said, and then through Theophrastus, whose lost survey of physical opinions fed the whole later doxography: Aetius, the heresiologist Hippolytus, Diogenes, the commentator Simplicius. Hermann Diels reconstructed that chain in 1879.

works.t: On the Solstice; On the Equinox (attributed)
p: Diogenes Laertius reports that on some accounts Thales left nothing written, on others only these two short pieces; a third, a Nautical Star-Guide, was ascribed by some to Phocus of Samos instead. No line survives and no later writer quotes one. If the titles are real, the books were practical — risings and settings of stars set against the farming and sailing year, what later Greeks called a parapegma. Most historians hold that he published nothing, and that his reputation travelled orally until Aristotle gave it a philosophical shape.

works.t: The doctrine of water (testimonia in Aristotle)
p: In Metaphysics A.3 Aristotle says that Thales, the founder of this kind of philosophy, made water the principle, then guesses at his reasons: nourishment and seed are moist, heat is generated from moisture. The guessing is explicit, which means no argument of Thales lay before him. On the Heavens adds that the earth floats on water like a log. The term archē is Aristotle’s own, projected backwards. Against any picture of a secular thinker stands On the Soul, where Thales credits the magnet with soul because it moves iron.

Herodotus says Thales foretold the year of a solar eclipse, which stopped a battle between Lydians and Medes at the Halys; astronomers date it to 28 May 585. No sixth-century method could predict where such an eclipse would be visible, so the story is at best a garbled lucky guess. The olive presses, in Aristotle’s Politics, are told to make a point — a philosopher could be rich if he cared to — and read as fable, as does Plato’s stargazer falling into a well while a Thracian girl laughs. The geometry comes from Proclus, nine centuries later.

legacy: Aristotle’s decision to open his history of philosophy with Thales is the single fact that made him first. Theophrastus then arranged the Milesians into a succession, teacher to pupil, and that scheme governed every later handbook. What Aristotle credited him with was narrow: a material principle and an explanation of the earth’s stability. What readers took was wider — that a storm is weather rather than anger.

Modern scholarship has been correspondingly cautious. Harold Cherniss argued in 1935 that Aristotle reshapes his predecessors to fit the four causes, which makes the earliest testimony also the least reliable. In Diels-Kranz, Thales is number 11 and has no authentic fragments, only reports. He survives as a threshold rather than a doctrine: the point at which Greeks began asking what everything is made of.

read.first: A collection of the Presocratics that prints each testimony with the name and century of the author reporting it, so the distance between Thales and his evidence stays visible; then Aristotle, Metaphysics A.3, which is short.
read.note: Every sentence attributed to Thales is somebody else’s summary, written two centuries or more later and usually to serve that author’s own argument.

thales.caveat: Nothing written by Thales survives and it is unclear whether he wrote at all; the eclipse prediction, the pyramid measurement and the geometrical theorems are reported only by much later sources and are doubted by most historians of ancient science.

anaximander.sub: who suspended the earth in nothing and gave a reason
world: Anaximander’s Miletus exported people as deliberately as it exported cloth. Colonies ringed the Black Sea, and each needed coastlines and distances. So a drawn map was a commercial instrument before it was a philosophical one. He lived to see that world end. In 546 Harpagus reduced Ionia for Cyrus, and Miletus continued on Persian terms rather than its own.

The deeper condition was linguistic. Authoritative Greek speech had been hexameter verse, sanctioned by the Muses. Within a few decades Ionians began writing plain prose, Anaximander first so far as we know, then Hecataeus. Hecataeus opened by saying he wrote what seemed to him true because the tales of the Greeks were absurd. Prose is a claim about authority. Anaximander’s vocabulary of penalty and assessment comes from the law court.
life: Apollodorus reported that he was sixty-four in 547 or 546 and died soon after, which gives the conventional birth around 610. Theophrastus called him the companion and successor of Thales, a pairing that may be doxographic tidiness. Aelian says he led a colony to Apollonia on the Black Sea. Diogenes credits him with a gnomon set up at Sparta, though Herodotus says the Greeks took the gnomon from Babylon.

He wrote a book. Themistius says he was the first Greek known to have published a written account of nature. The title On Nature is a later convention, applied by Hellenistic librarians to almost every early physicist. The book was still readable in Theophrastus’ library in the fourth century BCE, and Theophrastus quoted from it. What reached Simplicius nine hundred years later was that quotation, not the book.

p: The reported doctrine begins with a refusal. The source of things cannot be any familiar stuff, because the opposites are at war and an unlimited quantity of one would long since have swamped the rest. Aristotle preserves that argument in the Physics, and it is the earliest surviving piece of reasoning in Greek philosophy. So the source is the apeiron, the boundless: unlimited in extent, indefinite in quality, described as deathless and ageless and as steering all things. From it the opposites separate out, a sphere of flame bursting into wheels of fire wrapped in mist. Sun and moon are that fire showing through vents.

works.t: Fragment B1, the single surviving sentence
p: Simplicius, commenting on Aristotle’s Physics, writes that things perish into those things out of which they come to be, according to necessity, for they pay penalty and retribution to one another for their injustice according to the assessment of time. He adds that the words are put rather poetically. That remark is why the sentence is treated as verbatim at all. An older reading took the injustice to be the act of coming into separate existence, an offence against the boundless. The dominant reading now fits the words better: opposites encroach on one another, summer on winter, and each repays what it took on a schedule time assesses. The metaphor is judicial, not moral.

works.t: The map of the world; the earth at rest
p: Agathemerus, drawing on Eratosthenes, credits Anaximander with the first map of the inhabited earth, which Hecataeus corrected and enlarged. The earth he made a squat drum, three times as wide as deep, with people on one flat face. It rests at the centre held up by nothing, because a thing equidistant from everything at the extremes has no cause to move one way rather than another. Aristotle records that argument and rejects it. He also sized the heavenly wheels in earth-diameters: the first cosmos drawn to scale.

legacy: The suspended earth has aged best. Every rival cosmology in the ancient Near East propped the earth on something. Anaximander removed the prop and replaced it with a symmetry argument. Karl Popper called it one of the boldest ideas in the history of human thought. The zoogony has been oversold the other way: humans first growing to maturity inside fish-like creatures is an argument about infant helplessness, not descent with modification.

Because so little text survives, Anaximander attracts readers looking for a beginning. Nietzsche gave him a chapter. Heidegger devoted a long essay to the fragment in 1946. Jean-Pierre Vernant argued that the centred, balanced cosmos mirrors the civic space of the emerging polis. Charles Kahn’s study of 1960 remains the standard sober treatment. What survives is a model rather than a doctrine: a world running on an impersonal equilibrium.

read.first: Read the fragment inside its Simplicius paragraph rather than as a standalone epigram, in an edition printing the surrounding commentary. Then the reports on the apeiron and on the earth’s rest, which are the two arguments actually preserved.
read.note: Roughly one sentence of a whole book survives, so every account of Anaximander is a reconstruction, and the confident ones are the least trustworthy.

anaximander.caveat: One sentence survives, and even its boundaries and the extent of Theophrastus’ paraphrase within it are disputed.

anaximenes.sub: who supplied the mechanism his teachers lacked
world: Anaximenes worked in a Miletus that had just lost its independence. Harpagus reduced Ionia for Cyrus in 546, and the city kept its wealth on Persian terms, governed by tyrants the Persians found useful. The revolt and the destruction of Miletus lay a generation ahead, in 494. He is therefore the last Milesian to think in an intact city. Nothing in the reports connects his physics to that situation.
life: His dates are conventional and weakly founded: Apollodorus fixed his prime by the fall of Sardis, yielding a birth around 586 and a death around 526. Theophrastus called him a companion of Anaximander and thought him important enough for a separate monograph, according to Diogenes Laertius. Diogenes also records that he wrote in simple, unadorned Ionic. That verdict implies a real book still being read in the Hellenistic libraries.

p: Anaximenes made air the principle, which looks like a retreat from the boundless. The advance is elsewhere. He explained how one stuff becomes many by a single process: rarefied, air becomes fire; condensed, it becomes wind, then cloud, water, earth, stone. Difference of kind reduces to difference of density, and no decree is needed. Plutarch reports a supporting observation, that breath through pursed lips is cold and through an open mouth warm, which is an appeal to something anyone can repeat.

The one sentence attributed to him says that just as our soul, being air, holds us together, so breath and air encompass the whole world. Most editors doubt the wording, which survives only in Aetius, a compiler of the first or second century CE, and whose vocabulary is Stoic. The analogy is well enough attested to be his. It lets one substance be both the material of the world and the principle keeping it ordered.

legacy: Aristotle and Theophrastus took Anaximenes more seriously than his flashier predecessor, and the reason is method. A principle that says only what things are made of settles nothing. Rarefaction and condensation explain how the many arise, and they do it by quantity rather than quality. That strategy runs forward to the atomists, who replace density with arrangement. It never really leaves physics. Air returned as the principle in Diogenes of Apollonia.

read.first: A collection of the Milesian testimonia read as a set, with Anaximenes taken immediately after Anaximander. The shift from what things are made of to how they change is then visible on the page.
read.note: Read the rarefaction doctrine as the point of the system rather than as a footnote to the choice of air.

anaximenes.caveat: The single supposed fragment survives only in a late compiler and is generally judged a paraphrase in later vocabulary rather than his own words.

pythagoras.sub: a religious founder around whom a science accumulated
world: Samos in Pythagoras’ youth was a naval power under the tyrant Polycrates, who took control around 538. He spent lavishly: an aqueduct tunnelled through a mountain from both ends by Eupalinos, a harbour mole, an enormous temple of Hera. Herodotus calls the three the greatest works of any Greek city. The engineering shows a milieu in which measurement had prestige. It also shows why a man might leave.

The west was richer and less stable. Croton, Sybaris, Metapontum and Tarentum were large colonies on the Italian coast, with famous athletes, a celebrated medical tradition at Croton, and aristocratic clubs that doubled as political factions. Croton destroyed Sybaris in 510. Pythagorean societies took part in that politics as a faction and paid for it. The tradition records a rising led by one Cylon, and a later burning of Pythagorean houses.
life: Born on Samos around 570 to a man named Mnesarchus, he emigrated to Croton about 530 and founded a community with rules governing diet, speech, property and daily conduct. That much is broadly agreed. The travel narratives — study in Egypt, Babylon, with the Magi — grow longer as the sources grow later. None can be checked. He died at Metapontum, probably in the 490s, after the community was attacked.

The earliest evidence is contemporary and hostile, which makes it valuable. Xenophanes mocked him for stopping a man beating a puppy because he recognised a dead friend’s voice in its yelping, the first testimony to transmigration. Heraclitus named him as proof that much learning does not teach understanding. The wonder stories — a golden thigh, appearing in two cities on one day — go back to Aristotle’s lost treatise. They are therefore early rather than late decoration.

works.t: Nothing written: the akousmata and symbola
p: Pythagoras published nothing, and the school made that a principle. Doctrines were credited to the founder. Their reported form of proof was that the Man himself said so. What circulated were akousmata, things heard — question-and-answer formulas and riddling prohibitions preserved by Aristotle and later by Iamblichus. What is wisest? Number. Do not step over a yoke; do not poke a fire with a knife; abstain from beans. A school that attributed every discovery to one man by policy destroyed the evidence for attributing anything to him.

works.t: The theorem and the harmonic ratios
p: The relation between the sides of a right triangle appears on Old Babylonian tablets more than a thousand years earlier. Plimpton 322, from about 1800 BCE, lists whole-number triples. Problem texts apply the rule as routine. The attribution to Pythagoras rests on Proclus, writing in the fifth century CE, and on a story that he sacrificed an ox in celebration. Ancient readers noted that this was impossible for a school forbidding animal sacrifice. The musical ratios stand firmer: octave, fifth and fourth answer to lengths of two to one, three to two and four to three, demonstrable on a stretched string.

Diogenes Laertius lists three books under his name, on education, statesmanship and nature, and reports that others thought them forgeries. The doubt was already standard. The Golden Verses, moral hexameters widely read in late antiquity and again in the Renaissance, is a much later compilation. Around these grew a body of pseudo-Pythagorean treatises circulated under the names of Archytas, Timaeus of Locri and Ocellus. The first Pythagorean whose own fragments survive and are largely accepted is Philolaus of Croton, born about 470.

legacy: Plato’s successors did the decisive work. Speusippus and Xenocrates read the Academy’s number-metaphysics back into Pythagoras. Aristotle’s habit of writing about the so-called Pythagoreans, never attributing a doctrine to the man, shows him resisting a transformation already underway. Neoplatonist biography completed it. Porphyry and Iamblichus, around 300 CE, produced Lives in which the sage is a divine man and the source of all Greek wisdom.

Walter Burkert argued in 1962 that the mathematical Pythagoras is a projection backwards and the historical one a religious teacher of transmigration and ritual purity. That is now the mainstream position, though Leonid Zhmud and others press a case for real mathematics in the early school. What survives is not a doctrine traceable to the man but a programme: that the structure of things is expressible as ratio. Copernicus and Kepler both invoked him by name.

read.first: Start with the earliest witnesses — the lines of Xenophanes and Heraclitus, Herodotus, and Aristotle on the so-called Pythagoreans — before touching Porphyry or Iamblichus. Read Philolaus for what an actual early Pythagorean argued.
read.note: The Lives by Porphyry and Iamblichus are devotional literature written eight centuries later. Reading them first leaves a picture that almost nothing supports.

pythagoras.caveat: Pythagoras wrote nothing, and the school attributed its discoveries to him as a matter of rule. Scholars remain divided over whether the historical man did any mathematics at all.

heraclitus.sub: who found the order inside the change
world: Ephesus was a sanctuary city as much as a trading one. The temple of Artemis was rebuilt on a colossal scale from about 560, with columns paid for by Croesus of Lydia and inscribed with his name. It drew pilgrims, deposits and the traffic that follows both. After 546 the city lived under Persian administration and, in stretches, under tyrants the Persians favoured. Heraclitus belonged to the old priestly aristocracy of such a city. That is why his contempt lands on the citizens rather than on the empire.

He lived through the Ionian revolt. Aristagoras of Miletus raised it in 499. Sardis burned in 498. The Greek fleet was destroyed at Lade in 494 and Miletus sacked, its men killed and the rest deported. Herodotus reports that Athens fined the playwright Phrynichus a thousand drachmas for staging the capture and reminding them of it. No surviving fragment mentions any of this. The greatest catastrophe of his lifetime leaves no visible trace in his book.

Two other conditions do show. Lydian electrum coinage was minted from around 600 and taken up quickly by the Ionian cities. It created an economy in which every commodity had an exchange value in one measure — the exact structure of his image of all things exchanging for fire as goods do for gold. Richard Seaford has argued that money underwrites the very idea of an underlying substance. That is a thesis rather than a consensus. Mystery religion is the other. Heraclitus attacks the rites while taking over their vocabulary of the initiated and the sleeping.
life: The Ephesian tradition makes him a member of the house descended from Androclus, the city’s founder. It says he resigned to his brother the hereditary title of basileus, by then a priestly office. He refused to write laws for the Ephesians. One fragment says they would do well to hang themselves, every grown man of them, and leave the city to the boys, for expelling Hermodorus on the ground that no one should be pre-eminent. The temper is aristocratic but not simply so: his central political word is the common, the xynon.

Almost everything else in the biography is manufactured. Diogenes Laertius reports that he played knucklebones with children in the temple precinct, withdrew to the mountains to live on grass, contracted dropsy, and tried to cure himself with dung. Hellenistic biographers routinely spun anecdotes out of an author’s own sentences. Each of these traces to a fragment about children, or dry souls, or riddling speech. The epithet the Obscure is ancient. The pairing with Democritus as the weeping against the laughing philosopher is a later convention.

His book he is said to have deposited in the temple of Artemis, a normal way of securing a text. Socrates is credited with the verdict that what he understood was excellent, and that the rest needed a Delian diver. Whether it was a continuous treatise or a designed sequence of self-standing sentences is disputed. The material reads as aphorisms, and Charles Kahn argued the form is deliberate. Aristotle complained in the Rhetoric that in the opening sentence one cannot tell which word the adverb belongs to — a defect on his terms, quite possibly the point on Heraclitus’.

p: Diogenes Laertius says the book fell into three parts, on the universe, on politics and on theology. That division is probably a later editor’s arrangement. Its length is unknown. Roughly a hundred and thirty sentences are numbered as genuine in Diels-Kranz, more than for most Presocratics. Since the book was short, that is probably a sizable share of the whole. The transmission depends on unfriendly readers. Clement of Alexandria quotes the most, using him to show that pagan wisdom anticipated Christian truth. Hippolytus preserves a long coherent block in the Refutation of All Heresies, believing Heraclitus the source of a heresy about Father and Son. Sextus preserves the opening. A fourth-century BCE papyrus from Derveni quotes the sentence on the sun’s measures.

works.t: Fragment B1, the opening of the book
p: The book began by saying that of this logos, which holds forever, men prove uncomprehending, both before they hear it and once they have heard; that although all things come to pass in accordance with this account, they are like people with no experience of it; and that other men are as unaware of what they do awake as of what they do asleep. The adverb rendered “forever” can attach to either clause. So the sentence says at once that the account holds always and that men always fail it.

Logos does double duty. The doubling is the argument. It is his own account, the book in the reader’s hands, and also the structure that account reports, the measure by which things happen. From this follows the epistemology of the second fragment. The logos is common and publicly available, yet most people live as though each had a private understanding. The failure he diagnoses is not ignorance of something hidden but inattention to something in plain view.

works.y: quoted by Arius Didymus, Plato and Plutarch
p: The best-attested wording says that upon those who step into the same rivers, other and other waters flow. Read closely it is not a statement that everything dissolves. It says the river stays the same river, and does so precisely because the water is always different. Identity lies in the pattern of the flow, not in the material. That is nearly the opposite of the doctrine usually hung on it. The formula “everything flows” is not a fragment at all. It is Simplicius’ summary phrase. Behind it stands Plato’s report in the Cratylus that Heraclitus says all things move and nothing stays. The textbook Heraclitus of universal flux comes from Plato and Aristotle using him as a foil. It comes also from Cratylus, who pushed the doctrine until, Aristotle says, he stopped speaking and only pointed.

works.y: quoted by Hippolytus, Clement and Plutarch
p: The road up and the road down are one and the same. Sea water is purest and foulest, life-giving for fish and deadly for men. The unapparent connection is stronger than the apparent. War is father of all and king of all, and justice is strife. The bow and the lyre are named as the model, structures held together by tension pulling opposite ways. But the crucial adjective is corrupt, and editors still argue between back-turning and back-stretched.

Fire is chosen for the same reason. The world-order, the same for all, was made by no god and no man, but always was and is and will be an ever-living fire, kindled in measures and quenched in measures. A flame is not a thing that changes but a process persisting by consuming. It is a standing pattern in moving material, which is exactly what he says a river is. Hence the exchange image, all things exchanging for fire as goods for gold. That he taught a periodic conflagration is doubtful. That reading is Stoic.

works.y: quoted by Clement, Stobaeus and Plutarch
p: A different group of sentences turns the inquiry inward without changing its terms. He says he searched out himself. You would not find the limits of soul, though you travelled every road, so deep is its logos. For souls it is death to become water; a dry soul is wisest. Character is a man’s guiding spirit, a sentence relocating fate from the outside of a life to its inside. On knowing and the divine he is deliberately oblique. The lord whose oracle is at Delphi neither speaks out nor conceals, but gives a sign — a description of the god that doubles as a description of his own method. Nature loves to hide. Much learning, he adds, did not teach Hesiod, Pythagoras, Xenophanes or Hecataeus.

legacy: The first readers pulled him apart. Cratylus took the flux to its limit and concluded one could not step into the same river even once. Plato, whom Aristotle says learned Heracliteanism in youth, kept the sensible world in flux and looked for stability elsewhere. That is one of the roads leading to the Forms. The Stoics claimed him as a founder, took over the logos and the cosmic fire, and fitted them with providence and a conflagration he probably never taught. Through Stoicism the word reached Philo of Alexandria and, by a route often overstated, the prologue of the Fourth Gospel.

Modern philosophy has treated him as a resource rather than a subject. Hegel said in his Berlin lectures that there was no proposition of Heraclitus he had not taken up into his own Logic. Nietzsche gave him the warmest pages of his book on the tragic age of the Greeks. Lenin filled a notebook with the unity of opposites as a dialectical law. Heidegger devoted a seminar with Eugen Fink to the fragments in 1966. Each reading works from a different handful of sentences, which the aphoristic survival makes unusually easy.

Scholarship has concentrated on order and authenticity. Miroslav Marcovich’s edition of 1967 and Charles Kahn’s of 1979 take opposite views of how much literary design can be recovered. Kahn arranges the fragments as a composed sequence, and his critics hold that the original order is simply lost. What remains beyond dispute is the achievement: the strongest statement in ancient thought that stability is a kind of process, and a river that has been doing work in arguments about identity ever since.

Whether Parmenides read him is an old question and an open one. The third way of fragment six, on which mortals hold that it is and is not the same and not the same, has been taken since antiquity as a hit at Heraclitus. It has been taken just as often as a description of ordinary belief in general. The two men’s dates are close enough that priority cannot be shown either way.

read.first: Read the fragments straight through in one sitting, in a translation that prints the ancient quoting author beside each. Then read them again slowly. Only afterwards take up a commentary that proposes an order.
read.note: Resist the summary that he taught universal flux. The words “everything flows” are not his, and the surviving river sentence says something more interesting and nearly opposite.

heraclitus.caveat: The book is lost, the original order of the fragments is unrecoverable, several famous sayings attributed to him are later paraphrases, and much of his biography was fabricated by ancient writers out of the fragments themselves.

parmenides.sub: who followed an argument past the whole visible world
world: Elea was a refugee city. When Harpagus reduced Ionia for Cyrus around 545, the people of Phocaea put to sea rather than submit. After a costly sea battle off Alalia in Corsica, the survivors settled on the Lucanian coast of Italy and founded Elea, which the Romans called Velia. It was small, hemmed in by Lucanians inland and by far greater Greek cities along the coast. Parmenides was born there a generation after the founding, into a community that had carried Ionian habits of inquiry a thousand miles west.

The Italian Greek world of his lifetime was violent and intellectually crowded. Croton destroyed Sybaris in 510. Pythagorean brotherhoods rose and were burnt out. The tyrants of Syracuse and Acragas fought Carthage at Himera in 480. Xenophanes of Colophon, another Ionian exile, was reciting in the west. He attacked the anthropomorphic gods of Homer and Hesiod in verse, and proposed one god unlike mortals in body or thought. That precedent made philosophical hexameter a going form, so a young Eleate with a metaphysical argument had a genre ready for it.

Excavations at Velia in the 1960s turned up inscriptions naming Parmeneides son of Pyres. He is described there as a natural philosopher and given the cult title Ouliades, of Apollo the healer, alongside officials of a healing shrine. Peter Kingsley built on these a reading of Parmenides as an initiate of an incubation cult. That reading fits the proem’s journey into darkness. The inscriptions are of Roman date, centuries later than the man. Most scholars treat the inference as suggestive rather than established. The Persian Wars, meanwhile, were fought at the other end of the Greek world and left no mark on the poem.
life: The dates rest on two incompatible foundations. Apollodorus put his prime around 504, which places his birth near 544. Plato’s Parmenides instead shows him at about sixty-five, visiting Athens with Zeno, then about forty, and meeting a very young Socrates. That yields a birth around 515. It is the chronology now generally used. Plato refers to the meeting again in the Theaetetus and the Sophist, and speaks of Parmenides with a respect he shows no one else. But a Platonic dramatic date is not a document.

On his training the reports diverge. Aristotle passes on the claim that he heard Xenophanes, which the doxographers hardened into a school succession. Sotion, quoted by Diogenes Laertius, says he associated with Xenophanes but followed a Pythagorean named Ameinias, poor but noble. On Sotion’s report Ameinias converted him to the contemplative life, and Parmenides built a shrine for him after his death. The story is circumstantial in a way invented ones usually are not. It points to a Pythagorean formation.

The one solid public fact is legislative. Speusippus, Plato’s successor, reported that Parmenides drew up laws for his city. Plutarch adds that the Eleate magistrates swore each year to abide by them. Whatever the poem argues about the unreality of change, its author organised a functioning constitution. His pupils were Zeno, whom one late source calls his adopted son, and, at a distance, Melissus of Samos. Melissus was an admiral before he was a philosopher. The Eleatic school as an institution is a doxographer’s construction.

works.t: On Nature (a hexameter poem, conventionally titled)
p: About a hundred and sixty lines survive, across nineteen numbered fragments in Diels-Kranz, out of a poem whose full length nobody knows. The title is a doxographic convention, not his. The metre is the dactylic hexameter of Homer and Hesiod, forced to carry deduction. Survival is owed almost entirely to two men with opposite motives. Sextus Empiricus quoted the proem nearly whole in order to allegorise it as a sceptical epistemology. Simplicius transcribed the long stretches of the central argument while writing his commentary on Aristotle’s Physics in the 530s CE. He explained that he did so because copies had become scarce. That decision by a late commentator is why the founding text of Western metaphysics exists at all.

Thirty-two lines open the poem. A young man is carried by mares along a road as far as his heart could wish. The daughters of the Sun, having left the house of Night, throw back their veils and lead him. They reach the gates of the paths of Night and Day, whose alternating key Justice holds. A goddess takes his right hand. She says he shall learn both the unshaken heart of well-rounded truth and the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true reliance.

The frame is Hesiodic: Hesiod met the Muses on Helicon, and they authorised his song. What follows the claim is the surprise. The goddess does not pronounce, she argues. She instructs him to judge by reasoning the much-contested refutation she is about to deliver. Revelation opens the door and hands over to proof. The reader is told to check the proof. The authority of the argument is meant to survive even if the mares and goddesses are read as ornament.

works.t: The Way of Truth (B2 to B8.49)
p: The goddess sets out the only two routes conceivable: that it is and cannot not be, and that it is not and must not be. Nothing can be learned on the second, since what-is-not can neither be known nor pointed out. Fragment three says that the same thing is there for thinking and for being. Mortals wander a third, backward-turning way on which being and not-being are taken to be the same and not the same.

Fragment eight lists the marks of what-is and proves each. It is ungenerated and imperishable: what could have made it grow, and out of what? Not out of what-is-not, which cannot be said or thought. No necessity could have stirred it to arise later rather than sooner. It is whole and of one kind, indivisible, all alike with no more of it here and less there; unmoving; complete. The argument closes with a simile: like the bulk of a well-rounded ball, equally balanced from the middle in every direction. The verb translated “is” has no expressed subject anywhere. Its sense — existential, predicative or veridical — is contested.

works.t: The Way of Opinion (B8.50 to B19)
works.y: quoted by Simplicius, Plutarch and Clement
p: At the midpoint the goddess ends her trustworthy account and announces a deceptive ordering of words. Mortals, she says, made up their minds to name two forms, of which they should have named only one: flame, gentle and rare, and against it dark night, dense and heavy. A cosmology follows in scraps — rings of fire and night packed together, a goddess in the middle who steers all things and devised Love first of the gods, and a moon night-shining, wandering round the earth with a light not its own. That last is a real astronomical claim. Parmenides is also credited with recognising that morning and evening star are one. Why a poem that has just proved change impossible should then give a physics is the question every reader must answer. The fragments do not decide it.

works.t: Fragment B16 and the account of thinking
p: Four dense and damaged lines say that as each man has the mixture in his much-wandering limbs, so thought is present to him; that what the nature of the limbs thinks is the same in each and all; and that what is full is thought. Aristotle cites them in Metaphysics Gamma to illustrate the early view that thinking is a bodily condition. Theophrastus discusses them in his treatise on the senses. The interest lies in the fragment’s position. It belongs to the Way of Opinion, and it makes cognition a matter of physical mixture. That is the sort of account the Way of Truth appears to rule out, since there thinking and being are said to be the same. Any interpretation must declare itself here.

legacy: The next two generations wrote in his shadow, rebuilding a world that could satisfy his rules. Zeno defended him obliquely by showing that plurality generates worse contradictions than unity. Melissus of Samos restated the argument in prose and changed one term. He made what-is unlimited in extent, where Parmenides had made it complete and comparable to a sphere. Empedocles supplied four eternal roots that mix and separate without ever coming to be. Leucippus and Democritus conceded the whole argument, then said that what-is-not, the void, nevertheless is — the precise move the poem forbids. Atomism is a Parmenidean invention.

Plato took him more seriously than any predecessor. The Parmenides lets him demolish the young Socrates’ theory of Forms, then runs eight deductions from the hypothesis that it is one. The Sophist calls the necessary correction a parricide of father Parmenides and performs it, showing that not-being is not nothing but difference, so that a false statement can be about something after all. Aristotle’s Physics opens by disarming the argument through the distinction of senses of being.

Since then his fortunes have followed metaphysics itself. Hegel began the Science of Logic with pure being, acknowledging the debt. Heidegger circled the identity of thinking and being for four decades. The twentieth-century analytic recovery — G. E. L. Owen, Charles Kahn on the veridical use of the verb, Alexander Mourelatos’s study of 1970, Jonathan Barnes — turned the poem back into premises and inferences to be assessed. What survives is not the conclusion, which almost nobody accepts, but the demonstration that an argument can be followed against the whole testimony of the senses.
The date given for the poem is an inference from the birth date and nothing else. No ancient source says when it was composed. On Apollodorus’ chronology it would fall a generation earlier.

read.first: Read the surviving poem entire, proem included, in a facing-page translation. It takes twenty minutes. Then work through fragment eight line by line, with a commentary that flags where the Greek is ambiguous. Only then read a general account.
read.note: The poem is short enough to read three times before reading anyone about it. That is the best defence against adopting an interpretation without noticing that a choice was made.

parmenides.caveat: The subject of the poem’s central verb is never named. The sense of that verb is disputed among existential, predicative and veridical readings. The ordering of the fragments is partly conjectural. The purpose of the Way of Opinion remains an open question.

zeno-elea.caveat: The book is lost. The motion paradoxes survive only as Aristotle’s summaries, written to be refuted. No formulation in Zeno’s own words exists for any of them. The identity of his intended opponents is unknown.
legacy: Mathematics eventually answered the arithmetic. An infinite series of halves sums to a finite whole, a fact made rigorous only in the nineteenth century by Cauchy and Weierstrass. Measure theory later allowed an infinite set of extensionless points to compose a segment of finite length. Bertrand Russell’s account of motion as being at different places at different times disposes of the Arrow on its own terms. Russell judged even so that Zeno’s arguments underlay nearly every subsequent theory of space, time and infinity.

What the mathematics does not settle is the metaphysics, which is why the paradoxes are still assigned. Debate continues over supertasks: Max Black’s infinity machines, James Thomson’s lamp switched infinitely often in two minutes. It continues too over whether a continuum of points is the right model of a moving body. Adolf Grünbaum and Wesley Salmon pursued that question. Bergson raised it by objecting that the mathematics describes the track and not the traversing.
life: He was born at Elea around 490. Plato’s Parmenides describes him as about forty at the dramatic date. It has Zeno explain that he wrote the book in his youth out of a competitive spirit, and that it was taken from him and circulated before he chose to publish. Aristotle, in a lost dialogue reported by Diogenes Laertius, called him the inventor of dialectic, which for Aristotle meant arguing from an opponent’s premises rather than one’s own.

The death is a set piece. Zeno joined a conspiracy against a tyrant, was arrested and tortured, refused to name his associates, named the tyrant’s own friends instead, and finally bit off his tongue and spat it at him. Diogenes Laertius gives several versions, drawing on Heraclides, Antisthenes and Hermippus. The sources cannot agree on the tyrant’s name, calling him Nearchus, Diomedon or Demylus. That disagreement is the clearest sign the story is a martyrdom rather than a memory.

read.first: Read Plato’s Parmenides 127 to 128 for Zeno’s own statement of his method. Then the plurality fragments as Simplicius gives them. Only then Physics VI.9, for the four motion arguments in Aristotle’s words.
read.note: Take the motion paradoxes as arguments with premises rather than puzzles with tricks. Notice that the standard mathematical reply answers some of those premises and leaves others standing.

zeno-elea.sub: who defended the one by wrecking the many

p: Proclus reports that the book contained forty arguments, each of the form: if things are many, then such and such follows, and its contrary follows too. Plato states the method in the Parmenides — not a positive doctrine but a counterattack, so that those who mock Parmenides for saying all is one will find their own assumption of plurality yields consequences more ridiculous still. Simplicius had a copy in the sixth century CE and quoted from it directly. That is why the arguments against plurality survive in Zeno’s own Ionic prose, while the paradoxes of motion reach us only through Aristotle.

If there are many things, each must have no magnitude at all, since a genuine unit has no parts and what has no magnitude adds nothing when added to something; and each must also be unlimited in magnitude, since whatever has size has parts, and those parts have parts, without end. If there are many, they must be exactly as many as they are, and so limited in number; and also unlimited, since between any two there is always another. Simplicius preserves the millet seed as well: if a bushel poured out makes a sound, one grain ought to make its proportionate share.

Aristotle sets them out in Physics VI in order to refute them. The Dichotomy: to cross a stadium one must first reach the halfway point, and before that its half, endlessly. Achilles: the swiftest never overtakes the slowest, since he must first reach where the tortoise started, by which time it has moved. The Arrow: at every instant the flying arrow occupies a space equal to itself and so is at rest. The Stadium: rows of equal bodies passing each other in opposite directions yield half a time equal to its double. Aristotle answers that the infinity involved is potential rather than actual, and that time is not composed of indivisible nows.

world: Elea in Zeno’s lifetime was still a modest Phocaean foundation on the Lucanian coast, prosperous and politically unremarkable. The centre of gravity in Greek intellectual life was shifting to Athens. After 478 Athens was converting a naval alliance into an empire and drawing arguers from across the Greek world. Plato’s report of Zeno and Parmenides arriving for the Great Panathenaea places him at that hinge.

The surroundings were full of problems about the small and the many, though we cannot show which he had in view. Italian mathematics was contending with incommensurable magnitudes. Anaxagoras asserted that of the small there is no smallest. An older consensus held that Zeno attacked a Pythagorean mathematics of unit-points. That consensus is now widely doubted, since the evidence for such a mathematics is late and thin. Safer to say his target is anyone holding that things are many.

empedocles.sub: the poet who answered Parmenides by making the elements four
world: Acragas was among the richest cities in the Greek world. Its ridge of temples was paid for by grain, olives and the spoils of Carthage's defeat at Himera in 480. Empedocles grew up under the tyrant Theron. He lived through the collapse of tyranny around 471, when the Sicilian cities turned to democracies that lasted a generation. Sicily was also where the teaching of public speech first became a craft with handbooks and fees.
life: Born about 494 into a leading Acragantine family, he was a physician, an orator and a religious teacher as much as a natural philosopher. The tradition says he refused a kingship. Aristotle, quoted by Diogenes Laertius, called him the inventor of rhetoric. He wrote in Homeric hexameter. Nothing survives whole: we have quotations in later authors, chiefly Simplicius, and a papyrus at Strasbourg published in 1999 that added some seventy lines.

p: The poem keeps the Eleatic rule that nothing comes to be from nothing. It then rescues the visible world by multiplying what there is. Four roots, earth and water and air and fire, are ungenerated. Birth and death are only their mixing and separation. Love and Strife work that mixing and separation in a cycle running from total blending out to complete dispersal and back. Aristotle argued with its zoogony, in which stray limbs wander, monsters form, and only well-fitted creatures last.

The other poem is religious. A spirit that has shed blood or sworn falsely is exiled from the blessed for thirty thousand seasons and driven through the elements and through mortal bodies. Empedocles says of himself that he has already been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird and a fish. Whether the two poems are one work, and how the physics squares with the transmigration, remains the open question. The Strasbourg papyrus sharpened that question rather than settling it.

legacy: Four elements passed through Aristotle into medicine and into European cosmology as far as the seventeenth century, usually with no name attached. Lucretius praised him and then refuted him. Modern readers have made him a proto-Darwinian, a shaman and a physicist by turns. The choice shows which poem they weighted. The story that he leapt into Etna leaving a bronze sandal comes from Heraclides through Diogenes Laertius. It is legend.

read.first: A translation of the fragments that prints the ancient quoting contexts alongside the verse, so it is clear who preserved what and why.
read.note: Read the physics and the transmigration together before deciding which one is the real Empedocles.

empedocles.caveat: The order of the fragments, the number of poems and the shape of the cosmic cycle are all modern reconstructions. The competing reconstructions differ substantially.

anaxagoras.sub: the first to give Mind a part in the making of the world
world: Anaxagoras arrived in Athens when tribute from the allied cities was rebuilding the Acropolis and paying for the fleet. He stayed roughly thirty years. Pericles was his friend and, on several reports, his pupil. That connection was also his danger. The decree of Diopeithes made it an indictable offence to teach doctrines about things in the heavens. Contemporaries understood the prosecution that followed as a blow aimed through the philosopher at the statesman.
life: Born at Clazomenae in Ionia about 500 to a wealthy family, he is said to have given away his property in order to pursue enquiry. Accounts of the impiety trial disagree flatly: one names Cleon as prosecutor, another Thucydides son of Melesias; in one version Pericles argues him down to a fine, in another he is condemned in absence. All agree that he withdrew to Lampsacus, was honoured there, and died about 428.

p: A single book, of which some twenty quotations survive, nearly all in Simplicius, writing nine centuries later. It opened with all things together. It denied a smallest: of the small there is no smallest, so nothing is ever wholly cut off from anything else. Everything accordingly holds a portion of everything, which is how bread turns into flesh. The exception is Mind, unmixed and self-ruling, which set going a rotation that sorts the mixture out. Socrates in the Phaedo describes buying the book, expecting Mind to explain why each thing is arranged for the best, and finding air and aether doing all the work instead.

legacy: Aristotle repeated that complaint, remarking that Anaxagoras wheeled Mind on like a stage machine whenever he was stuck for a cause. His astronomy drew more attention than his seeds: the sun a burning stone larger than the Peloponnese, the moon made of earth and lit from the sun, eclipses caused by shadow. Later readers found in nous either an anticipation of a creator or a warning about half-hearted teleology. The prosecution gave Athens its first philosophical exile, a generation before Socrates.

read.first: The fragments with Simplicius' framing preserved, followed immediately by the passage of Plato's Phaedo on the disappointment of Mind.
read.note: The doctrine that everything contains everything sounds absurd until one asks how nourishment becomes bone.

anaxagoras.caveat: The date of the trial is disputed between the 450s and the 430s. The sources disagree on whether he was convicted, fined or acquitted.

protagoras.sub: the first man to charge a fee for teaching argument
world: Athens in the mid fifth century was the capital of an empire and the richest city in Greece. Tribute from two hundred allied cities paid for the fleet, the buildings and the jurors' wages. Power ran through speech: a man got his way by persuading thousands in the assembly. He defended his property before juries of hundreds, in courts that had no advocates and made him speak for himself.

Into that market came the Sophists, teachers who charged fees for training in argument and civic competence. Protagoras was the first and the dearest. His fee bought entry to the political class, which is why rich men paid and comic poets sneered. Pericles is said to have given him the drafting of laws for the colony at Thurii in 444. The plague of 430 and the long war hardened the city toward clever foreigners.
life: Born at Abdera in Thrace about 490, he taught for some forty years, moving between cities and returning repeatedly to Athens. Plato sets him there among crowds of pupils. He was the first, on Plato's account, to call himself a sophist and to say plainly what he sold: good counsel in a man's own affairs and in those of the city. His fee was reportedly enormous.

Death came about 420, by a persistent report in a shipwreck on the way to Sicily. Tradition adds that Athens condemned him for the opening of his book on the gods and burned copies in the marketplace. Scholars doubt it: Plato's Meno, written within living memory, says he kept his high reputation to the end. Of everything he wrote, two or three sentences remain.

works.t: Truth, or the Overthrowing Arguments (Alētheia, Kataballontes)
p: The book opened with the famous sentence: man is the measure of all things, of those that are that they are, and of those that are not that they are not. Plato takes this in the Theaetetus to mean that each thing is to me as it appears to me and to you as it appears to you, so that no appearance is false. He then turns it against itself: if whatever seems true to a man is true for him, and most men think Protagoras wrong, then by his own rule he is wrong.

One sentence survives, quoted often enough in antiquity to be secure: concerning the gods he is unable to know either that they are or that they are not, or what they are like in form, since the obscurity of the matter and the shortness of human life prevent it. That is agnosticism rather than denial. Its ground is methodological: the same shortness of life constrains enquiry everywhere else. In a city where cult was civic duty rather than private conviction, the tradition of a prosecution records how the sentence was heard.

Two books, and the source of the doctrine that on every matter there are two accounts opposed to one another. From it comes the boast that he could make the weaker argument the stronger. Aristotle records that claim about forensic craft as his, and Aristophanes then fastened it onto Socrates in the Clouds, with consequences at the trial of 399. The technique was training rather than scepticism: argue both sides until it is clear which considerations carry weight. Later rhetorical handbooks are built on the method, as is the anonymous Dissoi Logoi.

legacy: Plato is the reason we have him and the reason he is misread. The Protagoras gives him a long and dignified speech, with the myth of Prometheus, arguing that political skill is shared by all men and improvable by teaching. The Theaetetus gives him a doctrine built in order to be refuted. Because Plato won the long argument about what philosophy is, sophist became a term of abuse.

The measure doctrine keeps returning. Ancient sceptics claimed him. Hobbes and Nietzsche took up the conventionality of value. Twentieth-century debates on relativism still open with the self-refutation objection and still dispute whether it lands. His other claim, that civic excellence can be taught to ordinary people and not inherited, is now the unexamined assumption of every school system in the world.

read.first: The handful of genuine fragments, then Plato's Protagoras and the central pages of the Theaetetus, read as evidence given by an opponent.
read.note: Keep separate what Protagoras is quoted as saying and what Plato has him say. Almost every popular account of him confuses the two.

protagoras.caveat: Nothing of his survives beyond a few sentences, so every account of his position is reconstructed from Plato, Aristotle and Sextus Empiricus, all of them arguing against it.

gorgias.sub: the orator who argued that argument settles nothing
world: Leontini was a Chalcidian city in eastern Sicily under pressure from Syracuse. In 427, early in the war with Sparta, it sent Gorgias at the head of an embassy to ask Athens for help, and he got it. A squadron sailed west, the first step to the catastrophe of 415. The Athens he addressed was rich, litigious and just out of the plague.
life: Born at Leontini about 483, reportedly a pupil of Empedocles, he lived past a hundred and died in Thessaly around 375. He settled nowhere, travelling to give paid displays at Olympia and Delphi and charging heavily for instruction. Unlike Protagoras, he denied teaching virtue at all. He taught speaking. Three short works survive complete under his name, with fragments of a funeral oration.

works.t: On Not-Being, or On Nature (Peri tou mē ontos)
p: Three theses: nothing is; if anything is, it cannot be known; if known, it could not be conveyed. Eleatic machinery is turned against its owners. The text is lost. It reaches us in two paraphrases, one in Sextus Empiricus, one in the pseudo-Aristotelian treatise on Melissus, Xenophanes and Gorgias, which do not agree on the arguments. Whether it is joke or serious cannot be decided.

A defence of Helen on four counts: she went to Troy by divine will, by force, by persuasion or by love, and on none can she be blamed. Speech, Gorgias says, is a great lord which with the smallest and least visible body accomplishes the most divine works, acting on the soul as a drug acts on the body. The last line calls the whole performance a plaything.

A model courtroom defence spoken by the hero whom Odysseus falsely accused of betraying the Greeks, and a technical exercise in argument from probability. Palamedes shows in sequence that the treason could not have been arranged, since no meeting, no messenger and no payment was possible. It is the best surviving evidence of what the Sophists actually taught in practice.

legacy: His rhythmic antitheses and rhyming clause-endings, the Gorgianic figures, marked Greek prose from Thucydides to Isocrates, who reportedly studied with him. Plato named a dialogue after him and used it to set rhetoric against philosophy in terms that held for two thousand years. Scholars of rhetoric now read the Helen as an early theory of language as force rather than mirror.

read.first: The Encomium of Helen and the Palamedes complete, which takes an hour, and then a translation of the two paraphrases of On Not-Being printed side by side.
read.note: The paraphrases are worth comparing precisely where they diverge, since that is where the reconstruction becomes guesswork.

gorgias.caveat: His one philosophical work survives only in two paraphrases that cannot both be accurate. The arguments usually attributed to him are therefore a scholarly composite.

leucippus.sub: the founder of atomism, of whom almost nothing is known
world: By the middle of the fifth century the Greek cities had absorbed the Eleatic argument that what is must be one, ungenerated and motionless. The reason given was that motion requires empty space, and empty space would have to be what is not. Physics had stalled on it. Abdera, on the Thracian coast, was a prosperous colony founded by Ionians fleeing Persian rule. Miletus and Elea, the other cities named as his home, were the seats of the two traditions atomism welded together.
life: Nothing certain is known. The sources place him at Abdera, at Miletus and at Elea, associate him with Zeno or with Melissus, and offer no dates beyond a floruit around 440. He was prominent enough for Aristotle and Theophrastus to name him the originator of atomism, and obscure enough that Epicurus, according to Diogenes Laertius, said there had never been any philosopher called Leucippus. Erwin Rohde revived that doubt in 1880 and Hermann Diels answered it. Most scholars now accept that he existed.

p: Theophrastus assigned this book to Leucippus, while Thrasyllus, cataloguing Democritus three centuries later, listed it among Democritus' works. The dispute cannot be settled. Its content is known through Aristotle's reports. What is not, the void, exists as genuinely as what is. The full is divided by it into infinitely many indivisible bodies differing in shape and size, which move everlastingly, collide and interlock. A vortex sorts like to like and forms worlds, of which there are countless, some lacking a sun or moon.

One sentence survives, the only words we have from him: nothing happens at random, but everything from reason and by necessity. It is the earliest plain statement of universal causal determinism in Greek. It sits awkwardly beside the picture of colliding atoms, since the necessity intended is mechanical rather than purposive. Epicurus found the consequence intolerable and introduced the swerve to escape it.

legacy: Aristotle almost always writes Leucippus and Democritus together, and the doxographers followed him. Any individual contribution is therefore unrecoverable. The founding move, granting existence to the void, is credited to him on Aristotle's authority and nothing else. Through Epicurus and then Lucretius the theory reached the seventeenth century. Gassendi revived it in the 1640s. It passed into the corpuscular physics of Boyle and Newton.

read.first: The testimonia in a collection of Presocratic sources, read straight through, since there is no continuous text to read.
read.note: Notice how often a report about Leucippus turns out to be a report about Leucippus and Democritus jointly.

leucippus.caveat: Some ancients denied he existed, Epicurus reportedly among them. No work can be securely assigned to him rather than to Democritus.

democritus.sub: the atomist who wrote on everything and survives in maxims
world: Abdera was a wealthy Ionian colony, a port for the trade of the Thracian interior and, after the Persian wars, one of the heaviest contributors to the Athenian alliance. Its assessed tribute stood among the largest paid by any member. That wealth made travel possible. Democritus is said to have spent his inheritance on it. He reportedly visited Athens, told nobody who he was, and passed unnoticed.

His life spanned the Peloponnesian war, the plague at Athens and the fall of the city in 404. Nothing in his physics answers to any of it. Atomism replies to an argument, not to a crisis. The ethics is another matter: a settled and cheerful mind, moderated ambition and staying clear of public business read like the advice of a man who watched Greek cities spend a century destroying one another.
life: Born at Abdera around 460, he was the pupil of Leucippus and, by some accounts, of Persian magi left behind by Xerxes' army. He travelled to Egypt and perhaps further east. One surviving line claims that no one of his time had covered more ground or met more learned men. He lived to a great age, perhaps ninety, and died about 370.

More was written by him than by any Greek before him. Thrasyllus, the astrologer at Tiberius' court who also arranged Plato, organised the corpus into thirteen tetralogies covering physics, ethics, mathematics, music and medicine. All of it is lost. What we have is roughly three hundred ethical sayings, most in Stobaeus' anthology, plus reports of the physics in Aristotle and Simplicius. A further set circulates under the name Democrates, and whether those are his is unsettled.

p: Ancient catalogues could not decide whether this book belonged to Democritus or to his teacher. Its physics is known only at second hand. Atoms are uncuttable and infinite in number, differ in shape, arrangement and position and nothing else, move in void, and account by their combinations for everything there is. Sweet and bitter, hot and cold, and colour exist by convention. In reality there are atoms and void. Aristotle rejected nearly all of it, yet treated it with more respect than any other Presocratic system, and so preserved most of what we know.

A cosmogony that appears to have run on into an account of human beginnings: men without arts or cities, taught by need, arriving at fire, shelter, farming and law, and settling on language by agreement rather than nature. Diodorus of Sicily preserves a history of that shape. Since Karl Reinhardt's study of 1912 many have traced it to this book, though the attribution is inference, not evidence. If it is right, Democritus wrote the first naturalistic history of culture, with no divine gift behind civilisation and no golden age before it.

The ethical writing survives only as detached sentences of uneven authenticity, but the position is legible. The end is euthymia, a good condition of the mind. It is reached by keeping desire in proportion, and by measuring what one wants against what is available rather than against what others have. No bridge is built from the physics to the ethics, which has disappointed readers looking for a system. One fragment shows him alert to the strain: the senses answer the mind that has overthrown them, telling it that their fall is its own.

legacy: Plato never names him, and a report in Diogenes Laertius has him wishing to burn the books. Aristotle argued with him constantly. Epicurus took the atoms, added the swerve to make room for choice, and denied owing anything to his predecessors. Through Lucretius the system reached the Renaissance nearly intact. Gassendi's revival in the 1640s made it the frame of the new corpuscular science.

Laughing philosopher is a later invention. Pseudonymous letters elaborated it, describing Hippocrates summoned to Abdera to cure Democritus of his laughter and finding him the sanest man there. It gave painters a subject and Montaigne an essay. Genuinely lost is an enormous body of work: the mathematics, the writing on music and on painting, and any ethical argument in continuous form.

read.first: The ethical fragments in a good collection, then the Aristotelian testimonia on the atoms, which carry the physics that the fragments do not.
read.note: Bear in mind throughout that the maxims are the least reliable part of the corpus. The physics survives only in the words of men who rejected it.

democritus.caveat: Not one of the seventy-odd reported titles survives. The ethical maxims attributed to him are of contested authenticity. His physics is known only through hostile summaries.

socrates.sub: the questioner who turned philosophy toward how to live
world: Socrates was born around 470 into the most confident city in the Greek world and died in one that had lost everything. The league formed against Persia had become an Athenian empire. Its tribute paid for the Parthenon, begun in 447. Democracy in his adult lifetime was radical by any ancient standard: assembly, allotted council, and jury pay that let poor men serve. He fought as a hoplite. Plato has him praised for steadiness at Potidaea in 432 and Delium in 424.

The Peloponnesian War ran from 431 to 404 and took a quarter of his life. Plague killed perhaps a third of the population. Two episodes fixed his political reputation. In 406, presiding by lot when the assembly wanted to try the Arginusae generals together in violation of law, he alone refused to put the motion. Under the Thirty in 404 he was ordered to help arrest Leon of Salamis and simply went home.

That is also why he was killed. The amnesty of 403 barred prosecution for anything done before it. So the political grievance — that he had taught Alcibiades, who betrayed Athens, and Critias, who led the Thirty — came into court as impiety instead. Athens had no creed and no clergy but it had a civic cult. Refusing the city’s gods was a real offence. Add a public used to seeing him lampooned on stage as a fee-taking crank, and the charge had somewhere to land.
life: He came from the deme of Alopece, son of Sophroniscus, said to have been a stonemason, and Phaenarete, said to have been a midwife — a detail Plato turns into his central image for the method. He married Xanthippe, whose reputation for temper is a later invention. He had three sons, the youngest still small when he died. Poor by choice rather than birth, he refused payment for teaching.

Plato’s Phaedo has him describe an early enthusiasm for natural philosophy and a decisive disappointment with it. Whatever the truth of that phase, the mature Socrates asked only how a person should live. His friend Chaerephon’s question to the Delphic oracle, and the answer that no one was wiser, became the story he told to explain a life spent cross-examining people who thought they knew things.

In 399 Meletus, backed by the politician Anytus and the orator Lycon, indicted him for not acknowledging the city’s gods, introducing new divinities, and corrupting the young. A jury of five hundred and one convicted him so narrowly that, on the Apology’s account, a shift of thirty votes would have acquitted him. Invited to propose an alternative to death, he suggested free meals at public expense and then a small fine. The second vote went against him by more than the first. An embassy to Delos delayed the execution about a month. Friends arranged an escape, and he refused it.

p: Not a dialogue but a courtroom speech in three parts: defence, counter-proposal, and address to the jury after sentence. Socrates separates the old slander, which he traces to Aristophanes, from the formal charge. He ties Meletus in knots over whether anyone would corrupt his own associates deliberately. Then he declines to plead.

The core is the oracle and the mission. He examined politicians, poets and craftsmen, and found each ignorant of what mattered most and confident that he was not. He concluded that his only wisdom is knowing he does not know. He calls himself a gadfly on a sluggish horse. He says the god stationed him where he stands. Whether the speech reproduces what was said in 399 or is Plato’s composition on the theme cannot be settled.
A short piece set in the prison, where an old friend arrives with money, a plan and every conventional reason to run. Socrates answers that the only question is whether escaping would be just.

He then imagines the Laws of Athens confronting him. They gave him birth, education and a lifetime’s option to leave. By staying he agreed to abide by their judgements even when a verdict wrongs him. The argument is prized as the first statement of tacit consent and attacked for proving far too much. As stated it would forbid disobeying any law at all — which is exactly what the Apology’s Socrates says he would do if ordered to stop philosophising. Reconciling the two remains a standing problem.

The earliest surviving portrait, and a hostile one. A farmer in debt enrols his son in Socrates’ Thinkery to learn the argument that makes the weaker case defeat the stronger. The son learns it and uses it to justify beating his father. Socrates appears suspended in a basket studying the heavens and teaching that the Clouds have replaced Zeus.

The play took third prize. The text we have is a partial revision. As evidence it is doubly compromised, since comedy assigns stock traits and the figure blends natural philosopher, sophist and atheist into one target. It matters anyway, because the Apology treats it as the source of the prejudice that convicted him twenty-four years later.

Xenophon knew Socrates, left Athens to soldier in Persia, and wrote to rebut the charges head-on. His Socrates is conventionally pious, sacrifices regularly, gives practical advice on managing an estate and choosing friends, and improves the young rather than unsettling them.

The result is a man it is hard to imagine anyone bothering to execute. Scholars long dismissed it for that reason. The verdict has softened. Xenophon is a plain and literal reporter with no metaphysics to sell. Where he and Plato agree — on the constant questioning, the refusal of fees, and self-mastery as the heart of virtue — the agreement is worth more than either witness alone.

works.t: The lost Socratic literature and Aristotle's testimony
p: Conversations with Socrates became a recognised genre after 399. Most of it is gone. Aeschines of Sphettus was admired for catching his manner. Antisthenes, Aristippus, Euclides of Megara and Phaedo of Elis all wrote, and all survive only in quotation and report.

Against this Aristotle supplies the one comparatively cool witness. He states that Socrates concerned himself with ethics and not with nature, that he sought universal definitions and inductive arguments, and, crucially, that he did not separate universals into a world of their own, whereas Plato did. That remark is the main external ground for distinguishing the historical Socrates from Plato’s spokesman. Aristotle, though, was born fifteen years after the execution and knew the man only through the same books.

legacy: Nearly every Hellenistic school claimed descent from him and drew opposite conclusions. Antisthenes took the self-sufficiency and indifference to comfort. That passed through Diogenes the Cynic to Zeno of Citium and became Stoicism, where Socrates is the standing example of the sage. Aristippus took the ease and freedom and founded the hedonist Cyrenaics. Euclides at Megara took the argumentative rigour and produced logicians.

The death did the rest. Early Christian apologists, Justin Martyr among them, enlisted him as a pagan who suffered for opposing false gods. Erasmus in a colloquy of 1522 has a character all but pray to saint Socrates. Hegel read the trial as a genuine tragedy in which city and man each defended something real. Kierkegaard made his irony a dissertation subject in 1841. Nietzsche in 1872 blamed him for killing tragedy by making everything answerable to reason.

What survives is a method and a problem. The method — press a claim until its consequences break it — is now ordinary equipment in philosophy. The problem is that no source is disinterested, so any reconstruction must choose its evidence first. Gregory Vlastos’ influential proposal is that the Socrates of Plato’s earliest dialogues is close to the man while the later one is Plato speaking. It remains the most used solution and is not a settled one.

One document stands outside all of them. Favorinus, writing in the second century CE, claimed to have seen the indictment preserved in the Athenian archive. Diogenes Laertius quotes its wording. That is why the three charges can be stated without relying on either advocate.

read.first: Read the Apology, then the Crito and Euthyphro, in that order and at one sitting. Follow with a few chapters of Xenophon’s Memorabilia to feel how differently a friend of comparable standing remembered the same man.
read.note: Every witness is an advocate, so read them against each other rather than blending them into a single portrait.

socrates.caveat: He wrote nothing. The Socratic problem — deciding which arguments in Plato are his rather than Plato’s — has no agreed solution and probably admits of none.

plato.sub: the dialogue-writer who made the eternal Forms the object of knowledge
world: Plato was born into a city at war. Athens had opened the Peloponnesian War in 431, lost Pericles to the plague in 429, and by 428 governed a tribute-paying empire from behind the Long Walls. Its democracy was direct and amateur: an assembly open to every adult male citizen, offices filled by lot, juries of hundreds paid a day’s wage. Persuasion, not office, was the currency of power.

The war ended badly and then worse. The expedition sent to Sicily in 415 lost Alcibiades to a religious scandal, then lost fleet and army outside Syracuse in 413. Defeat at Aegospotami in 405 and surrender in 404 brought down the Long Walls and installed the Thirty, a Spartan-backed junta that killed perhaps fifteen hundred men in eight months. Democracy returned in 403 under an amnesty covering everything before it. Four years later it executed Socrates.

Recovery came, and it was partial. Athens rebuilt a fleet and formed the Second Athenian League in 378/7, inside a balance the King’s Peace of 387/6 had left Persia to arbitrate. Thebes broke Sparta at Leuctra in 371. From 359 Philip II assembled a Macedon no Greek city could match. Plato died in 348/7, a decade before Chaeronea. He never saw the polis fall, but he wrote inside its visible decline.

Athens had no censor and no publisher. Books could nonetheless be bought: in the Apology Socrates says the works of Anaxagoras go for a drachma at most from the orchestra. What the city did have was the impiety charge. Plutarch reports a decree of Diopeithes allowing the impeachment of men who did not acknowledge the divine. Anaxagoras was prosecuted and Diagoras of Melos condemned in his absence. The report that Protagoras’ books were collected and burnt in the agora is late and doubted. Under the Thirty, Xenophon reports, Critias and Charicles forbade Socrates to teach the art of words.

The form he chose was not his invention. Aristotle in the Poetics counts Socratic conversations as a kind of imitation that has no name of its own. Xenophon, Antisthenes and Aeschines of Sphettus wrote them too. Diogenes Laertius reports a dispute about who wrote the first dialogue: some named Zeno of Elea, and Aristotle in the first book of On Poets named Alexamenus of Styra or Teos. Xenophon’s Socrates and Plato’s do not match. Which is nearer the man has been argued ever since.

None of this produced the theory of Forms: the metaphysics answers Heraclitus and Parmenides, not Sparta. What the politics produced was the question whether any regime can be arranged so that knowledge rather than flattery decides. The sophists had made argument a paid profession and set nature against convention. Isocrates opened a rival school around 393. And Greek geometry was becoming a deductive science under Theodorus, Archytas and Eudoxus: certain knowledge of unseen objects, immune to disagreement, and the model for what Plato wanted knowledge to be.
life: He was born in 428/7 into a rich Athenian family with a dangerous address book. His mother Perictione traced descent from Solon’s circle. Her cousin Critias and her brother Charmides both served the Thirty and died in the fighting of 403. His brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus are the young men who press the case against justice in the Republic. The tradition that his given name was Aristocles is late and unverifiable.

Socrates was the decisive fact of his youth. The Seventh Letter, whoever wrote it, describes a young aristocrat expecting to enter politics. In it he is repelled first by the Thirty, who tried to implicate Socrates in an illegal arrest, then by the democracy that tried him in 399. Plato left Athens after the execution. Later biographers send him on to Egypt, Cyrene and southern Italy, an itinerary plausible in outline, undocumented in detail.

Around 388/7 he reached Sicily and met Dion, brother-in-law of the tyrant Dionysius I. The story that he was sold as a slave on Aegina is later embellishment. The same tradition has the ransom money buying the Academy’s ground. The friendship produced two disastrous journeys. In 367 Dion summoned him to educate the new tyrant Dionysius II. In 361 he went again, was effectively detained, and got out with help from Archytas of Tarentum.

Between the first and second Sicilian journeys he founded the Academy, about 387, in a grove outside the walls sacred to the hero Academus. It was no university: a property, a cult association in legal form, and a standing conversation that charged nothing. Diogenes Laertius preserves what he gives as Plato’s will, disposing of estates at Iphistiadae and Eiresidae and saying nothing about the school. Aristotle arrived from Stagira in 367 at seventeen and stayed twenty years. Tradition names two women among the members, Axiothea and Lasthenia.

Across some fifty years he wrote dialogues and never spoke in his own voice. He appears three times by name, twice at Socrates’ trial and once as absent from his deathbed. Their order is reconstructed from style and cross-reference. The statistical form of that reconstruction begins with Lewis Campbell’s edition of the Sophist and Politicus in 1867. The placement of individual works is disputed. Plato died in 348/7. Speusippus took the school. Where every other classical philosopher survives in fragments or in later summary, his corpus came through entire, arranged in antiquity into nine tetralogies.

Publication meant copying. A finished roll went to friends, and from them to anyone who would pay a scribe, with no control by the author after that. Dionysius of Halicarnassus writes that Plato was still combing and curling his dialogues at eighty. Diogenes Laertius reports a tablet found after his death carrying the opening of the Republic written out in several arrangements. These are stories about a working method, not documents of one.

The Laws was posthumous. Diogenes Laertius reports that Philip of Opus copied it out from the wax tablets it was left on. Some ancient readers gave Philip the Epinomis that follows it. The corpus was ordered more than once. An arrangement into trilogies is attributed to Aristophanes of Byzantium. The nine tetralogies are credited to Thrasyllus, an astrologer at the court of Tiberius. That is the order the manuscripts keep. What a modern reader holds is a copy of copies. The oldest full witness is Codex Clarkianus 39 in the Bodleian, written in 895 for Arethas of Caesarea. It carries the first six tetralogies. Parisinus graecus 1807, of the ninth century, carries the later ones. Fragments on papyrus reach much further back, one of the Phaedo among the Petrie papyri to the third century BCE.

works.t: The Socratic dialogues: Apology, Crito, Euthyphro, Laches, Charmides, Gorgias
