p: The short early works share a shape. Socrates asks what some quality is — courage, piety, temperance — refuses examples in place of a definition, and shows the confident answerer that his own beliefs contradict him. Nobody reaches an answer. The point is that the man discovers he never had one.

Two do more. The Apology, a defence speech rather than a conversation, gives the mission from the Delphic oracle. Socrates tells the jury that a shift of thirty votes would have acquitted him. In the Crito the personified Laws of Athens argue that Socrates owes obedience even to an unjust verdict. The Euthyphro asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious or is pious because they love it. That dilemma has outlived every theology aimed at it.

The Gorgias is the longest of the group and the harshest. Socrates denies that rhetoric is a craft at all and calls it a knack for flattery, standing to justice as cookery stands to medicine. Polus will not accept the consequence, that doing injustice is worse for the doer than suffering it. Callicles then drops the pretence and argues that justice by nature is the strong taking what they can. Under all of these run the two claims the tradition calls the Socratic paradoxes: that virtue is knowledge, and that no one does wrong willingly.

The question is whether virtue can be taught. The dialogue never answers it. Meno raises the paradox that inquiry is impossible: a searcher who knows what he seeks need not seek it, and one who does not would not recognise it. Socrates answers that the soul saw the truth before birth, so learning is recollection. He takes an uneducated slave through the construction of a square double a given square.

The demonstration proves less than it claims, but it is the first appearance in Western writing of the thought that some knowledge cannot come from experience. Socrates also borrows a method from the geometers: if the answer is out of reach, ask on what hypothesis it would follow. Anytus, who will be one of Socrates’ prosecutors, joins the conversation and takes offence. Socrates has just observed that the best Athenians, Themistocles and Pericles among them, failed to teach their virtue to their own sons.

The dialogue closes on a distinction that never went away. True belief gets to Larisa as well as knowledge does, but will not stay put until tied down by an account of the reason why. Virtue is left to divine dispensation.

Socrates’ last day doubles as the fullest statement of the two-world picture: philosophy is practice for dying, because the philosopher wants what the body obstructs. It reaches the reader at one remove. Phaedo tells the day at Phlius to Echecrates, and notes that Plato was absent, being ill. Suicide is ruled out at the start, on the ground that we are the gods’ possessions and may not desert the post. Four arguments for immortality follow — from the generation of opposites, from recollection, from the soul’s affinity with what is unchanging, and finally from the Forms, since soul brings life as fire brings heat and so cannot admit death.

Simmias proposes that soul is an attunement of bodily parts and dies with them. Cebes grants survival but not indestructibility. Socrates answers Simmias well and Cebes only by helping himself to the theory under defence. The passage on Anaxagoras, who invoked Mind and then explained everything by air and aether, prompts the turn to explanation by Forms as a “second sailing”.
Then the hemlock, and the last request, that a cock be paid to Asclepius.

Speeches in praise of Eros at a party held in 416 for the tragedian Agathon’s first victory. The evening reaches the reader third-hand: Apollodorus repeats it years later, having had it from Aristodemus, who was there. Aristophanes supplies the myth of the original double humans, split by Zeus, each half hunting ever since for its other. Socrates then reports what Diotima of Mantinea taught him and undoes that myth. Love is not of a lost half but of the good, and of possessing it forever, so every love is a bid for immortality.

Diotima makes Eros neither god nor mortal but a spirit between the two. Love is a pregnancy seeking birth in beauty, in bodies for some and in poems, laws and arguments for others. From this follows the ascent, from one beautiful body to all bodies, to souls, laws and studies, and at last to Beauty itself. Then Alcibiades crashes in drunk, praising not love but Socrates, whom he compares to a plain statuette with a god inside. Every reader knew that Alcibiades wrecked the Sicilian expedition the following year.

Ten books that open on whether the just man is better off than the unjust and close as a theory of knowledge, education, art and the soul. Thrasymachus defines justice as the interest of the stronger. Glaucon and Adeimantus, unsatisfied by his refutation, restate the case seriously and offer the ring of Gyges as the test. Book I ends in the aporia of the early works. Some scholars have argued it was written first as a separate dialogue. The claim is stylistic and contested.

Socrates answers by building a city in speech. Three classes match three parts of the soul. Justice is each part doing its own work. The city rests on a lie its rulers must tell, that the citizens were formed underground with gold, silver or bronze in them. Along the way come the censorship of poetry, the abolition of family and property for the guardians, the admission of women to the guardian class on equal terms, and the rule that philosophers must govern. Books VI and VII give the images that carried the tradition — sun, divided line, cave — and put the Form of the Good beyond being itself.

Books VIII and IX then run the constitutions downhill: timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny, each paired with the man whose soul matches it. The tyrant, having every liberty, is the unhappiest man alive. Book X banishes the imitating poets as three removes from what is, and ends with the myth of Er, where souls choose their next lives and the responsibility is theirs.

The twentieth century largely read the proposals as the first totalitarian manifesto, most influentially in Karl Popper’s The Open Society and Its Enemies of 1945. The defence, which has the text on its side, is that the city is a paradigm laid up for the soul.

The only dialogue set outside the city. Socrates and Phaedrus walk up the Ilissus and lie down under a plane tree. Phaedrus has a written speech by Lysias arguing that a boy should give himself to a man who does not love him. Socrates improves on it, then stops, saying he has offended a god. Diogenes Laertius reports that some in antiquity made this Plato’s first work, on the ground that the subject is juvenile. The date remains disputed.

The recantation makes madness a gift when a god sends it. Soul is self-moving and therefore ungenerated. It is a charioteer with two horses, one obedient and one not. It once rode the rim of heaven and saw what is. Beauty alone among those things has a visible copy here, which is why the sight of it unsettles a man.

The second half asks what would make rhetoric an art rather than a trick, and answers: knowledge of the truth, and of the kinds of soul it addresses. Then comes the story of Theuth, who offers writing to the Egyptian king Thamus and is refused. Writing is a drug for reminding, not for memory. It gives the look of wisdom without the thing. A text repeats itself to everyone alike and cannot defend itself when questioned. Serious teaching is written in the learner’s soul. What goes on papyrus is play. That verdict stands inside a written dialogue, by a man who wrote for some fifty years.

Plato’s attack on his own theory. A very young Socrates presents the Forms to the aged Parmenides and to Zeno, who take them apart. The meeting is generally judged unhistorical. Socrates is asked first what there are Forms of, and is confident about justice and beauty, hesitant about man and fire, and repelled by the thought of a Form of hair or mud. A Form shared among many things is then either cut into parts or present whole in each. Parmenides offers a sail spread over many men as the test. Then comes the regress: if large things are large by Largeness, then Largeness and the large things need a further Form to explain what they share, without end. Aristotle later called this the Third Man.

Worse is the greatest difficulty: if Forms relate only to each other and particulars only to each other, divine knowledge cannot reach our world and ours cannot reach the Forms. Parmenides does not conclude that Forms should go — without them, he says, thought has nowhere to turn — but prescribes exercise. The second half delivers eight deductions about what follows if the One is and if it is not.

The late date is orthodoxy rather than a finding. G. E. L. Owen argued in 1953 that the Timaeus belongs with the middle dialogues, written before the Theaetetus and the Parmenides, and attacked the stylometry the traditional placement rests on. H. F. Cherniss defended the late date against him. The question has never closed.

What is knowledge. The conversation arrives as a document inside its own fiction. Euclides of Megara says he wrote it from notes and checked it with Socrates more than once. He left out the reported speech so that it reads straight. The young mathematician Theaetetus, a real person who worked on irrational magnitudes, makes three attempts. Knowledge is perception. Socrates expands that into Protagoras’ doctrine that man is the measure of all things set in a Heraclitean flux. He then refutes it by noting that Protagoras must count the majority view that he is wrong as true. Knowledge is true belief, which fails because a jury persuaded of a truth does not thereby know it. Knowledge is true belief with an account. Every reading of “account” collapses.

Between the attempts comes a long detour on how false belief is possible at all. Two models are tried and both fail: a block of wax that takes impressions, and an aviary in which one reaches for a bird and catches the wrong one. Midway stands the digression on the philosopher, who does not know the road to the market place and cuts a ridiculous figure in court.

The dialogue ends in failure. Socrates says his art is his mother’s: a midwife delivering other people’s thoughts and testing whether they are viable. The Forms, which would settle the question at a stroke, are never invoked. Whether that is discipline or lost confidence is sharply disputed.

Socrates is present but silent while a visitor from Elea runs the conversation. The task is to define the sophist by dividing kinds, a method practised first on the angler. Six definitions come out before the hunt stalls on a real problem. The sophist trades in falsehood, falsehood is saying what is not, and Parmenides had ruled that what is not cannot be said or thought.

Before the answer comes the quarrel about being, staged as a battle of gods and giants. On one side are men who admit only what can be handled. On the other are the friends of the Forms, who admit only what never changes. The Visitor offers a mark that might satisfy both: to be is to have some power to act or be acted on. He puts it as a proposal, not a doctrine.

The Visitor then commits what he calls parricide against father Parmenides. Not-being is not the opposite of being but difference: to say motion is not rest is to say motion is other than rest. Five greatest kinds — being, sameness, difference, motion, rest — combine and exclude in determinate ways, which makes true and false statement alike possible and yields the first genuine theory of negation. The last definition then lands the sophist in the art of making appearances, an imitator who does not know the thing he imitates.

A near-monologue on the origin of the cosmos, offered explicitly as a likely account rather than a demonstration. It opens as a sequel, with a summary of a city much like the Republic’s, and hands on to Critias and his unfinished story of Atlantis. A craftsman god, the Demiurge, imposes order on a disorderly receptacle by looking to an eternal model, makes the world a living animal with a soul, and makes time as a moving image of eternity.

Between the eternal model and its copy stands a third thing, the receptacle, which must have no character of its own in order to take on all of them. The physics is geometrical: the elements are built from two kinds of triangle, so they transform into one another by rearrangement. The solids are assigned — tetrahedron to fire, octahedron to air, icosahedron to water, cube to earth. Reason does not command the world but persuades necessity. What will not yield is left to the wandering cause.

Whether the creation is meant literally was contested inside the Academy itself, Xenocrates reading it as exposition and Aristotle insisting Plato meant it. Cicero translated part of it into Latin. Through Calcidius’ partial Latin version it was very nearly the only Plato the Latin Middle Ages possessed. That makes it the most consequential dialogue of all.

The longest work and the last, left unrevised at his death. Socrates does not appear. An unnamed Athenian walks to a Cretan cave with a Spartan and a Cretan and designs the laws of a colony, Magnesia, in exhausting detail: land allotments, marriage age, festivals, drinking parties as a test of character, and a mixed constitution balancing monarchic against democratic elements. The households are fixed at 5,040, a number chosen because it divides so many ways.

This is the second-best city, built for people as they are rather than as the Republic wished. Its best idea is the preamble: a law should be preceded by persuasion explaining why it is right, because a free citizen is not a slave to be ordered. Book X then argues that soul precedes body because self-moving motion must precede transmitted motion. It is aimed at three errors about the gods — that there are none, that they exist and take no interest, that they can be bought off with sacrifice. It prescribes death for obstinate impiety, which sits badly after the Apology. Above the magistrates sits a Nocturnal Council, meeting before dawn, whose business is to understand the ends the laws are for.

Thirteen letters travel with the corpus, most of them certainly spurious. The seventh is different: a long apologia addressed to Dion’s supporters after his murder in 354, narrating political disillusionment under the Thirty and then the democracy, the execution of Socrates, and the Syracusan misadventure. If genuine it is the only autobiography by a major Greek philosopher. It gives a reason for going to Syracuse at all: shame at being a man of words only.

Its centre is a digression arguing that the deepest matters cannot be written down at all. Name, definition, image and knowledge are four things one must pass through, and the fifth, the thing itself, arrives suddenly after long shared work. That argument runs alongside what the Phaedrus says about writing. The two passages are the main textual support for the claim that the Academy taught what it did not publish. Authenticity has been argued both ways for two centuries and remains open. Even sceptics generally place it inside the Academy within a generation of his death.

The most sustained recent attack is Myles Burnyeat and Michael Frede’s The Pseudo-Platonic Seventh Letter, published in 2015, which argues that the philosophical digression is incompetent and the letter not Plato’s at all.

legacy: The school outlived him by nine centuries and spent much of that time disagreeing about him. Around 265 Arcesilaus turned the Academy sceptical, holding that the aporetic dialogues showed the real Plato suspending judgement, a line Carneades sharpened and Cicero carried to Rome. Antiochus of Ascalon broke with that in the 80s BCE and went back to doctrine. The oldest institutional quarrel in philosophy is thus the quarrel over whether Plato had a system.

Between Antiochus and Plotinus the reading hardened into a syllabus. Alcinous’ Didaskalikos sets out Platonic doctrine as numbered topics. Numenius of Apamea is credited with the question of what Plato is but Moses speaking Attic. In these writers the Forms become thoughts in the mind of a god, generally judged a development rather than a reading.

Doctrine won. In the third century Plotinus built from the Parmenides a hierarchy descending from a One beyond being. Christian writers took what they needed. Augustine records in the Confessions that the books of the Platonists taught him to conceive an immaterial God. The writings under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite smuggled Proclus into medieval theology. Justinian closed the Athenian school in 529.

Arabic readers got much less of him than of Aristotle, and mostly in summary. Al-Farabi wrote on the philosophy of Plato and summarised the Laws. Averroes, with no Arabic Politics to hand, wrote his political commentary on the Republic instead. It survives only in Hebrew translation.

The Latin Middle Ages, by contrast, had almost no Plato — Calcidius’ Timaeus, and from the twelfth century versions of the Meno and Phaedo. Recovery was a Renaissance event: Marsilio Ficino, working for the Medici in Florence, translated the whole corpus into Latin and printed it in 1484. His commentary on the Symposium put the phrase Platonic love into European use. Henri Estienne’s Greek edition of 1578 supplied the page references still used to cite Plato in every language.

Modern reading begins with Schleiermacher, whose translations from 1804 insisted the dialogues be read as literary wholes. Three durable quarrels followed: Popper’s indictment of the Republic; the analytic recovery of Plato as an arguer whose mistakes can be diagnosed; and the Tübingen school’s claim that the unwritten doctrines are the true centre. Gregory Vlastos led the second. His Socrates: Ironist and Moral Philosopher of 1991 tried to separate the Socrates of the early dialogues from Plato’s own. Hans Joachim Krämer and Konrad Gaiser led the third, resting it on Aristotle’s reports and on Aristoxenus’ account of a lecture on the Good. Leo Strauss and his students pressed a fourth line, reading the dialogues as dramas that conceal as much as they state. What survives is not the two-world metaphysics but what was built on its site: realism about universals and mathematical objects, the Euthyphro dilemma, and the cave as the standing image of ideology.

read.first: Begin with the Apology and Crito, which need no scaffolding, then the Meno, then the Symposium, and only then the Republic straight through without stopping to master Books VI and VII. The Phaedrus repays being read after it, since its closing pages argue against trusting written philosophy. Any translation with the Stephanus numbers in the margin makes a reference traceable anywhere.
read.note: These are plays as well as arguments, so notice who is speaking, who has gone quiet, and what the argument costs the person on the receiving end.

plato.caveat: The order of composition is reconstructed from style and cross-reference and is disputed in detail. The Seventh Letter may not be his. The “unwritten doctrines” are known only from Aristotle and later reports, so how far the dialogues represent the whole of his philosophy cannot be settled. Several works travelling in the corpus are doubted: the Epinomis is given to Philip of Opus by ancient report, and the authenticity of the Alcibiades I and the Hippias Major has been argued both ways. Nearly everything told about the life comes from Diogenes Laertius in the third century CE and from later biographers. The oldest complete manuscripts are later still, by about thirteen centuries, so the text in hand is an edited reconstruction from copies rather than anything Plato touched.

aristotle.sub: the philosopher who put form back inside the thing
world: Aristotle was born in 384 BCE at Stagira on the Chalcidice. It was a small Greek city within reach of a kingdom about to swallow the Greek world. His father Nicomachus served Amyntas III of Macedon as court physician. The family was thus tied to that court before it mattered. Philip II took the throne in 359 and remade it: a standing army built around the long sarissa, financed by the gold of Mount Pangaeum, extended southward by siege, bribery and marriage. Philip destroyed Stagira in 349. Tradition says he later rebuilt it at Aristotle’s request. Plutarch reports that restoration in the Life of Alexander, some four centuries after the event.

Fourth-century Athens was no longer an imperial power. It was still where philosophy was done. The democracy restored after 404 had watched a second naval league rise and fall. Public argument narrowed to one question: fight Macedon or join it. Demosthenes built a career on the first answer and Isocrates on the second. Chaeronea decided the matter in 338. The League of Corinth left the city autonomous in name and supervised in fact. With no censor and no licensing of books, the city prosecuted impiety instead. Socrates had been tried and executed on that charge in 399. Similar prosecutions of Anaxagoras and Protagoras are reported by later sources and are less secure.

Philip was murdered in 336. Alexander crossed into Asia in 334. Within a decade he had destroyed the Persian empire and marched to the Punjab. He died at Babylon in June 323. The conquests enlarged what a Greek writer could describe. But the story that Alexander shipped specimens home to his tutor is late and thin. Pliny the Elder tells it in the Natural History, four centuries on. Relations had soured well before: in 327 Alexander had Callisthenes, Aristotle’s kinsman and the expedition’s official historian, arrested and killed. Callisthenes had refused the Persian court ritual of prostration. Arrian gives two versions from his own sources: Ptolemy says Callisthenes was tortured and hanged, Aristobulus that he was carried about in chains and died of disease.

None of this made Aristotle an Athenian. He taught as a metic, a resident foreigner who could not own Attic land. On returning in 335 he therefore bought no property, as Plato had for the Academy. He lectured instead in a public gymnasium in the grove of Apollo Lyceus. Legal standing came later, when Theophrastus secured the right to hold ground — through Demetrius of Phalerum, Diogenes Laertius reports. The precariousness told in 323: Athens rose against the Macedonian garrison. A charge of impiety was laid over an old hymn Aristotle had written for a dead friend. A foreigner with court connections had no defence. Diogenes Laertius names Eurymedon the hierophant as the accuser. Athenaeus credits the indictment to Demophilus, at Eurymedon’s prompting. Antipater crushed the revolt at Crannon in 322 and garrisoned Munychia. The democracy gave way to a constitution limited by a property qualification. Aristotle’s will names Antipater as its executor.

Publication in this world was copying: no publishers, no editions, no property in a text. A work was published when copies passed out of the author’s hands. What Aristotle published were dialogues and exhortations written for readers outside the school. Cicero praised their golden flow of speech, a judgement on books we no longer have. The lecture courses were school material and were not written to circulate. Aulus Gellius preserves a letter in which Alexander complains that the acroamatic doctrines had been made public. It belongs to the forged correspondence. The distinction it turns on, between exoteric works and the school’s own, is nonetheless old: Aristotle himself refers to exoteric discussions.
life: Nicomachus died while his son was young. Aristotle was raised by a guardian, Proxenus of Atarneus. Proxenus’ son Nicanor returns at the end, as heir in the will and as the man Aristotle wished his daughter to marry. His mother Phaestis came from Chalcis on Euboea, a detail that would matter at the end of his life. The medicine in the family may explain the interest in animal structure. But Aristotle nowhere claims a medical training. The ancient biographies are late and anecdotal.

In 367, aged seventeen, he went to Athens and entered Plato’s Academy. He stayed twenty years, until Plato died in 347. The Academy was not only Plato. It practised division, diairesis, as the route to a definition, a method he later attacked for proving nothing. He was not a docile pupil. The criticism of separate Forms that runs through the surviving works reads like an argument made inside the school over decades rather than a convert’s repudiation. When Speusippus took over the Academy, Aristotle left. The succession and the anti-Macedonian mood have both been proposed as reasons. The sources do not settle it.

He went east to Assos in the Troad, invited by Hermias, the ruler of Atarneus. He married Hermias’ kinswoman Pythias. From there he crossed to Lesbos. It was there, with the young Theophrastus of Eresus, that the biological research was done. The lagoon at Pyrrha recurs in the animal works like a field site. Botany stayed the subject of Theophrastus, whose Enquiry into Plants survives. Hermias was seized by the Persians and executed around 341. Diodorus reports that Mentor of Rhodes took him by a ruse. Aristotle composed a hymn in his memory that would be used against him thirty years later.

In 343 or 342 Philip called him to Mieza to teach the thirteen-year-old Alexander. What was taught is almost entirely unknown. The teaching cannot have run long: Alexander was regent in Macedon by 340 and commanding a wing at Chaeronea in 338. The correspondence between them that circulated in antiquity is forged. He returned to Athens in 335 and began the school at the Lyceum. The covered walk there, the peripatos, eventually gave his followers their name. Pythias died. He then lived with Herpyllis of Stagira, who bore him a son, Nicomachus.

He left Athens in 323, so that the city should not, in a saying reported much later, sin twice against philosophy. He withdrew to the family property at Chalcis and died there the following year, aged sixty-two. His will survives in Diogenes Laertius: provision for Herpyllis, freedom for several slaves, the request that Pythias’ bones be laid beside his own. The will does not call her a wife. The ancient reports differ on what she was. What survives is not what he published. The polished dialogues that made his ancient reputation for style are lost but for fragments. The corpus we read is the school’s internal material, lecture courses cut, restated and revised.

What that corpus looks like is what a working school leaves behind. Bekker’s Greek text runs to page 1462, much of it not reading like a finished book. Treatises cross-refer to one another in both directions, some of them to arguments the named work does not contain. The same material turns up twice in different versions, three books standing in both the Nicomachean and the Eudemian Ethics. The Metaphysics is fourteen books nobody has shown to be one composition. The ancient catalogues sharpen the problem rather than solving it. Diogenes Laertius lists about 150 titles and a total of 445,270 lines, a catalogue that matches what we read only in part. Other lists survive under the name of Hesychius and in an Arabic tradition attributed to Ptolemy al-Gharib. Whether Aristotle, his students, or a much later editor gave the treatises their present shape is not settled.

works.t: The Organon: Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Posterior Analytics, Topics, Sophistical Refutations
p: Aristotle never called these six works the Organon. The name, the instrument of the sciences, is a later Peripatetic label. The Categories sorts what can be said of a subject into ten kinds and gives priority to the individual: this man, this horse, is substance in the strictest sense. On Interpretation, treating statements that can be true or false, raises in its ninth chapter the sea battle that may or may not happen tomorrow: the founding text on future contingents.

The Prior Analytics is the beginning of formal logic anywhere: schematic letters standing for terms, the syllogism defined as an argument in which something other than what was laid down follows of necessity, the valid moods sorted into three figures. Moods of the second and third figures are proved by reducing them to the first, and where that fails by reductio or by setting out an instance. The Posterior Analytics asks what a science is: demonstration from premises prior to and explanatory of the conclusion, resting on first principles that cannot themselves be demonstrated. Its last chapter asks how those principles are known, and answers: induction from perception, through memory and experience, to a state Aristotle calls nous. Kant could still say that logic had neither advanced nor retreated since Aristotle. He was wrong — the Stoics had a propositional logic he lacked — but the remark measures how completely this held the field until Frege.

Two of the six are older and less read. The Topics trains dialectic, which argues from endoxa: the opinions held by everyone, or by most people, or by the wise. It is drill rather than theory, organised around the four predicables — definition, genus, property, accident — and several hundred topoi, or lines of attack. Sophistical Refutations, counted in antiquity as its last book, sorts fallacies into those that turn on language and those that do not. It ends with a remark worth the whole set. On rhetoric, Aristotle says, there was much earlier work to build on. On reasoning there was nothing at all. He began from nothing.

Not physics in the modern sense but a general theory of natural things, those with an internal principle of motion and rest. Book II sets out the four causes — material, formal, efficient, final — which are four kinds of answer to the question why. The final cause is the contested one: regular outcomes in nature are aimed at without anyone doing the aiming. Nature does nothing in vain. Later books treat place, void, time as the number of motion with respect to before and after, and the continuum, where Zeno’s paradoxes get their first serious answer. The dynamics are wrong. They were attacked from inside the tradition by Philoponus in the sixth century and by the impetus theorists of the fourteenth.

Book I clears the ground against Parmenides. Coming to be is not something out of nothing but needs three things: a substratum, a form, and the privation of that form. Book III then defines motion itself, as the actuality of what exists potentially, in so far as it is potential. Descartes mocked the scholastic version of that definition. Book IV holds that the place of a thing is the innermost motionless boundary of what contains it. It denies the void, partly on the ground that motion in a void would stand in no ratio to motion through a medium. Book VIII argues that motion is eternal and requires a first mover that is not itself moved. Metaphysics XII takes that argument up.

This cosmos has two regions and two physics. Below the moon are the four elements, each with a natural motion in a straight line, up or down. Above it is a fifth body, argued for from the claim that circular motion is natural to nothing else. That body is ungenerated, indestructible and unalterable, and moves in circles for ever. The heavens therefore have no history. The eternity of the world follows, and became the hardest of his doctrines for readers who had a creation to defend.

The arguments about the earth are better than the book’s reputation. The earth is spherical: the shadow it throws in a lunar eclipse is curved, and the stars overhead change as one travels north or south. Aristotle reports that mathematicians who calculate the circumference make it 400,000 stades. That is the earliest surviving estimate of the size of the earth. How long a stade was is uncertain, so the figure cannot be converted with confidence. The earth is also at the centre and at rest, against the Pythagoreans who had moved it. Galileo’s Dialogue of 1632 argues at length against the incorruptible heavens of this book.

The soul, in the definition this treatise builds towards, is the first actuality of a natural body having life potentially: not a thing lodged in the body but what the body is organised to do. Asking whether soul and body are one, Aristotle says, is like asking whether the wax and its shape are one. Souls come in nested capacities: nutrition, perception, locomotion, thought. A plant therefore has a soul in the same sense a person does. Perception is the reception of the sensible form without the matter, as wax takes the seal without the iron. Each sense has its own object, colour for sight and sound for hearing. Book III adds phantasia, the capacity for images, and holds that the soul never thinks without one.

The difficulty is Book III, chapter 5, on the intellect that makes all things and is called separable, unaffected and unmixed. It is a compressed page. It generated the medieval controversy over the agent intellect, from Alexander of Aphrodisias through Averroes’ single shared intellect to Aquinas’ rejection of it.

works.t: History of Animals, Parts of Animals, Generation of Animals
p: About a third of the surviving corpus is biology, the part most often skipped. The History of Animals is the data: some five hundred kinds of animal described by habitat, anatomy, diet, breeding and behaviour, much of it gathered by dissection and from fishermen and beekeepers. The main division is between blooded and bloodless animals, which falls close to the modern line between vertebrates and invertebrates. The Academy’s method of dividing by repeated pairs is refused, in favour of many differences taken at once. Aristotle records that one arm of the male octopus is modified for reproduction, dismissed as fable until the hectocotylus was confirmed in the nineteenth century. He records too a placenta-like attachment in the smooth dogfish, which Johannes Müller verified in 1842. He knows that dolphins and whales bear live young and breathe air. He opened hens’ eggs on successive days to watch the embryo, and reports the heart beating first. Much else in them is false.

Parts of Animals supplies the method. Its first book is the best statement of Aristotelian science anywhere: explain the organ by the function it serves, subject to what the material makes possible. And do not scorn humble creatures, since in all natural things there is something wonderful. Generation of Animals is the theoretical summit and the worst offender. Development is genuine epigenesis. But the male supplies form and motion while the female supplies only matter, an asymmetry that did centuries of damage. It is not bare prejudice: semen is concocted blood, held to transmit the motions that shape the female contribution into an animal. Darwin, reading Ogle’s translation in 1882, wrote that Linnaeus and Cuvier had been his two gods but were mere schoolboys beside old Aristotle.

works.y: compiled from work of c. 350–330 BCE
p: The title means only “after the Physics”, whether in an editor’s arrangement or in the order of study. No ancient source says who coined it. Book I surveys earlier thinkers, in what is for several of the Presocratics our fullest ancient report of what they held. Book V is a lexicon: about thirty terms, each taken through its several senses. The short second book is reported in an ancient note to be the work of Pasicles of Rhodes. Fourteen unequal books do not argue one thesis from start to finish. What holds them together is the project of Book IV, a science of being qua being. It rests on the claim that being is said in many ways but all with reference to substance. The same book defends the principle of non-contradiction, not by proving it, which is impossible, but by showing that a denier who says anything determinate has already conceded it. Books VII to IX ask what substance is and answer, against Platonists and common sense alike, that it is form. Book XII argues to an unmoved mover, pure actuality, causing motion as an object of desire does, whose life is thought thinking itself. That book also counts the movers, at forty-seven or fifty-five, following the astronomers Eudoxus and Callippus. Books XIII and XIV then take apart the Forms and the mathematical objects of the Platonists, with the argument later called the third man among the weapons.

This is the most durable of the works. It begins from what people already want, eudaimonia, and asks what that consists in. The function argument holds that the human good is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, since the characteristic human work is rational activity. Virtue of character is a stable disposition, formed by repeated action rather than teaching, to feel and act rightly: a mean relative to us, fixed by practical wisdom, phronesis, not by a rule. Book III separates voluntary from involuntary action and introduces choice. Book V treats justice, and adds equity, the correction of a law where the law is too general to fit the case. Book VII takes up akrasia, acting against what one knows to be better, and asks in what sense the knowledge is present. Pleasure is analysed twice, in Book VII and again in Book X, in two accounts that do not agree. Two long books on friendship follow. Book X praises contemplation as the highest happiness, which sits awkwardly with the civic life described earlier. Anscombe’s 1958 attack on modern moral theory sent philosophers back to this text.

The Politics continues the Ethics. The good life is possible only in a city, so the study of character runs into the study of constitutions. Man is by nature a political animal. Whoever is outside the city is either a beast or a god. Book I also carries the defence of natural slavery, which fails on Aristotle’s own terms, since he concedes that enslavement by conquest is unjust. The same book separates the management of a household from the unlimited pursuit of money, and condemns lending at interest as money bred out of money. That argument was still doing work in the medieval prohibition of usury. Book II reviews existing constitutions and proposals, and rejects the common ownership of women and property in Plato’s Republic. The middle books are empirical, drawing on the 158 constitutions the school collected. Of those only the Constitution of the Athenians survives, from a papyrus published in 1891. He classifies constitutions by the number of rulers and whether they rule for the common good. He holds that the many deliberating together may judge better than the few experts. He concludes that the most workable state is dominated by a middle class. Books VII and VIII describe the best city and the education it would give, and break off unfinished.

Aristotle calls rhetoric the counterpart of dialectic and defines it as the capacity to see, in any case, the available means of persuasion. He distinguishes three sources of persuasion, the speaker’s character, the audience’s emotion and the argument itself, and three settings, assembly, courtroom and ceremonial occasion. Its logical core is the enthymeme, a syllogism drawn from premises the audience already holds. Alongside it stands the example, which argues from one case to another. What has worn best is Book II. It analyses anger, fear, pity, shame and envy by asking whom people feel each towards and in what state they are when they feel it: the earliest systematic psychology of the emotions. Book III turns to style and arrangement. Prose should be clear without being flat, should not fall into metre, and should take its ornament from metaphor rather than from compounds and rare words.

works.y: c. 335 BCE; only Book I survives
p: Poetry is imitation, mimesis. Tragedy is the imitation of a serious and complete action, arousing pity and fear and accomplishing the katharsis of such emotions. Six parts make it up: plot, character, thought, diction, melody and spectacle. Plot comes first and character second, since tragedy imitates action rather than persons. The best plots turn on reversal and recognition together, and on a change of fortune brought about by hamartia, an error rather than a vice. Events must follow one another by probability or necessity, which rules out the god lowered by machine to end the play. Poetry is more philosophical than history because it shows what would happen, not merely what did. Of style, Aristotle says that the great thing is to command metaphor. It is a sign of natural gift, and the one thing that cannot be learnt from another. Two cautions: katharsis is named in the definition and never explained, which is why the quarrel over purgation, purification and clarification has run for four centuries; and the neoclassical three unities are a Renaissance elaboration of the one unity, of action, that the text requires. The book on comedy is lost.

legacy: Theophrastus inherited the school, the library and the research programme, and Strato after him. Then the Lyceum faded. For two centuries Aristotle was known chiefly through the lost dialogues. Strabo tells a possibly embroidered story of the books passing to Neleus of Scepsis, hidden in a cellar, damaged, and carried to Rome after Sulla took Athens in 86 BCE. Around the middle of the first century BCE Andronicus of Rhodes catalogued Aristotle’s writings and grouped related treatises together. How far the corpus we read is his work rests on one late report in Porphyry. Jonathan Barnes argued in 1997 that the story will not carry the weight usually put on it. Commentary then became the discipline: Alexander of Aphrodisias around 200 CE, then Neoplatonists such as Simplicius and Philoponus, who preserved the texts while reading Plato into them. The commentators are a library in their own right: the Berlin Academy printed them as the Commentaria in Aristotelem Graeca between 1882 and 1909, in twenty-three volumes.

Transmission ran east before it ran west. Syriac-speaking Christian scholars translated the logic from the sixth century. Their successors staffed the Abbasid translation movement at Baghdad in the ninth, where Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his circle turned the corpus into Arabic. Al-Farabi earned the title of the Second Teacher. Avicenna absorbed Aristotle so thoroughly that he rebuilt him. Maimonides, writing in Arabic in the twelfth century, built the Guide of the Perplexed on Aristotelian physics and psychology. Averroes, at Cordoba in the twelfth century, wrote short, middle and long commentaries on nearly everything and became simply the Commentator. Several of those long commentaries survive complete only in Hebrew or in Latin, the Arabic being lost. Without that chain the Latin West would have inherited a fragment.

Latin Europe had only part of the logic, in Boethius’ translations, until the twelfth century. Then the rest arrived twice over: from Arabic at Toledo, notably through Gerard of Cremona, and from Greek, by James of Venice and later by William of Moerbeke, who translated for Aquinas in the 1260s. They were disruptive enough to be banned. A Paris council forbade lecturing on the natural works in 1210. The ban was renewed in 1215 and softened in 1231. By 1255 the arts faculty required them all. Aquinas wrote line-by-line commentaries on a dozen of the works and called their author simply the Philosopher. The radical Aristotelians of the arts faculty, Siger of Brabant among them, taught the eternity of the world and one intellect shared by all men. The reaction culminated in Bishop Tempier’s condemnation of 219 propositions in 1277, aimed at the radical Aristotelians but catching some Thomist theses. Both of those doctrines are on the list. Only the articles touching Aquinas were annulled, in 1325, two years after his canonisation.

The revolt was correspondingly violent. Humanists mocked scholastic Latin, Galileo demolished the physics, and Bacon named his Novum Organum of 1620 against the old one. Luther’s Disputation against Scholastic Theology of 1517 set Aristotle against theology as darkness against light. The break was not clean. Pomponazzi used Aristotelian arguments in 1516 to conclude that the immortality of the soul cannot be demonstrated. Zabarella at Padua worked a theory of scientific method out of the Posterior Analytics. Whether it reached Galileo has been argued both ways and is unsettled. The Greek text had meanwhile been printed by Aldus Manutius at Venice between 1495 and 1498. What returned, once the polemic cooled, was more than the critics expected: Bekker’s Berlin edition of 1831 still supplies the numbers by which the corpus is cited; Jaeger’s thesis of 1923 reopened the question of how the works were composed; Anscombe, Foot and MacIntyre revived the ethics; and philosophers of biology now read the animal works as science. Some of that is live rather than historical. Nussbaum’s capability approach takes the function argument as a starting point. Hylomorphism has returned in the philosophy of mind. Lukasiewicz reconstructed the syllogistic as a formal system in 1951. The argument over how well that reconstruction fits the Greek has not stopped.

Aristotle left a second ethical treatise, the Eudemian Ethics. Three books belong to both: Nicomachean V, VI and VII are Eudemian IV, V and VI. Which treatise they were written for is disputed. The answer decides which account of pleasure and of practical wisdom is the later one.

read.first: Begin with the Nicomachean Ethics, Books I to III and X, in a modern translation with facing commentary. Then Physics II on the four causes, De Anima II, and Metaphysics VII and XII. Use an edition printing the Bekker numbers in the margin, since those are how everyone cites him. The Revised Oxford Translation, edited by Jonathan Barnes in 1984, is the standard complete Aristotle in English.
read.note: These are lecture notes, not prose written to be read, so the argument often moves faster than the sentences do. A good commentary is not a luxury here.

aristotle.caveat: The dating and internal order of almost every treatise is conjectural. Several works are compilations later editors assembled. The authenticity of some pieces — among them the Categories and the surviving Constitution of the Athenians — remains genuinely disputed. The same doubt attaches to Book X of the History of Animals and to the whole of the Magna Moralia. The three books shared by the two Ethics were written for one of them. Which one is unsettled. Almost everything said here about how the corpus was assembled rests on late sources: Strabo, Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, Porphyry. None of them was in a position to know at first hand.

antisthenes.sub: the Socratic who kept the hardness and dropped the metaphysics
world: Athens after the defeat of 404 was poorer, smaller and suspicious of itself. The empire had gone, the fleet had gone, the long walls were pulled down, and the men who had trained its politicians were widely blamed. Socrates was executed in 399. Antisthenes, son of an Athenian father and a Thracian mother, exercised at the Cynosarges, the gymnasium outside the walls reserved for those of mixed descent.
life: Born about 446, he studied first with Gorgias and taught rhetoric himself before attaching himself to Socrates. He walked several miles into the city each day to hear him. He was present at the death. Xenophon gives him a speech praising his own poverty as the greatest of riches. He quarrelled bitterly with Plato. Diogenes Laertius lists some sixty titles in ten volumes. Two declamations survive, and the rest is fragments and report.

p: Two short paired speeches contesting the arms of Achilles, with Ajax speaking for deeds and plain courage and Odysseus for intelligence and results. They are the only continuous prose we have from him. Their authenticity has been questioned, but is generally accepted. Read next to his ethics, they look less like a rhetorical exercise than an argument about where excellence lies. The Cynic answer is given to the man who loses the contest.

works.t: Sathon, or On Contradicting (Sathōn, ē peri tou antilegein)
p: Three books against Plato, whose name the title deforms into an obscenity. Behind the abuse lay a philosophical charge, that Forms are redundant: later commentators report him saying he could see a horse but could not see horseness. He held that contradiction is impossible, because each thing has its own proper account and one cannot say of a thing what it is not. Aristotle records the doctrine and calls it simple-minded.

legacy: Doxographers put him at the head of a succession running to Diogenes, then Crates, then Zeno of Citium. That made him ancestor of the Stoics as well as of the Cynics. Modern scholarship doubts the chain: Diogenes may never have met him. The succession may be later tidying by writers who wanted every school descended from Socrates. What is not in doubt is that he stated the premise both schools start from, that virtue suffices for happiness, can be taught, and consists in deeds.

read.first: The two declamations, short enough to read at a sitting, followed by Xenophon's Symposium for the only portrait of him by someone who knew him.
read.note: Resist reading him backwards from Diogenes. The connection between them is the weakest link in the standard story.

antisthenes.caveat: Almost nothing survives. The two declamations are of debated authenticity. His traditional role as founder of Cynicism rests on a succession list that many scholars regard as a later construction.

diogenes-sinope.sub: the Cynic who made the argument by living it
world: Sinope was a Black Sea colony of Miletus, prosperous on the trade in fish, timber and iron. It struck its own silver coinage. The father of Diogenes had charge of that coinage. Sinopean coins of the fourth century defaced with punch marks have in fact been found, an unusual case of an archaeological trace sitting close to an anecdote. But it proves nothing about who defaced them.

His years in Athens and Corinth coincided with the end of Greek civic independence. Philip won at Chaeronea in 338. Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 and by 323 ruled from the Adriatic to the Punjab. Citizenship of one city, the frame of Greek ethics for three centuries, counted for less. The claim to be a citizen of the world, apparently first made by Diogenes, belongs to that moment, as does the Hellenistic turn toward self-sufficiency.
life: He came to Athens as an exile, driven from Sinope for tampering with the currency. The phrase, deface the coinage, became his motto for what he did to convention. Tradition makes him a pupil of Antisthenes, though the chronology strains. Pirates are said to have captured and sold him at Corinth. There he tutored the sons of his purchaser Xeniades and died about 323, by tradition on the same day as Alexander.

Every famous scene belongs to tradition and to no contemporary record: the storage jar he lived in, the lamp carried in daylight to find a human being, the cup thrown away on seeing a boy drink from his hands, the reply to Alexander that he should stand out of the light. All of it comes through Diogenes Laertius, compiling in the third century CE, six hundred years after the fact. The anecdotes may preserve his manner. None can be verified as an event.

p: The book is reported to have described a community without money, temples, law courts or marriage, with women and children held in common and knucklebones for currency. It is reported also to have held that incest and eating human flesh are forbidden by convention alone. Philodemus, in the first century BCE, quotes enough to establish that the book existed and scandalised readers. Its authenticity was already contested in antiquity. Diogenes Laertius reports that Sosicrates and Satyrus denied he wrote anything, while other sources list titles. It remains the strongest evidence that Cynicism had positions and not only gestures.

Seven titles are reported, among them Thyestes, Medea and Oedipus, with a handful of lines quoted. They seem to have turned the tragic form against itself, staging the taboo subjects of myth in order to argue that the horror attached to them is a matter of custom. Ancient readers doubted them too: one source hands them to Philiscus of Aegina, a follower. The pattern is familiar: wherever a Cynic text would be most useful as evidence, someone in antiquity has denied it is genuine.

Fifty-one short letters circulated under his name, addressed to his father, to Crates, to Alexander and to various cities. None is by him. They were written centuries later, most likely as school exercises in adopting the Cynic voice. They matter for two reasons. They set out Cynic positions in continuous prose, which the anecdotes never do. They show how completely the man had turned into a mask that any competent writer could put on.

legacy: The chreia, a compressed scene ending in a retort, was the vehicle. Easy to memorise, collected in schoolbooks and used to teach composition for a thousand years, it carried Cynicism as anecdote rather than doctrine. That is why the movement never acquired a curriculum and never quite died. Crates of Thebes passed it to Zeno, and Stoicism began as Cynicism with a physics attached.

Later ages took whatever they needed. Egyptian ascetics inherited the technique of public poverty. Julian attacked the Cynics of his day for copying the beard and not the discipline. Rabelais, Diderot in Rameau's Nephew, Nietzsche and Foucault each found a use for the figure. The modern sense of cynic, meaning distrustful of other people's motives, has drifted nearly to the opposite of what he meant.

read.first: Book VI of Diogenes Laertius entire, which is the whole ancient dossier, read with its date of composition kept in mind.
read.note: Treat each anecdote as a report about what Cynics found worth repeating, not as a report about an afternoon in Corinth.

diogenes-sinope.caveat: He left nothing, the works attributed to him were already disputed in antiquity, and the entire biography rests on collections of anecdotes compiled some six hundred years after his death.

pyrrho.sub: who wrote nothing and gave scepticism its name
world: Pyrrho's adult life covered the conquest and the break-up that followed it. He went east with Alexander's army in the 320s, as far as Bactria and India, in the company of the philosopher Anaxarchus. After Alexander died in 323 the empire fell to the wars of the successors. The Greek world became larger, richer, less stable and governed by soldiers.

Ancient sources say he met the naked sages of India and the magi of Persia. Modern scholars have argued about whether Indian thought shaped his position. The evidence is thin and the question open. Clearer is the local demand. Hellenistic philosophy sold tranquillity to men who no longer decided anything about their own cities. Pyrrho, Epicurus and the first Stoics all offered it, by very different routes, within the same fifty years.
life: Born at Elis in the Peloponnese about 360, he was a painter before he was a philosopher. A modest picture of his was still shown at Elis generations later. After the eastern expedition he returned home and lived quietly with his sister, a midwife, selling poultry in the market. Elis honoured him, made him a high priest, and on his account is said to have exempted philosophers from taxes. He died about 270.

No school was founded and no book written. His pupil Timon of Phlius put the teaching into satirical verse. The doxographers used Timon. Aenesidemus revived the name at Alexandria two centuries later and built a systematic scepticism on it. Sextus Empiricus, writing around 200 CE, produced the manual that survives. Every reconstruction of what Pyrrho himself held must pass through at least two of those hands. Each had purposes of his own.

p: Diogenes Laertius reports that Pyrrho wrote nothing whatever apart from a poem addressed to Alexander, for which he was paid ten thousand gold pieces. Not a line of it survives. The report may be no more than a way of accounting for a philosopher without books. Its interest is negative. The founder of a tradition of argument left no arguments. Everything ascribed to him is therefore either a description of how he behaved or a summary composed by somebody else.

works.t: Silloi and Indalmoi, by Timon of Phlius
p: Timon's lampoons ridiculed nearly every philosopher in hexameters that parody Homer, exempting only Pyrrho, whom he praised for an untroubled calm. From his verse comes the one connected statement of the position, quoted by Aristocles of Messene and preserved in Eusebius: things are equally indifferent, unmeasurable and undecidable; therefore neither our perceptions nor our opinions are true or false; therefore we should hold no opinions, and from that follows speechlessness, and then tranquillity. Whether the first clause claims something about reality or only about our access to it is the central dispute in modern scholarship.

works.t: Outlines of Pyrrhonism (Pyrrhōneioi hypotypōseis), by Sextus Empiricus
p: The surviving handbook of the tradition, written five centuries after its subject and not by him. Sextus sets out the modes for generating opposed appearances of equal weight, the suspension of judgement that results, and the tranquillity that follows suspension unsought, as he puts it, the way a shadow follows a body. He insists that the sceptic still lives by appearances, by custom and by the practice of a craft. That answers the charge that suspension makes ordinary life impossible.

legacy: Little happened for two centuries. The sceptical initiative passed instead to Plato's Academy under Arcesilaus and Carneades, who fought the Stoics with borrowed weapons. Aenesidemus, breaking with the Academy in the first century BCE, took up Pyrrho's name as a banner for a stricter position. Then the whole tradition nearly vanished, surviving in the manuscripts of Sextus and in the ninth book of Diogenes Laertius.

Printing changed that. The Latin Sextus of 1562 reached Montaigne, who wrote the Apology for Raymond Sebond out of it. The crisis that followed runs through Descartes' search for certainty, Bayle's dictionary and Hume's observation that nature cures the doubts argument cannot. Epistemologists still work with the Agrippan modes. Whether a man can live his scepticism is still asked in the terms Sextus set.

read.first: Book I of Sextus' Outlines of Pyrrhonism, then the Aristocles passage from Eusebius and the life in Diogenes Laertius, in that order.
read.note: Sextus is a wonderfully clear writer, but he reports a mature system and not the practice of the man whose name it carries.

pyrrho.caveat: Pyrrho wrote no philosophy. Scholars remain divided over whether his position was a claim that reality is indeterminate or a claim that we cannot know how things are.

epicurus.sub: the physicist who made freedom from fear the whole of ethics
world: Alexander died in 323 BCE. Within a year Athens had gambled on independence in the Lamian War and lost. A Macedonian garrison held the harbour hill of Munychia. The property qualification for citizenship rose or fell according to which general held the city. Demetrius of Phalerum governed for Cassander from 317. Demetrius Poliorcetes expelled him in 307. Athenian politics had become a function of somebody else’s army.

That loss of scale did not empty the temples. Public cult continued as before, and to it were added honours for kings. A processional hymn greeted Poliorcetes as a god who was actually present, unlike the others, who were deaf or far away. Beneath it ran an older and more private anxiety about eclipses, thunder and what waits after death. Epicurus wrote physics as a remedy for that anxiety, which is why his atoms arrive wrapped in consolation.

Teaching still concentrated in Athens, though Ptolemy I’s Museum at Alexandria had begun drawing away the mathematicians. Four schools competed for pupils within a few miles: Academy, Lyceum, the Stoa from about 300, and the Garden. That competition was legally visible. In 307/6 one Sophocles of Sunium carried a law requiring the council’s approval for anyone to head a school. The philosophers left the city until it was repealed a year later.
life: Born in 341 BCE on Samos, where his father Neocles had settled as one of the Athenian colonists and taught school, Epicurus grew up an Athenian citizen abroad. That status brought him back to Athens about 323 for two years of military service. While he was away Perdiccas expelled the settlers from Samos. His family moved to Colophon and he joined them there. He studied under Nausiphanes at Teos, a follower of Democritus, and afterwards denied owing him anything.

His own teaching began at Mytilene in 311, went badly, and continued at Lampsacus, where he gathered the men who would run the school: Metrodorus, Hermarchus, Polyaenus, Idomeneus. About 307/6 he bought a house in Athens and a garden between the city wall and the Academy. The Garden was a household as much as a school. Women attended, including Themista and Leontion, who wrote against Theophrastus. So did slaves, one of whom, Mys, is named in the will.

Members memorised summaries, corresponded heavily with allied groups abroad, and dined together monthly. The political counsel was withdrawal — lathe biosas, live unnoticed — which was an accurate reading of what an Athenian assembly could still decide. Death came in 270 from a urinary blockage. The will, quoted in full by Diogenes Laertius, freed four slaves and endowed the memorial dinners. A letter of his last day tells Idomeneus that recollection of their conversations weighed against extreme pain.

p: The shortest and most quoted of the letters compresses the ethics into a few pages. It opens by insisting that philosophy has no right age, then removes the two great fears. The gods exist and are blessed and incorruptible, therefore neither angry nor grateful. Popular piety slanders them by expecting favours. Death is nothing to us, since sensation is the condition of anything mattering and death is its end. Then comes the classification that does the practical work. Desires are natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, or empty, and only the first class must be met. Pleasure is defined negatively, as absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance, which is why bread and water can be a limit case of the good life. Prudence turns out to be the chief virtue, because prudence does the accounting.

The physics in epitome, written for students who could not work through the thirty-seven books of On Nature and needed something they could hold in memory. Nothing comes to be from nothing, and nothing perishes into nothing. The whole is bodies and void. Bodies are compounds or the indivisible atoms out of which compounds are made. Atoms are unlimited in number and the void unlimited in extent, so there are innumerable worlds. Perception is explained by thin films of atoms, eidola, streaming off surfaces and striking the sense organs. That grounds the claim that all sensations are true, and that error lies in the judgement added to them. The prose is telegraphic and hard, a mnemonic rather than an argument. Much of the reasoning behind its assertions has to be recovered from Lucretius.

The third letter treats things in the sky: the size of the sun, the phases of the moon, thunder, hail, earthquakes, comets. Its governing principle looks perverse until the purpose is clear. Where several explanations are consistent with what we observe, all should be accepted as possible. Insisting on one is the error of the astronomers. This is not indifference to truth but a therapeutic move, since fear of the heavens is fed by the sense that celestial events are signs of divine intention. Any sufficient natural account dissolves it. Some scholars doubt whether the letter is Epicurus’ own composition rather than a pupil’s digest of his meteorology. The question is unsettled. The doctrine of multiple explanations is certainly his, since Lucretius uses it at length.

Forty numbered sentences, evidently made to be learned by heart and recited. The first four are the core of what Philodemus later calls the fourfold remedy: the divine is not to be feared, death is not to be felt, the good is easy to get, the terrible easy to endure. Doctrines five to thirty concern pleasure, prudence and friendship, including the claim that no pleasure is bad in itself but that some cost more than they yield. The last stretch sets out a contract theory of justice. Justice is not a thing in itself but an agreement neither to harm nor be harmed, binding only among those who make it and revisable when circumstances change what is advantageous. A companion set of eighty-one sayings, the Vatican Sayings, surfaced in a Vatican manuscript in 1888.

The main work, in thirty-seven books, written over decades and never transmitted whole. What survives is physical: charred rolls from the library of the villa at Herculaneum, buried in 79 CE and dug out in the eighteenth century. They have been unrolled, drawn, and more recently read by imaging that does not destroy them. The fragments show that Epicurus argued in detail rather than asserting, and that the summaries flatten him. Book twenty-five is the most consequential recovery. It discusses how a developed character becomes responsible for its own actions, and how an atomist who explains everything by atoms can still hold people to account. That is the problem for which the swerve, prominent in Lucretius, is one part of the answer. Work on the rolls continues. The text is still growing.

legacy: No ancient school held its doctrines so still. Epicureans transmitted summaries for four centuries rather than developing them, which made the movement durable and static. Philodemus of Gadara taught it in Italy in the first century BCE, and Lucretius versified it. About 120 CE a rich provincial named Diogenes had a long Epicurean text carved on a portico wall at Oenoanda, so that passers-by could read the remedy.

Opposition was equally durable. Stoics and Academics attacked the physics and the hedonism. Christian writers found a mortal soul and indifferent gods intolerable. Dante puts Epicureans in burning tombs with the heretics. The name became a byword for gluttony, close to the opposite of what the Garden practised. No medieval copyist preserved On Nature. The school survives chiefly because Diogenes Laertius filled his tenth book with the letters, the doctrines and the will.

Recovery ran through Lucretius. Poggio Bracciolini’s find of 1417 put the physics back in circulation. Pierre Gassendi in the 1640s rehabilitated Epicurus for Christian readers. His corpuscular atomism fed Boyle and Locke. Jefferson called himself an Epicurean in 1819. Marx wrote his 1841 dissertation on Democritean and Epicurean physics, taking the swerve as the point where necessity admits freedom. Modern imaging of the Herculaneum rolls has made him an ancient author whose text is still growing.

The poem is De rerum natura, six books of Latin hexameter written in the middle of the first century BCE. It is the fullest surviving exposition of Epicurean physics in any language. Much of the reasoning the letters merely assert has to be recovered from it.

read.first: Read the Letter to Menoeceus and then the Principal Doctrines. Together they take an hour and contain the whole ethics. Follow with the Letter to Herodotus only if the physics interests you, and with Lucretius if it does.
read.note: The word pleasure is a trap in English. He means the state of a body in no pain and a mind in no fear, and almost nothing the modern word suggests.

epicurus.caveat: Nothing survives whole in his own hand: the three letters, the Principal Doctrines and the will reach us inside Diogenes Laertius, the Vatican Sayings through one manuscript, and On Nature only as carbonised fragments from Herculaneum. The Letter to Pythocles is of contested authorship.

zeno-citium.sub: the immigrant who turned a public colonnade into a school
world: Citium was a Phoenician-founded city on the south coast of Cyprus, contested between Ptolemy and Antigonus and rich on copper and the purple dye trade. Zeno was a merchant’s son of Phoenician descent. In Athens he remained a resident foreigner with no political rights — a condition his school’s indifference to office and birthplace would eventually turn into doctrine.

Athens had stopped being a power. Macedonian garrisons came and went. The tyrant Lachares stripped the gold from Athena’s statue. The Chremonidean War ended in surrender to Antigonus Gonatas in the year Zeno died. What remained was the city’s eminence as a place of instruction. His choice of the Stoa Poikile, a public colonnade on the Agora, was therefore pointed: no walls, no gate, no endowment, anyone could stop and listen.
life: The tradition recorded by Diogenes Laertius three centuries later says Zeno reached Athens about 312 BCE after a shipwreck cost him a cargo of purple. On that account he wandered into a bookseller’s, heard Xenophon’s Memorabilia read aloud, asked where such men were found, and was pointed at Crates the Cynic walking past. The story is too neat to trust and too well attested to discard. His teachers certainly included Crates, Stilpo of Megara, the logician Diodorus Cronus, and Polemo of the Academy.

Teaching began about 300 in the painted porch. His pupils were first called Zenonians, then Stoics after the building. He declined Antigonus Gonatas’ invitation to Macedon and sent his student Persaeus instead. Diogenes Laertius quotes an Athenian decree honouring him with a gold crown and a public tomb in the Kerameikos, praising a life consistent with his teaching. He died in 262. Cleanthes succeeded him.

p: His most notorious book, written early and under Cynic influence — ancient wits said it was written on the Dog’s tail. It described a community of the wise with no temples, lawcourts, gymnasia or coinage, no conventional marriage, and one dress for men and women. The ground was that such institutions exist to manage people who are not virtuous. Later Stoics found it an embarrassment. Some denied it was his. Everything we have comes from hostile summaries, chiefly in Diogenes Laertius and in Philodemus’ charred treatise on the Stoics.

works.t: On the Nature of Man; On Impulse
p: The ethical treatises produced the formula that defined the school: the end is to live in agreement, to which with nature was attached. The sources disagree over whether Zeno said both words or Cleanthes supplied the second. Beneath it lay oikeiosis, the claim that an animal’s first impulse is self-preservation rather than pleasure, and that developing reason extends the same concern to others. Zeno also drew the hard line later Stoics had to defend: only virtue is good, only vice bad, and health and wealth are indifferent though naturally preferred.

His theory of knowledge survives mainly through Cicero, who reports the gesture used to teach it. An open palm is an impression; fingers slightly bent, assent; a closed fist, the grasping of the object, katalepsis; the fist gripped by the other hand, knowledge, which only the wise man has. The crucial term is the cognitive impression, an appearance that comes from a real object and could not have arisen from anything else. Arcesilaus attacked that criterion at once. Most of what survives is preserved inside the attack.

legacy: The school outlasted every institution he knew. None of his own words came with it. Cleanthes and then Chrysippus reworked the system so thoroughly that separating Zeno’s positions from theirs is a standing problem of Hellenistic scholarship. The evidence is Diogenes Laertius’ seventh book, Cicero, Stobaeus, Galen and the Herculaneum papyri, all later, and most of it either hostile or summarising.

His afterlife is largely retrospective claiming. Plutarch read the Republic as a vision of humanity as one community under one law. Modern histories of cosmopolitanism regularly begin there, owing as much to Plutarch as to Zeno. The recent revival of popular Stoicism draws almost entirely on Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius. The founder is therefore the least read of the Stoics and the hardest to read.

read.first: There is no book to read. Start with the seventh book of Diogenes Laertius in any complete translation, then a modern collection of Hellenistic sources printed with commentary.
read.note: Any continuous account of Zeno’s thought is a modern reconstruction from fragments. Honest ones say so on the page.

zeno-citium.caveat: Not one of Zeno’s books survives. The biography rests on anecdotes collected centuries after his death. The boundary between his doctrines and Chrysippus’ systematisation of them is genuinely disputed.

chrysippus.sub: the logician who made Stoicism a system that could be defended
world: Soli, where he was born about 279 BCE, was a Greek city in Cilicia inside the Seleucid orbit. Its name had already given Greek the word solecism for provincial speech — a joke made at Chrysippus’ expense in antiquity. The eastern Mediterranean he crossed to reach Athens was a world of competing royal capitals in which Greek learning had become an export and a court ornament.

Athens by then was politically finished and intellectually decisive. What drove his enormous output was an argument inside that small world. Arcesilaus had turned the Academy sceptical and aimed it squarely at the Stoic criterion of truth. Cleanthes had no adequate reply. The school was losing pupils. Chrysippus wrote to answer this, at a reported five hundred lines a day. He had a habit of quoting whole passages of Euripides that his own readers complained of.
life: He came to Athens young, possibly after his family property was confiscated, and trained under Cleanthes. Diogenes Laertius reports that he also studied in the Academy with Arcesilaus and Lacydes. That would mean he learned the sceptical case from the men making it. He is said to have told Cleanthes that he needed only the doctrines and would find the proofs himself — arrogance that turned out to be an accurate job description.

Taking over the school about 230, he ran it until his death around 206. He produced a catalogue that Diogenes Laertius lists at over seven hundred books, more than three hundred of them on logic. Unusually for a Hellenistic intellectual of his standing, he held no court appointment. Two comic accounts of his death circulated, one involving undiluted wine and one a donkey eating figs. Both are the kind of anecdote ancient biography collected, and neither carries weight.

p: A carbonised roll from Herculaneum preserves parts of this work and is nearly the only physical remnant of Chrysippus’ own writing. What it and the doxographies show is a propositional logic unlike Aristotle’s logic of terms. The variables stand for whole statements. The system rests on five indemonstrable argument forms — among them if the first then the second, but the first, therefore the second — from which other valid arguments are derived by stated rules. Nineteenth-century logicians dismissed all this. After Frege it was recognised as the ancient anticipation of sentential logic.

The physics defended a fully determined cosmos, a single living being pervaded by pneuma. In it every event follows from prior causes, and the whole is periodically consumed by fire and repeated. The obvious objection is that responsibility disappears. His answer, preserved by Cicero and Aulus Gellius, is the cylinder: someone must push it to start it rolling, but that it rolls rather than skids follows from its own shape. Impressions arrive by fate. Assent comes from the character that is ours. Against the lazy argument he replied that outcomes are co-fated with the actions producing them.

The therapeutic core of his ethics argued that emotions are not irrational forces contending with reason but judgements: fear is the opinion that something bad is at hand, grief the fresh opinion that it is present, and their excess is reason itself in a bad state. This unifies the soul at the cost of making passion look like simple error. Posidonius later broke with it. Almost all of the text survives inside Galen’s long attack in On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato, so its best witness is its most determined opponent.

legacy: The ancient verdict was blunt: if there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa. He gave the school arguments that survived two centuries of Academic assault, and a vocabulary Cicero, Seneca and Epictetus inherited without rebuilding. Not one of the seven hundred books came through the manuscript tradition. What we have is fragments in Galen, Plutarch, Cicero and Stobaeus, assembled by von Arnim in 1903 into the collection scholars still cite.

His logic had the strangest fate. Misunderstood in late antiquity, ignored once Aristotle became the logic of the schools, and dismissed by Kant as a science that had learned nothing new, propositional logic was reinvented in the nineteenth century by people who did not know it had existed. Only after Lukasiewicz and Mates in the twentieth was Chrysippus recognised as its inventor. The modern argument about determinism and responsibility still runs on a version of his cylinder.

read.first: Begin with Cicero’s On Fate and the second book of On the Nature of the Gods, then a modern anthology of Hellenistic sources that prints the logical fragments with commentary.
read.note: Everything attributed to him is quoted by someone arguing against him. The arguments read better once that filter is kept in view.

chrysippus.caveat: Over seven hundred titles are reported, and none survives whole. So every account of his logic, physics and ethics is reconstructed from quotation by opponents and from damaged papyri.

cicero.sub: the statesman who built a Latin vocabulary for Greek thought
world: The Republic Cicero served destroyed itself in his lifetime. Sulla’s proscriptions in 82 had shown what a Roman army could do to Roman politics. The alliance of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus in 60 emptied the constitutional forms of content. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49, won at Pharsalus, was made dictator for life and killed in 44. The second triumvirate proscribed its enemies the next year. Soldiers caught Cicero near Formiae in December 43.

Roman opinion had long treated Greek philosophy as suspect. The senate expelled philosophers and rhetoricians in 161 BCE. Cato wanted Carneades sent home quickly in 155 for arguing both sides of justice. By Cicero’s day the senatorial class was educated in Greek and studied at Athens or Rhodes, but Latin had no technical vocabulary for any of it. Books were made by household copyists. He dictated to his freedman Tiro, who ran the production of the entire corpus.
life: Born in 106 BCE at Arpinum into local gentry, Cicero was a novus homo with no consular ancestors and made his way by advocacy. He trained in law under Scaevola. He heard Philo of Larissa when the head of the Academy fled to Rome in 88, and later studied at Athens under Antiochus of Ascalon and at Rhodes with the Stoic Posidonius. Consul in 63, he executed the Catilinarian conspirators without trial and was exiled for it in 58.

The philosophical corpus is a product of defeat. Pardoned after Pharsalus but politically finished, he lost his daughter Tullia in February 45.
