He wrote a Consolation for himself, now lost, and then in roughly twenty months produced the Academica, On Ends, the Tusculan Disputations, On the Nature of the Gods, On Divination, On Fate, On Old Age, On Friendship and On Duties. He said himself that the writing stood in for the public life he no longer had.

works.t: On the Nature of the Gods (De Natura Deorum)
p: Three books in which an Epicurean, a Stoic and an Academic argue about the gods in a Roman house. Velleius states the Epicurean theology and is demolished. Balbus gives the Stoic case from cosmic order at length. Cotta then takes that apart too. The work closes with Cicero remarking only that Balbus seemed nearer to a semblance of truth. The refusal to conclude is the Academic method working as intended. Because the Greek originals are lost, this is our fullest account of Hellenistic theology. Hume took its form for the Dialogues concerning Natural Religion.

Written in a few weeks as Antony consolidated power, and addressed to his son studying in Athens, this is his most practical and most influential book. The first two parts follow the Stoic Panaetius on the honourable and the expedient. The third, where Panaetius stopped, argues Cicero’s own thesis that the two never genuinely conflict, since nothing dishonourable is truly advantageous. He tests it on cases: the grain dealer sailing into starving Rhodes who knows other ships are coming, the general Regulus keeping an oath to his captors. The reasoning is uneven. The book became a school text for eighteen centuries.

works.t: On the Republic; On Laws (De Re Publica; De Legibus)
p: The earlier pair, written while he still had a career, argue for the mixed constitution and for law grounded in nature rather than decree. The passage Lactantius preserves — that true law is right reason in agreement with nature, unchanging and valid for all nations — carried natural law into Roman jurisprudence and the whole later Western tradition. On the Republic was then lost except for its closing Dream of Scipio, which survived because Macrobius wrote a commentary on it. In 1819 Angelo Mai found much of the rest in the Vatican, beneath a copy of Augustine on the Psalms.

legacy: He gave Latin its philosophical language, coining or fixing terms European thought still uses: qualitas for what-sort-ness, moralis for the study of character, and, on Seneca’s report, essentia. Augustine dated his own turn to philosophy to reading the now-lost Hortensius. In the Latin Middle Ages Cicero simply was classical philosophy. Petrarch’s discovery of the letters to Atticus at Verona in 1345, which revealed a vacillating politician behind the moralist, is a conventional starting point of humanism.

Modern judgement has swung hard. Mommsen treated him as a windbag. The nineteenth century denied him an originality he had never claimed. Rehabilitation rests on two grounds: that a good expositor choosing between schools is doing philosophy, and that he is irreplaceable as evidence. For Stoic theology, Epicurean physics and Academic scepticism alike the Greek texts are gone. His summaries stand in their place. That means his framing has shaped what those debates now look like.

read.first: On Duties first, for the argument and the influence, then On the Nature of the Gods for the method of arguing every side. On Friendship and On Old Age are short and read easily.
read.note: He is a witness as much as an author. The pleasure of the dialogues comes from watching a working politician test doctrines against cases he had actually faced.

cicero.caveat: A large part of the philosophical corpus is lost, including the Hortensius and the Consolation. On the Republic survives only in the fragments recovered from a palimpsest in 1819.

lucretius.sub: the poet who argued atomism as a cure for terror
world: Rome in the 60s and 50s BCE was rich, violent and badly governed. Sulla’s proscriptions were in living memory. The revolt of Spartacus was put down in 71, and Catiline conspired in 63. Armed gangs under Clodius and Milo fought in the streets, while Pompey, Crassus and Caesar divided the provinces. Public religion there was a branch of the state: magistrates took auspices, augurs could invalidate legislation, diviners were consulted on portents. An attack on religio was not abstract.

Epicureanism had meanwhile become fashionable among the class that ran that state. Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul in 58, kept the Epicurean Philodemus of Gadara in his household. The library excavated at Herculaneum is probably Philodemus’ own. Latin verse was a young medium, Catullus was writing in Lucretius’ lifetime, and Greek philosophical terms had no Latin equivalents. Lucretius complains of the poverty of his ancestral tongue and invents as he goes.
life: Nothing reliable is known about him. The name is Titus Lucretius Carus. The poem addresses a Memmius, generally identified with Gaius Memmius, praetor in 58 and patron of Catullus. The only near-contemporary notice is a sentence in a letter of Cicero to his brother Quintus in February 54, remarking on the poems of Lucretius. Even the sense of that sentence is disputed. Whether the work appeared in his lifetime is unknown.

Jerome’s chronicle, written around 380 CE from a lost work of Suetonius, states that Lucretius was driven mad by a love philtre, wrote his books in lucid intervals, and killed himself at forty-four. It states also that Cicero afterwards corrected them. No earlier source knows any of it. The details fit a familiar pattern of hostile Christian biography, and most scholars discount the whole story. It has nonetheless shaped the picture of him down to Tennyson’s monologue of 1868.

works.t: On the Nature of Things, Books I-II (De Rerum Natura)
p: The poem opens with a hymn to Venus as the generative force of the world, then turns to demolish the fear of the gods it seems to invoke. The first two books lay down the physics: nothing is created from nothing, nothing returns to nothing, the universe is atoms and void, both without limit. Book two adds what Epicurus’ surviving letters barely mention: the swerve, a minimal uncaused deviation in the fall of atoms, needed to let atoms collide at all and to leave room for the will. The method is stated openly, as honey smeared on the rim of a cup of bitter medicine.

works.t: On the Nature of Things, Books III-IV
p: Book three is the psychological centre. It argues by accumulation rather than by one proof that mind and spirit are bodily, made of especially fine atoms, born with the body and dissolved with it. It concludes that death is nothing to us, since there will be no one for it to happen to. The closing tirade, in which Nature rebukes a man complaining at the end of a life he used badly, is the most sustained rhetoric in Latin poetry. Book four explains sensation by films of atoms and ends with an unsparing attack on sexual passion.

works.t: On the Nature of Things, Books V-VI
p: The last books take the doctrine outward. Book five denies that the world was made for humanity, and insists it had a beginning and will have an end. It gives a naturalistic history of civilisation: the emergence of living things, fire and metals, language growing from need rather than invention, religion originating in dreams and in terror at the sky. Book six explains thunder, magnets and plagues, then breaks off inside an account of the plague at Athens taken from Thucydides. Whether that ending is deliberate, unfinished or damaged has been argued for four centuries.

legacy: Virgil read him closely and answered him in the Georgics. After that the materialism made the poem unwelcome. Christian writers attacked it, and it came within a copy or two of vanishing. The surviving text descends from Carolingian manuscripts now at Leiden. Poggio Bracciolini, hunting in a German monastery in 1417, put it back into circulation. Machiavelli copied it out in his own hand, and a Florentine synod banned it from schools in 1517.

Its second life was as a scientific text rather than a poem. Montaigne quoted it constantly, Gassendi used it to reconstruct Epicurean atomism, Newton owned and annotated it, and eighteenth-century materialists took over its account of the origin of religion. Stephen Greenblatt’s The Swerve, in 2011, made the rediscovery famous again. Specialists criticised it for overstating the darkness before it. The durable claim is narrower: the poem gave early modern Europe its fullest ancient account of a universe running without design.

read.first: Read Book Three whole, in a verse translation, before anything else. Then Books One and Five. A prose crib is useful alongside for the technical passages.
read.note: It is an argument in verse, not a poem decorated with science. Skipping the reasoning leaves only the set pieces.

lucretius.caveat: Almost nothing about the author’s life is known. Jerome’s account of madness, a love philtre and suicide is four centuries late, unsupported and probably polemical. The poem’s state of completion is disputed.

philo.sub: the Alexandrian who put Moses and Plato in the same book
world: Alexandria under Augustus and Tiberius held the largest Jewish community outside Judaea, perhaps a third of the city. Its members spoke Greek, read the Torah in the Septuagint, and had no Hebrew. A philosophy that could not be conducted in Greek was no use to them.

The city was also where Greek learning had been catalogued rather than invented: the Library, the grammarians, the commentary as a form. Philo inherited the commentary and used it on scripture. The politics were less hospitable. The pogrom of 38 CE burned synagogues and killed in the streets, and Philo led the delegation that went to Rome about it.
life: Almost nothing is known of him apart from what he wrote and one dated episode. He was born into the richest Jewish family in Alexandria around 20 BCE. His brother Alexander was an official wealthy enough to gild the Temple gates in Jerusalem, and his nephew Tiberius Julius Alexander abandoned Judaism, governed Egypt for Rome, and commanded at the siege of Jerusalem.

In 39 or 40 CE Philo led the embassy that put the Alexandrian Jews' case to Caligula, who wanted his statue in the Temple. He wrote an account of it. He seems to have died soon after 50 CE. He calls himself elsewhere a man dragged from contemplation into public affairs, and it reads as more than a formula.

p: A verse-by-verse reading of Genesis 2 and 3 in which nothing is what it says. Adam is mind, Eve is sense-perception, the serpent is pleasure, and the garden is virtue. The method is not Philo's invention — Greek readers had been allegorising Homer for centuries — but turning it on a sacred text with a law attached to it is. He does not deny the literal sense: the commandments still bind, and he attacks those who think allegory dissolves the obligation to keep them. What the allegory adds is a second reading underneath, in which the Pentateuch turns out to contain Greek philosophy.

works.t: On the Creation of the World (De opificio mundi)
p: Genesis 1 read through the Timaeus. God creates by thinking an intelligible world first and then making a sensible copy of it, which puts the Platonic forms inside the divine mind rather than beside it. The six days are not a sequence in time but an order of rank. Between God and the world stands the logos, God's reason and the instrument of creation, which Philo calls at different points the image of God, the firstborn son, and a second God — language he never systematises and which later readers were not slow to use.

works.t: On the Embassy to Gaius (Legatio ad Gaium)
p: The report of his mission to Caligula, and the one place his philosophy touches an actual emergency. It describes the riot of 38, the desecration of the synagogues, and an audience in which the emperor wandered through a building giving orders about window glazing while the delegation tried to speak. The argument is that Jewish practice is compatible with Roman order and that the emperor's own predecessors had granted as much. It is also the earliest sustained account of a pogrom by someone who was there.

legacy: The synagogue did not keep him. No rabbinic source names Philo, and his works survive because Christians copied them — Clement and Origen in his own city, then Ambrose and Eusebius, who reports the legend, certainly false, that Philo met Peter in Rome. The logos that stands between God and the world, at once God's thought and something that can be called son, was too convenient to the fourth-century debates to be left alone. Whether the Johannine prologue owes him anything directly is disputed and probably unanswerable.

What he founded is the technique rather than any doctrine: the claim that a revealed text and a philosophical tradition can be made to say the same thing, held by reading the text as a figure. Origen, Augustine, Maimonides and Aquinas all work inside it. Sixteen centuries of scriptural philosophy run through a method first used systematically by a Greek-speaking Jew with no Hebrew.

read.first: On the Creation of the World, which is short and shows the whole manoeuvre; then the first book of the Allegorical Interpretation to see the method applied at length. The Embassy to Gaius can be read on its own as history.
read.note: The Loeb edition runs to twelve volumes and much of it is repetitive commentary. Sampling is not a compromise here; it is how the corpus is used.

philo.caveat: How far Philo is a philosopher and how far an exegete using philosophical vocabulary is still argued. He nowhere states a system, and reconstructions of one depend on which treatises are weighted.

seneca.sub: the Stoic who wrote about virtue from inside Nero’s court
world: The Principate kept republican forms and abolished republican politics. The senate still met and still supplied consuls and governors. But power ran through the emperor’s household. Prosecution for treason was the routine instrument of court faction: informers took a share of the condemned man’s estate, and exile to an island was ordinary. Provincial families like the Senecas of Corduba rose into that senate. Their advancement depended entirely on standing with one man.

Stoicism gave such men a language for keeping their self-respect under a monarchy they could not change. Cato’s suicide at Utica gave them a model. That made philosophers politically suspect. Nero, Vespasian and Domitian all expelled philosophers from Rome. Thrasea Paetus and Helvidius Priscus were killed on the charge of ostentatious virtue. Historians now doubt whether the so-called Stoic opposition was ever an organised faction. The danger of being taken for one was nonetheless real.
life: Born at Corduba about 4 BCE, son of the rhetorician Seneca the Elder, he was brought to Rome as a small child. There he heard the Stoic Attalus and the Pythagorean Sotion, whose vegetarianism he abandoned when Tiberius made foreign rites dangerous. Chronic respiratory illness nearly killed him young and took him to Egypt for years. He entered the senate under Caligula, who reportedly wanted him executed for a speech. In 41 Claudius exiled him to Corsica for adultery with the emperor’s niece.

Agrippina recalled him in 49 to tutor her twelve-year-old son. From Nero’s accession in 54, Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus effectively governed for some years. Seneca wrote the speeches, including the one excusing Agrippina’s murder in 59. He grew immensely rich. Tacitus and Dio both report resentment at his provincial loans. He withdrew from court in 62 and wrote the letters to Lucilius in retirement. In 65 Nero ordered his suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy.

p: A hundred and twenty-four letters in twenty books, written in the last years of his life to a friend serving as procurator in Sicily. Aulus Gellius quotes a book twenty-two, so more once existed. They are letters in form and a graduated course in substance. They begin with the use of time, crowds, travel and illness, and move into technical questions of virtue and the good. Letter forty-seven, on treating slaves as fellow human beings and dining with them, is the most quoted and is characteristically short on institutional conclusions. The manner is aphoristic and quotable. It made him the most imitated prose moralist in Europe.

works.t: Dialogues (Dialogi), including On the Shortness of Life and On Anger
p: The twelve pieces transmitted as dialogues are essays with an addressee rather than conversations. On the Shortness of Life argues that life is long enough and is squandered on other people’s business. That argument is aimed at exactly the careerism Seneca practised. On Anger gives the fullest surviving Stoic analysis of a single passion, distinguishing the involuntary first shock, which is not yet anger, from the assent that makes it so. The consolation sent from exile to Polybius, Claudius’ freedman, flatters the emperor at length and is hard to read as anything but a plea for recall.

Addressed to an eighteen-year-old Nero in his second year, and unembarrassed about what it is: an argument that the emperor should be merciful, made to the emperor, in public. Clemency is distinguished from pity, which is a passion and therefore a defect. Clemency is defended on grounds of security as much as virtue, since a ruler who does not need to kill is safer than one who does. The treatise founds the mirror-for-princes genre in Latin. John Calvin’s first published book, in 1532, was a humanist commentary on it.

legacy: The charge of hypocrisy began in his lifetime and has never gone away: Dio reports it as fact, Tacitus weighs it, and the man who wrote on the contempt of wealth left one of the largest fortunes in Rome. Late antiquity solved the problem by annexation. A forged correspondence between Seneca and St Paul, probably fourth-century, circulated widely enough that Jerome listed him among Christian writers. Dante placed him in Limbo.

His tragedies, closet dramas on Greek subjects, gave Elizabethan playwrights their structure of revenge, ghosts and stichomythia. Kyd and Marlowe worked directly from them. Justus Lipsius’ On Constancy, in 1584, made him the centre of neo-Stoicism. Montaigne read him beside Plutarch. Modern scholarship, following Miriam Griffin’s study of 1976, has largely stopped asking whether he lived up to his essays. It reads them as the work of a man who knew he had not.

read.first: Start with a selection of the Letters to Lucilius rather than the whole run, then On the Shortness of Life, which is twenty pages and complete in itself.
read.note: Read him with Tacitus’ Annals to hand. The friction between the essays and the career is not a distraction from Seneca but the most interesting thing about him.

seneca.caveat: The Octavia transmitted with his tragedies is not his. The correspondence with St Paul that secured his medieval reputation is a forgery.

epictetus.sub: the freed slave who reduced philosophy to what is up to us
world: Born about 50 CE at Hierapolis in Phrygia, he was owned in Rome by Epaphroditus, himself a freedman of Nero and one of the emperor’s administrative secretaries. That placed him inside the imperial household with no legal standing whatever, watching the machinery of power from underneath it. Nero fell in 68. Four emperors followed in a year. The Flavians took over. Epaphroditus was later executed by Domitian for having helped Nero die.

Domitian’s reign made philosophy a punishable posture. After the executions of senators associated with Stoic dissent, philosophers were expelled from Rome around 89 and again in the early 90s. Epictetus left for Nicopolis in Epirus, the city Augustus founded to commemorate Actium, on the main route between Italy and Greece. Wealthy Romans sent their sons there. So exile moved his teaching rather than ending it, and gave the lectures their subject: what a man can lose.
life: Lame in one leg — Simplicius says from a master’s cruelty, others from disease, and the sources disagree — he was permitted while still a slave to attend the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the leading Roman Stoic of the day. Freed at some point after Nero’s death, he taught in Rome until the expulsion. He lived with almost nothing, owned an earthenware lamp after a thief took the iron one, never married, and in old age took in an abandoned child.

He wrote nothing at all. Around 108 a young Greek-speaking Roman of senatorial rank, Arrian — later consul, governor of Cappadocia and historian of Alexander — attended the school and took down what was said. Arrian’s prefatory letter claims he recorded the words as spoken, for his own use, without intending publication. Whether that is fact or a literary convention of the period is debated. The plain spoken Greek, unlike Arrian’s polished writing, counts in its favour. Epictetus died about 135.

p: Four books survive of an original eight. These are not the formal reading and exposition of Stoic texts but the discussion that followed. They read like it: a visitor is questioned, a student mocked for wanting to be admired, an argument broken off. The organising claim is the division between what is up to us — judgement, impulse, desire, aversion — and everything else, including the body, reputation and office. From it he builds three disciplines, of desire, action and assent, and applies them to Roman situations: an audience with the emperor, a lawsuit, a dead child.

Arrian’s fifty-three-chapter distillation of the Discourses, made to be carried and memorised. It opens with the dichotomy of control and proceeds by short imperatives: remember you are an actor in a play whose part is not your choosing; men are disturbed not by things but by their opinions about things; wish events to happen as they do. The compression is its value and its danger, since the same sentences, stripped of the classroom exchanges and the humour, read as counsel to accept whatever occurs — the standard misreading of Stoicism as passivity.

Four books of the Discourses were lost, probably early. What remains of them is a small set of quotations, chiefly in Stobaeus’ anthology and in Aulus Gellius, who reports an Epictetan argument about a philosopher who turned pale in a storm. The loss matters because the surviving books are unevenly distributed across the three disciplines and may have been fuller on logic, which Epictetus insisted his students study. Marcus Aurelius thanks Rusticus for lending him a personal copy of Epictetus’ memoranda, which suggests circulation beyond the published books.

legacy: Marcus Aurelius is the first great reader and quotes him more than anyone else. Origen, arguing with Celsus in the third century, remarks that ordinary readers admired Epictetus more than Plato. Simplicius wrote a long Neoplatonic commentary on the Handbook in the sixth century. Byzantine monks produced Christian paraphrases with Socrates replaced by St Paul, which is why the text survived in monastic libraries at all.

Poliziano’s Latin translation of 1479 launched him in the West. Pascal wrestled with him as the most dangerous of the pagan moralists. Shaftesbury filled notebooks in imitation. Frederick the Great carried him on campaign. In the twentieth century the American naval officer James Stockdale credited the Handbook with getting him through seven years as a prisoner in Hanoi. Cognitive behavioural therapy adopted the sentence about opinions rather than things as a slogan — accurate about the psychology, silent about the theology holding it up.

read.first: Read the Discourses first and the Handbook second, which reverses the usual order for good reason: the classroom voice explains what the maxims are for.
read.note: Book One of the Discourses is enough to decide whether he suits you. If he does, the whole is short.

epictetus.caveat: Not a word survives from his own hand. The Discourses are Arrian’s transcript, whose fidelity is Arrian’s own claim, and half of them are lost.

marcus-aurelius.sub: the emperor who kept a notebook against his own vanity
world: The Antonine succession worked by adoption. Marcus inherited an empire that looked stable and stopped being so at once. He ruled from 161 with Lucius Verus as co-emperor, the first such arrangement. The eastern war against Parthia brought back with the returning armies an epidemic, probably smallpox, that ran through the provinces from 165 for a generation. Ancient testimony and modern estimates of mortality differ widely, but its scale is not in doubt.

War on the northern frontier consumed the rest of the reign. Marcomanni and Quadi crossed the Danube and reached northern Italy. Marcus spent most of his last decade in camps in Pannonia, debasing the silver coinage and auctioning palace property to pay for it. Avidius Cassius revolted in the east in 175 on a false report of his death. Christians were executed at Lyon in 177 under his authority. None of this appears as narrative in the notebooks.
life: Born at Rome in 121 into a wealthy senatorial family of Spanish origin, Marcus was noticed early by Hadrian. At Hadrian’s direction he was adopted in 138 by Antoninus Pius, whom he then served as heir for twenty-three years. Fronto, the leading Latin orator of the age, trained him in rhetoric. He turned from rhetoric to philosophy in his late teens. His teacher Junius Rusticus lent him Epictetus.

He became emperor in 161 and died in 180 on the Danube, succeeded by his son Commodus. Commodus was the first natural son to inherit in nearly a century, and the end of the adoptive sequence. The notebooks belong to the last decade, and some were written on campaign. The second book carries a note that it was written among the Quadi on the river Gran, the third that it was written at Carnuntum. No evidence suggests that anyone was meant to read them.

p: The first book stands apart from everything after it. It is a numbered inventory of what he owed to particular people. From his grandfather, good temper; from his mother, plain living and a horror of doing wrong; from Rusticus, the discovery of Epictetus and the lesson that he should stop writing showy prose; from Antoninus Pius, a long portrait of a ruler who worked steadily, listened, and did not perform. It is a moral audit rather than a memoir, probably written last, and the best evidence for how a Roman aristocrat understood a moral education to be transmitted.

The rest is short, unordered entries, some a line long, addressed to himself in the second person. Stoic doctrine is not argued for but assumed and applied. The exercises are a small set repeated hundreds of times: view the matter from above, until reputation and grievance shrink to their real size; remember that both of you will shortly be dead; strip an impressive thing to its physical description, so that vintage wine becomes fermented grape juice. The repetition is evidence of failure — a man writes the same instruction for ten years because it does not take. Its author had unlimited power, and was reminding himself hourly not to be corrupted by it.

Rediscovered in 1815 by Angelo Mai beneath a later text in a palimpsest from Bobbio, this exchange with his rhetoric teacher shows a Marcus nobody had seen: affectionate, playful, preoccupied with his health and his reading, apologising for having caught only a few hours of sleep, describing a day spent picking grapes. Fronto is exasperated by his pupil’s turn to philosophy and says so. The letters are the only substantial external window on his inner life. They show the ordinary young man the Meditations are addressed to.

legacy: The book almost did not survive. No ancient author cites it until Themistius in the fourth century. The printed tradition rests on a manuscript used for the Zurich edition of 1559 and since lost, checked against a single Vatican codex. Once available it was read as the record of a philosopher-king. Gibbon fixed that picture for English readers. The equestrian statue on the Capitoline escaped the melting-down of pagan bronzes because it was mistaken for Constantine.

Two modern readings compete. Popular Stoicism treats the Meditations as maxims for personal effectiveness, which turns a record of struggling into a manual of success. Scholarship, following Pierre Hadot, reads it instead as hypomnemata, notes-to-self in a recognised ancient genre of spiritual exercise, whose repetitions are the practice rather than a defect of composition. The second reading explains the form. The first explains why a private notebook now sells in millions.

read.first: Read Book One, then Books Four to Seven, in a modern translation that does not archaise. It can be opened anywhere, which is how it was written.
read.note: The repetition is the point. Reading straight through in a day flattens a book meant to be entered a few lines at a time.

marcus-aurelius.caveat: The work had no title and no intended reader. Its arrangement into twelve books may not be the author’s. The text depends on a thin manuscript tradition with corrupt passages.

sextus.sub: the physician whose handbooks preserve an entire lost school
world: Second-century medicine was divided into sects that argued about method as much as treatment: Dogmatists who reasoned from hidden causes, Empiricists who claimed to rely on observation and precedent alone, and Methodists who worked from evident common conditions. Galen, practising in Rome in the same decades, attacked all his rivals in print. The dispute matters because scepticism about unobservable causes was a live professional position, not an academic pose. Sextus writes as a doctor who held one.

Philosophy by then was organised around commentary, handbooks and epitomes. Pyrrhonism was itself a revival. Aenesidemus had broken with the Academy in the first century BCE, on the ground that under Antiochus it had turned dogmatic. He reconstituted a sceptical tradition under the name of Pyrrho of Elis. Agrippa, a century or so later, sharpened its machinery. Sextus writes at the end of that line, for readers who wanted the whole apparatus in usable form.
life: Almost nothing is known. His floruit is conventionally placed around 180 to 200 CE on indirect grounds. Diogenes Laertius names him in a list of Pyrrhonist teachers, giving him a teacher, Herodotus of Tarsus, and a pupil, Saturninus. His city is unknown. Alexandria, Rome and Athens have all been proposed on the strength of passing remarks in his own text. None of the arguments is decisive.

The name Empiricus attaches him to the Empiric medical sect. But at one point in the Outlines he says Methodism is the medical school closest to scepticism. Nobody has agreed how to square that with the name. He writes throughout in the first person plural, as spokesman for a school with settled formulae rather than as an innovator. How much of the content is Aenesidemus, how much Agrippa and how much his own remains open.

p: Three books, and the clearest statement of ancient scepticism that exists. The first sets out the method: for every appearance or argument produce an opposing one of equal weight. The result is suspension of judgement, after which tranquillity follows, Sextus says, as a shadow follows a body. He then catalogues the machinery — the ten modes of Aenesidemus, turning on the variability of perception, and the five of Agrippa: disagreement, infinite regress, relativity, unproved assumption and circular reasoning. The sceptic is not paralysed. He lives by appearances, custom, natural feeling and training in a craft, and merely declines to assert how things really are.

works.t: Against the Logicians, Physicists and Ethicists (Adversus Mathematicos VII-XI)
p: A longer and more technical assault on the theoretical disciplines, aimed above all at the Stoics. It is our best single source for the Hellenistic debate about the criterion of truth, quoting positions on both sides at a length nobody else preserves. Its treatment of signs and proof — that no sign can be shown to indicate anything hidden without begging the question — is the ancient form of an argument still current. The book is repetitive and reads as a compilation of prepared attacks. That is why it is valuable: the works it quotes are lost.

Six books against the teachable arts — grammar, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astrology and music — arguing in each case that the subject has no coherent object and that nothing can be taught or learned. The traditional numbering confuses matters, since these six were transmitted with the other five as one series although they belong to a different project. The material on grammar and music preserves definitions and disputes otherwise lost. The general argument supplies the sharpest form of the charge that scepticism, followed out, undoes its own transmission.

legacy: He was barely read for thirteen centuries. A handful of Greek manuscripts came through Byzantium. Then Henri Estienne printed a Latin translation of the Outlines in 1562, and Gentian Hervet the rest in 1569. The effect on early modern Europe was out of all proportion to the size of the books. Montaigne wrote the Apology for Raymond Sebond with Sextus beside him, had sceptical maxims painted on his ceiling beams, and struck a medal showing a pair of scales.

The crisis that followed shaped modern philosophy directly. Descartes built the Meditations to answer a doubt he had met in this form. Bayle and Hume worked in its wake. Richard Popkin’s history of 1960 made the line of transmission standard scholarship. Agrippa’s five modes, and especially the regress, are the usual framing of the contemporary problem of justification. Whether a sceptical life is possible at all was pressed against him in antiquity and is argued still.

read.first: Book One of the Outlines of Pyrrhonism, which is short, systematic and complete in itself. The rest of the corpus is for those who want the arguments against particular schools.
read.note: He is a compiler with a purpose. The flatness of the prose is deliberate, since the aim is to induce a state rather than to persuade of a thesis.

sextus.caveat: His dates, city and biography are essentially unknown. How much of the doctrine is his own rather than inherited from Aenesidemus and Agrippa cannot be determined.

plotinus.sub: the Platonist who made everything flow from a single source
world: The decades of Plotinus’s maturity were the worst the Roman state had known. Between 235 and 284 some twenty men were acclaimed emperor and nearly all died violently. Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian in 260, Gothic raiders reached the Aegean, and the silver coinage sank to washed copper. Plotinus taught in Rome throughout, and the Enneads mention none of it.

What pressed on him was the religious traffic of the capital: Christians, Gnostic teachers with elaborate cosmologies, readers of Chaldaean revelation. His own seminar contained Gnostics whose books he set pupils to refute. Philosophy had meanwhile become commentary, Plato read through five centuries of debate with Aristotle’s Categories folded in. He works inside that culture, but argues with the text rather than repeating it.
life: Nearly everything known about him comes from Porphyry’s memoir. Born about 204, probably at Lycopolis in Egypt, he would not discuss his parentage or sit for a portrait. At twenty-seven he found Ammonius Saccas in Alexandria and stayed eleven years. In 243 he joined Gordian III’s Persian expedition, hoping to meet Indian philosophers; the emperor was killed and he escaped to Antioch.

He reached Rome about 245, aged forty, and taught for the rest of his life, writing nothing for ten years. From 253 he composed fifty-four treatises answering questions from the seminar. His method explains their texture: he worked an argument out in his head, wrote it through without rereading, and would not revise. Gallienus nearly gave him a ruined Campanian town to refound under Plato’s Laws.

p: Fifty-four essays sorted by Porphyry into six sets of nine, running from ethics through the physical world and soul to Intellect and, last, the One. There is no system-book; the doctrine must be assembled from occasional pieces. Its core is a descent. The One lies beyond being and beyond thought, since thinking already divides thinker from thought, and can be named only by denial. From it comes Intellect, which thinks itself and holds the Forms; from Intellect, Soul, which orders bodies and generates time; at the far edge lies matter, where the outflow fails. Nothing is decided or lost: the source gives as the sun gives light.

The earliest treatise by Porphyry’s chronology, and the most read. Plotinus attacks the Stoic account of beauty as proportion among parts by observing that a single colour and a single note are beautiful and have no parts. Beauty is the presence of form in matter, and the soul recognises it because the soul is of the same stock. The essay then climbs, from beautiful bodies to souls to the virtues to Intellect itself, closing with the instruction to work on oneself as a sculptor works on a statue.

Porphyry cut one long composition into four separated pieces; this is its polemical end. Plotinus answers people in his own lecture room who held the visible world to be the botched work of a fallen power. The cosmos, he replies, is the best image an intelligible order can have in matter, so contempt for it is contempt for what produced it. And the Gnostics multiply levels of reality without argument, while promising rescue by initiation to people who have not troubled to become good.

legacy: The school ran on through Porphyry, then Iamblichus, who added ritual theurgy, and Proclus, who made the scheme deductive. Latin readers got Plotinus through Marius Victorinus’s translations, which supplied Augustine with what he calls the books of the Platonists. In Arabic an abridgement of Enneads IV to VI circulated as the Theology of Aristotle, so that Avicenna built on Plotinus believing he built on Aristotle.

Ficino’s Latin Enneads of 1492 returned him whole to the West, and he shaped the Cambridge Platonists, Schelling and Bergson. Two misreadings matter. One takes him for a mystic rather than an arguer, on the strength of Porphyry’s report of four episodes of union; the treatises are dense technical argument. The other credits his doctrine to India, for which there is no evidence.

read.first: Read Porphyry's Life, which stands at the front of every complete edition, then On Beauty (I.6), then the treatise on the three primary levels (V.1).
read.note: The six-by-nine arrangement is Porphyry's subject scheme, not an order of composition, so nothing is gained by starting at the beginning and reading through.

plotinus.caveat: Almost every biographical fact about Plotinus rests on Porphyry alone, who was both a devoted pupil and the editor with an interest in how the corpus looked.

porphyry.sub: the editor whose one deferred question outlived his answers
world: Porphyry lived into the recovery that followed the third-century collapse. Diocletian took power in 284 and rebuilt the state as a tetrarchy, with a reformed coinage and provinces cut small. Part of that restoration was religious: an empire reassembled around traditional cult had an obvious quarrel with a church that would not sacrifice. The Great Persecution opened in 303.
life: He was born about 234 at Tyre and named Malchus, “king” in his own language. Longinus at Athens turned it into Greek as Porphyrius, after the purple Tyre produced. He came to Plotinus in Rome in 263, argued with him for three days about whether the objects of thought lie inside the intellect, and was won over. A depression later brought him near suicide, and Plotinus sent him to Sicily.

works.t: Life of Plotinus and the edition of the Enneads
p: Porphyry had a teacher who wrote in no order and left fifty-four occasional essays. He sorted them into six groups of nine by subject rather than date. He cut at least one long composition into separate treatises to make the arithmetic work, and listed what was written when. That list is why anything can be dated. The arrangement is why the corpus is called the Enneads.

A short introduction to Aristotle’s Categories, explaining genus, species, difference, property and accident. Porphyry declines to discuss whether genera and species subsist in themselves or only in thoughts, and if they subsist whether they are bodily or bodiless, separate from perceptible things or in them. He never came back to it. Boethius translated the passage. The deferred question became the medieval problem of universals.

Fifteen books, the most formidable criticism a pagan philosopher produced, surviving only in fragments quoted by opponents. Constantine ordered it burned in 325 and Theodosius II repeated the order in 448. Enough remains to show close reading. He set the gospels against each other, and argued from the accuracy of its prophecies that the book of Daniel was written in the second century BCE.

legacy: The Isagoge became the first book of the logic curriculum in Greek, Syriac, Arabic and Latin, and stayed there a thousand years. Its five terms are still called the predicables. Realists and nominalists alike began from the sentences in which Porphyry declined to answer. His own positions, more concessive to Aristotle and popular religion than his teacher’s, were superseded by Iamblichus.

read.first: The Life of Plotinus, brief, vivid and the model for later philosophical biography. Then the first two pages of the Isagoge, which is all the universals problem needs.
read.note: The Isagoge repays reading as a school text rather than a thesis, since its influence came from its clarity and its silences rather than its doctrine.

porphyry.caveat: Against the Christians survives only in quotations by hostile writers. Whether a large body of anonymous objections preserved by Macarius Magnes belongs to it is still disputed.

proclus.sub: the last scholarch, who left Neoplatonism as a deductive system
world: By the fifth century the Roman West had fallen and the Athenian Academy was a pagan school in a Christian empire, tolerated rather than protected. Its teachers held the old cults and said so carefully. Justinian closed it in 529, forty-four years after Proclus died.

Philosophy by then meant commentary. A teacher's originality showed in how he read Plato and Aristotle, not in announcing a new view, and the curriculum ran through Aristotle to Plato and ended in the Parmenides. Proclus worked entirely inside that convention and produced, within it, the most systematic metaphysics anyone had written.
life: Born in Constantinople around 412 to a family from Lycia, he was sent to Alexandria to study law and turned to philosophy instead. He came to Athens at about twenty, studied under Plutarch of Athens and then Syrianus, and succeeded Syrianus as head of the school, which he ran for close to fifty years.

His pupil Marinus wrote a life of him which is our main source and is frankly hagiographical: Proclus is said to have slept little, written seven hundred lines a day, kept every pagan festival of every nation, and been visited by Athena. He never married. He was exiled from Athens for a year, probably for the openness of his paganism, and went to Lydia. He died in 485.

p: Two hundred and eleven propositions, each with a proof, in the manner of Euclid. It is the only work of ancient metaphysics built that way, and the form is the argument: if the structure of reality is necessary, it should be demonstrable. The content is the doctrine of procession and return — everything that proceeds from a cause remains in it, goes out from it, and turns back to it — together with the triadic unfolding of the One into intellect and soul. The proofs are tight enough that the work can be read as a formal system, and were tight enough to survive translation into Arabic, Latin and Georgian.

The Parmenides' second half, a series of apparently sterile deductions about whether the one is, had been read since Plotinus as a coded theology. Proclus gives the fullest version: each hypothesis describes a level of reality, and the first, which concludes that nothing whatever can be said of the one, establishes that the first principle is beyond being and beyond speech. The Latin translation by William of Moerbeke carried this reading into the thirteenth century.

works.t: Commentary on Euclid's Elements, Book I
p: Valuable for two reasons that have nothing to do with each other. It is a Neoplatonic account of what mathematical objects are — projections of innate reason-principles onto the imagination, neither Platonic forms nor abstractions from sense — and it is our single best source for the early history of Greek geometry, since Proclus summarises a lost history by Eudemus. Almost everything said about mathematics before Euclid rests on this book.

legacy: His reach is mostly indirect and mostly anonymous. Around the year 500 someone writing under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, Paul's Athenian convert, took Proclus' hierarchies and his negative theology and put them into a Christian frame. The forgery was accepted for a thousand years and gave the Latin and Greek churches their angelic orders and their mystical vocabulary. Aquinas comments on it respectfully, without knowing the source.

The Liber de Causis, an Arabic compilation of propositions from the Elements of Theology, circulated in Latin as Aristotle's. Aquinas, reading Moerbeke's new translation of Proclus in 1268, saw what it actually was and said so — a piece of source criticism four centuries early. Ficino and the Florentine Platonists then read him directly, and Hegel, who called the Elements the culmination of ancient philosophy, took the triadic movement of remaining, procession and return more seriously than he took most of antiquity.

read.first: The Elements of Theology in E. R. Dodds' edition, which prints the Greek, a translation and a commentary that is itself a short history of Neoplatonism. Read the first sixty propositions slowly; the rest depends on them.
read.note: Do not start with the commentaries. They assume the system the Elements sets out, and they are very long.

proclus.caveat: Whether the system is Plato's, and whether Proclus thought it was, are separate questions. He presents himself throughout as an expositor, which modern readers generally take as a convention rather than a claim.

augustine.sub: the bishop who turned philosophy inward
world: Augustine was born in 354, forty years after Constantine legalised Christianity and a generation before Theodosius made the Nicene faith the religion of the state. In his lifetime sacrifice was outlawed, temples closed, and bishops given jurisdiction over civil disputes. A church with the machinery of empire at its disposal had to decide what it would use. He spent decades answering that in practice.

Roman Africa was rich, urbanised and split. Out of the persecution of 303 came the Donatist schism, a rival church holding that clergy who surrendered scriptures forfeited their orders and their sacraments. By Augustine’s time it was the majority church in Numidia. He argued against it for twenty years, secured a weighted conference at Carthage in 411, then defended coercion of heretics against his own earlier instincts.

Then the west began to fail. Alaric’s Goths sacked Rome in August 410. Refugees crossed to Africa with the charge that the city fell because it had abandoned its gods. Among them came Pelagius, whose confidence in human moral capacity occupied Augustine’s last eighteen years. In 429 the Vandals crossed from Spain. In 430 they besieged Hippo, and he died on 28 August.
life: His father Patricius was a town councillor at Thagaste in Numidia, pagan until his deathbed. His mother Monica was Christian and relentless. A patron, Romanianus, paid for schooling at Madauros and Carthage. At nineteen he read Cicero’s Hortensius, now lost, which turned him toward philosophy. He took a concubine he never names, lived with her some fifteen years, and spent nine of them among the Manichees.

Teaching rhetoric took him to Rome in 383. Through the pagan senator Symmachus he reached the chair at Milan in 384. Ambrose’s preaching showed him that the Old Testament could be read figuratively, removing his chief objection to the church. He also read the books of the Platonists, probably Plotinus and Porphyry, in the Latin the Confessions associates with Marius Victorinus. That reading gave him an incorporeal God and evil as an absence.

Visiting Hippo Regius in 391 he was seized by the congregation and pressed into ordination. He became bishop about 395 and stayed thirty-five years in a busy port, preaching several times a week and judging property disputes. The output runs to over a hundred treatises, three hundred letters and five hundred sermons. It still grows: unknown letters surfaced in 1975, unknown sermons in 1990.

The turn came in the summer of 386, in a Milan garden and, on his own account, at a child’s voice telling him to take up and read. He resigned the chair. He spent the winter at the country estate of Cassiciacum writing his first dialogues — on scepticism, on the happy life, on order, and the Soliloquies — and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Monica died at Ostia later that year as they waited for a ship home.

p: Nothing quite like it had been written. It is addressed not to a reader but to God, in the second person throughout. A life story is therefore carried inside a prayer, and the reader overhears. Nine books reach Monica’s death. The last four turn to memory, to time and to the opening of Genesis, which looks like a change of subject and is not. Book XI is the most influential philosophy he wrote. If the past no longer is, the future is not yet, and the present has no duration, then time cannot be measured in things. What is measured lies in the mind: a present of things past, which is memory, a present of things present, which is attention, and a present of things future, which is expectation.

works.t: The City of God (De civitate Dei)
p: Twenty-two books answering the charge that Christianity brought Rome down. The first ten dismantle it: the gods never protected Rome, its own historians record worse catastrophes than 410, and Roman greatness rested on a lust for domination that pagan moralists had themselves denounced. The remaining twelve trace two cities, defined not by institutions but by two loves. The one love is of God to the contempt of self, the other of self to the contempt of God. They are mixed in history and separated only at the judgement. So he identifies the earthly city neither with the empire nor the heavenly city with the visible church, a distinction later readers repeatedly lost. Book XIX holds the politics. Without justice a state is a large robber band. Peace is the tranquillity of order, which is all a political community can honestly promise.

A manual for reading and preaching scripture, and by accident a founding text of the theory of signs. Augustine divides everything into things and signs. He then treats language as the paradigm case of a thing used to point beyond itself. His interpretive rule is startling: a reading that builds up love of God and neighbour is not fatally wrong even if it misses what the author meant. A reader who habitually goes astray will nonetheless eventually go badly astray. Book IV defends the use of pagan rhetoric on the argument that the Israelites carried Egyptian gold out of Egypt. That settled for the Latin Middle Ages whether a Christian might study the liberal arts. Its account of signs stands behind medieval semiotics.

Fifteen books written slowly and, he complains, circulated before he had finished. The first half works through the technical problem of saying that three are one. He adopts the word person with visible reluctance, remarking that it is used not in order to say something but in order not to be silent. The second half is the original part. If the mind is made in God’s image, the image should be findable by looking. So Augustine hunts triads in the mind itself: mind, its knowledge of itself, its love of itself; then memory, understanding and will. The search matters more than any one triad. It made the will a distinct power of the soul in a way no Greek text had, with consequences running through medieval psychology to Descartes.

A long series running from On the Spirit and the Letter to On the Predestination of the Saints. Pelagius held that God does not command the impossible, so we can keep the commandments. On his account grace is the gift of a free will, the law and the example of Christ. Augustine answered that the will is damaged rather than neutral, that we inherit from Adam a condition and not merely a bad example, and that the first movement toward God is itself God’s gift. His reason is that grace earned by merit would not be grace. He did not evade the consequences: election is gratuitous and the rest of humanity justly condemned. Carthage condemned Pelagianism in 418. The West took his side in a mitigated form, leaving the harder doctrine for Gottschalk, Luther and Calvin.

In his seventies Augustine went back through ninety-three of his own works in the order he had written them, said what prompted each, and corrected what he now thought wrong. No ancient author had done anything comparable. It is why his chronology is better known than that of any other writer of the period. It also records a real difficulty. His early On Free Choice of the Will had argued that evil enters through a defect in a created will and is a privation, a failing away from good, rather than anything God made. The Pelagians were quoting it against him. He does not disown it, explaining that he had written against the Manichees before the question of grace was forced on him.

legacy: The Latin Middle Ages had Augustine as they had no one else. Anselm and Bonaventure work inside his psychology. Aquinas, who reorganised theology around Aristotle, treats his authority as something to interpret rather than contradict. Original sin, the privation account of evil, the analysis of the will, the two cities and the practice of writing about oneself all reach later Europe through him.

He was claimed by both sides in every later quarrel. Luther and Calvin took the theologian of grace, their opponents the theologian of the church and the sacraments, the Jansenists of Port-Royal the anti-Pelagian. Descartes had to answer the charge that his starting point came from a line in the City of God about the impossibility of being deceived about one’s own existence.

Modern assessment divides cleanly. As a psychologist of desire, memory and self-deception he is read by people with no theological interest. The account of time in Book XI remains a live position. As the man who fixed original sin, predestination and the legitimacy of religious coercion in the West, he draws criticism often sharpened by admiration for the rest.

read.first: Start with the Confessions, reading Books I to IX and XI, and coming back to X, XII and XIII later. Then read Book XIX of the City of God on its own.
read.note: The City of God does not reward being read straight through on a first attempt. The anti-Pelagian treatises make better sense once the Confessions has shown why a divided will mattered so much to him.

augustine.caveat: Which Neoplatonic texts he read in Latin at Milan, and how much came from Plotinus rather than Porphyry, remains unsettled. So does how far the garden conversion scene is a literary shaping of the event.

boethius.sub: the last Roman, and the West's only Aristotle for six centuries
world: Italy in Boethius’s lifetime was ruled by a Gothic king who preserved every Roman form. Theodoric killed Odoacer in 493 and governed from Ravenna for thirty years with the senate sitting and the courts working. One fault line remained: the Goths were Arian Christians and their subjects Catholic. The senatorial aristocracy to which Boethius belonged kept its estates, its Greek and its habit of looking east.

In 519 a thirty-five-year schism between Rome and Constantinople was healed. The emperor Justin began legislating against Arians. A stable division became a question of loyalty, and senators with eastern correspondents looked like traitors. Theodoric, old and without a male heir, grew suspicious. Boethius was caught in exactly that shift. So, shortly afterwards, was Pope John I, who died in the king’s custody.
life: Born about 477 into the Anicii. His father, consul in 487, died early. The senator Symmachus raised him and gave him his daughter Rusticiana in marriage. His Greek was already rare in the West. He formed young the plan of translating all of Plato and Aristotle and showing that they agreed. He was consul in 510 and in 522 saw his two sons hold the consulship jointly.

That year he became master of offices. In 523 he defended the senator Albinus against a charge of treasonable correspondence with Constantinople. He said that if Albinus was guilty so were he and the whole senate. He was arrested, with further charges of sacrilege and magic. Condemned without a hearing, imprisoned near Pavia and clubbed to death, he was about forty-seven. The translation project had reached the logic and no further.

works.t: The Consolation of Philosophy (De consolatione Philosophiae)
p: Written in prison, alternating prose with thirty-nine poems in a wide range of metres. Lady Philosophy appears to a prisoner composing self-pitying verse, dismisses the Muses, and treats him as a patient. She shows that Fortune promised nothing and has taken back only what was hers, and that the goods men chase are fragments of a single good which is God. Book V argues that divine foreknowledge does not destroy freedom, because God does not foresee at all. Eternity is the complete and simultaneous possession of unbounded life. So God sees all times at once, as we see a present act, and what is seen is not thereby necessitated.

He translated Porphyry’s Isagoge and Aristotle’s Categories, On Interpretation, Prior Analytics, Topics and Sophistical Refutations, commented twice on the first two, and wrote handbooks on syllogism and topical argument. Until the middle of the twelfth century this was the whole of Aristotle available in Latin. In the second Isagoge commentary he answered the question Porphyry had refused. Universals are not things, since one thing cannot be wholly present in many. But neither are they empty, because the mind abstracts what is common from particulars. Thinking apart is not thinking falsely.

Five short pieces applying logical technique to Christian doctrine, the first sustained attempt to do so in Latin. One argues that the categories cannot be applied to God unchanged, since predicating substance of God says what he is and not what he has. On the Hebdomads proceeds from axioms in the manner of a geometrical proof. It distinguishes a thing’s being from the thing that is, a distinction Aquinas took over and built on. A third supplies the definition of person every later scholastic quotes: an individual substance of a rational nature.

legacy: The Consolation was among the most read books in Europe for a thousand years. It was turned into Old English in Alfred’s circle, into Middle English by Chaucer and into English again by Elizabeth I. Dante places Boethius in the heaven of the sun. The logical corpus carried the vocabulary of Latin philosophy into the schools and handed the twelfth century the problem of universals as he had left it.

The absence of any Christian reference from the Consolation provoked centuries of unease and, in the nineteenth century, the theory that he had abandoned Christianity. That collapsed in 1877, when a fragment of Cassiodorus was published attributing the theological tractates to him. The better explanation is that the book is deliberately an argument philosophy can make on its own. That is why the schools could use it.

read.first: The Consolation, whole and in order, in a version that keeps the alternation of verse and prose rather than reducing it to argument.
read.note: Book V, on foreknowledge and freedom, is the hardest and the most rewarding. Everything before it is arranged to make it possible.

boethius.caveat: Whether Boethius was guilty of anything cannot be determined, since the only account of the charges is his own, written under sentence of death. Even the year of execution is given variously as 524, 525 or 526.

anselm.sub: faith seeking understanding, and one very short argument
world: Anselm’s adult life ran alongside two upheavals. The Normans took England in 1066 and rebuilt its church: English bishops replaced by Normans, sees moved to towns, cathedrals begun again on a scale the island had not seen. Lanfranc, Anselm’s own teacher, ran that reconstruction from Canterbury after 1070. Bec, founded in 1034 by a knight who could barely read, had become the best school in northern France.

The second upheaval was the reform of the papacy. Gregory VII’s claim that laymen could not invest bishops with the symbols of their office set off a fifty-year contest with the emperors and with the Norman kings of England. Anselm inherited that quarrel with the archbishopric. Scholars were meanwhile applying dialectic to doctrine. The argument over whether logic had any business in theology was bitter.
life: He was born at Aosta in 1033 to a landholding family. He left home about 1056 to wander in Burgundy and France for three years. Lanfranc’s fame drew him to Bec, where he took vows in 1060, became prior in 1063 and abbot in 1078. Everything of philosophical interest that he wrote was written there, for monks who asked for it, in the intervals of running an estate.

In 1093 William Rufus, who had kept Canterbury vacant four years to draw its revenues, gave it to Anselm during an illness he thought fatal. Anselm quarrelled with him over papal recognition and was exiled from 1097 to 1100, finishing Cur Deus Homo in southern Italy. He then quarrelled with Henry I and went again from 1103 to 1106. The settlement of 1107 was largely his.

p: Written at the request of his monks, who wanted the reasons for what they already believed set out without appeal to scripture. Anselm obliged completely: nothing in it argues from authority. He begins from the observation that things are good in different degrees, and that comparison implies a standard through which they are good. The same move is run through existence, so that whatever exists through another leads back to something existing through itself. Lanfranc, sent the draft, was cool about a work on God that quoted no one.

He wanted a single argument needing no other, and after nearly abandoning the search found one. God is that than which nothing greater can be thought. The fool of the psalm who says there is no God must understand those words in order to deny them, so the thing is at least in his understanding. But what exists in reality is greater than the same thing existing only in the understanding. Chapter three goes further: such a being cannot be thought not to exist, a claim about necessity rather than mere existence.

works.t: Why God Became Man (Cur Deus Homo)
p: A dialogue with the monk Boso, written mostly in exile, which sets out to show by reason alone, setting Christ aside as though nothing were known of him, that God had to become man. Sin is a failure to render God his due, and it incurs a debt that must be either paid or punished. A human being owes the payment but, already owing everything, cannot make it. Only God could pay it, but God does not owe it. Hence one who is both.

legacy: The ontological argument has never stayed dead. A monk named Gaunilo answered it while Anselm lived, objecting that the same reasoning would conjure a perfect island. Anselm replied that only the greatest conceivable being cannot be thought not to exist, and had the exchange copied with his own text. Aquinas rejected it because we do not know God’s essence. Descartes and Leibniz revived it, and Kant answered that existence adds nothing to a concept.

Anselm is often called the father of scholasticism, which flatters and misleads. He had no school, wrote no summa, and worked before the recovery of Aristotle gave the schools their method. His procedure belongs to the monastery rather than the lecture hall. What passed into the schools was the satisfaction account of the atonement, which Abelard attacked at once and the Reformers hardened into something more penal than Anselm wrote.

read.first: The Proslogion, short enough to read at a sitting, together with Gaunilo's objection and Anselm's reply, which are always printed with it.
read.note: Read it as the meditation it announces itself to be before extracting the argument, since the surrounding prayer is not decoration.

anselm.caveat: Whether Anselm intended the Proslogion argument as a proof addressed to unbelievers or as an exercise in understanding a faith already held has been disputed since Karl Barth pressed the second reading in 1931.

abelard.sub: the logician who put universals in words and sin in the will
world: The schools of northern France were expanding fast when Abelard arrived. Teaching had left the monasteries for the cathedral towns. Paris held three centres within a mile of each other: Notre-Dame on the island, the canons of Saint-Victor, and the hill of Sainte-Geneviève, where a licensed master could set up and live on his students’ fees. There was no university yet. Reputation was made in public disputation.

Reform of the church was meanwhile enforcing clerical celibacy: the councils of 1123 and 1139 declared the marriages of clergy in major orders not merely illicit but void. That is the background of the disaster in Abelard’s private life. It explains Héloïse’s argument that marriage would end his career. The same decades produced Bernard of Clairvaux, who twice moved successfully against him.
life: Born in 1079 at Le Pallet in Brittany, eldest son of a knight, he gave up his inheritance to study. He learned logic from Roscelin, who held that universals are only words, and then from William of Champeaux. He attacked William so effectively in public that William changed his position and Abelard set up rival schools at Melun and Corbeil. By about 1115 he held the chair at Notre-Dame.

There he lodged with the canon Fulbert and became tutor to Fulbert’s niece Héloïse, a woman with a Latin education unusual for anyone. The affair produced a son, a secret marriage which she opposed, and, when Fulbert took his revenge, Abelard’s castration. A council at Soissons in 1121 made him burn his own book on the Trinity. Bernard secured a second condemnation at Sens in 1140. Abelard appealed to Rome, got as far as Cluny, and died in 1142.

p: His solution to the problem Boethius had transmitted is that a universal cannot be a thing, since every thing is one and particular. A common essence wholly present in Socrates and in an ass would make contraries inhere in the same item. What is universal is a word, though not an arbitrary noise: a term is predicable of many because those many agree in a status, in being a man, which is not a further thing and not nothing. This is conceptualism, and it needs no third realm.

A hundred and fifty-eight theological questions, each followed by quotations from the fathers supporting the answer yes and quotations supporting no, with no resolutions supplied. The prologue is the point: before concluding that authorities conflict, check the manuscript, ask whether the author later retracted the view, whether he was reporting rather than asserting, and whether a word is used in two senses. It is a teaching instrument, not a work of scepticism. Its shape became the standard form of scholastic argument.

Sin, Abelard argues, is not a deed and not a desire but consent to what one believes displeases God. The inclination is not itself sinful. Resisting it is what merit consists in. The deed adds nothing to the guilt of the consent, so two men who both consent to a killing are equally guilty though only one succeeds. He follows the principle where it leads: those who crucified Christ in genuine ignorance of who he was did not sin in doing it, a claim condemned at Sens.

works.t: The Story of My Misfortunes (Historia calamitatum) and the letters
p: A long letter of consolation to an unnamed friend, on the argument that other men’s troubles are smaller than his own. It is the first extended autobiography in Latin since the Confessions and could hardly be less like it: worldly, aggrieved, contemptuous of rivals, interested in vindication rather than in God. Héloïse read a copy and wrote to him. The exchange that follows is remarkable because she refuses the repentance he offers, insists she acted from love, and would rather be called his mistress than an emperor’s wife.

legacy: The method outlasted the man. Peter Lombard’s Sentences, the textbook every theologian in Europe commented on for four centuries, uses the procedure of Sic et Non with the resolutions filled in. His logic fared worse. When the rest of Aristotle arrived in Latin from the 1150s, work done on the older curriculum was superseded. He was not read seriously as a logician again until the twentieth century.

Outside philosophy he survives as half of a love story, which he would have resented and Héloïse perhaps not. Their letters were being copied by the 1230s, adapted by Jean de Meun and versified by Pope in 1717. The ethics of intention has aged better than anything else he wrote. That an act is judged by the consent behind it rather than by what happens is now so ordinary that its origin is invisible.

read.first: The Historia calamitatum with the first two letters of Heloise, then the Ethics, which is short and can be read for its argument alone.
read.note: The logical works are technical and edited from difficult manuscripts, so a good account of the position on universals is more use to most readers than the text itself.

abelard.caveat: The authenticity of the correspondence with Héloïse has been argued over since the nineteenth century, no manuscript being earlier than about a century after their deaths. Most scholars now accept the letters. But the further claim that an anonymous earlier exchange belongs to the same pair remains contested.

albertus.sub: the encyclopaedist who made the whole Aristotle usable in Latin
world: Albert’s working life falls in the decades when the Latin West gained a new institution and a new library. Paris won its privileges from Gregory IX in 1231, after the strike of 1229. Into the schools poured Aristotle’s natural books, turned into Latin at Toledo from Arabic and in Sicily from Greek, with Avicenna and Averroes attached. Paris had banned those books in 1210 and again in 1215; by 1255 the arts faculty required them. He wrote in the gap between prohibition and prescription.
life: Born at Lauingen in Swabia around 1200, he entered the Dominicans at Padua in the early 1220s. He lectured in the German convents, held a Dominican chair at Paris from 1245, and in 1248 went to Cologne to build a studium generale, taking with him a heavy, silent southern Italian student. Provincial of Teutonia, then bishop of Regensburg from 1260 until he resigned in 1262 to teach again, he died at Cologne in 1280, having outlived that pupil by six years.

p: The plan, announced in his exposition of the Physics, was to make all the parts of Aristotle intelligible to the Latins. He worked by paraphrase rather than gloss, in the manner he took from Avicenna, restating each book in his own order and adding digressions to supply what Aristotle lacked. Logic, natural philosophy, metaphysics and ethics were all covered. He warned that Aristotle was a man and could err, which kept the project on the safe side of the bans.

Twenty-six books: the first nineteen paraphrase Aristotle’s zoology in Michael Scot’s Arabic-derived version, the last seven are Albert’s own. What distinguishes them is the reporting: German falconers questioned, whales and herring described from northern accounts, insects examined by hand. His companion On Minerals states the rule — natural science does not simply accept what others have said, but investigates the causes at work in nature. The observations are uneven, but they are observations.

legacy: Later readers reduced him to Thomas’s teacher, and the reduction stuck. His naturalism had a separate life, feeding the German speculative tradition through his Cologne pupils Ulrich of Strasbourg and Dietrich of Freiberg, and less directly Eckhart. Legend made him a magician with a talking brazen head. Pius XI canonised him in 1931 and named him a doctor of the church.

read.first: A selection from the zoological and mineralogical writings rather than the theological summae — they show what he was for.
read.note: Only part of the enormous corpus exists in modern translation, and the Cologne critical edition remains unfinished after a century.

albertus.caveat: Several popular works long printed under his name are spurious, and the story that he travelled to Paris in 1277 to defend Aquinas’s teaching is late and widely doubted.

aquinas.sub: Aristotle and Christian doctrine joined without either dissolving
world: Paris in the 1250s was fighting over who might teach. The friars had taken chairs the secular masters regarded as theirs, and would not join the strikes that were the guild’s only weapon. William of Saint-Amour argued in 1256 that mendicancy itself was illegitimate. Alexander IV condemned the tract. Aquinas answered in print, and became a master at thirty-one in the middle of the quarrel.

Books applied the other pressure. Gerard of Cremona at Toledo, Michael Scot in Norman Sicily, and from the 1260s William of Moerbeke working straight from Greek had put nearly the whole Aristotle into Latin, with Averroes attached as “the Commentator”. Arts masters such as Siger of Brabant taught the philosophy as philosophy, including the doctrine that all men share one intellect. Opponents charged them with holding two contradictory truths at once. No surviving text of theirs says so.

Authority answered twice. In December 1270 Bishop Étienne Tempier condemned thirteen propositions at Paris. In March 1277 he condemned two hundred and nineteen. Robert Kilwardby banned thirty at Oxford eleven days later. Southern Italy meanwhile changed hands: Charles of Anjou destroyed the Hohenstaufen at Benevento in 1266. The Aquino family, ruined in the wars, had been on the losing side.
life: Thomas was born at Roccasecca about 1225, a younger son of a minor baronial family, and placed as a child oblate at Montecassino. War drove him to the new imperial university at Naples around 1239, where Aristotle’s logic and physics were ordinary curriculum. Joining the Dominicans in 1244 appalled his relatives, who held him at home for a year. He went to Paris in 1245, studied there under Albert, and followed him to Cologne in 1248.

Paris took him back in 1252 to lecture on the Sentences. He incepted as master in 1256 and taught until 1259. Nine years in Italy followed, at Orvieto, Rome and Viterbo, attached to the papal court. There he began the Summa Theologiae and worked beside Moerbeke. A second Paris regency from 1268 to 1272 was unusual, probably a rescue mission. In 1272 his order sent him to Naples.

On 6 December 1273, after Mass, he stopped dictating. His secretary Reginald of Piperno pressed him and received, as witnesses reported half a century later, the answer that everything he had written seemed like straw. He wrote nothing more. Summoned to the Council of Lyon, he fell ill on the road and died at Fossanova on 7 March 1274, not yet fifty.

works.t: Commentary on the Sentences (Scriptum super libros Sententiarum)
p: Every bachelor of theology lectured on Peter Lombard’s twelfth-century textbook. The resulting commentary was a young man’s licence to teach. Thomas’s is long and already recognisably his: the distinction of essence and existence is in place, so is the claim that the soul is the one substantial form of the body. It also shows him inside a frame he would abandon: the Sentences organise theology around Lombard’s division of things and signs, not around God as beginning and end. That dissatisfaction is the origin of the Summa.

What stands in printed editions as the rest of the third part is the Supplementum. His brethren assembled it after his death out of the early commentary on the Sentences. It fills the gap but represents the theology of the young bachelor of 1254, not the thought of the man who broke off in 1273.

works.t: On Being and Essence (De ente et essentia)
p: Thirty pages, written for his Dominican brethren before he was a master, and as compressed as anything he produced. Essence is what a definition signifies. In composite substances it includes matter as well as form. Then the move that matters: one can know what a man is, or what a phoenix is, without knowing whether any exists. Existence therefore belongs to the essence of nothing short of a being whose essence simply is to be. Everything else receives its existence, and receives it from that one. The distinction is Avicenna’s, but Thomas makes it the hinge of his metaphysics — creatures are composite not only of matter and form but of essence and the act of existing. How strong that distinction is was disputed within a generation.

Four books arranged by what reason can and cannot reach. The first three argue from premises an unbeliever might grant: that God exists and what he is not, that creation and providence follow, that human beings are ordered to a final end. The fourth turns to what only revelation supplies — Trinity, Incarnation, sacraments, resurrection. The old story that Raymond of Peñafort commissioned it as a handbook for missionaries in Spain is medieval but late. Most scholars doubt it. The book argues chiefly against Averroist positions. Part of the autograph survives, in the hand contemporaries called illegible.

Written, the prologue says, for beginners whom existing books confused with repetition and disorder. Its shape is a circuit: God; the going-out of creatures from him; the return of rational creatures through Christ. Each of several thousand articles poses a question, lists objections, cites a contrary authority, answers in a paragraph, then replies to the objections one by one.

The famous passages sit inside that machinery. The five ways — from motion, efficient causation, contingency, degrees of perfection and the governance of things — occupy one article and are all a posteriori. He rejects Anselm’s argument because we have no access to God’s essence. On religious language he steers between saying that “wise” means the same of God and of us, which makes God a large creature, or something wholly other, which makes theology noise. Such terms apply analogically, first to God and derivatively to us. The treatise on law defines natural law as the eternal law as a rational creature shares in it, which puts basic morality within anyone’s reach. He broke off partway through the third part.

Twelve of them, on the Physics, the Metaphysics, On the Soul, the Nicomachean Ethics and others, several left unfinished. They are close literal expositions written while he was teaching against the Paris Averroists. The point is partly polemical: to show that Aristotle, correctly read, does not teach one shared intellect and does not demonstrate the eternity of the world. Whether they state Thomas’s own philosophy or only report Aristotle’s is a standing scholarly argument.
