The commentary on the Book of Causes contains a real discovery — using Moerbeke’s new Latin Proclus, he identified that work as an Arabic compilation from the Elements of Theology.

These record the public disputations a master ran. They are where he argues at length: On Truth from the first Paris regency, On the Power of God and On Evil from the Italian and second Paris years, together with the Quodlibetal Questions, in which anyone present could raise anything at all. An article here may carry twenty objections where the Summa carries three. Readers who find the Summa thin on argument should come to this material. The discussion of free choice in On Evil, question six, goes well past anything in the textbooks.

legacy: The condemnation of 1277 caught positions he had defended — that matter individuates, that a human being has a single substantial form — three years after his death. Kilwardby’s Oxford ban named the last outright. His order defended him at once, made his doctrine official in 1309, and had the Paris articles touching him revoked in 1325, two years after his canonisation.

Thomism then became a school, which is not the same as being read. Cajetan systematised the doctrine of analogy further than the texts warrant. Vitoria at Salamanca replaced Lombard with the Summa as the theology textbook in the 1520s. The Spanish scholastics built international law on his natural law. Leo XIII’s Aeterni Patris of 1879 made him effectively normative for Catholic teaching.

Twentieth-century readers broke that consensus productively. Étienne Gilson insisted the centre was the act of existing rather than the essences the manuals dwelt on. Anscombe, Geach and MacIntyre carried his accounts of action, virtue and intention into analytic philosophy, where they now have readers with no theological commitments. Finnis and Grisez rebuilt natural law on him, controversially. The persistent misreading treats the five ways as his case for God rather than five compressed lines of a longer one.

read.first: The Summa Theologiae in a selection that follows one thread through — the treatise on happiness and law opening the second part is the best entrance — rather than front to back.
read.note: The article form looks forbidding and is not: read the body first, then the replies, and never the objections on their own.

aquinas.caveat: The Supplement printed with the Summa was assembled by others from his Sentences commentary. The chronology of the works rests largely on later catalogues. The December 1273 episode is known only from witnesses testifying almost fifty years afterwards.

scotus.sub: the subtle doctor for whom being meant one thing throughout
world: Scotus grew up intellectually in the shadow of 1277. Tempier’s articles had made a range of Aristotelian positions unsafe at Paris. The effect was less to silence philosophy than to license alternatives: if God could have done otherwise, the actual order is contingent, and arguments from necessity lose their grip. Oxford, where he first lectured, was not bound by the Paris censures but felt their weather.

His career then collided with high politics. In 1303 Philip IV of France, at war with Boniface VIII over taxing the clergy, required the Paris masters to endorse his demand for a general council against the pope. Scotus refused to sign and left the kingdom with some eighty others. Boniface was seized at Anagni that September and died within weeks.
life: The record is thin. He was ordained priest at Northampton on 17 March 1291, which places his birth around 1266. He came from Duns in the Scottish borders. A Franciscan from his teens, he studied and lectured at Oxford through the late 1290s. He moved to Paris around 1302, was readmitted there after the exile, took his mastership in 1305, and was sent on to Cologne in 1307.

He died at Cologne on 8 November 1308, about forty-two years old, leaving his principal work half-revised. That accident governs everything about how he is read. Students called him the Subtle Doctor, and the compliment cut both ways. The density is real, though his distinctions are generally doing work rather than decorating. John Paul II beatified him at Rome in 1993.

p: His own revision, meant for publication, of the Oxford lectures on the Sentences, and the statement of his views wherever he got it finished. Here he argues that “being” must be univocal: one can be certain that God is a being while doubting whether he is finite or infinite. A concept one is simultaneously certain and doubtful about cannot be two concepts. Against Aquinas’s analogy he holds that without univocity no argument can travel from creatures to God at all. It also carries the formal distinction: really identical things can hold formally distinct aspects before any act of mind.

The Oxford course the Ordinatio was meant to supersede, identified as a separate work only in the twentieth century by the Vatican editors. It matters because it is complete where the Ordinatio is not, and because comparing the two shows him changing his mind on substantial points. Individuation is the famous case: what makes Socrates this individual is neither his matter nor the common nature he shares with other men, but a further positive entity, later called haecceitas, thisness. His followers used that term far more freely than he did.

Twenty-one questions surviving from the public disputations of his Paris regency, mature and comparatively orderly in arrangement. They carry his most considered statements, among them his fullest account of the will. For him the will is self-determining as no other power is: given all the same conditions it could have willed otherwise. It inclines not only towards what benefits the agent but towards what is just in itself. Morality is therefore not simply read off necessary essences, since the commands beyond the first table of the law could have been given differently.

legacy: The Franciscans adopted him as the Dominicans had Aquinas. Scotism ran on into the eighteenth century. His argument that Mary was preserved from original sin at her conception — prevention being the more perfect redemption — carried the Paris faculty in 1387. It was substantially the case Pius IX adopted in 1854. The slogan that God could do it, it was fitting, and so he did it is a later summary.

Modern judgement divides. Peirce and Heidegger both read him closely, though Heidegger’s 1915 thesis was partly on a grammar now known to be by Thomas of Erfurt. Analytic metaphysicians have revived haecceity as a live option. Gilson and, later, the Radical Orthodoxy theologians blamed univocity for flattening God into one item within a common ontology, and so for modern secularity. Most medievalists find the charge anachronistic.

read.first: A selection of the key questions with facing Latin — univocity and individuation first — rather than any continuous stretch of the Ordinatio.
read.note: Expect to read each argument twice. The difficulty is compression rather than obscurity.

scotus.caveat: The corpus is a textual problem. The Ordinatio was unfinished at his death and was completed by students from his lectures. Editions down to Wadding’s of 1639 carried works now known not to be his.

ockham.sub: the nominalist who cut the world back to individuals
world: The papacy sat at Avignon from 1309. John XXII, elected there in 1316, ran the church as a legal and fiscal machine. His quarrel with the Franciscans over poverty began as an argument about property and ended as doctrine: the bull Cum inter nonnullos of 1323 declared it heretical to hold that Christ and the apostles owned nothing. For friars who had staked their identity on that claim, obedience and orthodoxy had come apart.

Empire and papacy were also at war. John refused to recognise Louis of Bavaria, who had himself crowned at Rome in 1328 and installed an antipope. Marsilius of Padua had argued in his Defender of the Peace of 1324 that coercive authority belongs to the community, not the clergy. Munich became the refuge of the excommunicated. Ockham reached it in 1330.
life: Born at Ockham in Surrey about 1287, he entered the Franciscans young and lectured on the Sentences at Oxford between 1317 and 1319. He never took up the regent mastership he had qualified for, which is why he is called the Venerable Inceptor, the beginner. Summoned to Avignon in 1324, he waited four years while a commission examined fifty-one propositions from his writings. Nothing was condemned.

Asked in 1327 by his minister general, Michael of Cesena, to study the poverty bulls, he concluded that John XXII was a heretic. On the night of 26 May 1328 he fled Avignon with Michael and Bonagratia of Bergamo. He was excommunicated, and took refuge with Louis of Bavaria. He died at Munich in 1347. The story that he offered to defend the emperor with his pen is legend.

p: A complete logic in three parts — terms, propositions, arguments — and the vehicle of his nominalism. Only individuals exist. A universal is a sign, and specifically a concept, standing naturally for many things. On that basis he rebuilds supposition theory, the account of what a term refers to in a given proposition. He also prunes the categories: quantity and relation are not further things beyond substances and their qualities. Thought itself, he argues, is a language with terms, syntax and truth conditions of its own, prior to any spoken tongue.

Seven sets of questions from his Oxford disputations, revised at Avignon, running from divine foreknowledge to the reality of motion. The principle of economy appears here in his own wordings: a plurality is not to be posited without necessity, and it is pointless to do with more what can be done with fewer. It licenses declining to posit an entity, not asserting that none exists. He suspends it wherever scripture or demonstration requires more. The familiar sentence about entities not being multiplied beyond necessity appears nowhere in his writings. That wording is seventeenth-century.

The Work of Ninety Days, written fast to answer John XXII’s bull Quia vir reprobus, defends the Franciscan distinction between using a thing and owning it. It develops a vocabulary of rights some historians read as a source of later subjective right. The unfinished Dialogue, cast as master and student and deliberately non-committal, is enormous. It argues that a pope may err, that a council may err, that the whole church may err, and that the faith could survive in a single believer. Papal fullness of power in temporal affairs he denies outright.

legacy: Fourteenth-century Oxford and Paris filled with debate over his positions. The label via moderna came to mark the nominalist route against the older realism. Whether he dismantled the scholastic synthesis or merely registered its collapse is arguable. What is clear is that on his account far less about God can be demonstrated, since omnipotence means the order of things could have been otherwise, and reason and revelation drift apart.

Gabriel Biel carried him into the German universities. Luther, taught in that school, called himself of Ockham’s party while attacking what it had made of grace. Later readers come for other reasons: the razor as a methodological rule he would half recognise, and the theory of mental language, which Fodor and others treat as an ancestor of the language of thought.

read.first: A philosophical selection in translation, then the first part of the Summa Logicae on terms and universals.
read.note: His Latin is plain and his arguments are numbered. What slows a reader is the count of distinctions, not the style.

ockham.caveat: The old claim that plague killed him depends on a death date of 1349. The documentary evidence now favours 1347, which makes the Black Death an unlikely cause.

suarez.sub: the last scholastic, and the first modern metaphysician
world: Spain in the later sixteenth century was the centre of Catholic Europe and of a second scholasticism that has no counterpart elsewhere. Trent had closed in 1563; the Society of Jesus, founded in 1540, was building a teaching order with a standard curriculum, and the Iberian universities were arguing about grace, about law, and about what Spain was entitled to do in America.

The new colleges needed textbooks. The medieval form — a commentary on the Sentences or on Aristotle, following someone else's order — suited a seminar and not a syllabus. That pressure, more than any doctrine, produced the book Suárez is remembered for.
life: Born at Granada in 1548 to a lawyer's family, he read law at Salamanca and entered the Society of Jesus in 1564 — on the second attempt, having been rejected as insufficiently able. He taught at Segovia, Valladolid, Rome, Alcalá and Salamanca, and from 1597 held the chair of theology at Coimbra, where he stayed until shortly before his death in 1617.

He was drawn into the two great controversies of his order. Against the Dominicans he defended the Jesuit account of grace and free will, which required a divine knowledge of what any free creature would do in any circumstance. Against James I of England he denied that kings hold power directly from God: authority is given to the community, which transfers it. James had the book burned in London, and the Parlement of Paris burned it too.

p: Fifty-four disputations, arranged by subject rather than by Aristotle's chapters, covering the whole of metaphysics in order from the concept of being to the kinds of non-being. It is the first freestanding systematic metaphysics in the Western tradition — not a commentary on anything — and it is why the discipline afterwards has the shape it does. Its positions matter as much as its form: being is a single concept that applies to God and creatures in the same sense, though unequally; individuals are individual in their own right and need no principle of individuation added to them; and essence and existence are not really distinct, against Aquinas. Disputation VII, on the kinds of distinction, is still the standard reference for what philosophers mean by distinguishing two things.

works.t: On Laws and God the Lawgiver (De legibus ac Deo legislatore)
p: Law is an act of a will that binds, but it binds because reason shows the act to be good, so Suárez stands between the voluntarists and the intellectualists and takes something from each. Political authority belongs to the community by nature and reaches the ruler only by the community's transfer, which makes tyrannicide arguable and divine right untenable. And he separates out the ius gentium: not natural law, since it could have been otherwise, but not the positive law of one state either — a body of custom holding between peoples. That is the law of nations in the sense the seventeenth century took up.

legacy: Descartes was taught from the Disputationes at La Flèche and cites Suárez by name in the Fourth Replies; the vocabulary of objective and formal reality that the Meditations uses without explanation is his. Leibniz said he read him as easily as a novel. Through the Protestant textbooks of Germany the work became the standard metaphysics in Lutheran universities as well, which is how Wolff and then Kant inherit a discipline organised the way Suárez organised it. Heidegger's claim, in the 1927 lectures, is that the Disputationes stands between the Greeks and modern philosophy, and that everyone after reads Aristotle through it.

Grotius took the law of nations from him and from Vitoria without much acknowledgement. The doctrine that authority originates in the people, meant to defend papal jurisdiction against kings, had a longer life than its purpose: it is in the Jesuit textbooks that carried it, and in a diluted form, into eighteenth-century constitutional argument.

read.first: Disputation I on the object of metaphysics and Disputation VII on distinctions, both available in translation. Then the first book of De legibus.
read.note: The complete Disputations run to well over a thousand folio pages. Nobody reads them straight through, and the internal cross-references make sampling workable.

suarez.caveat: Calling him the first modern metaphysician is a claim about form and transmission, not about doctrine; on most questions he is defending a scholastic position. How much of Descartes' framework is actually Suarezian is still argued.

al-kindi.sub: the man who made Greek philosophy speak Arabic
world: Al-Kindi worked in the Baghdad of al-Ma'mun and al-Mu'tasim, during a translation movement funded by caliphs, viziers and physicians who wanted Greek science in Arabic for their own uses. The Bayt al-Hikma of later legend was more plausibly a palace library than an academy. The same court ran the mihna, the inquisition of 833 that obliged officials to affirm the created Qur'an. Al-Kindi stood near that party and lost ground when it fell.
life: Of the royal line of Kinda — hence the honorific, philosopher of the Arabs — he was a governor's son and tutor to Ahmad, son of al-Mu'tasim, for whom several treatises were written. He seems not to have translated himself but commissioned, corrected and rewrote. His circle produced the Arabic Plotinus that circulated for centuries as The Theology of Aristotle. Later biographers report that under al-Mutawakkil he was beaten and his library seized for a time.

p: Dedicated to al-Mu'tasim, it is the founding text of philosophy in Arabic. Only its first part survives, in a manuscript recovered last century. It insists that truth has no nationality and that gratitude is owed to anyone who brings even a little of it. Then it breaks with Aristotle: nothing actual can be infinite. Body, time and motion entail one another and are all finite, so the world began. The argument runs to al-Ghazali and into modern cosmological arguments still called kalam.

A few pages, wholly out of proportion to its size in influence. Al-Kindi sorts intellect into four: one always in act and separate from the soul, one potential in us, one that has acquired its forms and can use them at will, and one in the act of thinking. Stitched together from Aristotle's De anima and its Greek commentators, it fixed the terms of every later argument, Arabic and Latin, about how a mind lays hold of a universal. It travelled west as De intellectu.

legacy: Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist credits him with some 260 titles, on optics, pharmacology, cryptanalysis and music as well as metaphysics. Most are lost, and about two dozen surfaced together in one Istanbul codex. Successors were unkind: al-Farabi rebuilt logic on firmer ground and superseded him. Later writers thought his Greek half-digested. What lasted was the founding decision, that the Qur'anic God and Greek demonstration belonged in one conversation.

read.first: On First Philosophy, in an annotated modern translation, followed by the short epistle on dispelling sorrow.
read.note: Read him as a founder rather than a finisher. The prose is stiff, and the arguments are often first drafts of positions others completed.

al-kindi.caveat: His birth and death years are conventional rather than documented. Most of his output is lost. His supervision of particular translations rests on later report.

al-farabi.sub: the logician who gave falsafa its shape and its politics
world: The Baghdad al-Farabi came to was politically hollow. After 861 the caliphs were creatures of their Turkish troops. In 945 the Buyid amirs took the city and reduced the caliph to a figurehead. The mihna had collapsed with al-Mutawakkil's reversal, and Mu'tazilite rationalism was in retreat. Philosophy there was largely the business of Syriac Christians. Al-Farabi learned his logic from them.

An episode of 932 shows what he faced. Before a vizier, the grammarian al-Sirafi argued against the Christian logician Abu Bishr Matta that Aristotle's logic was merely the grammar of Greek and held no authority over Arabic. By most accounts he won. Al-Farabi's lifelong claim—that logic governs meanings rather than words, and so belongs to no single language—answers that charge.
life: He was born around 870, either in Farab on the Jaxartes or in Faryab in Khurasan. The sources disagree, as they do over his family's Turkic or Persian origin. In Baghdad he studied logic with the Nestorian Yuhanna ibn Haylan and moved in Abu Bishr Matta's circle. He inherited a curriculum that covered the whole Aristotelian Organon when Latin Europe had two of its books.

Around 942 he left the disintegrating capital for the Hamdanid court of Sayf al-Dawla at Aleppo. He died at Damascus in 950, about eighty. Tradition made him an ascetic in Sufi dress who wrote in the margins of borrowed books. That is late embroidery. He was also a working music theorist whose treatise on instruments and intervals is a technical document.

works.t: The Principles of the Opinions of the Inhabitants of the Virtuous City (Mabadi' Ara' Ahl al-Madina al-Fadila)
p: It begins with God and ends with politics. The order is the argument. From the First, which thinks itself, separate intellects proceed, each generating the next with its sphere, until the tenth—the Active Intellect—brings human minds from potential to actual thought. Only then does al-Farabi turn to cities. The best is ordered on the same plan, its ruler standing to the citizens as the First stands to being. That ruler is philosopher and lawgiver at once, which is to say prophet, since revelation is what imagination makes of philosophical truth for those who cannot follow a demonstration. The ignorant cities, devoted to wealth or honour, are described with an accuracy suggesting he had some in view.

works.t: The Enumeration of the Sciences (Ihsa' al-'Ulum)
p: A map of what there is to know, in five chapters: language, logic, the mathematical sciences, physics and metaphysics, and finally politics, with jurisprudence and dialectical theology folded in beneath it. The order is his own rather than Aristotle's. The placement is a claim. Putting law and kalam last, as subordinate practical arts, says plainly what he thought of the religious sciences as sciences. Gerard of Cremona translated it at Toledo. Dominicus Gundissalinus rebuilt his own division of philosophy out of it. This short handbook therefore helped shape the medieval Latin curriculum.

works.t: The Harmonization of the Two Opinions of the Two Sages, Plato the Divine and Aristotle (Kitab al-Jam' bayna Ra'yay al-Hakimayn)
p: It argues that the quarrels between Plato and Aristotle—over forms, the eternity of the world, the soul—dissolve once each is read in his own idiom. It leans on the pseudo-Aristotelian Theology to show that Aristotle too taught creation. The thesis mattered: for the falasifa there was one philosophy rather than competing schools, and a philosopher's job was to expound it, not to take sides. It circulated under his name from an early date and shaped how the tradition read both Greeks. Several scholars have since argued on stylistic and doctrinal grounds that al-Farabi did not write it. The question is open.

legacy: The title tradition gave him, Second Teacher after Aristotle, was earned in logic. He put the whole Organon into working Arabic. He separated demonstration from dialectic, rhetoric and poetics, giving later writers a way to rank kinds of argument—which is how Averroes could sort people by the proofs each can follow. Avicenna said a small treatise of his finally explained what Aristotle's Metaphysics meant.

His political philosophy had a stranger afterlife. Little read in Arabic outside a narrow circle, it was recovered in the twentieth century by Leo Strauss and Muhsin Mahdi. They took the account of prophecy as philosophy accommodating revealed religion rather than the reverse. That reading is contested. Some think it makes him more subversive than he was. Latin Europe knew him chiefly as a logician.

read.first: The Virtuous City in a heavily annotated translation, then the short Enumeration of the Sciences for the shape of his system.
read.note: His prose is dry and orderly to the point of severity. The reward is that almost nothing in it is decoration.

al-farabi.caveat: His birthplace, ethnic origin and the authorship of the Harmonization are all genuinely disputed. Much of the biographical tradition postdates him by centuries.

avicenna.sub: the system-builder whose metaphysics became the common language
world: Avicenna was born in the last decade of Samanid Bukhara, a Persian dynasty ruling Transoxiana and Khurasan from a court where Arabic learning sat beside a reviving Persian literature. He describes entering its library as a young man and finding rooms of books sorted by subject, some of which he never saw again anywhere. In 999 the Qarakhanids took the city and the dynasty ended.

West of him the Buyid amirs held Baghdad and kept the Abbasid caliph as an ornament. Much of Iran and Iraq lay under Shi'i rule, tolerant of learning and violently unstable. So a philosopher who wanted a salary took service with a prince and shared the prince's luck. Avicenna served as court physician and twice as vizier, was jailed when a patron's regime fell, and hid between appointments.

Intellectual conditions mattered more. The translation movement had finished its work: the Aristotelian corpus, the Greek commentators, Galen and Ptolemy were all in Arabic. Nobody had yet built a system from them. Kalam meanwhile had its own atomist metaphysics in which God remakes the world at every instant. He wrote with both in view, which is why his questions stayed the questions for six centuries.
life: Born in 980 at Afshana near Bukhara, he was the son of a Samanid official whose house entertained Isma'ili missionaries. The boy listened and was unpersuaded. A travelling scholar, al-Natili, taught him elementary logic and was soon outpaced. The autobiography he dictated to al-Juzjani reports that he read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times without grasping its purpose, until a cheap commentary by al-Farabi made it plain in one night.

At about seventeen he cured the Samanid ruler Nuh ibn Mansur and gained the palace library. No post lasted long thereafter. In Hamadan he served the Buyid amir Shams al-Dawla as physician and then vizier. He survived a mutiny of troops demanding his execution, and spent four months in the fortress of Fardajan when the next regime suspected his letters. He wrote in prison.

The most productive years came at Isfahan under 'Ala' al-Dawla, where he held sessions on Friday nights, revised the Canon, and worked through the night with students. Al-Juzjani, with him for twenty-five years, completed the autobiography and catalogued the works. Avicenna died in 1037, aged fifty-seven, of a colic he treated himself and, by his student's account, treated too aggressively. He was buried at Hamadan.

p: Not a cure for the body but for ignorance: a complete curriculum in four parts — logic, natural philosophy, mathematics, metaphysics — following the Aristotelian order while quietly replacing Aristotle's arguments wherever Avicenna thought he could do better. The metaphysics carries his central move. What a thing is can be considered apart from whether it is. A full account of horse tells you nothing about whether any horse exists. So in everything but one case existence comes to an essence from outside, which is to say from a cause. Every contingent thing depends at every moment on something else. The series cannot regress without end. There is therefore a being whose essence just is to exist: the Necessary Existent, simple, uncaused and one. That proof starts from neither motion nor the world's beginning. The psychology of the same work carries the flying man. Its Latin parts shaped scholastic metaphysics more than any Greek text but Aristotle.

works.t: The Canon of Medicine (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb)
p: Five books: general principles, simple drugs alphabetically, diseases head to foot, diseases of the whole body, compound remedies. The achievement is organisational rather than experimental — Galen and the Greek tradition systematised and cross-referenced so exactly that a physician could find what he needed. Avicenna also lays down rules for testing a drug: unmixed, on a simple rather than a composite illness, and in more than one case before the effect is credited. Gerard of Cremona translated it at Toledo. It was printed in Latin dozens of times after 1473 and remained a set text at Padua and Montpellier into the seventeenth century. Paracelsus reportedly burned a copy at Basel in 1527 because it stood for the authority he wanted broken. Its persistence is also its indictment: a book that good made it harder to see what Galenic medicine had wrong.

The late work, and deliberately unfinished as argument: compressed to obscurity, gesturing at proofs rather than laying them out, arranged in ten sections that run from logic through physics and metaphysics to the states of the mystics. Composed for readers already trained in his system, it assumes the Shifa' throughout and explains almost nothing twice. Avicenna told his readers to keep it from the unworthy. Whether the ending marks a turn towards something beyond demonstration, or simply his own psychology pushed to its limit, has been argued since the twelfth century. The commentary tradition on it became a genre of its own. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's hostile reading was answered point by point by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. Later students read all three together as one running argument.

An epitome of the Shifa' assembled largely out of its own text. For centuries it was the way most readers actually met Avicenna, since few could sit down with the full encyclopedia. Its version of the flying man is the one usually quoted. Imagine a person created whole in mid-air, in a void, blindfolded, limbs held apart so that nothing touches, with no sensation since birth: he would still affirm that he exists, while affirming nothing of a body. Avicenna takes this to show that self-awareness is primitive and reaches us by no sensory route. The thought experiment appears in three of his works with slight variations. Modern readers dispute its form — whether it proves immateriality, makes a point about reference, or draws attention to something one has always had.

Avicenna refers to a work setting out philosophy as it is in itself, without the concessions to the Peripatetic school that the Shifa' makes for its readers. Almost all of it is gone. A section of the logic survives, with a preface. Twelfth-century readers, and many since, took the title to promise an esoteric oriental wisdom opposed to Greek rationalism. Suhrawardi built an Illuminationist tradition partly on that expectation. Recent scholarship, Dimitri Gutas above all, argues the reverse: the label is geographical, marking the philosophy of Khurasan against that of the Baghdad school, and what survives suggests a different order of exposition rather than a different doctrine. The evidence is thin enough that the argument continues.

legacy: Within a century Avicennism was not a school but the water everyone swam in. His opponents argued in his vocabulary: al-Ghazali attacked twenty of his theses and adopted his logic entire. Post-classical kalam is largely Avicennan metaphysics contested from inside. In Iran the line runs through Suhrawardi and Tusi to Mulla Sadra in the seventeenth century, who inverted the essence-existence distinction to make existence the primary reality.

Latin Europe met him at Toledo, where Dominicus Gundissalinus worked with a Jewish collaborator identified as Abraham ibn Daud, decades before the full Aristotle arrived. William of Auvergne, Albert the Great and Aquinas take the essence-existence question from him. Aquinas's third way rebuilds the argument from contingency. Duns Scotus on being as metaphysics' subject is unimaginable without him. Whether Avicenna meant a real distinction or one of consideration is still disputed.

The Jewish reception went as deep: Maimonides told Samuel ibn Tibbon that Avicenna was worth studying. Hebrew philosophy took his psychology as its baseline. What has aged worst is the cosmology of nested intellects and spheres, which fell with Ptolemy. What has aged best is the flying man, still cited in philosophy of mind, and the insistence that existence is not one more property a thing has.

Three of the twenty — the world's pre-eternity, God's knowing particulars only in a universal way, and the denial of bodily resurrection — al-Ghazali declared not merely false but unbelief, a capital charge. Every later Avicennan in the Sunni world argued inside that boundary.

read.first: The Metaphysics of the Healing in a facing-page translation, entering at the treatment of the necessary and the possible. Then the psychology for the flying man.
read.note: He rewards patience and punishes skimming, because the terminology is built up in order and later arguments assume every earlier definition.

avicenna.caveat: The autobiography is the source for nearly everything about his early life, and is a composed self-portrait rather than a document. The dating of individual works rests largely on al-Juzjani's catalogue.

al-ghazali.sub: the theologian who learned philosophy in order to break it
world: Al-Ghazali's career belongs to the Seljuk state at its height and to its sudden crisis. Turkish sultans ruled in the name of a caliph who had authority but no army. The vizier Nizam al-Mulk built a network of state madrasas to train a Sunni scholarly class loyal to that arrangement. In 1092 Nizam al-Mulk was assassinated, reportedly by the Nizari Isma'ilis. Sultan Malikshah died weeks later.

The Isma'ili challenge was not merely doctrinal. Alamut taught that certainty comes only from an infallible living imam. That teaching answered a real problem and was winning converts. The caliph al-Mustazhir commissioned a refutation from him. Avicenna's system, meanwhile, struck many educated Muslims as more coherent than anything the theologians offered. His whole output answers one anxiety from three directions: how does anyone know that what he believes is true.

One thing is conspicuously absent. He was in Damascus and Jerusalem in the mid-1090s. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099. He says essentially nothing about it anywhere in his writing. That silence is a useful corrective to any account making medieval Islamic thought a reaction to Christendom. The arguments that gripped him were internal ones, and Latin Europe barely registered as a rival.
life: He was born at Tus in Khurasan around 1058, though recent work argues for 1055. Orphaned young, he was educated through the charitable machinery of the madrasas. He reached Nishapur and studied under al-Juwayni, the leading Ash'arite theologian of the age. Nizam al-Mulk took him into his entourage. In 1091 the vizier installed him, aged about thirty-three, at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, the most prestigious chair in the Sunni world.

In July 1095 he left it. He describes a physical collapse: for months he could not speak in the lecture hall. The physicians told him the cause lay in his heart, not his body. He distributed his wealth and vanished for eleven years—Damascus, Jerusalem, Hebron, Mecca, then Tus. Whether the crisis was purely spiritual, or also a well-timed exit from a capital where his patrons had just been killed, no source settles.

By 1106 Nizam al-Mulk's son had pressed him back into teaching at the Nizamiyya of Nishapur. The son was himself assassinated within the year. Al-Ghazali justified the return by arguing in print that the century needed a renewer of religion, a claim about his own office. He soon withdrew again to Tus, kept a small lodge for students and Sufi companions, and died there in December 1111.

works.t: The Aims of the Philosophers (Maqasid al-Falasifa)
p: Before attacking the philosophers he set out their logic, metaphysics and physics without comment, in a summary clean enough to serve as a competent Avicennan textbook. Refutation without comprehension, he says, is worthless. He wrote it at Baghdad at the height of his teaching, a year or two before the attack itself. The consequence was comic and enormous. It was translated at Toledo in the twelfth century without its framing preface. That translation filed Algazel among the Arab philosophers, an ally of Avicenna, for some three hundred years, until the Incoherence reached Latin and the mistake became visible. Latin readers thus spent three centuries citing as an authority the man who had written to demolish that authority. The book also shows how much he absorbed of what he opposed: he learned syllogistic here and never gave it up.

works.t: The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahafut al-Falasifa)
p: Twenty discussions, each taking a philosophical thesis and showing that the philosophers cannot demonstrate it by their own standards. That is the crucial tactic: he usually does not assert the opposite, only that the proof fails. Their claim to demonstrative certainty therefore collapses into opinion. Seventeen theses he calls innovation. Three he declares unbelief—the eternity of the world, the claim that God knows particulars only in a universal way, and the denial of bodily resurrection. The seventeenth discussion is the famous one. The connection between what we call cause and what we call effect is not necessary. The reason is that observation shows only that burning occurs when fire touches cotton, never that the fire produces it. The regularity is God's settled habit. Whether that makes him a thoroughgoing occasionalist, or leaves room for secondary causes whose powers are real but not independent of God, divides the scholarship. That is because the discussion offers two positions and does not clearly choose.

works.t: The Revival of the Religious Sciences (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din)
p: Forty books in four quarters—acts of worship, the customs of daily life, the vices that destroy, the virtues that save—written mostly in retreat and running to thousands of pages. It is the constructive work the polemics cleared room for, and the one most Muslims have actually read. Its argument is that the religious sciences had become a technology of legal correctness with no account of what happens inside a person. The inner life, it holds, is the point of the outward act. It domesticates Sufism for the Sunni mainstream, presenting the states and stations of the mystics as ordinary religious psychology grafted onto orthodox law. Maliki scholars in the west burned copies. Ibn al-Jawzi and later Ibn Taymiyya complained of its weak hadith and its philosophical residue. It is still commonly called the most widely read book in Islam after the Qur'an.

A short intellectual autobiography written near the end and organised as a search: theologians, philosophers, Isma'ilis and Sufis are examined in turn, and certainty found only in the last. It opens with a genuine sceptical crisis—reason convicts the senses of deceiving, and then reason itself goes into the dock. For nothing guarantees rational judgement any more than sense guaranteed itself. He reports that the state lasted about two months and ended not in proof but in a light God cast into his breast. The parallel with Descartes has been drawn since the nineteenth century, and holds as far as the doubt goes. The exits are entirely different. As autobiography it is retrospective and shaped, an apologia for a controversial career rather than a diary. It sorts his enemies into four schools rather more neatly than life does.

works.t: The Distilled Essence of Legal Theory (al-Mustasfa min 'Ilm al-Usul)
p: His last major book, a work of Islamic legal theory prefaced by a compressed introduction to Aristotelian logic. The preface makes the blunt claim that whoever has not mastered logic cannot be relied on for knowledge at all. Coming from the author of the Incoherence, that settled the question for the madrasas: logic is a neutral instrument, not a foreign import contaminated by the metaphysics it usually travelled with. Within a century syllogistic was standard equipment for jurists and theologians across the Sunni world. Manuals of it were written for students who would never read a line of Aristotle. Nothing shows more clearly that al-Ghazali partitioned philosophy rather than rejecting it. He kept the method and refused a specific set of conclusions.

legacy: The claim that al-Ghazali killed philosophy in Islam is the most repeated thing said about him. It owes less to the sources than to nineteenth-century European scholarship, Ernest Renan's above all. That scholarship wanted a villain to explain why the Arabic tradition supposedly stopped. It is now heavily qualified: philosophy continued as post-Avicennan kalam in Fakhr al-Din al-Razi and Tusi, the Iranian traditions ran on into the seventeenth century, and al-Ghazali transmitted more Avicennism than he destroyed.

Averroes answered him eighty years later, line by line, and accused him of writing one thing for the elite and another for the crowd. The charge stuck in the West. It misses how consistent his practice of matching argument to audience was. His claim that necessary connection is never observed anticipates Hume by some six hundred and fifty years. No route of transmission has been demonstrated. The resemblance is best treated as two men finding the same crack in the same wall.

Elsewhere his standing never dipped. The Ihya' is still taught and printed across the Muslim world. The Niche of Lights, with its Neoplatonic hierarchy of veils, keeps the question of a hidden Avicennan al-Ghazali open. The modern picture—a man who absorbed the philosophers' tools so completely that he changed what Sunni orthodoxy could say—is more interesting than either the demolisher of the old story or the crypto-philosopher of the new one.

read.first: Deliverance from Error first, for the shape of the life and the mind. Then the seventeenth discussion of the Incoherence on causation, which stands on its own.
read.note: Read the Incoherence alongside Averroes's reply where possible. The reply quotes it at length, and the two were built to be read against each other.

al-ghazali.caveat: His birth year, the nature of the 1095 breakdown, and the authenticity of the final section of the Niche of Lights are all contested. So is whether the Incoherence commits him to strict occasionalism.

averroes.sub: Aristotle's most patient reader, and Latin Europe's scandal
world: Averroes lived his whole life under the Almohads, a movement born among Berber tribes of the High Atlas around Ibn Tumart. Ibn Tumart was a self-declared mahdi who preached a severe doctrine of divine unity against Almoravid anthropomorphism. By the 1140s they held the Maghreb, by the 1170s most of Muslim Iberia. Their ideology was theological throughout, which cut two ways: their caliphs took philosophy seriously as few Muslim rulers had, and the same seriousness could turn on a philosopher without warning.

Al-Andalus was under permanent military pressure. Christian kingdoms had taken Toledo in 1085 and were pressing south. Almohad rule depended on winning battles. The victory at Alarcos in 1195 was followed within seventeen years by catastrophe at Las Navas de Tolosa. Averroes's disgrace fell in the middle of that mobilisation, which is why historians read it as a concession to religious scholars whose support the war effort needed.

Andalusian philosophy was thinner than Baghdad's and stranger for it: a small affair of a few men in contact with each other—Ibn Bajja, Ibn Tufayl, Averroes—working from a partial library, without any Arabic version of Aristotle's Politics. Al-Ghazali's Incoherence had arrived from the east and was widely taken as settled. Averroes wrote as a man restoring something he believed corrupted in the east and abandoned at home.
life: Born at Córdoba in 1126 into a dynasty of Maliki jurists—grandfather and father were both chief qadi of the city—he trained in law and medicine. Law remained his profession, while the philosophy was formally the sideline. His handbook on the points where the legal schools disagree is still consulted. His medical compendium reached Latin as the Colliget.

Al-Marrakushi, writing generations later, reports that Ibn Tufayl brought him before the caliph Abu Ya'qub Yusuf, who asked what philosophers held about the eternity of the heavens. Averroes hedged in terror until the caliph took up the question himself. From that audience, the story goes, came the commission to explain Aristotle. The anecdote is late and neat; the patronage is documented. He became qadi of Seville in 1169, chief qadi of Córdoba in 1182, and court physician at Marrakesh.

In 1195 the caliph Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur turned on him: condemned before an assembly of scholars, stripped of office and banished to Lucena, with philosophical books burned and the sciences restricted. The reasons are not documented. Within two years he was restored and summoned to Marrakesh, where he died in December 1198. The young Ibn 'Arabi describes watching the coffin carried back to Córdoba on one side of a beast, the books balancing it on the other.

That handbook is the Bidayat al-Mujtahid wa-Nihayat al-Muqtasid, begun about 1168. It remains the most widely read of his books in Arabic — the reverse of his Latin reputation, which rests on works his own tradition let drop.

p: He commented on nearly the whole corpus at three levels. The levels are pedagogy rather than repetition. The epitomes summarise a work's doctrine for a beginner without following its text. The middle commentaries paraphrase closely, smoothing the argument for a reader who can already follow it. The long commentaries—only five, on the Posterior Analytics, Physics, On the Heavens, On the Soul and the Metaphysics—quote Aristotle lemma by lemma and expound each piece at length. That is a form taken from the Greek commentators and unprecedented in Arabic at that scale. The programme rests on a conviction: that Aristotle got the structure of the world essentially right, that later readers had buried him under emanation schemes drawn from books he never wrote, and that the work required was excavation. Where a text was missing he says so.

works.t: Long Commentary on On the Soul (Sharh Kitab al-Nafs)
p: Here he reaches the position that made his name notorious. The potential or material intellect must be able to receive any form whatever, so it cannot itself be a particular material thing. But anything individuated by a body is particular. Averroes concludes that the material intellect is one separate substance shared by the whole human species, not a faculty each of us privately owns. What is mine is the images my imagination supplies. Thinking happens when that shared intellect is joined to them. He reached this only at the end, having held different views in the epitome and the middle commentary. The development can be traced. The Arabic is largely lost. The work survives complete only in Michael Scot's Latin, which is how Christendom met it, with consequences its author could not have foreseen.

works.t: The Incoherence of the Incoherence (Tahafut al-Tahafut)
p: Al-Ghazali is quoted at length and answered paragraph by paragraph, which is why so much of the Incoherence survives embedded in its refutation. The central counter is that abolishing necessary causation abolishes knowledge: if fire has no nature that makes it burn, nothing has a definition, and there is nothing to know about anything. Averroes also charges his opponent with incompetence in Avicenna's own terms and with saying different things to different audiences, while himself insisting elsewhere that different audiences require different arguments. He does not simply defend the falasifa. A good part of the book argues that Avicenna misrepresented Aristotle, so that al-Ghazali attacked a target Averroes had no wish to defend. It is also, throughout, a defence of philosophy's right to exist, written by a sitting judge who knew the risk.

Cast formally as a legal ruling on whether the Law permits, forbids or requires the study of philosophy, and answering that for those capable of it, philosophy is obligatory. Since scripture commands reflection on creation, and demonstration is the perfected form of reflection, the demonstrative class has a religious duty to philosophise. Truth does not contradict truth, so where a text appears to conflict with a demonstration the text has an inner sense and must be interpreted. But only the trained may interpret it, and never in public, because dialectical and rhetorical minds are harmed by arguments they cannot assess. This is not the double truth later attributed to him: there is one truth, addressed in three registers. The treatise circulated little in Arabic and never reached Latin, which is why the misreading had a clear field.

Averroes wrote on the Republic because Aristotle's Politics had never reached Arabic, and he says so. The commentary follows Plato's argument for the philosopher-ruler and the education of the guardians, and drops the theory of forms as unproved. It turns the analysis of degenerate regimes on states he knew, the Almoravids serving as a case of a regime founded on virtue decaying into one founded on honour and then wealth. His remark that the women of his own cities are kept like plants, a burden on the men who support them and a loss to the whole community, is unusually direct. The Arabic is lost. The text survives only in Samuel ben Judah's Hebrew translation of 1320, which shows plainly who was still reading him.

legacy: In Arabic he had almost no school. Within two generations Andalusian philosophy was finished, and the eastern tradition had long since taken the Avicennan road. His commentaries were copied rarely. Much of his output survives only because others translated it. Ibn Khaldun, writing in the fourteenth-century Maghreb, knew and used him, but as one authority among many rather than as the head of a living tradition.

In Hebrew and Latin he was the Commentator, cited by the title alone. Jewish scholars translated nearly the whole corpus and for two centuries read Aristotle through his eyes. At Paris, Michael Scot's Latin arrived as the arts faculty was absorbing the full Aristotle. The unity of the material intellect became a crisis. Taken to mean that no individual soul thinks or survives death, it was condemned by Bishop Tempier in 1270 and again in 1277. Aquinas wrote a treatise against it.

Latin Averroism is now read as a construct. The men so named, Siger of Brabant among them, were radical Aristotelians who agreed with him on some points and not others. The double truth that Tempier's preface complains of is a position nobody is known to have held. Renan's book of 1852 then remade him as a free-thinking martyr to clerical reaction—an image the Decisive Treatise, the work of a chief qadi arguing from scripture, does not support.

read.first: The Decisive Treatise, which is short and states the whole programme; then selections from the Incoherence of the Incoherence read against al-Ghazali.
read.note: The commentaries are demanding and rarely read whole outside universities, but the long commentary on the soul is worth sampling to see how the notorious doctrine is actually built.

averroes.caveat: Several major works survive only in Hebrew or Latin translation. The reasons for the 1195 disgrace are undocumented. The celebrated first audience with the caliph rests on a single much later report.

maimonides.sub: the codifier of Jewish law who wrote a book for the perplexed
world: The Almohads ended a way of life. Taking Córdoba in 1148, they abolished the arrangement by which Jews and Christians paid a tax and were left alone, offering conversion, exile or death. Communities centuries old scattered, some converting outwardly and continuing as Jews in private. What a Jew may say under compulsion, a question Maimonides treated early and leniently, was not academic for him.

Egypt was another world. Fatimid rule ended in 1171 when Saladin, having served as its vizier, restored Sunni allegiance and founded the Ayyubid state. The Crusader wars ran through Maimonides's whole Egyptian career. Fustat, the old city beside Cairo, left the enormous cache of documents called the Geniza. That is why the daily texture of his life is better known than that of almost any medieval philosopher.
life: Born at Córdoba in 1138, he was taught by his father, a rabbinic judge, in the Arabic and Hebrew learning of al-Andalus. The family moved within Spain, reached Fez around 1160 and Acre in 1165, and settled at Fustat in 1166. His brother David supported the household by trading gems and drowned in the Indian Ocean around 1169. Maimonides wrote that the grief laid him up for a year.

Medicine then became his living, since he refused payment for teaching Torah. He served al-Qadi al-Fadil, Saladin's chief minister, later Saladin's son al-Afdal, and headed the Jewish community of Egypt. A letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon describes riding to the palace each morning, returning to a courtyard full of patients of every faith, and working until night. He died in 1204 and was buried at Tiberias.

p: Begun in Spain at about twenty-three and finished in Egypt, written in Judeo-Arabic so that ordinary readers could use it, this was meant to make the Mishnah intelligible without the Talmud. Two inserted essays outgrew their setting. The Eight Chapters presents a Greek doctrine of the mean as the plain sense of rabbinic virtue. The introduction to the tenth chapter of Sanhedrin sets out thirteen principles that every Jew must hold. Judaism had never had a creed. The list provoked argument for centuries and entered the liturgy as a hymn, a peculiar fate for a philosophical proposal.

Fourteen books covering the whole of Jewish law, including the Temple rites nobody could perform, arranged by subject in clear Mishnaic Hebrew and stating each ruling flatly, without the sources or the debates behind it. That decision made it the most useful and the most resented book in rabbinic literature. Abraham ben David of Posquières objected that a code without sources invites obedience without understanding and stands between the reader and the Talmud. It opens not with ritual but with the existence and incorporeality of God, which puts metaphysics at the foundation of the law.

works.t: The Guide of the Perplexed (Dalalat al-Ha'irin)
p: Written in Judeo-Arabic and sent in instalments to one former student, it addresses a reader who has studied philosophy and now finds his religion unintelligible. It warns at the outset that its chapters are scattered on purpose and contain deliberate contradictions. The first part dismantles the language of scripture: no positive attribute can be predicated of God without dividing his unity, so we can say only what he is not. The second declines the decisive question, since neither the eternity of the world nor its creation can be demonstrated and scripture may therefore decide. That refusal, a philosopher marking the exact limit of proof, is the most admired move in the book.

legacy: Samuel ibn Tibbon translated the Guide into Hebrew at once, consulting the author by letter. A freer version by al-Harizi followed, from which a Latin Dux neutrorum reached the schoolmen by the 1240s. Aquinas cites Rabbi Moses repeatedly on divine names and on the undemonstrability of the world's beginning. Within Judaism the reaction was fiercer: his books were banned in some communities and burned at Montpellier in 1232.

He has never stopped being contested. The book's own design is the reason. Because it announces that it conceals, every generation has asked what. Spinoza attacked him for making scripture say whatever philosophy required. Leo Strauss read the contradictions as deliberate cover for a radical Aristotelianism, splitting the field. The Mishneh Torah meanwhile stayed in daily use, which no other medieval philosopher's book can claim.

read.first: The Guide, beginning with the introduction on contradictions and the chapters on divine attributes. The Eight Chapters make a shorter way in.
read.note: The Guide is designed to be difficult and says so. Read it slowly and with a commentary rather than expecting a treatise's straight line.

maimonides.caveat: His birth year is given as both 1138 and 1135. Whether the Guide's contradictions conceal a doctrine at odds with its surface remains the central dispute in Maimonides scholarship.

ibn-khaldun.sub: the historian who asked what makes states possible at all
world: The fourteenth-century Maghreb was a machine for making and unmaking dynasties. Hafsids at Tunis, Zayyanids at Tlemcen and Marinids at Fez fought each other and their own tribal allies without pause. A competent secretary could serve four of them in a decade. Further east, the Mongols had sacked Baghdad in 1258 and ended the caliphate. Sunni learning had shifted to Mamluk Cairo, where he would end his life.

Then the plague. The Black Death reached Tunis in 1348 and killed both his parents and several of his teachers. He returned to it in the Muqaddimah, writing that civilisation itself seemed to have been called to extinction. His theory of the life cycle of states was written by a man who had watched a society come apart and wanted to know what holds one together.
life: Born at Tunis in 1332 to a family of Andalusian Arab descent that had left Seville before the Christian conquest, he took the standard religious and literary training. Then he entered chancery service. The career was mobile and repeatedly disastrous: office under the Hafsids, two years' imprisonment at Fez for backing the wrong claimant, an embassy from Granada to Pedro of Castile in 1364, and negotiations with Berber tribes for whoever was paying.

In 1375 he withdrew to a fortress at Qal'at Ibn Salama in what is now western Algeria and stayed four years. There, he says, he wrote the Muqaddimah in five months. From 1382 he lived in Cairo, teaching and serving six separate terms as Maliki chief qadi, dismissed from each. A ship carrying his wife and daughters went down off Alexandria in 1384. In 1400 he was lowered by rope over the wall of besieged Damascus to meet Timur. The city was sacked anyway.

p: Formally the prolegomenon to a universal history, in practice a new subject, which he calls the science of human social organisation. Its premise is that historians are credulous, repeating army figures no economy could feed. The remedy, on that premise, is knowledge of how societies work, against which a report can be tested. Its engine is asabiyyah, the solidarity binding a kin group so that its members will die for one another. It is strongest among hard peripheral peoples. It carries them to power over softer settled populations and then decays: the founders have it, the second generation remembers it, the third keeps only the comfort. By the fourth the dynasty is defended by paid strangers and falls to a fresh group from the margin. Around this he argues about taxation, the division of labour, crafts and prices, offering them as causal regularities rather than moral lessons.

The universal history the Muqaddimah introduces, running from the Arabs and the ancient peoples down to his own day. Its eastern sections are compiled from earlier writers and are not why anyone reads it. Its treatment of the Berber dynasties of North Africa is another matter, drawing on his own service, his own negotiations with tribes, and documents he had handled. It remains a primary source without which much of the medieval Maghreb would be unrecoverable. The gap between the halves is instructive, since the theory was built where the evidence was firsthand.

Appended to the history, it is one of the fullest self-accounts surviving from the premodern Arabic world. It lists his teachers and theirs, reproduces official correspondence, and narrates the sackings, imprisonments and dismissals of his career with administrative calm. It is the source for the meeting with Timur and for the composition of the Muqaddimah. The self-portrait is arranged, as such things are. He presents his frequent changes of allegiance as the ordinary conduct of a scholar-official rather than opportunism. Readers have divided over whether to accept that.

legacy: He founded nothing. No school followed him in Arabic. For two centuries the book was read chiefly as a literary curiosity. Ottoman scholars took him up in the seventeenth century, partly because a theory of dynastic decline was of urgent interest in Istanbul. The Muqaddimah was translated into Turkish. Europe found him late: extracts from Silvestre de Sacy in 1806, de Slane's French translation in the 1860s, Rosenthal's English in 1958.

A long argument about what he was has followed. Arnold Toynbee called the Muqaddimah the greatest work of its kind produced by any mind in any time or place. A century of writers have claimed him as the first sociologist or the first economist. The claims need discounting, since the framework describes the arid belt he actually knew. Reading his tax argument as supply-side economics flattens it. What survives is the insistence that societies have regularities which can be stated and used.

read.first: The Muqaddimah in the abridged one-volume version of the standard English translation. Take the opening on historical method and the chapters on group feeling and dynasties.
read.note: The sections on the occult sciences and letter magic are part of the book and should not be skipped as embarrassments. They show what a fourteenth-century science of society included.

machiavelli.sub: the first writer to describe rule without excusing it
world: Charles VIII of France crossed the Alps in September 1494 with a professional army and bronze siege guns. The Italian balance of five powers collapsed in a season. Naples fell almost without a battle. Within a few years France, Spain and the Empire were settling their quarrels on Italian ground. The wealthy, subtle, militarily hollow city-states had become terrain rather than agents.

Florence expelled the Medici in that same crisis and spent eighteen years a republic, first under Savonarola, burned in 1498, then under the gonfaloniere Piero Soderini. It hired mercenaries and failed for a decade to retake Pisa. In 1512 it watched Spanish infantry sack Prato and scatter its citizen militia. Machiavelli wrote about force as a man who had seen force settle everything.
life: Born in Florence in 1469 to a lawyer of good name and small means, Machiavelli owed his education to his father’s books. He enters the record in 1498, weeks after Savonarola’s execution, as second chancellor of the republic and secretary to the Ten of War. For fourteen years he drafted despatches and rode on legations to Cesare Borgia, Louis XII and the Emperor. He pressed for the citizen militia meant to replace hired troops.

The restored Medici dismissed him in November 1512. In February his name turned up on a conspirator’s list. He was racked before an amnesty for the election of Leo X freed him. From a farm at Sant’Andrea in Percussina he told Francesco Vettori, on 10 December 1513, of his evenings with the ancient historians and of a small work he had composed on principalities. He died in 1527, passed over by the republic he had hoped would recall him.

p: Twenty-six short chapters sorting principalities by how they were acquired and what keeps each, dedicated at last to Lorenzo de’ Medici, duke of Urbino. The scandal lies in chapters fifteen to eighteen: since men are not good, a ruler who insists on being good among them will be destroyed. He must learn how not to be good and use that knowledge as necessity dictates. Chapter twenty-five gives fortune half of what happens and leaves the rest to us. The last chapter drops analysis and calls on the Medici to drive the foreigners out of Italy.

works.t: Discourses on the First Ten Books of Livy (Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio)
p: Three books on Livy’s account of early Rome, read to the young patricians of the Orti Oricellari. The argument is republican: liberty is better kept by a people than by a prince, armed citizens are worth more than hired soldiers, and the tumults between plebs and senate that Roman writers deplored were what made Rome free. Conflict given a lawful outlet is a constitution’s working part, not its disease. Much that The Prince offers as advice appears here as diagnosis, which is why the relation between the two is still argued over.

works.t: The Art of War (Dell’arte della guerra)
p: The only major political work Machiavelli published in his lifetime, cast as a conversation in the Rucellai gardens with the condottiere Fabrizio Colonna as its speaker. It argues for conscript infantry drilled on Roman lines, against the mercenary companies that had failed Florence. It insists that military and civil institutions stand or fall together. The tactical detail was already dated: he underrated firearms. Reprinted across Europe, it carried his name further in the sixteenth century than either of the others.

legacy: Rome placed The Prince on the Index in 1559. Innocent Gentillet’s Anti-Machiavel of 1576 fixed the caricature for France and England. The stage Machiavel of Marlowe and Shakespeare is that caricature in costume, an atheist poisoner with an Italian name. The adjective entered European languages long before most of its users had read a page of him. It has never been dislodged.

Serious readers ran the other way. Spinoza called him acute and took The Prince for a warning to free peoples. Rousseau called the book a satire and its author a republican. Modern scholarship follows the Discourses: Skinner set him in Florentine civic humanism, Pocock traced his republicanism into Anglo-American hands, and Isaiah Berlin argued that his real offence was to expose two incompatible moralities with no way of ranking them.

read.first: Read The Prince in an edition with the Vettori letter attached, then the Discourses before forming a view. The second book is where his politics actually lives.
read.note: The prose is fast and unhedged. It is easy to mistake its coldness for approval of what it describes.

machiavelli.caveat: The composition of The Prince and the Discourses overlaps in time. Whether the shorter book is counsel, audition, satire or warning has been disputed for five centuries without resolution.

montaigne.sub: who invented the essay in order to find out what he thought
world: France between 1562 and 1598 fought eight civil wars over religion. Montaigne's own region changed hands repeatedly; the massacre of St Bartholomew's Day in 1572 fell in the year he began writing. Neighbours killed each other over doctrines neither could demonstrate, which is the condition his scepticism answers rather than the subject it discusses.

Two other things shaped the book. Sextus Empiricus had been printed in Latin in 1562, and the ancient sceptical arguments were suddenly available whole. And the New World had produced reports of peoples whose customs were coherent, ancient and entirely unlike Europe's — a fact Montaigne takes more seriously than almost anyone else of his century.
life: Born in 1533 at the château de Montaigne near Bordeaux to a family enriched in the fish and wine trades and ennobled two generations earlier. His father had him woken by music and taught Latin as a first language by a tutor forbidden to use French. He trained in law and sat for thirteen years in the Bordeaux parlement.

There he met Étienne de La Boétie, whose death in 1563 he never got over and whose friendship the essay Of Friendship is about. In 1571, at thirty-eight, he retired to his tower library, had sentences from Sextus and Lucretius painted on the beams, and began to write. He was twice elected mayor of Bordeaux, travelled to Italy for his kidney stones, negotiated between Henry of Navarre and the Catholic League, and died in 1592 with the third edition unfinished.

p: Three books and a hundred and seven chapters, on cannibals, on thumbs, on the education of children, on smells, on repentance, on experience. The word essai means an attempt or a trial, and the method is to take a subject and see what happens: quote the ancients, contradict them, contradict himself, and record the contradiction rather than resolve it. He never revised by deletion. Later editions add layers around the earlier text, so the book shows a mind changing over twenty years with all its stages left visible — which is a large part of what makes it unlike anything before it.

The longest chapter and the philosophical centre. It begins as a defence of a natural theologian and turns into a demolition of human cognitive pretension: the senses deceive, reason cannot certify itself without circularity, animals may reason as well as we do, and the customs we call natural are local. The motto he had struck on a medal — Que sais-je?, what do I know? — is offered as a question rather than a thesis, because a thesis of doubt would refute itself. Pascal read it and it terrified him; Descartes read it and the First Meditation answers it.

legacy: The essay as a form is simply his. Bacon's Essays of 1597 take the name and almost nothing else; the line that actually descends from Montaigne runs through Cowley and Hazlitt to Emerson, Woolf and the modern personal essay. Shakespeare read Florio's translation of 1603 and used it in The Tempest, where Gonzalo's commonwealth is lifted from Of Cannibals.

In philosophy his effect is as a problem to be answered. Descartes' method of doubt is built to defeat exactly the Pyrrhonism the Apology revives, and Pascal's fragments circle him with a mixture of admiration and alarm. Later he is read differently again: as the first writer to make the study of a single ordinary self a legitimate subject, and by Nietzsche as proof that a philosopher could be cheerful.

read.first: Of Cannibals (I.31), Of Friendship (I.28), Of Experience (III.13) and Of Repentance (III.2). Then the Apology for Raymond Sebond if the scepticism is what you came for.
read.note: Screech's Penguin translation marks the layers added in each edition, which is worth having. Read a chapter at a time; the book is not built to be read continuously.

montaigne.caveat: Whether the scepticism of the Apology is Montaigne's settled view or a position tried on in one chapter is a long-running dispute. The later essays are markedly less sceptical and more confident about experience.

bacon.sub: the Lord Chancellor who tried to reorganise all knowledge
world: Bacon’s England was a litigious, quickly enriching kingdom whose government ran on patronage and whose Crown was chronically short of money. Careers were made at court and in the law. Parliament met when the Crown wanted a subsidy, and used the occasion to press grievances. That friction over prerogative and monopolies became the constitutional quarrel that ended in civil war.

The learned world he wanted to overturn still taught Aristotle from Latin textbooks at Oxford and Cambridge. Outside the universities things moved: Gilbert on the magnet in 1600, Kepler’s new astronomy, Galileo’s telescope in 1610, and William Harvey, Bacon’s own physician, working towards the circulation of the blood. Printing, gunpowder and the compass were his standing examples of what unphilosophical inventions could do.
life: Born in London in 1561, son of Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, and of Anne Cooke, a formidable Calvinist translator. He went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, at twelve, and spent three years with the embassy in France. He came home in 1579 to find his father dead and himself unprovided for. The Earl of Essex became his patron. Bacon helped prosecute him for treason in 1601, and the stain never came off.

Under James he rose steadily: Attorney General in 1613, Lord Chancellor in 1618, Viscount St Alban in 1621. That same year the Commons charged him with taking gifts from litigants. He confessed without excuse, was fined forty thousand pounds and barred from office. The five years at Gorhambury that followed were his most productive: the final Essays, the History of the Reign of King Henry VII, and the Latin recasting of his survey of learning.

works.y: 1605; expanded in Latin as De augmentis scientiarum, 1623
p: Two books in English, dedicated to a new king who thought himself learned. The first defends learning against the charges made at court, that it breeds irresolution, impracticality and irreligion. The second surveys the whole of knowledge, sorted by the faculty that produces it: history from memory, poesy from imagination, philosophy from reason. Bacon lists the gaps as carefully as the holdings. That catalogue of deficiencies is the real work. The scheme, enlarged into Latin in 1623, later supplied the tree of knowledge for the French Encyclopédie.

The second part of a six-part Great Instauration he never finished. It is written in numbered aphorisms, so that no reader could mistake it for a system. Book I clears the ground with the four Idols: of the Tribe, built into human nature; of the Cave, peculiar to each mind; of the Marketplace, planted by loose words; of the Theatre, inherited from philosophical systems. Book II gives the method — tables of presence, of absence and of degrees, then elimination rather than counting — and works it through on the form of heat. He concludes that heat is a species of motion. He was right about heat, and right that a negative instance outweighs a hundred confirmations.

An unfinished utopian fable, printed with Sylva Sylvarum the year Bacon died. Sailors blown off course reach Bensalem. Its real government is Salomon’s House, a state-funded college of research with a division of labour: some men gather experiments from abroad, some perform new ones, some draw axioms, some direct the next round. The point is institutional rather than doctrinal. Discovery is slow and cumulative, and needs buildings, money and staff. The founders of the Royal Society read the fable as a prospectus and said so.

legacy: The Royal Society adopted him as its patron ghost. Thomas Sprat’s official History of 1667 is built around his programme, and Boyle and Hooke wrote up experiments in something like his manner. Diderot and d’Alembert put him first among the moderns and borrowed his classification of knowledge outright. The slogan that knowledge is power has outlived every particular thesis he defended.

As a description of how discovery works, the method failed. Bacon had little use for mathematics, rejected Copernicus, and expected axioms to rise from tables of instances without the bold guessing scientists do. Harvey remarked, according to Aubrey, that he wrote philosophy like a Lord Chancellor. What survived is the other half: science as public, cooperative, funded work aimed at relieving the human condition rather than at contemplation.

read.first: Book I of the Novum Organum for the Idols, then New Atlantis, which is short and shows what he wanted built.
read.note: The tables of Book II reward patience rather than admiration. Read them as an early attempt at experimental design, not as a working recipe.

bacon.caveat: The story that Bacon died after stuffing a fowl with snow to test refrigeration comes from Aubrey, who had it from Hobbes. The Victorian claim that he wrote Shakespeare’s plays has no standing among scholars.

hobbes.sub: the materialist who derived the state from fear
world: A century of confessional war had made religion the central political problem of Europe rather than its solace. The Reformation split Christendom into rival churches. From the 1560s France, the Netherlands and finally the Empire fought over the consequences. The Thirty Years’ War, which ended three years before Leviathan, killed a large share of the German population. It settled nothing about doctrine, only about who would decide it.

England came late to the same crisis. Charles I ruled eleven years without parliament, then summoned two in 1640. The second fought him. The king was executed in January 1649, and England spent eleven years a commonwealth and protectorate. Hobbes wrote about the dissolution of a commonwealth while one dissolved around him. He thought the cause plain: authority had been divided between king, parliament, pulpit and common law.

Meanwhile the mechanical philosophy was replacing the Aristotelian one. Galileo had shown that motion, not rest, is a body’s natural state. Mersenne’s circle in Paris treated nature as matter in motion and geometry as the model science. Hobbes took that method whole, resolving the commonwealth into its parts in thought and reassembling it, which gives his politics its unnerving air of proof.
life: Born at Westport near Malmesbury in April 1588, son of a country vicar who abandoned the family. An uncle in the glove trade paid for his schooling and for Magdalen Hall, Oxford. In 1608 he entered the Cavendish household as tutor and secretary, and stayed attached to it for seventy years. According to Aubrey he came to geometry only at forty, opening a Euclid at the forty-seventh proposition and refusing to believe it until he had traced it back.

On the last of three long continental journeys he met Galileo in Florence and joined Mersenne’s circle in Paris. He fled to Paris in November 1640 as the Long Parliament assembled, having circulated a manuscript defending royal power. He stayed eleven years, tutoring the exiled Prince of Wales. Leviathan appeared in 1651. The exiled court read its attack on ecclesiastical power as betrayal. Hobbes went home and made peace with the Council of State.

The Restoration brought a royal pension and no safety. After the plague and Fire of 1666 a Commons committee proposed to examine Leviathan as a cause of atheism. Hobbes burned papers and never published on religion in England again. He fought John Wallis over mathematics into his eighties, and answered Bishop Bramhall on liberty and necessity. He died at Hardwick Hall in December 1679, aged ninety-one.

works.t: Eight Bookes of the Peloponnesian Warre (translation of Thucydides)
p: Hobbes’s first book, made from the Greek when English readers had only versions filtered through French and Latin. He published it, he said, because his countrymen needed to see what democracy had done to Athens. His preface calls Thucydides the most politic historiographer that ever writ. The choice fixed his temperament before any doctrine of his own existed: history as the record of what men do once restraint slips, and the Corcyra chapters on faction, where words change meaning to suit the violence.

works.t: The Elements of Law, Natural and Politic
works.y: circulated in manuscript 1640; printed without his authority 1650
p: Written as the Short Parliament collapsed and passed round among royalist gentlemen, this is the whole system in miniature. The first part takes human nature apart mechanically: sense is motion in the organs, imagination is decaying sense, deliberation an alternation of appetite and aversion, the will simply the last appetite before acting. The second part builds the commonwealth on that base. A printer split the manuscript in 1650 into Human Nature and De Corpore Politico without asking. So the first published version of Hobbes’s politics was a piracy.

Third in the plan of his philosophy and first into print, because, as he explained, his country was boiling with questions of right and obedience. Latin, ordered under the headings Liberty, Dominion and Religion, it is the most disciplined statement of the political theory. The natural condition appears as a war of all against all.
