The laws of nature are derived as theorems of self-preservation. Church power is folded into civil power. Continental readers, Pufendorf and Spinoza among them, met Hobbes through this book rather than through Leviathan.

works.t: Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Common-Wealth Ecclesiasticall and Civill
p: The argument runs from the mechanics of sensation to men without a common power. They are equal enough that any one may kill any other, they want the same scarce things, and no promise binds where nobody enforces it. So they are in a war of every man against every man, where there is no industry, no navigation, no arts, and the life of man is solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. This is not a claim about prehistory. Hobbes reaches it by taking a commonwealth apart in thought. In fact he can point only to approximations: civil war, and the posture of sovereign states towards each other.

The way out is a covenant of every man with every man authorising one man or assembly to act in the name of all. The sovereign is not party to it and cannot break it. He is an artificial person, and because his subjects author what he does they cannot justly complain of it. Authority must be undivided, since divided power is civil war postponed. Two limits survive: the right to preserve one’s life cannot be given away, and obligation lapses when the sovereign can no longer protect. Half the book concerns scripture and the church. Those pages had it called atheist within a year.

The foundation of the system, published thirteen years after the part meant to rest on it. Its subject is body and motion, which for Hobbes is every subject there is. Nothing is incorporeal, and to say otherwise is to misuse words. Sensation, memory and desire are motions in matter. Reasoning is computation, the adding and subtracting of names. The book also contained a claimed squaring of the circle. John Wallis, Savilian professor of geometry at Oxford, demolished it within months. The two abused each other in print for twenty years. Hobbes never conceded, and spent on the quarrel the credit his politics had left him.

works.y: written c. 1668, licence refused; pirated 1679, authorised edition 1682
p: Four dialogues on the causes of the civil war, submitted to Charles II, who refused a licence. So the book appeared in pirated form only in the year he died. It blames the war on seducers of opinion: Presbyterian preachers, Catholic clergy, universities teaching Aristotle’s politics, and gentlemen who had read Cicero and mistaken the Roman republic for a model. The history is partisan and often wrong in detail. But it states his conviction plainly: opinion is a material force, and a sovereign who does not govern doctrine will not govern long.

legacy: Hostility came first and lasted. Hobbism became a byword for atheism and moral licence. Bramhall, Clarendon and the Cambridge Platonists answered him at length. In 1683 Oxford condemned Leviathan and De Cive and burned copies. Most of the abuse was aimed at the materialism and the biblical criticism rather than at the politics. The two were rarely distinguished by men who wanted him silenced.

The serious uptake was continental. Spinoza and Pufendorf built on the derivation of civil right from self-preservation. How far Locke wrote against him is disputed, since the named target of the Two Treatises is Filmer. Rousseau thought him the one writer who had seen the problem clearly. Germany rediscovered him through Ferdinand Tönnies. Oakeshott’s edition of 1946 restored him to English philosophy. Taylor and Warrender argued that the laws of nature bind only as divine commands, which provoked decades of dispute.

What survives is the machinery. The state of nature as an analytical device is standard equipment in political theory and in game theory. Game theory formalised the Foole’s objection as a problem about cooperation. His account of representation, the sovereign as an artificial person whose acts are authored by those he represents, remains the sharpest statement of that puzzle. The common misuse is to file him among realists in international relations on the strength of one chapter.

The Latin version of 1668 was printed at Amsterdam by Blaeu, inside the collected Opera philosophica. No English licence was obtainable after 1666. Hobbes made it himself. In place of the Review and Conclusion he put an Appendix in three dialogues, on the Nicene creed, on heresy, and on the objections his book had drawn.

read.first: Leviathan parts one and two, in a modern-spelling edition with the 1651 frontispiece reproduced. Read chapters thirteen to eighteen twice.
read.note: Parts three and four are hard going. But they are half the book and the half that made him notorious, so a reader who skips them should say so.

hobbes.caveat: Whether Hobbes was an atheist, a heterodox Christian or a sincere if idiosyncratic one is genuinely unsettled. The late religious writings can be read either way.

descartes.sub: the doubter who rebuilt knowledge from one certainty
world: Descartes came of age inside the wars of religion and served in them. Educated by Jesuits at La Flèche, he enlisted with the Protestant Maurice of Nassau at Breda in 1618. A year later he enlisted with the Catholic Duke of Bavaria, as the Thirty Years’ War opened. He never wrote about the fighting and took no confessional side in print. The war shaped his life chiefly by keeping him moving.

In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo for holding that the earth moves. Descartes had almost finished Le Monde, whose whole structure required a moving earth. Learning the news that November, he told Mersenne he would rather suppress the work than publish a syllable disapproved by the Church. Everything afterwards was written with censors in view. The Discourse appeared anonymously. The Principles dressed the same cosmology in a formula by which the earth rests in the vortex carrying it.

He lived over twenty years in the Dutch Republic, which had cheap presses and no Inquisition. Even there he was pursued. Gisbertus Voetius, rector at Utrecht, had Cartesian teaching condemned in 1642 and pressed charges of atheism that took diplomatic help to blunt. His setting was the new mechanical philosophy, learned from Isaac Beeckman, who first showed him that physical problems could be posed mathematically.
life: Born in Touraine in 1596, he lost his mother in infancy. La Flèche, from 1606 or 1607 until 1614 or 1615, gave him eight or nine years of Jesuit mathematics and Aristotle. A law degree at Poitiers followed in 1616. Then he left for the army and met Beeckman in November 1618. On 10 November 1619, in a stove-heated room in Germany, he had three dreams that he took as a vocation to a unified science.

From 1628 he lived in the Dutch Republic, moving house constantly and corresponding with Europe through Mersenne. Le Monde was shelved in 1633. The Discourse and its three essays appeared in 1637, the Meditations in 1641. A daughter, Francine, was born in 1635 to a servant, Helena Jans van der Strom. She died of fever at five, a loss he called the greatest of his life.

In May 1643 Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, exiled at The Hague, wrote to ask how an unextended soul could move a body. The correspondence ran for years and produced the Passions of the Soul. Late in 1649 he accepted Queen Christina’s invitation to Sweden. There he found himself tutoring her at five in the morning through a northern winter. He caught pneumonia and died in February 1650.

works.t: Rules for the Direction of the Mind (Regulae ad directionem ingenii)
p: Thirty-six rules planned in three books of twelve, twenty-one written, the last three left as bare titles. The programme is already there: the sciences are one because they are one mind at work; only intuition and deduction yield knowledge; complex problems must be broken into their simplest components and rebuilt in order. Rule Four announces a universal mathematics of order and measure, whatever the subject. What is missing is metaphysics: no doubt, no God, no thinking substance. That absence is why the Rules matter: the method arrives first, as a mathematician’s working habit. The philosophy is built later to license it.

works.t: The World, or Treatise on Light (Le Monde), with the Treatise on Man
p: A complete mechanical cosmology. Descartes describes an imaginary matter in an imaginary space, gives it three laws of motion, and shows that it would settle into vortices carrying planets around stars — a world, he says, indistinguishable from ours, which asserts the earth’s motion without appearing to. The companion Treatise on Man explains the body as a hydraulic machine of nerves and valves, and claims that everything an animal does could be produced without a soul. Suppressed in 1633 and printed only after his death, it circulated in manuscript and supplied the physics of the Principles.

works.t: Discourse on the Method (Discours de la méthode), with the Dioptrics, Meteorology and Geometry
p: Published anonymously at Leiden in French. The Discourse is a preface: four rules of method, a provisional morality for living while one’s beliefs are under demolition, and a compressed sketch of the doubt and the cogito. The three essays were the demonstration that the method paid. The Meteorology gives the first quantitative geometry of the rainbow, computing by the law of refraction the angles that Theodoric of Freiberg had traced qualitatively around 1304. The Geometry fuses algebra with geometry, letting curves be handled as equations, and fixed the notation still used for knowns, unknowns and powers. Written obscurely on purpose, it became usable only through van Schooten’s Latin editions. That is how Newton and Leibniz received it.

works.t: Meditations on First Philosophy (Meditationes de prima philosophia), with the Objections and Replies
works.y: 1641; second edition with a seventh set of objections, 1642
p: Six days of first-person reasoning. The doubt is a demolition tool: the senses have deceived him, dreaming is not reliably distinguishable from waking, and an all-powerful deceiver could falsify even arithmetic. What survives is the doubting. Whenever the proposition is put forward it is necessarily true that he is, at minimum, a thing that thinks. Two proofs of God do the rebuilding: in the Third Meditation, that his idea of an infinite being requires a cause with as much reality as the idea represents; in the Fifth, that existence belongs to a supremely perfect being as three angles belong to a triangle. A God who does not deceive then guarantees whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived.

Descartes commissioned the Objections and Replies and printed them with the book. They are part of it, and skipping them removes the argument’s hardest test. Arnauld lands the blow still called the Cartesian circle, that clear and distinct perception is certified by God while God is proved by clear and distinct perception. Descartes distinguishes what is perceived now, indubitable while perceived, from what is merely remembered as proved. Most readers find that a real distinction and an insufficient answer.

works.y: 1644; French translation with a new preface, 1647
p: A textbook in numbered articles, meant to displace the scholastic manuals in Jesuit colleges. Part II makes matter identical with extension, denies the vacuum, and states laws of motion including the principle that a moving body continues in a straight line. Parts III and IV run the vortex cosmology. Much is wrong. His measure of motion is size times speed without direction, and his rules of impact are mostly false, as Huygens and Leibniz showed. It is still the first modern attempt at a complete physics deduced from stated principles. For fifty years it was the system Newton had to beat.

works.t: The Passions of the Soul (Les passions de l’âme)
p: Two hundred and twelve short articles, grown out of the letters to Elisabeth. The passions are perceptions in the soul caused by movements of the animal spirits. Descartes places their meeting in the pineal gland, chosen because it sits at the centre of the brain and, unlike the other parts, is not doubled. Two images from two eyes can therefore unite in one. Six passions are primitive — wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness. The remedy is not suppression but générosité, a settled self-esteem grounded in the free use of the will.

legacy: The durable objection came from Elisabeth. She asked how a thinking substance with no extension could determine the animal spirits to move, since pushing requires contact and surface. Descartes answered that the union of mind and body is a primitive notion, grasped in ordinary life rather than by the intellect. Elisabeth replied that she would sooner grant matter and extension to the soul than grant an immaterial thing the power to move a body. That is not an anecdote but the objection. No Cartesian ever met it.

His successors conceded the point. Cordemoy, Geulincx and Malebranche took causal interaction to be impossible and made God the agent on every occasion. Spinoza collapsed the two substances into one with thought and extension as attributes. Leibniz denied interaction and set the two in pre-established harmony. Gilbert Ryle’s Concept of Mind buried the whole picture in 1949 under the phrase the ghost in the machine.

The physics went down with Newton. The vortices were gone from French science by the 1740s. The mathematics did not go down: coordinate geometry is universal, and the notation of the 1637 Geometry is on every blackboard. Still contested is the reading, widespread since Reid, that Descartes trapped philosophy behind a veil of ideas. Recent scholarship pushes back: the doubt is a device internal to a constructive project. He also spent far more pages on optics and physiology than on doubting.

The caution did not finally save him. Louvain's theologians condemned his philosophy in 1662. In November 1663 Rome placed his works on the Index of Prohibited Books donec corrigantur, where they stayed.

read.first: The Meditations in an edition that prints the Objections and Replies, with the correspondence with Elisabeth read alongside the Sixth Meditation.
read.note: It is a short book that rewards slow reading. The argument moves in the transitions between meditations, not in the famous sentences.

descartes.caveat: The three dreams of November 1619 are known only from Baillet’s paraphrase of a notebook now lost. The occasional claim that Descartes was poisoned in Stockholm has no support among historians.

pascal.sub: who founded the calculus of chance and then bet everything on one throw
world: France under Richelieu and Mazarin was centralising, taxing and putting down revolts. Pascal's father was a tax official who lost his post for protesting a cut to government bonds and regained favour by being sent to assess taxes in Rouen — the drudgery that made his son build a calculating machine.

The other condition is Port-Royal. Jansenism held an Augustinian doctrine of grace against the Jesuits, and by the 1650s was under formal attack: the Sorbonne censured Arnauld in 1656, the convent was eventually dispersed and its buildings razed. Pascal's two great works are both products of that fight, one directly and one at a distance.
life: Born at Clermont in 1623 and taught at home by his father, who is said to have kept mathematics from him and been overruled by the boy's own rediscovery of geometry. At sixteen he wrote a theorem on conic sections that Descartes refused to believe was his. At nineteen he built the Pascaline to do his father's sums. In the 1640s he arranged the Puy-de-Dôme experiment, carrying a barometer up a mountain to show the mercury fell, which was evidence for the vacuum that Descartes denied could exist.

In 1654 he had, on the night of 23 November, an experience he recorded on a paper beginning Feu — fire — and sewed into his coat, where it was found after his death. He withdrew to Port-Royal, wrote the Provincial Letters anonymously while the censure of Arnauld was in progress, and spent his last years in pain, on an apology for Christianity he never assembled. He died in 1662, aged thirty-nine.

works.t: Correspondence with Fermat on the problem of points
p: A gambler's question: two players are interrupted mid-game, so how should the stake be divided? Pascal and Fermat answer it by asking not what has happened but what would have happened, and weighting each possible completion by its chance. That move — valuing an uncertain prospect by summing outcomes against their probabilities — is expected value, and with it the mathematics of decision under uncertainty begins. The Treatise on the Arithmetical Triangle, written the same year, sets out what is now called Pascal's triangle and, in passing, the first clear statement of proof by induction.

Eighteen anonymous letters defending Arnauld and attacking Jesuit casuistry, particularly the doctrine that one may follow any probable opinion even if a more probable one opposes it. Pascal's device is to let a complacent Jesuit explain his own position at length and to say almost nothing in reply. The letters were condemned and burned, and they made moral laxity the accusation the Society could never afterwards shake. Voltaire, who agreed with nothing in them, called them the first work of French prose.

Some hundreds of notes toward an unfinished apology, found after his death and arranged by others, which is why editions disagree about their order. The wager treats belief as a decision rather than a proposition. Whatever the odds, an infinite payoff dominates a finite stake, so the rational act is to bet on God. Pascal then adds that the person convinced by the argument still will not believe, and must act as if he did until habit does the rest. Elsewhere: the heart has reasons reason does not know; first principles are known without proof, so reason cannot ground itself; man is a thinking reed, crushed by a universe that does not know it is crushing him.

legacy: The mathematics propagated immediately and anonymously. Huygens turned the Fermat correspondence into the first printed treatise on probability in 1657, and everything from insurance to statistical inference sits on the notion of expectation the two of them worked out in a summer. Decision theory is the direct descendant, and the wager is still the standard first example in it, usually with the objection that infinite utilities break the framework.

The Pensées had a different audience. Voltaire attacked them at length and thereby kept them in print. The nineteenth century made Pascal a precursor of existentialism, which Kierkegaard's admiration and Nietzsche's furious respect both encourage — Nietzsche calls him the only logical Christian and says Christianity ruined him. The claim that reason cannot certify its own starting points is now more often credited to others, but it is stated flatly in the fragments.

read.first: The Pensées in Krailsheimer's translation, which follows the Lafuma order. Read the wager fragment, the thinking reed, and the two orders; then the first four Provincial Letters for the prose.
read.note: Editions number the fragments differently. Lafuma and Sellier follow the two surviving copies of Pascal's own arrangement; Brunschvicg regroups them by topic and is easier to browse but further from the manuscript.

pascal.caveat: The arrangement of the Pensées is an editorial act, and how much of an argument the finished book would have made is unknowable. Readings that depend on the order of the fragments should be treated with care.

spinoza.sub: the rationalist who made God identical with nature
world: Spinoza's Dutch Republic was the richest state in Europe and the least conventional: a federation without a king, run by merchant regents. From 1650 the stadtholderate stood empty. From 1653 Johan de Witt governed as Grand Pensionary. In 1672 the French invaded, a mob tore De Witt apart in The Hague, and the republican experiment ended.

Amsterdam's Portuguese Jewish community was two generations old, built by converso families who had lived outwardly as Catholics in Iberia and had to relearn a Judaism they had lost. Its rabbis policed orthodoxy hard, because the toleration they enjoyed was conditional. The city's presses printed what no other city would, often behind false imprints.

Descartes had lived in the Republic for two decades and left it quarrelling: Utrecht condemned his philosophy in 1642, Leiden restricted its teaching. Optics was the growth science. Christiaan Huygens ground lenses a short walk from his rooms in Voorburg. He took his living from lenses and his vocabulary, though not his conclusions, from Descartes.

What that toleration would not cover was shown in 1668. Adriaan Koerbagh, of Spinoza's own circle, published in Dutch and under his own name that God is identical with nature and that miracles are impossible. He was tried for blasphemy and died in prison the next year. The Theological-Political Treatise appeared within two years, anonymously and in Latin.
life: Born in Amsterdam in November 1632 to a Portuguese merchant family, Spinoza left the congregation's school before rabbinic training and ran the import business after his father died in 1654. On 27 July 1656, aged twenty-three, the Talmud Torah congregation pronounced a herem on him in terms far harsher than its usual formula, forbidding anyone to come within four cubits. It names no doctrine, and was never lifted.

He studied Latin with Franciscus van den Enden, an ex-Jesuit with radical politics, and by 1661 had left Amsterdam for Rijnsburg, then Voorburg, then The Hague. He ground lenses for telescopes and microscopes, skilled work Huygens took seriously, and lived on that and subsidies from friends. In 1673 he declined a chair at Heidelberg, doubting the promised freedom would reach far enough.

Publication was governed by calculation: one book under his name, one anonymously and ruinously, the rest withheld. He died at The Hague on 21 February 1677, aged forty-four, of a lung complaint that glass dust probably worsened. Within the year his friends printed the Opera Posthuma with only his initials on the title page. The States of Holland banned it in 1678.

works.t: Short Treatise on God, Man, and His Well-Being (Korte Verhandeling van God, de Mensch en deszelvs Welstand)
p: The earliest full statement of the system, written for a circle of friends and never printed. The Latin original is lost. What survives are two Dutch translations, unnoticed until the middle of the nineteenth century. The doctrines are already recognisable — one infinite substance, thought and extension as its attributes, the passions as forms of inadequate knowledge, salvation as the mind's union with God. The manner is not. It argues in ordinary prose, with dialogues, scholastic apparatus and traces of Descartes and of Neoplatonic sources. It is loose where the Ethics is exact. Its value is evidential: the mature metaphysics was in place long before the geometrical order was imposed on it.

works.t: Descartes' Principles of Philosophy (Renati Des Cartes Principiorum Philosophiae Pars I et II, more geometrico demonstratae)
p: This was the only book Spinoza published under his own name. It began as tutoring: he was taking a student, Johannes Casearius, through Descartes. Friends persuaded him to write it up. What he produced is Descartes' metaphysics and physics recast as definitions, axioms and demonstrated propositions — the first sustained trial of the method he would later turn on his own philosophy. Lodewijk Meyer's preface warns that the author does not accept everything he here proves, singling out free will and the real distinction between mind and body. Appended is Metaphysical Thoughts, scholastic definitions handled with visible impatience. The book made his European reputation as an expositor of Descartes, which is not what he was.

Published anonymously with a false imprint naming a Hamburg printer who did not exist. The sheets came from Jan Rieuwertsz in Amsterdam. Its programme is to separate theology from philosophy so that neither can discipline the other. Prophecy is vivid imagination, not superior knowledge. Miracles cannot break a natural order that is God's own nature. Scripture must be read like any other ancient document, and read that way it teaches obedience and justice, not physics. He denies that Moses wrote the Pentateuch and points to a later compiler. The closing chapters defend freedom of thought as a condition of civil peace. Church councils condemned it. The States of Holland banned it in 1674.

works.t: Treatise on the Emendation of the Intellect (Tractatus de Intellectus Emendatione)
p: Spinoza's one piece of autobiographical writing, and he abandoned it. It opens with a man who has learned that wealth, honour and pleasure are not worth what they cost, and who sets out to find a good whose enjoyment is continuous. The method follows: four ways of perceiving, from hearsay through vague experience and inference to the direct grasp of a thing through its essence, only the last counting as knowledge. He then turns to what makes a definition true. The text breaks off mid-argument. Beside the Ethics it shows what the geometrical order was for — not proof as ornament, but a cure for the intellect.

Five parts, built from definitions and axioms through numbered propositions, with scholia where Spinoza argues in his own voice. Part I proves there can be only one substance: a substance is in itself and conceived through itself, two sharing an attribute could not be told apart, and none can produce another. It is infinite, and it is God, or Nature. Its attributes are what the intellect perceives as its essence. Of infinitely many we know two, thought and extension. Everything else is a mode, nothing is contingent, and purpose in nature is a human projection.

Part II makes mind and body one thing under two attributes, so the order of ideas is the order of things. Part III grounds the emotions in the conatus, each thing's striving to persevere in its being. Parts IV and V argue that we are enslaved by affects we do not understand and freed by understanding them. Knowledge comes in three kinds — imagination, reason, and the intuition that moves from God's essence to the essence of particular things. The third yields the intellectual love of God, part of God's love of himself. He had it ready in 1675, heard what Amsterdam was saying, and took it home.

Written in his last two years and stopped by his death in the chapter on democracy. Where the earlier treatise argued for freedom, this one asks how institutions can be built so freedom does not depend on the character of whoever holds office. Right extends exactly as far as power. Men are moved by passion. A constitution must be arranged so that officials acting from ambition and fear produce the common good anyway. Spinoza works through monarchy, aristocracy and democracy in turn, sizing councils so faction is unprofitable. The debt to Machiavelli is acknowledged in the text. It is the least read of his books, and plainly the work of a man who had watched a republic collapse.

legacy: For a century his name was an accusation. Spinozist meant atheist. Refutations were printed by men who knew him only through Pierre Bayle's hostile article. The books circulated anyway, in Latin and in clandestine French, through the manuscript underground of the early Enlightenment. John Toland, who coined the word pantheist, was among the readers.

Rehabilitation came in Germany, and suddenly. In 1785 Friedrich Jacobi published his account of a conversation in which Lessing confessed himself a Spinozist. The Pantheismusstreit that followed with Moses Mendelssohn made Spinoza's God the central question of German letters. Goethe read the Ethics all his life. Hegel held that one must be a Spinozist before one can be a philosopher.

Two lines outlived the metaphysics. The historical reading of Scripture set out in the Theological-Political Treatise became ordinary biblical scholarship. Its case for free expression became ordinary liberalism. Since the 1960s the Ethics has been read again as a philosophy of mind and emotion, by Gilles Deleuze and by naturalists who want affect without a soul.

read.first: Begin with the Theological-Political Treatise, which is written in continuous prose and shows the mind working, then take the Ethics in a modern annotated translation with the letters bound in.
read.note: Read the Ethics by following the scholia and appendices first and picking up the demonstrations on a second pass. Going straight through from Part I proposition one defeats most readers.

spinoza.caveat: The grounds of the 1656 herem are nowhere recorded, so every account of why he was expelled — his metaphysics, a dispute over his father's estate, his associations outside the community — is reconstruction.

locke.sub: the mind as white paper, and government as a trust
world: Locke was born in 1632 into a country sliding toward civil war. His father, a Somerset attorney, rode as a captain of parliamentary horse. He entered Westminster School in 1647, a few hundred yards from the scaffold where Charles I was executed. He welcomed the Restoration. His earliest political writing defended the magistrate’s right to impose forms of worship. The Clarendon Code then made dissent a crime. Toleration became for him a practical question before it was a principled one.

His other setting was the new experimental philosophy and the Atlantic trade beside it. Locke assisted Robert Boyle, practised medicine with Thomas Sydenham, absorbed the corpuscularian account of matter that underwrites his primary and secondary qualities. He also served the Lords Proprietors of Carolina, helped draft their Fundamental Constitutions in 1669, held stock in the Royal African Company, and sat on the Board of Trade from 1696.

Then came the crisis that produced his politics. The Exclusion Crisis of 1679 to 1681 was fought over whether parliament could bar a Catholic heir from the throne. Royalists reprinted Filmer’s Patriarcha in 1680 as ammunition for divine right. Shaftesbury lost. After the Rye House Plot of 1683 his associates fled or died. Locke spent five years in the Dutch Republic, where toleration was practised well ahead of any English theory of it.
life: Educated at Westminster and at Christ Church from 1652, Locke found the scholastic curriculum sterile and drifted into medicine, chemistry and experimental work. He was elected to the Royal Society in 1668. He kept his Christ Church studentship until Charles II ordered him stripped of it in 1684. The clinical habit — observe, record, distrust systems — runs through everything he wrote.

In 1666 he met Anthony Ashley Cooper, soon Earl of Shaftesbury, and joined his household the next year. In 1668 he organised the operation that drained an abscess on Shaftesbury’s liver and probably saved his life. Thereafter he was physician, secretary and political agent to the most dangerous politician in England. The Essay began in 1671, when friends in his rooms stuck on a question of morality and revealed religion. Locke proposed they first examine what the understanding is fit for. He spent 1675 to 1679 in France, returned into the Exclusion Crisis, and in 1683 fled to Holland under an assumed name.

He came back in the fleet that carried Princess Mary and published nearly everything within a year: the Epistola de Tolerantia in Latin at Gouda in 1689 and in English soon after; the Two Treatises anonymously late in 1689, dated 1690; the Essay in December, the only one under his name. He acknowledged the anonymous books only in a codicil to his will. He spent his last years as a paying guest of the Mashams at Oates in Essex, defending the Essay against Bishop Stillingfleet until his death on 28 October 1704.

p: Four books and some twenty years of work, aimed at fixing what people can know before they quarrel about what they cannot. Book I attacks innate principles: if truths were stamped on every mind, children and the mentally impaired would have them. Book II builds the positive account — the mind as white paper furnished by sensation and by reflection on its own operations. It distinguishes the extension, shape and motion that bodies really have from the colour, sound and taste that are only powers to produce sensations in us.

The chapter on identity, inserted in 1694, makes personal identity a matter of continuity of consciousness rather than of soul or body, treats person as a forensic term, and supplies the prince and the cobbler. Book III argues that our species terms mark essences of our own making. Book IV defines knowledge as the perception of agreement among ideas. It also allows that God might have superadded thought to matter, which brought Stillingfleet down on him.

The First Treatise is a patient demolition of Filmer’s claim that kings inherit Adam’s paternal authority. The Second builds from a state of nature that is a condition under a law of nature knowable by reason. In it each person owns himself and acquires property by mixing his labour with what is common, subject to leaving enough and as good for others and taking nothing that spoils. Consent to the use of money then lets holdings become unequal before any government exists. Political power is not dominion but a trust held for the public good. When rulers break the trust, power devolves to the people.

Peter Laslett’s edition of 1960 dated the composition to the Exclusion Crisis, with the Second Treatise written first. On that dating it is not a decorous justification of 1688 after the fact, but a revolutionary manuscript published, with a new preface, once a revolution had made it safe. The chapter on slavery defines it as a state of war continued between a lawful conqueror and a captive, which cannot license hereditary chattel slavery. That sits badly beside Locke’s Royal African Company stock and his work on a Carolina constitution granting masters absolute power over their slaves. Scholars divide over whether this is hypocrisy, a built-in exemption, or a contradiction he never confronted.

works.t: A Letter concerning Toleration (Epistola de Tolerantia)
p: Written in Dutch exile for his friend Philipp van Limborch and published anonymously, it rests on two claims: the magistrate’s commission covers life, liberty and estate, not souls; and force could not do the work anyway, since penalties act on the will while belief follows what the mind takes to be true. Locke separates the church, a voluntary society, from the commonwealth. The limits are as revealing as the argument: nothing for those whose allegiance runs to a foreign prince, and nothing for atheists, whose promises he thought could not bind.

Assembled from letters written in exile to his friend Edward Clarke about the upbringing of Clarke’s son, it addresses the education of a gentleman. Locke wants habit rather than precept: a hardened body, plain food, early rising, and virtue and breeding before book learning. He is contemptuous of rote Latin grammar, hostile to beating except for obstinacy, and insistent that curiosity be encouraged rather than corrected. The book ran through many editions and translations. Rousseau engaged with it closely.

works.t: The Reasonableness of Christianity, as Delivered in the Scriptures
p: Published anonymously and argued entirely from scripture, it asks what a person must believe to be a Christian and answers: that Jesus is the Messiah, with repentance and an honest effort at obedience. Everything else is left as matter for study rather than a condition of salvation. The strategy matches the Essay: hold faith to what the evidence supports, and the grounds for excluding people shrink. John Edwards attacked it as Socinian, and Locke replied twice while still refusing to admit authorship.

legacy: The Essay dominated British philosophy for a century. Voltaire made it the centrepiece of his account of England, Condillac rebuilt it in France, and Leibniz wrote a chapter-by-chapter reply published only in 1765. Berkeley and Hume then pushed the way of ideas further than Locke wanted. The chapter on personal identity drew Butler’s objection that remembering an action presupposes the identity it was meant to constitute, and Reid’s brave officer, who by Locke’s criterion both is and is not the boy he once was. The modern literature still starts there.

The Two Treatises travelled a stranger road. Little cited in the 1690s, it was absorbed into the eighteenth-century Whig canon and carried to the colonies. It stands behind the American Declaration’s life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. Twentieth-century scholarship unsettled that inheritance. Laslett and John Dunn relocated the book in the theological world of 1681, arguing that its foundations are more Calvinist than liberal, while C. B. Macpherson read it as a charter of possessive individualism.

His letter on toleration has the longest afterlife of anything he wrote. Its exclusions are now taught alongside it, as the measure of how narrow even the generous position was in 1689. Beside that sits the ledger of his colonial employment. The man who wrote that no one may be subjected to the arbitrary will of another held stock in the Royal African Company from 1672 until he sold it in 1675, and in the Bahama Adventurers besides. That is not a footnote, and explaining it is now a standing question in political thought.

Locke’s preface warns that the reader has only the beginning and end of the discourse, the papers that should have filled the middle being, in his words, more than all the rest. The First Treatise breaks off in mid-sentence. What survives is less than half of what he wrote.

read.first: Read the Second Treatise whole. It is short and the argument moves. Follow it with the Letter concerning Toleration, then take the Essay in selections rather than straight through: Book II chapters 1 to 8 and 27, and Book IV chapters 1 to 4 and 15 to 19.
read.note: Locke repeats himself and digresses. Good editions mark the chapters he added after 1690, which is worth knowing before treating any of it as a single finished system.

locke.caveat: The composition dates of the Two Treatises rest on internal and circumstantial evidence and are still argued over. So is how much of the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina Locke authored rather than transcribed for his employers.

leibniz.sub: the polymath who built reality out of windowless minds
world: Leibniz's Germany was the one that came out of the Thirty Years War. The peace of 1648 left the Empire a patchwork of several hundred principalities, its confessional boundaries frozen and its population reduced by a third in places. Power lay with dynastic courts. An able commoner made his career as a jurist in somebody's chancery.

His working life coincided with the building of the learned institutions: the Royal Society founded in 1660 and chartered in 1662, the Paris Academy in 1666, the Acta Eruditorum at Leipzig in 1682. Europe could now publish a result in months rather than decades. Leibniz used all three, and supplemented them with a correspondence running to some fifteen thousand letters.

Louis XIV's wars framed his diplomacy. The confessional split framed his theology. He spent years on schemes to reunite the Catholic and Protestant churches, and more on the dynastic history meant to secure his employers' claim to an electorate and, in 1714, the British throne. The metaphysics was written in the margins of that salaried work.
life: Leibniz was born at Leipzig on 1 July 1646, the son of a professor who died when the boy was six. He taught himself Latin in his father's library and matriculated at fourteen. His Dissertation on the Art of Combinations of 1666 already carries the ambition he never gave up: a characteristica universalis in which reasoning becomes computation and disputants need only say, let us calculate. Leipzig withheld his doctorate in law. Altdorf granted it in 1667 and offered a chair, which he refused.

He entered the service of the Elector of Mainz and in 1672 was sent to Paris on a diplomatic errand. He stayed four years, and they made him. Huygens taught him mathematics from close to scratch. By 1675 he had the differential and integral calculus, in the notation still used. He also built a calculating machine that multiplied and divided by a stepped drum, and showed it in London.

From 1676 until his death he served the dukes of Brunswick at Hanover as librarian, councillor and court historian. A scheme to drain the Harz silver mines with windmills failed. The family history was never finished. He founded the Berlin society of sciences in 1700. The priority quarrel with Newton's partisans darkened his last decade. A Royal Society committee found against him in April 1712, and Newton had drafted the report it printed in 1713 as the Commercium Epistolicum. The modern verdict is independent discovery, Newton earlier, Leibniz first into print in 1684.

p: Thirty-seven short articles drafted at speed during a winter at the Harz mines, sent to Antoine Arnauld as a list of headings, and not printed for a hundred and sixty years. The core claim concerns individual substances. The complete concept of an individual contains everything that will ever be true of it. So anyone grasping the concept of Alexander would read off every one of his conquests. From this Leibniz derives that substances never act on one another, that each expresses the whole universe from its own position, and that God chose this world because it yields the greatest variety of phenomena by the simplest laws. Nearly every later doctrine is here in outline except the word monad.

Arnauld read the headings and replied that complete concepts made everything necessary and destroyed freedom. If the notion of Adam already contains the fall, God could not have created Adam and withheld the fall. The exchange that followed was conducted through a landgrave acting as intermediary. It forced Leibniz to distinguish the necessity of a demonstration from the certainty of what a free agent will in fact choose. It forced him also to explain how a body can be a genuine substance rather than a heap. Here he first states the harmony openly: substances agree not because they touch but because each was made to unfold in step with all the others. Arnauld conceded politely and stayed unconvinced.

works.t: New Essays on Human Understanding (Nouveaux essais sur l'entendement humain)
p: A chapter-by-chapter reply to Locke's Essay, cast as a conversation between Philalethes, who speaks Locke's text almost verbatim, and Theophilus, who answers. Locke died in October 1704, just as the manuscript was finished. Leibniz judged it unfair to publish against a man who could not reply. The book waited sixty-one years. Its central move saves innate ideas by making them dispositions rather than furniture: the mind is not a blank tablet but veined marble, whose grain the sculptor follows. To the maxim that nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses, he adds the exception of the intellect itself. The doctrine of minute unnoticed perceptions, which combine into the roar of the sea, is worked out here.

works.t: Theodicy (Essais de Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu, la liberté de l'homme et l'origine du mal)
p: The only philosophical book Leibniz published as a book, written in French for the salon audience of Sophie Charlotte of Prussia and aimed at Pierre Bayle. Bayle had argued that the existence of evil cannot be reconciled with reason and that faith must be held against it. Leibniz answers that God, surveying infinitely many possible worlds, actualised the best on balance. Evil, he answers, comes in three kinds: metaphysical, which is simply the finitude of creatures; physical suffering; and moral sin, which God permits without willing. The argument defends the choice of the whole, not the goodness of any particular misfortune. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, Voltaire made Pangloss out of it. The caricature has outlived the book.

Ninety numbered paragraphs written in Vienna, compressing the whole system for a reader who had not followed the correspondence. Since composites must be made of simples, the real things are simple substances: monads, without parts or shape, incapable of natural generation or destruction. They have no windows, because nothing can get into or out of what has no parts. What they have instead is perception, which represents the rest of the universe from a single point of view, and appetition, which drives the passage from one perception to the next. No two are alike, since things sharing all their properties would be one thing. Bodies are well-founded appearances of aggregates. The apparent traffic between mind and body is pre-established harmony, set at creation.

Its companion, the Principles of Nature and Grace Founded on Reason, was written in the same year for Prince Eugene of Savoy and printed in 1718. The 1720 publication of the Monadology was Heinrich Köhler's German translation, which also supplied the title. The French text Leibniz wrote waited until 1840.

Five letters and five replies, passed through Caroline, Princess of Wales, with Samuel Clarke writing for Newton and almost certainly with his help. Leibniz opened by charging that Newtonian physics makes God an incompetent clockmaker who must periodically rewind his own machine. He charged too that gravity acting at a distance is an occult quality dressed as science. The exchange then turned to space and time. If space were an absolute container there could be no sufficient reason for God to place the universe here rather than three feet east, and two arrangements differing only in position would be indiscernible and therefore identical. Space must instead be the order of coexisting things. Leibniz died before answering the fifth letter, and Clarke published the set.

legacy: Christian Wolff turned the philosophy into a textbook system that held the German universities for half a century. It was that version, not Leibniz himself, that Kant demolished and Voltaire ridiculed. Much of what histories call dogmatic metaphysics is in fact Wolff. The New Essays arrived in 1765 too late to change that quarrel and just in time to complicate it.

The papers stayed in Hanover. Leibniz left something on the order of two hundred thousand sheets, most never printed. The discipline has been catching up ever since: the French Monadology in 1840, the Discourse and the Arnauld letters in 1846, the logical papers in 1903. The critical edition begun in 1923 is still incomplete.

Louis Couturat and Bertrand Russell, working separately around 1900, argued that the metaphysics falls out of a logic of subject and predicate. That reading made Leibniz suddenly interesting to analytic philosophers, and is still contested. Frege's successors delivered a fragment of the characteristica. The binary arithmetic he published in 1703 became the arithmetic of machines.

read.first: Read the Discourse on Metaphysics with the Arnauld correspondence in the same volume, then the Monadology. A good selected-writings edition carrying the shorter essays and letters is worth more than any single book.
read.note: The short pieces are not digests of a hidden magnum opus. There is no such book, and the philosophy exists mostly as occasional writing addressed to particular correspondents.

leibniz.caveat: Leibniz did not title the Monadology. Many drafts carry no date. The chronology of the unpublished writings is still adjusted as the critical edition proceeds.

berkeley.caveat: Part II of the Principles was lost in manuscript and never rewritten. His account of spirits and of our knowledge of other minds survives only in scattered remarks.
legacy: The standard reception has been a misreading. Samuel Johnson kicked a stone and said he refuted him thus, which misses the argument, since Berkeley never doubted that stones are hard and stop the foot. Kant distinguished his own transcendental idealism from what he called Berkeley's dogmatic version. Thomas Reid rejected the premise that what we perceive are ideas rather than things.

What survived was the method. Hume took over the attack on abstract ideas and dropped the God. Mill's account of matter as permanent possibilities of sensation and the sense-data theories of the early twentieth century are Berkeleian in structure. The vision essay founded a durable programme in perceptual psychology. The Analyst stands as an outsider's objection the professionals had to concede.
life: Kilkenny College, then Trinity from 1700 and a fellowship in 1707. His first book, An Essay towards a New Theory of Vision of 1709, argued that distance cannot be seen but is inferred from cues we have read since infancy. It argued too that sight and touch share no ideas at all, so their connection is learned, like a language. Two more books followed before he was twenty-eight.

He went to London in 1713, wrote for Steele's Guardian and befriended Swift and Pope. In Italy he lost the manuscript of the second part of the Principles. De Motu of 1721 turned his criticism on force and absolute space. From 1728 he waited three years at Newport, Rhode Island, for a parliamentary grant for a Bermuda college that never came, writing Alciphron against the freethinkers. As Bishop of Cloyne from 1734 he promoted tar-water in Siris, his best-seller. He died at Oxford in 1753.

read.first: Start with the Three Dialogues, which state the whole position in accessible form. Turn to the Principles afterwards, for the compressed argument and the introduction on abstraction.
read.note: Hold on to the fact that he denies an unperceivable substrate, not the reality of ordinary objects. Readers who forget this spend their time arguing with a position he never held.

berkeley.sub: the immaterialist who denied matter to defend common sense

p: The introduction attacks abstract general ideas: nobody can form the idea of a triangle that is neither equilateral nor scalene. The puzzles requiring such ideas are self-inflicted. The body argues that sensible things are collections of ideas, that an idea can resemble nothing but another idea, and that matter — an unperceiving substrate beneath the qualities — is not merely unknown but unintelligible. What exist are minds and their ideas. Berkeley is not denying that the table is there. He denies that anything stands behind its perceptible qualities. He holds that their orderly succession is God's doing.
works.t: A Treatise concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, Part I

p: Incomprehension greeted the Principles, so Berkeley wrote it again as a conversation. Hylas begins a confident materialist and is walked through the collapse of the distinction between primary and secondary qualities. If heat and colour are mind-dependent because they vary with the perceiver, so are extension and figure. The case for God is clearest here: ideas of sense arrive involuntarily and in order, so another mind must produce them. And so is the insistence that immaterialism defends common sense rather than undermining it.
works.t: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous

p: Addressed to an unnamed infidel mathematician, generally taken to be Halley. Berkeley grants that the calculus reaches true results and asks how: computing a fluxion supposes an increment, divides by it, then makes it vanish, which is to have the quantity both ways. His famous phrase calls such vanishing increments the ghosts of departed quantities. He proposes that the right answers come from a compensation of errors. He adds that men who swallow this should not scorn the mysteries of religion. The objection was sound and was not properly met until limits were made rigorous.

world: Berkeley was born in 1685 into the Protestant minority that governed Ireland after the Williamite victory. It was perhaps a tenth of the population, holding most of the land, insulated by penal laws that shut Catholics out of office and the professions. Trinity College Dublin, where he spent his twenties, was that establishment's only college. He belonged to it entirely.

The intellectual weather in London was Newtonian and nervous. The Principia had settled physics. What it had not settled was what the new science implied about God. Freethinkers from John Toland to Bernard Mandeville were drawing conclusions the clergy disliked. Berkeley's career answers that situation: a defence of religion aimed not at the new science but at the metaphysics of matter grown up beside it.

montesquieu.sub: the comparatist who made liberty a matter of structure
world: Montesquieu came of age under the Regency. Louis XIV died in 1715. Philippe d’Orléans loosened the court, restored the parlements to political life, and let John Law build a paper-credit system that collapsed in 1720. Bordeaux, where Montesquieu owned vineyards and sat as a magistrate, lived by wine and the colonial trades. He watched money and law move together long before theorising the connection.

Censorship set the other condition. Books like his could not be printed openly in France. The Persian Letters therefore appeared in Amsterdam under a false imprint and The Spirit of the Laws in Geneva, both anonymous, both smuggled back over the frontier. Rome placed the second on the Index in 1751 and the Sorbonne prepared a censure. His Defence of 1750 conceded almost nothing.
life: Charles-Louis de Secondat was born at La Brède near Bordeaux in 1689 and trained in law. An uncle left him in 1716 the barony and the office of président à mortier in the Parlement of Bordeaux. Finding the work tedious, he sold the office in 1726 and moved to Paris, where the Persian Letters had made him famous. The Académie française elected him in 1728.

Then he travelled: Italy, Austria, Hungary, Holland, and England from 1729 to 1731, where he watched Parliament sit and was made a fellow of the Royal Society. Back at La Brède he spent some twenty years reading and dictating, and went nearly blind before finishing. The Spirit of the Laws appeared in 1748. He died in Paris in 1755, and d’Alembert eulogised him in the Encyclopédie.

p: Two Persians travel to France and write home. The letters are printed as though authentic. The device lets Montesquieu describe French religion, medicine and monarchy as a stranger would describe something arbitrary. The fable of the Troglodytes sketches a virtuous republic that cannot last. The joke cuts both ways: while the travellers philosophise about liberty, the harem they left behind decays into revolt and murder. The book sold hugely, was pirated within months, and fixed the century’s favourite manoeuvre — making the familiar look contingent by viewing it from outside.

works.t: Considerations on the Causes of the Greatness of the Romans and their Decline (Considérations sur les causes de la grandeur des Romains et de leur décadence)
p: A short history with a thesis, published anonymously at Amsterdam between his famous books. Rome rose and fell, Montesquieu argues, not by fortune or by the qualities of particular men but through general causes working over centuries: the constitution of the legions, the distribution of land, the corrosion of civic manners by conquest and wealth. Explanation in history becomes a search for structural causes rather than a gallery of characters. The book reads best as the workshop for his masterpiece, where the same method is turned on every polity at once.

works.t: The Spirit of the Laws (De l’esprit des lois)
p: Laws are relations: they answer to climate, soil, commerce, religion and the temper of a people, so a law suiting one nation may destroy another. He sorts governments into republics, monarchies and despotisms, each with an animating principle — virtue, honour, fear. He argues in Book XI that English liberty rests on holding legislative, executive and judicial power apart, so that power checks power. The climate chapters, deriving character from cold air on nerve fibres, are the weak joint. On slavery he is divided: Book XV carries the ironic defence abolitionists quoted for a century and, later, climatic arguments conceding servitude may suit hot countries.

legacy: The Americans read him hardest. Delegates at Philadelphia in 1787 and in the ratifying conventions cited him on both sides of every question. Madison, defending the constitution in Federalist 47, called him the oracle always consulted on the separation of powers. He then spent the paper explaining that Montesquieu never meant the branches to be wholly separate. Blackstone had already carried the doctrine into English law.

In France the reputation ran otherwise. Voltaire mocked the climate theory. The physiocrats found him unsystematic. Durkheim and later Raymond Aron claimed him as a founder of sociology for treating institutions as facts with causes. The climate chapters are dead. What survives is the comparative method, the insistence that liberty is an effect of arrangement rather than of intention, and one ironic page on slavery.

read.first: Start with the Persian Letters for the voice, then read The Spirit of the Laws selectively: Books I to III on the kinds of government, Book XI on England and the separation of powers, and Book XV on slavery. Use an edition keeping the original book and chapter numbers.
read.note: The Spirit of the Laws is built of very short chapters and rewards sampling. Read straight through, the accumulation of examples buries the argument.

montesquieu.caveat: How to weigh his treatment of slavery is genuinely contested. The ironic chapter of Book XV is unambiguous, but the climatic arguments a few chapters later are not. Scholars disagree over whether the book is an abolitionist document or a divided one.

voltaire.sub: the campaigner who made toleration a public cause
world: France under Louis XV licensed what could be printed and punished what could not: the Parlement of Paris burned books, the Sorbonne censured, the Bastille held writers without trial. The counterweight was commercial. Presses in Amsterdam, Geneva and Neuchâtel printed what Paris forbade. Pedlars carried the sheets in bales back over the frontier, so that a condemned book usually sold better than a licensed one.

Two events set his late direction. The Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755 killed tens of thousands on a feast day and made cheerful providence look obscene. The Seven Years’ War cost France Canada and India at the peace of 1763. In March 1762 the parlement of Toulouse had the Protestant merchant Jean Calas broken on the wheel for a murder he almost certainly did not commit.
life: François-Marie Arouet was born in Paris in 1694 and educated by Jesuits at Louis-le-Grand. He took the name Voltaire around his first success, the tragedy Oedipe of 1718, having spent eleven months in the Bastille for verses mocking the Regent. In 1726 the servants of the Chevalier de Rohan beat him in the street. When he pressed for a duel he was jailed and exiled, and spent three years in England.

The rest was flight and accumulation. He lived from 1734 with Émilie du Châtelet at Cirey, working on Newton; served Louis XV as historiographer; quarrelled with Frederick II after three years in Berlin; and, grown rich by speculation, bought Ferney in 1758, a few hours from the Swiss border, where he ran a watchmaking colony and conducted his campaigns by post. He died in Paris in 1778.

works.t: Letters concerning the English Nation (Lettres philosophiques)
p: Twenty-five short letters report on Quakers, Anglicans, Parliament, inoculation, commerce, Locke and Newton, and end by attacking Pascal. The method is comparison by implication: describing a country where dissenters trade peaceably and a merchant is honoured indicts France without naming it. The Parlement of Paris ordered the French edition burned in 1734. A warrant went out for the author, who withdrew to Cirey. The Elements of Newton’s Philosophy of 1738, written there with du Châtelet, did the harder work of explaining attraction and optics to readers raised on Descartes’s vortices.

works.t: Zadig, or Destiny (Zadig, ou la Destinée) and Candide, or Optimism (Candide, ou l’Optimisme)
p: Both are short, fast, and built to break a doctrine. Zadig tests providence through an oriental romance in which an angel justifies calamity and leaves the justification looking thin. Candide finishes the job: Pangloss keeps insisting that all is for the best while the earthquake, the Inquisition, the war and the mutilated slave in Surinam accumulate. It is less an argument against Leibniz than a demonstration that the argument cannot be held in the presence of the facts. The closing instruction to cultivate the garden is deliberately modest, and has been over-read ever since.

works.t: Treatise on Toleration (Traité sur la tolérance) and Philosophical Dictionary (Dictionnaire philosophique portatif)
p: The Treatise was written into a live case. Voltaire took up the Calas family, paid for lawyers and printing, and flooded Europe with pamphlets until the judgment was quashed in 1765. The book argues from the trial outward to the claim that civil peace requires the state to stop enforcing doctrine. The Dictionary is the same campaign in fragments, alphabetical and pocket-sized so it could be smuggled: brief entries on the soul, miracles, prophecies and fanaticism, ridiculing scripture with a straight face. Both books were publicly burned, and both were promptly reprinted everywhere.

legacy: The Revolution moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1791. “Voltairean” came to mean anticlerical wit rather than a doctrine. The Calas campaign matters more: a private citizen used publicity to reverse a court, the shape later taken by Zola in the Dreyfus affair. His most quoted sentence, on defending to the death the right to speak, was written by his biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall in 1906.

As a philosopher he built nothing systematic and did not pretend otherwise. He was a deist who thought religion useful for order, no democrat, and hostile to Jews in passages his admirers skip. What survives is Candide, still the most read book of the French eighteenth century, and the principle he made ordinary: that the state has no business punishing belief.

read.first: Read Candide first, in an edition whose notes identify the real events behind each disaster, then the Letters concerning the English Nation, then the Treatise on Toleration alongside a short account of the Calas trial.
read.note: The Philosophical Dictionary is meant to be opened at random rather than read in order. The collected works run to some fifty volumes, so every selection is somebody’s argument about him.

hume.sub: the empiricist who followed the premise all the way down
world: Hume was born four years after the Union of 1707 dissolved the Scottish parliament. That left the country with its own church, law and universities but no legislature. Edinburgh’s governing class were advocates, ministers and professors rather than politicians. The returns of union came slowly — linen, the Glasgow tobacco trade, agricultural improvement on the eastern estates. But by the 1750s they were real. They paid for the clubs and the presses on which his generation lived.

Twice in his lifetime that settlement was challenged by arms. The rising of 1715 stalled at the drawn battle of Sheriffmuir and broke up the following February. In 1745, Charles Edward Stuart held Edinburgh from September until November. The risings bore on the philosophy directly. They made the grounds of obedience urgent. Hume answered by denying that any government rests on a promise. Allegiance rests on interest and habit, which is why it survives revolutions.

Scottish intellectual life ran through clubs rather than faculties — the Rankenian, the Philosophical Society of Edinburgh, the Select Society founded in 1754 by the painter Allan Ramsay with Hume, Adam Smith and Lord Kames among its members, and the Poker Club of 1762. All of it carried a provincial anxiety: these men wrote a language they did not speak. Hume compiled a list of Scotticisms to be avoided.

Against that ran the power of the Kirk. Edinburgh’s town council appointed its professors. The clergy pressed hard on the choice. In 1745, Hume lost the chair of Ethics and Pneumatical Philosophy to William Cleghorn after charges of scepticism and atheism. In 1752, the logic chair at Glasgow was closed to him for the same reasons. In 1755, the General Assembly considered censuring him, but the Moderate party of William Robertson and Hugh Blair headed it off. Barred from teaching, he wrote for booksellers and a paying public. He learned to publish late, anonymously, or posthumously.

What the Kirk could not do, the law still could. England’s system of pre-publication licensing had lapsed in 1695 and nothing replaced it. Control worked after the fact instead, through prosecution for blasphemous and seditious libel. Thomas Aikenhead, a student, was hanged in Edinburgh for blasphemy in 1697, fourteen years before Hume was born. In 1763 Peter Annet stood in the pillory in London for a blasphemous libel. No one prosecuted Hume.

That trade was in London rather than Edinburgh. His first essays appeared in Edinburgh under Alexander Kincaid in 1741. Almost everything afterwards went to London houses — John Noon, then Thomas Longman, then Andrew Millar and William Strahan. It also meant an English publisher could pull a sheet already set in type. That happened during the printing of Four Dissertations.

The last third of his life ran with British power rather than against it. The Seven Years’ War ended in 1763 with Britain holding Canada. Hume went out to the Paris embassy that autumn. His letters from the Wilkes agitation of 1768 are contemptuous of the London crowds. In letters from 1775 he argued for letting the American colonies separate.
life: David Home — he changed the spelling in 1734 so the English would pronounce it — was born in Edinburgh on 26 April 1711 into minor gentry with an estate at Ninewells in Berwickshire. His father died when he was two. He entered the university at about eleven, left without a degree, and was pushed toward the law, which he abandoned for Cicero and Virgil.

Around 1729, his health and nerve collapsed for nearly five years. He described the episode in a long letter drafted for a physician in 1734 and probably never sent. The intended reader is usually identified as George Cheyne, sometimes as John Arbuthnot. Neither identification is secure. The letter reports palpitations, scurvy spots and a ravenous appetite, and calls the condition the disease of the learned. After a few months as a merchant’s clerk in Bristol, he crossed to France in 1734. After Paris and Reims, he settled in 1735 at La Flèche in Anjou, beside the Jesuit college where Descartes had been schooled. There, living cheaply and reading, he wrote A Treatise of Human Nature before he was twenty-seven.

How the Treatise reached print is part of its failure. In a letter of December 1737 Hume told Henry Home that he was castrating his work. He was cutting the reasonings concerning miracles, to give as little offence as possible. He sold the first two books to John Noon, on reported terms of fifty pounds and twelve bound copies for an edition of a thousand. Book III went to Thomas Longman in 1740. No second edition appeared in his lifetime. The text modern editors work from is that single printing, with the appendix and errata of 1740.

The Treatise failed. The next decade went to recovering from it. Two volumes of essays sold in 1741 and 1742. The Edinburgh chair did not follow. He answered the charges from the 1745 contest in an anonymous pamphlet. He took a tutorship with the deranged Marquess of Annandale in 1745. In 1746 he served as secretary to General James St Clair on the botched raid against L’Orient. In 1748 he accompanied him on a military embassy to Vienna and Turin. Out of those years came the recasting of Book I into the first Enquiry.

In 1752, the Faculty of Advocates made him Keeper of their library. The salary was forty pounds, which he handed to the blind poet Thomas Blacklock. The point was the thirty thousand volumes, and out of them came the History of England. In 1754, the curators struck three French books he had ordered as indecent. He nearly resigned the post. The History made him what philosophy had not — in his own phrase, not only independent but opulent.

He also spent thirty years managing what the Treatise had done to him. The Enquiries were not summaries of it. They were replacements, and he treated them as such. In October 1775 he sent Strahan an Advertisement to be prefixed to the collected Essays and Treatises on Several Subjects. It disowns the Treatise as a work projected before he left college and published too early. It asks that the later pieces alone be regarded as containing his philosophical sentiments. The notice appeared in the edition of 1777, after his death. The Treatise has been reprinted and taught ever since regardless.

The last phase was public and cheerful. From 1763 to 1766 he was secretary at the Paris embassy under the Earl of Hertford. There he became the pet of the salons, le bon David, dined by d’Holbach’s atheists, who found his caution about the word atheism comic. He brought Rousseau to England in 1766. The friendship exploded within months into a public quarrel. Pressed by his Paris friends, Hume printed his own account of it in 1766, first in French and then in English. After two years as Under-Secretary of State he retired to the Edinburgh New Town. He wrote a five-page autobiography in April 1776. He received Boswell in July with unbudging good humour about his own extinction. He died of an abdominal cancer on 25 August. Adam Smith’s published letter on those last months, calling him as near a perfectly wise and virtuous man as human frailty permits, brought Smith more abuse than anything he wrote on trade.

Two documents settled what would outlive him. His will of January 1776 left his manuscripts to Adam Smith. A codicil of August moved the Dialogues concerning Natural Religion to William Strahan, with the nephew named as fallback. That April’s autobiography, My Own Life, supplies most of the phrases his biographers still use, dead-born from the press among them. It is also a self-portrait composed for publication by a dying man.

works.t: A Treatise of Human Nature: Being an Attempt to Introduce the Experimental Method of Reasoning into Moral Subjects
works.y: Books I and II 1739, Book III 1740
p: Hume sold the first two books to John Noon for fifty pounds and published them anonymously in January 1739. The subtitle is the programme: a Newtonian science of man built from observation rather than definition. Its instrument is the copy principle — every simple idea is a faint copy of some simple impression. So an idea with no impression behind it is empty noise. Hume at once supplies his own counterexample, the shade of blue a man has never seen but could imagine in its place on a scale. He waves it aside as too singular to disturb the maxim. Applied to causation it bites. Between two billiard balls we see succession and contiguity, never a necessary connection, and what repetition adds is only a felt determination of the mind. Constant conjunction is in the world. Necessity is in us. On induction the argument is shorter and worse. Any inference from experience assumes that the future will resemble the past, which is the thing in question.

Two further parts of Book I are usually skipped and should not be. Part II denies that extension is infinitely divisible, building space and time out of indivisible minima. Part IV then turns the sceptical machinery on the machinery. Belief in body can be derived neither from the senses nor from reason. Hume’s answer is not a proof. It is that nature does not leave the question to us, and that whether there is body is a point we must take for granted. Belief itself is redefined on the way. It is not an extra idea but a conception held with more force and vivacity, produced by custom.

Book I ends by turning the instrument on the observer. Looking inward, Hume finds perceptions, never a self having them. The mind is a bundle, and the theatre he mentions has no stage. Book II builds the passions from association, and yields the line that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions. Book III derives morals from sentiment. It treats justice as an artificial virtue answering to scarcity, and observes that writers slide from is to ought without a word of explanation. The conventions of property grow, he argues, as two men learn to pull the oars of a boat together, without any promise between them. Promises are themselves naturally unintelligible on his account. They bind because a convention makes them bind. The whole, in his later phrase, fell dead-born from the press. In an appendix he confessed that he could not make the account of personal identity consistent, calling it a labyrinth. Perceptions are distinct existences. The mind perceives no real connection among them.

The essays were Hume’s trade and his first success. Politics can be made a science, he argues, because forms of government have regular effects independent of the virtue of the men who fill them. The essay on the original contract dismantles the founding myth of Whig legitimacy while conceding nearly all its practical conclusions. The Political Discourses of 1752, later absorbed into the collection, was the only book he called successful on first publication. Money is a counter whose quantity fixes prices but not real wealth. The specie-flow mechanism makes a permanent trade surplus impossible, so the jealousy of trade between nations rests on a mistake. Adam Smith took those arguments over largely intact. The same volumes carry the footnote on race added to Of National Characters in the 1750s. It asserts a natural inferiority, and in its first form extends the claim to every people other than whites. The revision printed in 1777 narrows it to the negroes. James Beattie attacked the note in 1770. Hume left it standing.

The collection was a working list rather than a book. Hume added, cut and reordered it through edition after edition until the year he died. Several early pieces were dropped and never restored, among them Of Love and Marriage and Of Moral Prejudices. Idea of a Perfect Commonwealth designs a republic, with counties and parishes and an indirect election of the senate.

works.t: A Letter from a Gentleman to his Friend in Edinburgh
p: Hume’s only public answer to the charges that cost him a chair. The pamphlet appeared anonymously in Edinburgh during the 1745 contest for the chair of Ethics and Pneumatical Philosophy. It prints the accusations drawn up from the Treatise — universal scepticism, the sapping of morality, the destruction of the arguments for God’s existence — and answers them one at a time. The defence is narrow. Denying that we can demonstrate a cause for every beginning of existence, he replies, is not denying that everything has a cause. He does not defend the reasonings on miracles, because he had cut them before publication. Its attribution to Hume is now accepted, and a modern edition was printed in 1967.

Twelve sections, long treated as a popularisation of Book I and better read as a rebuilding on a narrower footprint. Causation is sharpened into two definitions: a cause as an object followed by another where all like objects are followed by like, and as an object whose appearance conveys the mind to the other. The problem of induction is set out with a clarity the Treatise never reached. Section VIII adds the reconciling project: we mean by liberty the absence of constraint rather than of causes, so the dispute is largely verbal.

The additions made the book notorious. Section X argues that testimony draws its credit from experience, and so that none suffices to establish a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event reported. A miracle is defined as a violation of a law of nature, so the proof standing against it is as complete as experience can make one. Part II leaves the abstract argument and counts instead. No miracle has been attested by enough men of education and repute. Wonder is a pleasure people seek out. Reports of the marvellous cluster among ignorant nations. The miracles of rival religions cancel one another. The section closes on a joke that is also its thesis. Christianity cannot be believed by a reasonable person without a miracle in his own person. Section XI puts into an imagined Epicurean’s mouth the rule that we may infer only a cause proportioned to its effect. That leaves natural religion with a designer no better than the world evidences. Hume had cut the miracles essay from the Treatise out of prudence. Publishing it cost him the Glasgow chair.

Two things here outran the Treatise in influence. The first is the division of all enquiry into relations of ideas and matters of fact. The first sort is known by thought alone. The second can always be denied without contradiction. The book ends by using that division as a test: a volume holding neither abstract reasoning about quantity nor experimental reasoning about fact should go into the flames. The second is Section XII on scepticism. Total doubt can be neither refuted nor lived. What Hume recommends instead is a mitigated scepticism — modest claims, and enquiries kept inside the reach of experience.

works.t: An Enquiry concerning the Principles of Morals
p: Hume thought this incomparably the best of his writings. It is the least read. The method is frankly empirical: collect the qualities of character everyone praises and look for what they share. They are useful or immediately agreeable, to the person himself or to others. That fourfold division organises the book. Sentiment does the approving, but a sentiment corrected by a general point of view, since praise that shifted with the speaker’s position would be useless. The last section faces the sensible knave, who accepts the account and asks why he should not cheat when cheating pays. The answer, that he forfeits an inward peace worth more than his gains, is candidly weaker than the argument it closes.

The long central section is on justice, and it argues from circumstances rather than from principle. Suppose goods unlimited, or every man’s generosity unlimited. Rules of property would be pointless and nobody would invent them. Suppose famine or shipwreck instead. The rules are suspended and nobody calls that wrong. Justice is useful under conditions rather than sacred. Of the four appendices that follow, the first holds that reason settles the facts while sentiment alone makes the final approval. The closing catalogue of virtues is meant to provoke. It ranks wit, cheerfulness and cleanliness among them, and strikes celibacy, fasting and penance off the list.

The book separates two questions theologians had run together: religion’s foundation in reason and its origin in human nature. Hume grants that the first admits an easy answer and devotes himself to the second, which is a joke with a knife in it. Religion begins not in contemplation of natural order but in anxiety about the causes of harvest, illness and storm — hope and fear directed at unknown powers. Polytheism therefore comes first.
