Monotheism arises by competitive flattery rather than by argument, as worshippers heap superlatives on a favoured god until nothing is left to add. The corollary is unflattering. The purer the theism the more intolerant, and popular religion rewards the monkish virtues, which serve nobody.

The book was printed in Four Dissertations in 1757. Two essays were cancelled at press and one written to fill the gap. Hume dedicated the volume to John Home, whose tragedy Douglas had just set the Kirk against the Edinburgh stage. In the argument polytheism and theism alternate rather than progress. Men raise one god above the rest, find him too remote to petition, then fill the space again with saints and intercessors. Hume closes by offering doubt and suspense of judgement as the only result of an accurate scrutiny. Remarks answering him appeared the same year over Richard Hurd’s name, and are generally credited to William Warburton.

works.t: The History of England, from the Invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688
p: The work that made Hume famous and rich was written backwards: the Stuarts first, in 1754 and 1757, then the Tudors in 1759, then the medieval volumes in 1762. The opening volume met, by his account, one cry of reproach and detestation. He claimed that forty-five copies sold in twelve months. Whig history held that England possessed an ancient constitution the Stuarts had violated. Hume argued that no such thing existed, that Elizabeth’s prerogative was as large as anything James I claimed, and that the liberties in dispute were being invented rather than defended.

His Charles I and his Strafford are handled sympathetically without royalism. What carries the book is narrative intelligence and a refusal to let the outcome supply the moral. It ran through edition after edition, and remained the standard English history for some seventy years. The copy-money the booksellers gave him, by his own account, much exceeded anything formerly known in England. It was displaced only when Macaulay wrote a Whig answer good enough to replace it.

What the book argues is that the constitution was made and not inherited. Hume takes the English government through conquest, feudal tenure and Tudor prerogative, and finds no continuous liberty there to be violated. Liberty on his account is recent, largely accidental, and owed to parties he disliked. The precious spark, he wrote, was kindled and preserved by the puritans alone. Editors who have collated the editions report that his revisions moved steadily against the Whigs.

works.y: written from c. 1751, revised 1761 and 1776, published 1779
p: Three speakers argue in a garden, reported at second hand by a narrator the reader is invited to distrust. Demea defends a rationalist theology and divine incomprehensibility. Cleanthes presses the argument from design: the world is a machine whose adjustment of parts to ends proves an intelligence resembling ours. Philo attacks, cumulatively. The analogy is weak, since the universe resembles an animal or a vegetable at least as much as a watch. We have experience of many watches and of one universe, so no repeated conjunction licenses the inference. Granting a designer, proportioning cause to effect gives no reason to make him one rather than many, or perfect rather than a bungler at an early attempt.

The middle parts multiply alternatives until the design inference has nothing left to grip. Part V grants the analogy and asks what it licenses: many gods, or an infant deity, or a superannuated one. Parts VI and VII offer generation and vegetation as principles of order as good as thought. Part VIII revives an Epicurean hypothesis in which matter in eternal motion settles by itself into stable arrangements. Part IX gives Demea the a priori argument from necessary existence, and Cleanthes rather than Philo answers it. Nothing whose non-existence is conceivable can be demonstrated, and for all we know the material universe is the necessary being.

Parts X and XI turn to evil. Given the pain built into animal life, the world is at best consistent with an indifferent first cause. The old questions ascribed to Epicurus, about whether God is willing but unable, or able but unwilling, stand unanswered. Part XII then appears to concede that the cause of order probably bears some remote analogy to human intelligence. In 1751 he had asked Gilbert Elliot of Minto for help in strengthening Cleanthes’ side. Adam Smith declined to see the book through the press. A codicil then left the manuscript to his publisher William Strahan, to pass to his nephew if Strahan did not print it within two and a half years. The nephew published it in 1779, in an edition carrying no publisher’s name. A manuscript survives in Edinburgh, reported to carry revisions from the last year of his life.

works.t: Of Suicide; Of the Immortality of the Soul
p: Both essays were set in type for Four Dissertations and pulled at the last moment after William Warburton pressed the publisher. Hume substituted the essay on taste. Of Suicide proceeds by elimination. Ending one’s life cannot wrong God, since every human action alters the course of nature. If diverting a river is no encroachment on providence, neither is turning aside a few ounces of blood. It cannot wrong a society one merely ceases to benefit. And it cannot wrong oneself when life has become a burden. The companion essay finds no argument for immortality that survives inspection. The metaphysical argument from the soul’s substance proves nothing, since we have no idea of substance. The moral argument from divine justice would make God’s purposes turn on creatures of a day. The physical argument runs the other way, since everything we observe of mind and body shows them decaying together. Revelation alone is left holding the doctrine, and the compliment is generally read as ironic. Both were printed anonymously in London in 1777 and kept out of respectable editions for a century.

legacy: The first serious answer came from his own country. Thomas Reid argued that Hume had reduced the theory of ideas to absurdity, and that the theory, not common sense, should give way. His Inquiry into the Human Mind on the Principles of Common Sense followed in 1764. James Beattie made the same case in 1770 as a bestseller and, Hume thought, a piece of bigotry. Kant reported in 1783 that the recollection of Hume had interrupted his dogmatic slumber. What he had read, though, was mostly the first Enquiry, so the Hume who provoked the critical philosophy is partly a secondhand Hume. The route to the rest is usually traced through the German translation of Beattie in 1772, which quotes the Treatise at length.

Two lines out of Hume are not sceptical at all. Bentham said that reading Book III of the Treatise made the scales fall from his eyes. Adam Smith built the Theory of Moral Sentiments on sympathy, then broke with Hume on the point that mattered. Smith denied that we approve of a virtue because we perceive its usefulness.

Through the nineteenth century the historian eclipsed the philosopher. T. H. Green’s hostile introduction of 1874 argued that Hume had brought empiricism to its self-refutation. Selby-Bigge’s student texts then fixed the Treatise rather than the Enquiries as the standard Hume, reversing his own preference. What they produced is the version still most often taught: a pure sceptic assembled from Book I, with the naturalism of Books II and III left off. Norman Kemp Smith answered that reading in 1941, arguing that Hume is a naturalist and that Books II and III come first.

Twentieth-century philosophy took him up piecemeal. The logical positivists claimed his fork as a proto-verification principle. Popper built a philosophy of science on conceding that induction cannot be justified. The regularity analysis of causation became the default view to argue against. David Lewis named a whole metaphysical programme Humean supervenience, on the claim that everything supervenes on a mosaic of local matters of fact. The New Hume debate now divides readers over whether he denied causal powers in the world or only denied that we can know them. Galen Strawson’s The Secret Connexion of 1989 opened that dispute in its present form. The paragraph on is and ought became Hume’s Law.

Outside philosophy departments much survives: the specie-flow mechanism in economics, and the framework within which miracle testimony is still argued about. So does the footnote on race, which cannot be treated as incidental in a thinker who founded morals on shared human sentiment. Edinburgh renamed its David Hume Tower in 2020 after a student campaign. The man who dismantled inherited authority reproduced the prejudice of his century, and both facts belong in the same sentence.

Two of his arguments are still in dispute rather than in the archive. John Earman’s attack of 2000 holds that Section X is a botch by the standards of the probability theory Hume half anticipated. Philo could show the design inference weak without supplying any account of how a mechanism comes to fit its function. After 1859 there was one.

In 1740 Hume also published, anonymously, An Abstract of a Book Lately Published. It is a review of his own Treatise, and it states the argument about causation and belief more plainly than the book does. Long credited to Adam Smith, it is now accepted as Hume’s. Keynes and Sraffa reprinted it in 1938 and made the case that settled the question.

read.first: Start with the first Enquiry, which is short, finished, and the version Hume wanted read. Take sections IV, V, VII, VIII and X slowly. Then the Dialogues, which can be read in an evening and rewards a second. Only then go back to Book I of the Treatise. Read the Appendix immediately after the section on personal identity.
read.note: Hume is easy sentence by sentence and hard paragraph by paragraph. The prose slides past you at exactly the points where the argument is doing the most work.

hume.caveat: How far Philo speaks for Hume in the Dialogues remains genuinely unsettled. So does whether the concession in Part XII is sincere, ironic, or prudential. So does the composition history of a book he revised over twenty-five years and never risked publishing. The dead-born verdict is Hume’s own, written nearly forty years later. The Treatise was reviewed in several journals, so the phrase may understate its early reception. The reported terms of the Noon contract and the intended reader of the 1734 letter both rest on manuscript evidence that has been read more than one way.

rousseau.sub: the insider who turned the Enlightenment against itself
world: Geneva was a small Calvinist republic of some twenty thousand people, governed by councils drawn from a narrow patriciate. Full citizens were a minority. The artisan quarters had agitated about it for a generation. Rousseau was born a citizen, the son of a watchmaker, and signed his books “citizen of Geneva”. The city stands behind the political writing: a state small enough for citizens to assemble in person was something he had seen.

Paris, where he arrived in 1742, ran on the opposite principle. Patronage, salons, the académies and the theatre distributed reputation. A man of talent without birth advanced by pleasing. The Encyclopédie, begun in 1751 under Diderot and d’Alembert, was the collective enterprise of that world. Rousseau wrote its articles on music before turning on the whole culture of improvement it represented.

Censorship shaped what he could publish and where. Books went to Amsterdam or Geneva and came back by smugglers. 1762 showed what happened when the system was tested: the Parlement of Paris condemned Émile and ordered its author arrested, the Archbishop of Paris wrote against it, and the Genevan council burned both Émile and The Social Contract. The public that had made his novel a bestseller made the condemnation news.
life: Rousseau’s mother died days after his birth in 1712. His father Isaac fled Geneva after a quarrel when the boy was ten. Apprenticed to an engraver and beaten, he walked out of the city gates in 1728. He fell in with Madame de Warens, who arranged his conversion to Catholicism in Turin. Over a decade at Chambéry she became his patron and lover. He educated himself in music, Latin and the moderns.

In Paris he proposed a new musical notation, wrote for the Encyclopédie, and had an opera performed before the king in 1752. Walking to Vincennes in 1749 to visit Diderot in prison, he read the Dijon academy’s prize question. By his own account, he was overwhelmed by the answer that made him famous. He lived with Thérèse Levasseur, a laundry-maid, for the rest of his life. The five children she bore him were left at the Paris foundling hospital. Mortality there was appalling, and the records make identification impossible.

After 1762 he was a fugitive. He took refuge at Môtiers in Prussian Neuchâtel, where in 1765 a crowd stoned his house. He then accepted Hume’s offer of England in 1766, and destroyed the friendship within months by accusing Hume of conspiracy. He returned in 1767 under a false name, copied music for a living, and died at Ermenonville in 1778. The Revolution moved him to the Panthéon in 1794.

works.t: Discourse on the Sciences and Arts, and Discourse on the Origin and Foundations of Inequality among Men (Discours sur les sciences et les arts; Discours sur l’origine et les fondements de l’inégalité)
p: The first won the Dijon prize by answering no: the revival of learning has corrupted morals, because arts and sciences flourish on luxury and produce men skilled at seeming. The second, which did not win, is the serious book. Rousseau reconstructs a state of nature stripped of everything society supplies — language, foresight, comparison. What he finds there is not Hobbes’s war but a solitary animal, sufficient to itself and moved by pity. What ruins him is other people. Once men live together and rank each other, amour de soi, the simple care for one’s own preservation, is overlaid by amour-propre, the need to stand higher in others’ eyes. Property completes the work. Law secures it for the rich. The history is avowedly conjectural, and he says so.

works.t: Julie, or the New Heloise (Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse)
p: The bestseller of the century and now the least read of his books. Julie and her tutor Saint-Preux love each other across a gulf of rank. She marries Wolmar at her father’s command and confesses the past. The three build at Clarens a household of transparent virtue sustained by constant self-supervision. Readers wept, wrote to the author as though the characters were alive, and rented the volumes by the hour from booksellers who could not keep up. More than seventy editions appeared before 1800, which makes it the best-selling book of the century in French. The novel matters because it puts the moral argument where the treatises cannot reach: virtue as a daily discipline of feeling rather than obedience to a rule, passion taken seriously and then subordinated, and the lakeside around Vevey turned into a moral landscape.

works.t: Emile, or On Education (Émile, ou De l’éducation)
p: A fictional pupil is raised by a tutor who arranges circumstances rather than issuing commands. The boy learns from things and necessity before he learns from men. Rousseau delays books, reasoning and religion for years, on the argument that a child is not a defective adult but a creature with its own way of seeing. He stages each lesson when the pupil wants it. Book V, which trains Sophie for Emile rather than for herself, is the part later readers have found indefensible. Embedded in Book IV is the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, grounding religion in conscience and the order of nature while dismissing revelation and miracles. That section brought the condemnation. Paris and Geneva both burned the book. He had left his own five children at the foundling hospital.

The problem is to find an association in which each obeys only himself and remains as free as before. The answer is total alienation: each gives himself and his rights entirely to the community. Since every member does the same, no one gives himself to any particular master. What the assembled citizens then will, as a body and about matters touching all alike, is the general will. It is not a majority vote, not the sum of private interests, and not what a leader declares on the people’s behalf. Rousseau distinguishes it explicitly from the will of all. Book I, chapter 7 holds that whoever refuses to obey it may be forced to be free — compelled, in context, to keep the contract that constitutes him a citizen. Sovereignty, he adds, cannot be represented, which rules out most modern states.

works.t: The Confessions, and Reveries of the Solitary Walker (Les Confessions; Les Rêveries du promeneur solitaire)
p: The Confessions open by claiming an enterprise without precedent and keep the promise unexpectedly: not by confessing sins in Augustine’s sense but by reporting the theft, the humiliation, the sexual peculiarity and the abandoned children as facts about a self worth recording in full. They invented the modern autobiography, including its unreliability, since Rousseau writes from memory, decades late and at war with his former friends. He shapes the record as he goes. The Reveries are ten walks left unfinished at his death, published with the first part of the Confessions in 1782. They drop self-justification for something quieter: botany, the drift of thought on the Île Saint-Pierre, and a prose later read as the first sustained account of consciousness at rest.

legacy: Kant credited Rousseau with teaching him to respect ordinary people. The debt shows in the idea of autonomy as obedience to a law one gives oneself. German writers from Herder to Schiller took the critique of civilisation. Pestalozzi and later Froebel built schools on Émile. The taste for solitude, mountains, childhood and confessional prose that runs through European Romanticism is largely his invention.

The political reception has been one long fight over a single concept. Robespierre invoked him constantly. The Terror made the general will look like an instrument for telling citizens what they really want. Constant, then Taine, then Jacob Talmon in 1952 built the genealogy from Rousseau to totalitarian democracy. Against that stands the text: no representation, no executive holding sovereignty, and a scheme workable only in states the size of Geneva.

The diagnostic vocabulary is not in dispute. Amour-propre — the self-regard that needs other people’s eyes and is never satisfied by them — has proved more durable than the political machinery. Recent moral philosophy has returned to it to explain why comparison makes people miserable in societies growing richer. The Confessions stay in print. Julie is now read almost only by specialists.

read.first: Read the Discourse on Inequality first, complete and with its notes, then The Social Contract Books I and II, then Emile in a good abridgement that keeps the Profession of Faith entire. The Reveries can be read in an afternoon. They are the best introduction to his prose.
read.note: He contradicts himself across books and knows it. Treat the works as one long argument conducted with himself rather than a system to be made consistent.

rousseau.caveat: The Confessions are the main source for much of his early life. They were written years afterwards by a man convinced he was the object of a conspiracy. A good deal of the biography therefore rests on his testimony alone. Nothing outside his own writing documents the five children: the admission is made in the Confessions and in a letter of 1751 to Madame de Francueil, the hospital’s registers identify no one, and Rousseau’s own later inquiry after the eldest turned up nothing.

smith.sub: the moralist of sympathy who also wrote the first economics
world: The Union of 1707 gave Scottish merchants legal access to the colonial trades. Glasgow used it. By the 1750s the Clyde firms dominated the European tobacco business, importing Chesapeake leaf and re-exporting most of it to France. The profits went into banks, sugar houses and the deepening of the river. Smith lectured in a city visibly remade by commerce, among merchants he knew.

The universities were the other institution. Glasgow and Edinburgh taught in English rather than Latin, paid professors partly by student fees, and had made their peace with the Moderate party in the Kirk. Oxford, where Smith spent six years, endowed its fellows to do nothing, and he said so in print. Orthodoxy still had teeth: Hume was blocked from chairs at both Scottish universities.
life: Smith was born at Kirkcaldy in 1723, his father already dead. At fourteen he went to Glasgow, where Francis Hutcheson lectured on moral philosophy in English and treated benevolence as a natural fact. A Snell exhibition took him to Balliol from 1740 to 1746, where he read on his own and disliked it. Public lectures at Edinburgh made his name. Glasgow gave him the chair of moral philosophy in 1752.

In 1764 he resigned to tutor the young Duke of Buccleuch abroad for a life pension, meeting Quesnay and Turgot in Paris and Voltaire at Ferney. Ten years of work at Kirkcaldy produced The Wealth of Nations in 1776. Hume died that year. Smith’s published letter describing his friend’s cheerful unbelieving death brought him, he said, ten times more abuse than his attack on the whole commercial system.

p: Moral judgement begins in sympathy — not benevolence, but the imaginative act of putting oneself in another’s place and finding one’s own feeling matches his, or fails to. We approve of what we can go along with. Since we want that concord and cannot demand it, we learn to judge ourselves as others would and internalise the standard as an impartial spectator, the man within the breast. Smith revised the book for thirty years, adding in 1790 a chapter on how admiring the rich corrupts moral judgement. He thought it his better book.

works.t: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
p: The opening move is the division of labour, illustrated by the pin factory and limited by the extent of the market, which makes transport, towns and free exchange the engines of growth. Smith then builds an account of price, wages, profit and rent, and a long assault on the mercantile system, monopolies and colonial preference. It is no defence of businessmen. People of the same trade, he writes, seldom meet without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public. The invisible hand appears once, in Book IV, arguing why merchants prefer home investment.

works.t: Lectures on Jurisprudence, and Essays on Philosophical Subjects
works.y: lectures of 1762-64, student notes recovered 1895 and 1958; essays published 1795
p: Smith had his papers burned days before his death. So the missing middle of the system survives in two sets of notes taken by Glasgow students, found in 1895 and 1958. Neither set is in his own words. But both show him teaching law and government as a history of property through stages of subsistence, and rehearsing the economic arguments a decade before publication. The Essays, edited by Joseph Black and James Hutton, contain the early History of Astronomy. It treats scientific systems as imaginative machines built to soothe the mind’s discomfort at surprise.

legacy: The invisible hand is reported badly almost everywhere. The phrase occurs once in each of the two books and once in the early essay on astronomy, always inside a local argument and never as a name for a law of markets. Smith never wrote laissez-faire or capitalism. German scholars erred the other way and invented Das Adam Smith Problem, a supposed contradiction between the two books.

Economics took the parts it could use: Ricardo and Malthus the theory of value and rent, Marx the division of labour and the critique of the merchant. Political rhetoric took the slogan. Serious reading resumed with the Glasgow Edition from 1976, which printed the lectures and correspondence alongside the books. It recovered Smith as a moral philosopher whose economics was one department of a larger account of how people live together.

read.first: Read The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Parts I and III, before opening The Wealth of Nations. Then take Book I of the Inquiry for the division of labour and Book IV for the attack on the mercantile system, leaving the digression on silver for later.
read.note: The Wealth of Nations has a plain surface and buried qualifications. The sentences that get quoted are usually the ones with a condition attached in the following clause.

kant.sub: the man who put reason itself on trial
world: Königsberg in 1724 was a Baltic port of some fifty thousand people, capital of East Prussia and seat of the Albertina, a university founded in 1544. Grain and timber came down the Pregel from Poland and left on Dutch and English ships. A Prussian garrison held the middle of the town. Kant never travelled more than a hundred miles from it. He learned his cosmopolitanism at a customs house rather than on a grand tour.

Frederick II, king from 1740 to 1786, gave Prussian professors something rarer than money: room. He allowed unusual latitude in print, stocked the Berlin Academy with French freethinkers, and denied the clergy power to prosecute a professor for heterodoxy. Kant’s enlightenment essay of 1784 states the bargain in the king’s own reported terms: subjects may argue as much as they like, provided they obey. That settlement died with its author. The religious edict of 1788 put censors back to work.

Print had a centre. Kant wrote for it. The Berlinische Monatsschrift, edited by Johann Erich Biester and Friedrich Gedike, was the journal of the Berlin enlighteners. In a footnote of December 1783 the pastor Johann Friedrich Zöllner asked in its pages what enlightenment is. Kant answered in the issue of December 1784. He kept publishing there for a decade.

Frederick died in August 1786. His nephew Friedrich Wilhelm II preferred piety to freethinking. Johann Christoph Wöllner became minister for ecclesiastical affairs in July 1788. An examining commission tested clergy and schoolmasters on doctrine. Anything touching religion needed an imprimatur. Everything Kant published after that was written under a censor.

War reached the town twice. Russian troops occupied Königsberg in January 1758, early in the Seven Years’ War, and held it four years. The inhabitants swore allegiance to the Empress Elizabeth. Officers of the occupying army sat in on lectures. The regime proved more lucrative than harsh. Kant petitioned Elizabeth for the vacant chair of logic and metaphysics and was passed over. Thirty years later Prussia fought revolutionary France and withdrew at Basel in April 1795. Kant welcomed the Revolution and kept welcoming it through the Terror.

The Albertina ranked its faculties as German universities did. Theology, law and medicine were the higher three. Philosophy was the lower faculty and the poorest. A Privatdozent in it drew no salary and lived on fees handed over at the lecture-room door. The lower faculty could also be prosecuted. Christian Wolff was expelled from Halle in November 1723 on the complaint of the Pietist theologians, and given forty-eight hours to leave Prussia. That was five months before Kant was born. Frederick II recalled him in 1740.

Newton was the authority of the age. He reached Kant through Martin Knutzen, who taught Newtonian physics inside a still officially Wolffian curriculum. That double inheritance — a science that plainly worked, and a school metaphysics deducing the soul, the world and God from bare concepts — is the pressure that formed the critical philosophy. The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 sharpened it: Kant’s essays of 1756 explain the disaster by subterranean cavities and vapours, not divine punishment. When Jacobi announced in 1785 that Lessing had died a Spinozist, Kant met the pantheism controversy with a rational faith disciplined by criticism.
life: Kant was born on 22 April 1724, son of a harness maker, into a Pietist household that measured religion by inwardness and conduct. A family pastor, Franz Albert Schultz, placed him in the Collegium Fridericianum, whose compulsory devotions left him a permanent distaste for religious display. He entered the university at sixteen and fell under Knutzen, a Wolffian who lent him Newton and a telescope.

His father’s death in 1746 ended the studies. For six years from 1748 Kant worked as a private tutor in country households around Königsberg, acquiring the manners and the billiards that surprised visitors expecting an ascetic. He returned in 1754, took the master’s degree in 1755 with a Latin dissertation on fire, qualified to lecture with the New Elucidation, and began fifteen years as a Privatdozent paid directly by whoever turned up.

Teaching on that basis meant volume: logic, metaphysics, ethics, mathematics, physics, even fortification, plus the physical geography and anthropology courses he gave for four decades. He refused the chair of poetry in 1764. He took a sub-librarian’s post at the royal castle in 1766 for the salary. Logic and metaphysics came only in 1770, at forty-six. Having published steadily for twenty years, he then published almost nothing for eleven.

That silence was not idleness. Rousseau, he said, had taught him to honour ordinary people. Hume, by the account he gives in the Prolegomena, had interrupted his dogmatic slumber. Drafts accumulated until the Critique of Pure Reason was written out in a few months and printed at Riga by Johann Friedrich Hartknoch in 1781. Recognition came slowly, then completely, helped by Reinhold’s popular letters of 1786.

He told Marcus Herz that the book was the work of at least twelve years, put on paper in some four or five months. Riga lay in the Russian Baltic provinces. The book found few readers at first. The first friendly commentary came in 1784 from Johann Schultz, court chaplain at Königsberg. The hostile review that mattered had appeared anonymously at Göttingen in January 1782. Christian Garve wrote it. Johann Georg Heinrich Feder cut and sharpened it. Garve acknowledged the original as his in a letter to Kant in 1783. Moses Mendelssohn, in the preface to his Morgenstunden of 1785, called him the all-crushing Kant.

The Religion reached print by manoeuvre. The first of its four essays passed the Berlin censor in 1792. The second was refused. Kant then asked the theological faculty at Königsberg whether the book fell to biblical or to philosophical theology, and obtained an imprimatur from the philosophy faculty at Jena. Friedrich Nicolovius published it at Königsberg in 1793.

By the 1790s Kant was the most discussed man in German letters, twice rector of his university, and an object of tourism for people who wanted to see the afternoon walk. He was also under supervision: the cabinet order of 1794 demanded silence on religion. He kept it until Friedrich Wilhelm II died in 1797. He stopped lecturing in 1796 and died on 12 February 1804.

The last years are known mostly from the men who kept his house. Ehregott Andreas Christoph Wasianski, a former student, published an account of them in 1804. He reports the last words as “Es ist gut”. That report rests on his testimony alone. The story that Königsberg set its clocks by the afternoon walk is repeated everywhere and is probably embellished.

works.t: Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens (Allgemeine Naturgeschichte und Theorie des Himmels)
p: Published anonymously, and largely lost when the publisher went bankrupt and the stock was impounded, this is Newtonian cosmology pressed further than Newton would go. Kant proposes that the solar system and the Milky Way condensed out of diffuse matter under attraction alone, that the nebulae are other galaxies, and that the process still runs, systems forming and dissolving across an infinite universe. Newton had left the planets’ initial arrangement to God. Kant gives it to mechanics, keeping God as author of the laws rather than a hand inside them. Laplace reached a comparable hypothesis independently in 1796. The physics is loose, but the ambition is the one criticism later disciplined: how far natural explanation reaches, and where it stops.

Give me matter, Kant writes, and I will build a world out of it. A third part ranks the inhabitants of the other planets by their distance from the sun, the outer ones being the finer. It is offered as conjecture.

works.t: On the Form and Principles of the Sensible and Intelligible World (De mundi sensibilis atque intelligibilis forma et principiis)
p: This Latin disputation, defended on taking his chair, holds half the critical philosophy and not the other half. Space and time, Kant argues, are neither substances nor relations among things but forms belonging to the knowing subject, laws of sensibility shaping whatever is given to the senses. That is the doctrine of the Transcendental Aesthetic, reached eleven years early. Yet he still credits the intellect with an independent grasp of things as they are. Metaphysics therefore survives as a science of the real. The problem he could not then solve — how concepts arising in the mind apply in advance to objects it does not produce — he put to Marcus Herz in February 1772.

It also names the mistake it takes metaphysics to keep making. A condition of sensibility is smuggled into a claim about intelligible things. Kant calls this a fallacy of subreption. That everything is in space and time says nothing about what is. It says how anything must appear to us.

works.t: Critique of Pure Reason (Kritik der reinen Vernunft)
p: The question is how synthetic a priori judgements are possible — claims that add to what we know yet hold necessarily and in advance. Kant inverts the usual assumption: instead of asking how knowledge conforms to objects, he asks how objects must conform to the conditions of any possible experience. He compares the move to Copernicus setting the spectator turning rather than the heavens. Space and time, the Transcendental Aesthetic argues, are forms of our sensing, not features of things. The Transcendental Deduction, rewritten entirely for the second edition, argues that experience must belong to one subject able to attach “I think” to each representation, that such unity requires the manifold of sense to be combined under rules, and that those rules are the categories. Every event has a cause, then, not because nature reports it but because nothing else could count as nature.

Armed with that result, Kant turns on traditional metaphysics. Proofs of a simple, persisting soul confuse the formal unity of thinking with an object encountered. The four antinomies yield equally cogent demonstrations that the world is finite and infinite, made of simples and endlessly divisible, free and wholly determined, necessary and contingent. The first pair rests on treating appearances as things in themselves, so both sides fail. The second pair may both stand if one act is determined as appearance and free as it is in itself. Existence adds nothing to a concept, so the proofs of God fall too. What survives the demolition is a discipline. The ideas of reason keep a regulative use, directing inquiry toward a completeness it never reaches and naming no object on the way. Late in the book Kant reduces the interests of reason to three questions: what can I know, what ought I to do, what may I hope? The Göttingen review of 1782 nonetheless took all this for Berkeley’s idealism.

Between the two halves stands the Schematism, the shortest hard chapter in the book. It asks how a category, which contains nothing sensible, applies to an appearance, which contains nothing else. Time supplies the third thing. A schema is a rule for producing a temporal pattern: persistence for substance, succession by a rule for cause. Kant says the art involved is hidden in the depths of the human soul.

The book is also two books. A second edition was wanted within six years. Kant used it to rewrite rather than correct. The preface is new, the Transcendental Deduction is new, the Paralogisms are recast, and a Refutation of Idealism is added to show that inner experience presupposes outer objects. The new preface says he had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith. Editions since print both texts where they differ and cite them as A and B. Which edition carries the better argument has been disputed since Schopenhauer, who insisted on the first.

works.t: Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics (Prolegomena zu einer jeden künftigen Metaphysik)
p: Written quickly and in irritation after the Göttingen review, the Prolegomena reverses the order of the Critique. Instead of building up from the conditions of experience, it starts from sciences that indisputably exist — pure mathematics, pure natural science — asks what must hold for them to be possible, then whether metaphysics can qualify. It introduces a contrast between judgements of perception and judgements of experience that Kant later dropped. It appends a pointed complaint about the anonymous reviewer. It is the shortest way in, though whoever reads it alone misses the arguments that bear the weight.

Its parts follow four questions: how pure mathematics is possible, how pure natural science is possible, how metaphysics as a natural disposition is possible, and how metaphysics as a science would be. The last is the one the title promises.

works.t: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (Grundlegung zur Metaphysik der Sitten)
p: A short book with one object: to find and establish the supreme principle of morality. Kant starts from ordinary moral judgement, which already distinguishes acting because something is right from merely acting in accordance with duty. From that he extracts the idea of a will good without qualification. If moral demands bind unconditionally, they cannot depend on what we happen to want. A categorical imperative can therefore command nothing except conformity to law as such. Hence the first formula: act only on a maxim one could at the same time will to be a universal law. The false promise fails it, since universalised the maxim destroys the practice it exploits. Two further formulations follow: never treat humanity, in one’s own person or another’s, merely as a means; act as a legislating member of a kingdom of ends. Kant claims the three say one thing, which is disputed. His third section tries to prove that we are free and therefore bound, an argument he abandoned three years later. Hegel’s charge that the test is empty has never quite been answered and never quite stuck.

The pivot of the argument is autonomy. A will is bound only by a law it gives itself. Every rival principle — happiness, perfection, the command of God — puts the ground of obligation outside the will. Obligation then depends on something wanted, which Kant calls heteronomy.

works.t: Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science (Metaphysische Anfangsgründe der Naturwissenschaft)
p: The first Critique secures the form of nature and says nothing about bodies. This is the book that takes up matter. Its preface holds a claim Kant never softened: a doctrine of nature contains only as much proper science as it contains mathematics. Four chapters follow the four heads of the categories: phoronomy, dynamics, mechanics, phenomenology. Matter is defined as the movable in space. It fills that space not by solidity but by a balance of repulsion and attraction. Hard atoms and empty space drop out of the account. The laws of mechanics are then derived from the principles the first Critique established, rather than read off experiment. Whether anything can be derived that way is the objection the book has always faced.

works.t: Critique of Practical Reason (Kritik der praktischen Vernunft)
p: The second Critique reverses the strategy of the Groundwork. Rather than derive the moral law from freedom, Kant treats our consciousness of the law as a “fact of reason”. No argument delivers that fact and none is needed for it. He infers freedom from it: the law is how we know we are free, freedom is what makes the law possible. He then argues for the primacy of practical over theoretical reason. Morality commands a highest good in which happiness answers to virtue. Nothing in nature guarantees that pairing. Reason may therefore postulate immortality and God — not as knowledge, which the first Critique forbids, but as commitments practical reason may make.

Its architecture inverts the first Critique. The Analytic begins with the principle and works out to objects, because practical reason determines its object instead of receiving it. The good is therefore defined by the law, and not the law by the good. The book closes on the starry heavens above and the moral law within. Those words are inscribed at his tomb in Königsberg, now Kaliningrad.

works.t: Critique of the Power of Judgment (Kritik der Urteilskraft)
p: Kant’s third Critique was meant to bridge the gap between nature, which is determined, and freedom, which is commanded. Its instrument is reflective judgement, which searches for a rule instead of applying one. In aesthetics he argues that a judgement of beauty is disinterested, rests on the free play of imagination and understanding rather than on a concept, and yet demands everyone’s agreement. That is a universality without a rule, which is why disputes about taste are neither pointless nor decidable. The sublime arises where imagination fails and reason’s own vocation is felt. The second half treats organisms, which we cannot help describing as though each part existed for the whole. That purposiveness is a maxim for inquiry, not a discovery.

Taste is analysed in four moments taken from the table of categories: disinterested, universal without resting on a concept, purposive without a purpose, and necessary through a common sense that is presupposed rather than found. Fine art requires genius, which gives the rule to art and cannot state the rule it gave. Kant also denies that there will ever be a Newton of the blade of grass.

works.t: Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason (Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der blossen Vernunft)
p: Four essays, assembled into a book after the Berlin censor blocked the second. Kant argues that human beings have a propensity to subordinate the moral law to self-love — radical evil, innate in the sense of universal rather than inherited. The remedy, he argues, is a revolution in disposition, assisted by the idea of a humanity well-pleasing to God, which is what he takes the figure of Christ to mean. Statutory faith is a vehicle for pure moral religion and should empty itself into it. Friedrich Wilhelm II, through his minister Johann Christoph Wöllner, replied in October 1794 with a cabinet order accusing Kant of distorting Christianity. Kant promised silence as His Majesty’s loyal subject, then declared the promise lapsed when the king died in 1797.

The four parts run in order: the evil principle beside the good in human nature, the conflict of the two for mastery, the founding of an ethical commonwealth, and true as against false service of God. Moral progress, the third part argues, needs a community and not only a resolution. The invisible church is his name for that community.

Written months after Prussia’s separate peace with France, and cast in the form of the instrument it distrusts: preliminary articles, definitive articles, a secret one. The preliminary articles forbid mental reservations in treaties, the acquisition of states by inheritance or purchase, standing armies in the long run, and hostilities that make later trust impossible. The three definitive articles require a republican constitution in every state, a federation of free states rather than a world government, which Kant expects would become a despotism, and a cosmopolitan right confined to hospitality. The claim that republics enter wars less readily is the ancestor of democratic peace theory.

The title, Kant says, was painted on a Dutch innkeeper’s signboard above a picture of a graveyard. An appendix ends with a test of publicity: a maxim of public action that cannot be avowed openly is unjust. Nature is said to work toward the same end through commerce, which Kant offers as a guarantee of a sort.

works.t: The Metaphysics of Morals (Die Metaphysik der Sitten)
p: Here at last is the system the Groundwork was groundwork for, published at seventy-three and in prose that shows it. The Doctrine of Right works out the conditions of external freedom: property is no more than a claim until a civil condition secures it, the state exists to make right enforceable, punishment answers to desert rather than deterrence, and there is no right of revolution — a conclusion admirers of his enthusiasm for France have struggled to place. The Doctrine of Virtue handles what cannot be coerced: the ends we are obliged to adopt, our own perfection and the happiness of others.

The universal principle of right asks one question. Can the action stand together with everyone’s freedom under a universal law? One right alone is innate, freedom. The rest are acquired. Two conclusions have embarrassed readers ever since. Marriage is analysed as a right to a person of the kind normally held over a thing. Retribution is pressed until a society dissolving itself must first execute the last murderer in its prisons.

works.t: The Conflict of the Faculties (Der Streit der Fakultäten)
p: Three essays, published together once the king was dead. The preface prints the cabinet order of 1794 and Kant’s reply, and observes that the reply was worded to bind him to His Majesty alone. The first essay gives the book its title. Theology, law and medicine are the higher faculties because government licenses what they teach. Philosophy is the lower faculty, answerable to nothing but reason, and must be free to examine every doctrine in public.

The second essay asks whether the human race is continually improving. Kant answers by pointing not to the French Revolution but to the sympathy of spectators who had nothing to gain by it. Such disinterested enthusiasm is a sign that a moral disposition exists in the species. A sign is all he claims.

Thirteen fascicles of drafts, unfinished and unpublished, in which Kant tries to complete the system with a transition from the metaphysical foundations of natural science to physics itself. The gap is real: the first Critique secures the form of nature but says nothing about matter, forces or the ether. Kant attempts here an a priori argument for an all-pervading ether. Later sheets, written as his memory failed, move toward a doctrine of the subject positing both itself and its object. Whether that is a fresh departure or the residue of decline is contested.

The manuscript has a history of its own. Kant wrote to Christian Garve in 1798 of a gap left in his system. These sheets are the attempt on it. They stayed in private hands for most of a century. Rudolf Reicke printed selections in the 1880s. Erich Adickes proposed an order of composition in 1920. The full text appeared only in the Academy edition of 1936 to 1938, in an arrangement of the fascicles that is disputed.

legacy: Reception was immediate and quarrelsome. Reinhold made Kant readable. Jacobi then framed the objection that never went away — that one cannot enter the critical philosophy without assuming things in themselves that affect us, and cannot stay inside it while assuming them. Schulze and Maimon pressed sceptical variants. Fichte, Schelling and Hegel concluded that the thing in itself had to go. They built systems Kant repudiated in a public declaration of 1799.

Schopenhauer, who thought himself the only faithful heir, kept the distinction between appearance and thing in itself and named the latter will. After Idealism collapsed the sciences reclaimed Kant. Otto Liebmann’s book of 1865 ended chapter after chapter demanding a return to him. Neo-Kantianism governed German universities for half a century, Cohen and Natorp reading the first Critique as a theory of scientific objectivity.

Neo-Kantianism was not one school. Marburg, where Cohen and Natorp taught and Ernst Cassirer followed, read Kant outward into mathematics and physics. The Southwest school of Wilhelm Windelband and Heinrich Rickert read him toward history and value. Heidegger attacked both in 1929. His Kant and the Problem of Metaphysics made the imagination the common root of sensibility and understanding, and treated the second edition as a retreat. He and Cassirer argued it in person at Davos that spring.

Analytic philosophy arrived late and stayed. Strawson’s The Bounds of Sense of 1966 detached the argument that experience requires objective structure from the idealism he judged a liability. It made transcendental arguments a live genre. Rawls carried the universalising test into a theory of justice and Habermas into a theory of discourse. Korsgaard and O’Neill rebuilt Kantian ethics as a constructivism about reasons. Toward Perpetual Peace stands behind the League of Nations.

The analytic quarrel runs through the analytic-synthetic distinction. C. I. Lewis kept a pragmatic a priori in 1929, chosen rather than found. Quine’s “Two Dogmas of Empiricism” of 1951 denied there was a distinction there to keep. Sellars turned the attack on the given into a Kantian argument that experience is already conceptual. McDowell carried that into Mind and World in 1994. In aesthetics the third Critique drew its sociological counter-attack in Pierre Bourdieu’s Distinction of 1979, which treats disinterested taste as a class position.

Two misreadings have been historically decisive. The first is psychological: that Kant made space and time features of human mental equipment rather than conditions of objectivity, which invites the reply that other creatures might be built otherwise. The second is the two-world picture, appearances here and a hidden realm there, contested by readings on which phenomena and noumena are one thing considered twice. What survives is his question: not what there is, but what a mind must supply first.

One dispute is recent and unresolved. Kant’s essays and lectures on human variety set out a hierarchy of races, defended in print in the 1770s and 1780s. Pauline Kleingeld has argued that he abandoned the hierarchy in the 1790s. Charles Mills and others have held that the racism is not detachable from the account of humanity the ethics rests on. Part of why the argument stays open is the evidence: much of it is lecture material taken down by students.

The comparison is his, the label is not: Kant nowhere writes of a Copernican revolution. The Copernicus passage appears only in the preface added to the second edition of 1787. A reader who looks for it in the book of 1781 will not find it.

read.first: Begin with the Groundwork, which is short, self-contained and argued in the open; then the Prolegomena for the shape of the theoretical project; then the Critique of Pure Reason in a modern translation with a chapter-by-chapter commentary beside it, taking the two prefaces and the introduction first and the Transcendental Deduction last.
read.note: Kant’s technical vocabulary is fixed and unforgiving, so a glossary is worth more than speed. The sentences reward being read twice rather than being read faster. The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Immanuel Kant supplies the standard English texts. References in the literature are to the volume and page of the Academy edition.

kant.caveat: Much of what circulates under Kant’s name — the courses on logic, ethics, metaphysics and anthropology — survives only in students’ notes of uncertain date and reliability. The composition history of the first Critique is disputed enough that scholars still argue over whether its parts were written to fit one another. The logic, the physical geography and the pedagogy published under his name were assembled by editors — Jäsche in 1800, Rink in 1802 and 1803 — from Kant’s annotated handbooks and from notes. How much of the wording is his is not recoverable. The Opus postumum likewise reaches us in an order its editors decided.

wollstonecraft.sub: who argued that the character of women is an artefact of their education
world: London in the 1790s was arguing about France. Burke's Reflections of 1790 drew some fifty replies, and the circle around the publisher Joseph Johnson — Price, Priestley, Godwin, Paine, Blake — was on the other side. Wollstonecraft's first Vindication was the earliest of those replies into print.

The condition she wrote against was legal as well as intellectual. A married woman in English law had no separate existence, could not hold property or contract, and had no claim on her children. Girls of her class were educated in accomplishments, and the standard advice books — Fordyce, Gregory, and Rousseau's Emile — told them so explicitly.
life: Born in London in 1759 to a father who drank through an inherited fortune and beat her mother. She worked at the three occupations open to her — companion, schoolmistress, governess — and hated them; the Irish family who employed her as governess dismissed her, she said, because the children preferred her. In 1787 Johnson took her on as a reviewer and translator, and she supported herself by writing thereafter.

She went to Paris in 1792 and watched the Terror. There she had a daughter, Fanny, by the American Gilbert Imlay, who left; she attempted suicide twice and then travelled alone through Scandinavia on his business, producing a book about it that Godwin said made him fall in love with its author. She married Godwin in 1797 and died eleven days after the birth of their daughter Mary, later Mary Shelley, of puerperal fever.

works.t: A Vindication of the Rights of Men
p: The first published answer to Burke, written in weeks and printed anonymously, then under her name in the second edition. Against Burke's argument that the constitution's authority lies in inheritance and sentiment, she sets reason and natural right, and turns his own aesthetic against him: the Enquiry had made the beautiful small, weak and pleasing, and Wollstonecraft points out that this is precisely how women are made to be. The connection between his politics and his account of feminine charm is the germ of the book she wrote next.

works.t: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
p: The argument is not that women are equal in attainment but that no one knows what they would attain, because the evidence is contaminated: the qualities held to prove female frivolity are exactly what an education in accomplishments would produce in anyone. Virtue is one thing and its standard is reason, so a separate feminine virtue is a contradiction. Rousseau is the target throughout — Sophie, educated to please Emile, is refuted chapter by chapter — and the remedy proposed is national co-educational day schools. The book is not a demand for the vote, which it mentions once in passing; it is a demand that women be treated as rational creatures and educated accordingly.

works.t: Maria, or The Wrongs of Woman
p: A woman confined in a madhouse by her husband, who has taken her child and her property, tells her story to a servant whose own history is worse. Wollstonecraft is making an argument the treatise could not: that the disabilities are legal and economic as much as educational, and that they bear differently on a gentlewoman and on a working woman. Godwin published it with her Memoirs after her death.

legacy: Godwin's Memoirs of 1798, written in candid grief, disclosed the illegitimate child, the suicide attempts and the affairs, and destroyed her reputation for most of a century. She was a name to be used against the cause, not for it — Walpole's 'hyena in petticoats' is from this period. The book itself stayed in print but was cited carefully.

Mill's The Subjection of Women of 1869 makes the same argument about contaminated evidence without naming her. The recovery began with Victorian suffragists and completed in the 1970s, when the Vindication became the founding text of Anglophone feminist philosophy. What has lasted is the structural move: where an alleged nature is invoked to justify a training, ask whether the nature is the residue of the training.

read.first: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, chapters 2, 4 and 12. Then the Letters Written in Sweden for the prose.
read.note: The Vindication was written in six weeks and reads like it; it repeats and digresses. The argument is all in the early chapters and in the chapter on national education.

wollstonecraft.caveat: How far her position extends beyond women of her own class is contested. Maria complicates the treatise, but the Vindication's proposals assume a readership with the leisure to be educated.

bentham.sub: the reformer who made happiness a unit of account
world: Bentham grew up in a Britain industrialising faster than it could govern itself. Between 1748 and 1832 the population of England roughly doubled. Cotton mills turned Manchester and Leeds into cities with neither corporations nor members of Parliament. The criminal law answered the disorder by multiplying capital offences and transporting convicts to New South Wales. The statute book was a heap of precedent, fiction and local custom.

Politics handed him two provocations. At home an unreformed Commons was defended by Blackstone as the perfection of English liberty. Abroad the French revolutionaries, who made him an honorary citizen in 1792, founded their constitution on natural and imprescriptible rights. To him they were a fiction dressed as fact, since rights are the children of law, and a right claimed before law was nonsense upon stilts.
life: Born in Houndsditch in 1748 to a prosperous attorney, Bentham went up to Oxford at twelve, was called to the bar, and refused to practise. Having heard Blackstone lecture, he decided the law needed an anatomist rather than another advocate. His father’s death in 1792 left him independent. He spent forty years at Queen’s Square Place, writing every morning and finishing almost nothing.

Others finished what he began. Dumont turned his drafts into readable French. James Mill and Francis Place organised the philosophic radicals. The Westminster Review of 1824 gave them a platform. His own Panopticon consumed two decades and ended in 1813 with a parliamentary indemnity of £23,000 instead of a prison. He died on 6 June 1832, the day before the Reform Act received royal assent, having directed that his body be dissected before an audience and preserved.

p: Published anonymously, the Fragment attacks a few pages of Blackstone on the original contract, extracted from a much longer manuscript that stayed unprinted until 1928. Bentham’s method is to take a sentence of legal piety, ask what fact it asserts, and show that it asserts none. The social contract is a fiction. Obedience needs no fiction: subjects obey while obedience produces more happiness than resistance. The preface names the standard, that the greatest happiness of the greatest number is the measure of right and wrong. Readers briefly credited the pamphlet to eminent lawyers. Interest fell when the author proved to be a nobody.

works.t: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
p: Meant as the preface to a penal code he never completed, this is where utilitarianism acquires its machinery. It opens with nature placing mankind under two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. It proceeds to the felicific calculus: pleasures scored for intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent, so that legislation becomes in principle arithmetic. Most of the book classifies offences and the cases where punishment is groundless, inefficacious, unprofitable or needless. A late footnote extends moral standing beyond our species: the question is not whether animals can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer. The standing objection is that the calculus assumes a commensurability it never demonstrates.

The design came from his brother Samuel, an engineer in Russia. Bentham wrote it up as letters from Krichev. A ring of cells faces an unlit central tower. The inspector sees without being seen. The inmate, unable to know when he is watched, must behave as though always watched. Bentham proposed to run the prison himself as a contractor paid by results. Parliament authorised the scheme in 1794. It collapsed by 1803, a failure he blamed on the King and the landed interest and which hardened his radicalism. Foucault made the building the emblem of modern disciplinary power in 1975, a use of Bentham rather than a reading of him.

legacy: Utilitarianism entered British public life less as a philosophy than as an engine of administration: the New Poor Law of 1834, sanitary reform under Chadwick, codification, the reform of the civil service. James Mill and then John Stuart Mill carried the doctrine forward while amending it. Sidgwick gave it its most careful statement in 1874. The footnote on animals, ignored for a century, became a founding citation for Peter Singer.

His texts fared worse than his ideas. John Bowring’s edition of 1838 to 1843 rewrote and omitted silently, though it did bring his critique of the French Declaration into English at last, as Anarchical Fallacies. Work judged unpublishable was left out, including a manuscript of the 1780s arguing for the decriminalisation of homosexuality that waited until 1978. The Bentham Project has been editing the surviving folios since 1968. The figure emerging is stranger than the caricature of a bloodless calculator.

read.first: Start with the first two chapters of the Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, then the preface to A Fragment on Government. Together they give the whole position.
read.note: Bentham is a difficult stylist who improves in small doses. Any nineteenth-century collected edition should be checked against the modern Collected Works.

bentham.caveat: Much of what Bentham wrote remains unpublished or unreliably edited. Judgements about his views on religion, sexuality and colonial policy have therefore shifted repeatedly as the manuscripts appear.

fichte.sub: the idealist who began everything from the self-positing I
world: The German states of the 1790s had no revolution and a great deal of argument about one. Censorship varied by principality, which made jurisdiction decisive: Saxony could confiscate a journal that Weimar tolerated. Jena, protected by Duke Karl August and within reach of Goethe, was for a decade the most exciting university in Europe. Its enrolments were swollen by the fame of Kantian philosophy.

Then the political ground moved. Prussia was destroyed at Jena and Auerstedt in October 1806. The Peace of Tilsit stripped it of half its territory, leaving French troops in Berlin. That catastrophe produced the Stein-Hardenberg reforms, the new university of 1810, and a patriotism that was cultural and linguistic because the nation it addressed had no state. Fichte’s last years belong to the emergency.
life: Born in 1762 at Rammenau in Saxony to a ribbon-weaver, Fichte owed his schooling to a local nobleman, Baron von Miltitz. He studied theology, found no living, and was tutoring in Leipzig in 1790 when a pupil asked him to explain Kant. The encounter converted him. In 1791 he went to Königsberg and wrote an essay in a few weeks to introduce himself. Through Kant’s intervention he found a publisher.

Fame brought the Jena chair in 1794. Five years later it was gone. Fichte had published, in a journal he co-edited, an essay identifying God with the moral order of the world. A pamphlet denounced it as atheism, and Saxony confiscated the issue. He answered Weimar with a letter threatening resignation, which was accepted. He lived in Berlin by lecturing, and died of typhus in January 1814.

works.t: Attempt at a Critique of All Revelation (Versuch einer Kritik aller Offenbarung)
p: The book asks on what conditions a rational being could accept something as divine revelation. It answers within Kant’s framework. Revelation can never establish the moral law, which is autonomous, but may be accepted where its content agrees with that law and human weakness needs sensuous support. It appeared anonymously, the preface and the author’s name left out through the publisher’s haste, and was taken for the critique of religion Kant was known to be planning. Kant named the real author. An unknown tutor became famous in a fortnight.

works.t: Foundations of the Entire Science of Knowledge (Grundlage der gesamten Wissenschaftslehre)
p: Fichte held Kant’s thing-in-itself both unknowable and unnecessary, and cut it out. What remains must be generated from the subject. He starts from the I that posits itself: not a fact but an act, a doing that is its own awareness of itself. He then argues that a Not-I must be posited against it, so that nature is the resistance without which moral striving would be impossible. He rewrote the system repeatedly, in the nova methodo lectures and again in Berlin, most of it unpublished, because readers kept taking for a doctrine what was meant as an exercise in self-observation.

works.t: Addresses to the German Nation (Reden an die deutsche Nation)
p: Fichte gave these fourteen speeches in occupied Berlin over the winter after Tilsit, with French garrisons in the city. Their proposal is educational: a total reform of national schooling on Pestalozzi’s lines, to form a people capable of freedom. Their premise is not. Fichte argues that the Germans are an Urvolk with an original, unmixed living language and therefore alone capable of genuine philosophy and genuine renewal. The argument is cultural rather than racial, and its author remained a republican. But the vocabulary proved portable, and later nationalists quoted the Addresses with enthusiasm.

legacy: Fichte set the agenda Schelling and Hegel then fought over: if the thing-in-itself goes, philosophy must show how objectivity is produced rather than received. Schelling broke with him over the standing of nature. Hegel’s Difference essay of 1801 already treats his system as a station, not a destination. Novalis and Friedrich Schlegel took the self-positing I as licence for an art of infinite reflection.

For a century he was read mainly as a bridge. The Addresses overshadowed the philosophy in the worst possible way. That has changed. Dieter Henrich’s work on Fichte’s original insight put him at the centre of current debate about immediate self-awareness. The insight is that self-consciousness cannot be a subject inspecting itself, since the inspection presupposes what it was meant to explain.

read.first: Start with The Vocation of Man of 1800, written for a general audience and the only readable statement of the whole position. Then take the introductions to the Wissenschaftslehre rather than the 1794 text itself.
read.note: The Addresses repay reading, but read them as a document of 1808 under occupation rather than as the summary of his philosophy.

hegel.sub: the philosopher who made history the medium of reason
world: Hegel entered the Protestant seminary at Tübingen in 1788, a year before the Bastille fell. The Revolution was the political event of his life. The tradition that he, Hölderlin and Schelling planted a liberty tree outside the town is much repeated but thinly evidenced. Most scholars now treat it as legend. Hegel never disowned 1789, and never stopped insisting that the Terror followed from the same abstract freedom.

He grew up inside a constitutional quarrel of his own duchy. Württemberg had a standing assembly of estates, which most German territories did not, and a long history of friction between it and the duke. In 1798 he published his first work, anonymously: a translation of Jean-Jacques Cart’s letters against the rule of Bern over the Vaud. In the same years he drafted a pamphlet arguing that the magistrates of Württemberg must be elected by the citizens. His friends are reported to have advised against printing it, and he did not.

France dismantled Germany while he wrote. Napoleon broke the Prussian army at Jena and Auerstedt on 14 October 1806, in the town where Hegel was lecturing. Two months earlier Francis II had laid down the imperial crown. The Holy Roman Empire — which Hegel had already analysed as no longer a state at all — ceased to exist. The Confederation of the Rhine and the Code Napoléon followed. Hegel welcomed much of it.

Defeat forced Prussia to reform itself from above. Stein and Hardenberg abolished hereditary serfdom by the edict of October 1807, rebuilt the army, and founded the University of Berlin in 1810 on Humboldt’s plan. These reformers were bureaucrats, not democrats. They modernised property, administration and schooling, and left the monarchy untouched. Hegel’s mature politics, with its salaried civil service standing above particular interests, is unintelligible apart from that officialdom, which is also the class that hired him.

By 1818 the reforming moment had closed. After the student Karl Ludwig Sand murdered the dramatist August von Kotzebue in March 1819, Metternich pushed through the Carlsbad Decrees: press censorship, surveillance of universities, dismissal of suspect professors. Hegel’s own students were caught in the demagogue hunts. He put up bail for one of them. He kept his chair, published under a censor, and saw his last essay, on the English Reform Bill, stopped mid-serial by the king in 1831.

The rules decided what shape an argument could take. Under the federal press law of 1819 anything shorter than twenty sheets went to a censor before publication. Longer books were exempt from that prior reading, though they could still be seized afterwards. A system in fat volumes was safer than a pamphlet. Lecturing was safer again. A professor’s course was watched and reported on. No official passed the sentences before he spoke them.

Berlin attached him to a government. Altenstein, who ran the ministry of spiritual, educational and medical affairs, protected him and used him. Hegel sat from 1822 on the royal commission that examined candidates to teach in the Brandenburg schools. In 1827 he helped found the Jahrbücher für wissenschaftliche Kritik, a review with something close to official standing. He was never elected to the Prussian Academy of Sciences. Schleiermacher, who sat in it and disliked him, is generally credited with keeping him out.
life: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was born in Stuttgart in 1770, son of a minor revenue official in the duchy of Württemberg. He took the ducal scholarship to the Tübingen Stift in 1788. He completed the theology course in 1793 and never sought a pulpit. His leaving certificate noted a diligent student with poor command of philosophy, the kind of judgement that survives because it aged badly.

For seven years he was a house tutor, in Bern from 1793 and in Frankfurt from 1797, where Hölderlin found him the post. These were reading years: Gibbon, Montesquieu, the English economists — his commentary on James Steuart is lost — and notebooks of essays he never printed. His father died in 1799. The small inheritance bought him a chance at an academic career.

Schelling, five years younger and already a professor, brought him to Jena in 1801. Hegel habilitated with a Latin dissertation on the planetary orbits, co-edited the Critical Journal of Philosophy with him, and lectured as an unsalaried Privatdozent in real poverty. He was finishing the Phenomenology as the French entered the town. In 1807 his landlady bore him a son, Ludwig, whom he later took into his household.

The Phenomenology reached its publisher in pieces. Goebhardt of Bamberg had contracted for it, and Hegel sent sheets as he finished them. Niethammer stood surety for the missing remainder when the deadline passed. Hegel wrote to him on 13 October 1806 that he had seen the Emperor ride out of the city, “this world-soul”, and reported having finished the work. How much was still unsent on the day of the battle has been argued over. The preface was written last, in January 1807. Part of the print run carries the earlier title, Science of the Experience of Consciousness, changed during production.

The next decade he spent outside the university. He edited the Bamberger Zeitung in 1807–08, and then served eight years as rector of the Gymnasium at Nuremberg, teaching logic to adolescents and rebuilding a curriculum. He married Marie von Tucher in 1811. The most demanding book of the century was written by a working schoolmaster and published in instalments as he finished them.

The Logic came from Schrag of Nuremberg in three instalments: the doctrine of being in 1812, the doctrine of essence in 1813, the doctrine of the concept in 1816. Two sons were born in those years, Karl in 1813 and Immanuel in 1814. Karl became a historian. Ludwig, the son born in Jena, entered the household in 1817. He broke with his father, enlisted in Dutch service, and died at Batavia in 1831, a few months before him.

Heidelberg called him in 1816 and Berlin in 1818, to the chair Fichte had held. There he became something German philosophy had not produced before: an institutional power, with ministerial backing from Altenstein, a school, and halls full of law students and civil servants. He died on 14 November 1831 during a cholera epidemic, though the diagnosis has been disputed ever since. He was buried beside Fichte.

Most of what is read as Hegel was assembled after he was dead. An association of friends of the deceased brought out eighteen volumes between 1832 and 1845. Marheineke took the lectures on religion, Gans the philosophy of right and world history, Hotho the aesthetics, Michelet the history of philosophy. A critical edition on modern principles, the Gesammelte Werke, began in 1968 and is not yet complete.

p: These are the unpublished essays of the tutoring years, gathered and titled by Herman Nohl in 1907 after Wilhelm Dilthey drew attention to them. The bundle includes a Life of Jesus, The Positivity of the Christian Religion and The Spirit of Christianity and its Fate. Nohl’s label misleads: the animating question is political. Hegel asks how a religion becomes positive — external, statutory, imposed by authority on a people who no longer recognise themselves in it. What was once a community’s own life therefore confronts it as law.

His measure is the civic religion he imagined in the Greek polis, where cult and custom belonged to the people. Against it Christianity appears as the faith of private individuals under Roman despotism, and doctrine as the fossil of a lost freedom. The contrast he draws between Jewish law and Christian love reproduces the anti-Judaic commonplaces of his milieu, and is rightly criticised for it. Because the manuscripts surfaced a century late, they created a “young Hegel” who could be set against the system, a move Lukács and others exploited hard.

Two items show the range of the bundle. The Bern Life of Jesus of 1795 retells the gospel with the miracles gone and Jesus teaching a morality of pure practical reason. It opens by identifying reason itself with the deity. A separate sheet in Hegel’s handwriting, found by Franz Rosenzweig and published in 1917 as the oldest system-programme of German idealism, is attributed variously to him, to Schelling and to Hölderlin. The authorship is disputed and unsettled. The English volume T. M. Knox translated in 1948 leaves the Life of Jesus out.

Hegel drafted this in Frankfurt and Jena and never published it. The verdict is in its opening sentence: Germany is no longer a state. He means the claim technically. A body whose members raise their own armies, make their own treaties and answer to no power that can compel them has the forms of a state without the thing. Feudal privilege, confessional division and the guarantees written into the peace of Westphalia have left a machinery that cannot act.

The remedy is not a liberal one. Germany needs a common defence and a centre with power to coerce. He is willing for a conqueror to impose it. What such a state should not touch is unexpectedly wide: religion, custom, dialect and local law can be left alone, because uniformity is not what makes a state. Karl Rosenkranz quoted the manuscript in his biography of 1844. It was first printed in full in 1893, edited by Georg Mollat. The political thinker arrives well before the system.

works.t: The Difference Between Fichte’s and Schelling’s System of Philosophy
p: Hegel’s first publication under his own name is a partisan intervention, defending Schelling’s system against those who took it for a variant of Fichte’s. It was read as an act of discipleship, which within six years it had ceased to be. Its lasting interest lies in the opening pages, where he states what philosophy is for. When a culture’s life is torn apart — faith against reason, subject against object, individual against community — that division, Entzweiung, generates the need for philosophy. Philosophy does not choose its problems. An age hands them over.

The critical target is what Hegel calls reflection: the understanding’s habit of fixing distinctions and then treating them as final. Against it he sets an Absolute that is not a further thing lying behind the oppositions but the whole in which they are produced and reconciled. Faith and Knowledge, published in the Critical Journal he edited with Schelling in 1802, extends the attack. It reads Kant, Jacobi and Fichte as three versions of one defeat — philosophies that end by placing the infinite permanently out of reach.

Two other Jena essays matter more than the polemic. The Relationship of Scepticism to Philosophy, of 1802, separates the ancient scepticism he admires from the modern kind, which leaves everyday belief where it found it. On the Scientific Ways of Treating Natural Law, of 1802 and 1803, is his first sustained political argument. Empirical natural law abstracts a state of nature and then calls the abstraction human nature. Formal natural law, Kant’s and Fichte’s, gets no duties out of consistency alone. Against both he sets the ethical life of a people, citing Aristotle on the priority of the whole to its parts. Articles in the Critical Journal appeared unsigned. The authorship of some of them is still contested.

The book traces consciousness through every shape it can take, from sense-certainty’s claim to grasp the bare this-here-now to absolute knowing. Each shape sets its own standard for truth, tests itself by it, and fails on its own terms. The failure is the shape’s own experience, not something imposed from outside. The next shape is whatever survives the wreck. Hegel calls the route the highway of despair.

The book keeps outgrowing the plan it announces. Consciousness gives way to self-consciousness, then to reason, then to spirit, where the shapes examined are a culture’s rather than one mind’s. Greek ethical life, Roman legal personality, faith against the Enlightenment, the Terror, the moral view of the world: each is a shape that broke. Religion and absolute knowing close the sequence. The preface, written after everything else, states the programme. Substance must be grasped as subject, the true is the whole, and a result without the road that reached it is worth nothing. It also mocks a formalism that paints every difference one colour — the night in which all cows are black.
