Two passages have outlived the rest. In lordship and bondage two self-consciousnesses each demand recognition. One submits. The master wins acknowledgement from someone whose acknowledgement is now worthless. The bondsman, forced to work on the world, acquires through fear and labour the independence his master has lost. Freedom turns out to be a relation between persons rather than a possession.

The unhappy consciousness turns the same split inward. The self projects its own essence into an unreachable beyond and then suffers its distance from it, the inner form, he says, of medieval devotion. He finished the manuscript as Napoleon entered Jena. The seams show. Schelling, mocked in the preface, never forgave him.

It sold slowly. He never quite settled his account with it. In 1831 he began revising it. A note of his from that year, quoted by his editors, calls it a peculiar early work and says it is not to be reworked.

This is where dialectic is explained rather than performed. Hegel begins with pure being, shows that a thought with no content is indistinguishable from nothing, and lets the instability of the pair generate becoming. Every later category arises the same way: a determination is taken as adequate, pressed until it yields a contradiction internal to itself, then superseded by a richer one preserving what was true in it. He calls the crucial move determinate negation — negating something specific leaves a specific result, not a blank. He names the double sense of cancelling and keeping Aufhebung.

It follows that thesis, antithesis and synthesis is not his formula. He invoked the triad only to dismiss it as a lifeless scheme applied from outside. The slogan reached the world through Heinrich Moritz Chalybäus’s textbook of 1837. Its three books — being, essence, concept — rest on the claim that these categories are not our equipment for handling a reality that stands apart, but the structure of what there is. Logic and metaphysics therefore coincide. Readers divide still over whether the transitions are derivations or persuasions.

The three books are unequal in difficulty. Being runs through quality, quantity and measure, and contains the attack on the bad infinite, a progress that repeats forever without arriving. Essence is the hardest and the most modern, treating identity, difference, contradiction, ground, appearance and actuality as pairs that each collapse into their partners. Here he argues that contradiction is a feature of things and not only a fault in thinking. The Concept turns from what is presupposed to what develops itself: universal, particular and individual, then judgement, syllogism, mechanism, chemism, teleology, life and the Idea. He describes this content, taken before nature and finite spirit, as God as he is in his eternal essence. Whether that sentence is theology or a figure of speech is a standing quarrel.

works.t: Encyclopaedia of the Philosophical Sciences in Outline (Enzyklopädie der philosophischen Wissenschaften im Grundrisse)
p: The Encyclopaedia is the whole system in numbered paragraphs, written to be dictated and then expounded in class. It falls into three parts. The Logic, condensed from the larger work and usually read in its place, treats thought’s own determinations. The Philosophy of Nature moves from space and time through mechanics, physics and organic life. The Philosophy of Spirit runs from anthropology and psychology through objective spirit — right, morality, the state — to art, revealed religion and philosophy. These he calls absolute spirit, and distinguishes only by their form: image, representation, concept.

The Philosophy of Nature has aged worst and is often cited to embarrass him, since he backs Goethe against Newton on colour and handles contemporary chemistry with more confidence than it deserved. The underlying claim is subtler than the errors. Nature is not deduced a priori but exhibited as a graded series in which spirit is increasingly at home. Every English edition prints Zusätze, additions compiled by editors from student notebooks. They are the most readable pages in Hegel and they are not, strictly speaking, his text.

The three editions differ enough to matter. The Heidelberg text of 1817 has 477 numbered paragraphs. The 1827 revision is much larger and carries a new preface answering the charge of pantheism. The 1830 edition, the one usually translated, has 577. The remarks printed in smaller type below the paragraphs are Hegel’s own writing. The book ends by quoting Aristotle’s Metaphysics on thought thinking itself, in Greek and untranslated.

works.t: Elements of the Philosophy of Right (Grundlinien der Philosophie des Rechts)
p: The argument moves in three stages. Abstract right gives the person property and contract but cannot say what is worth willing. Morality, Moralität, supplies conscience and intention. Hegel credits Kant with establishing the standpoint of the free will, but charges that a conscience testing maxims for consistency has no content of its own. Ethical life, Sittlichkeit, is the answer. Family, civil society and state are institutions in which duty and inclination coincide because the agent was formed by them. His account of civil society is unsentimental: accumulating wealth produces a rabble of the impoverished.

The preface carries his two most argued-over sentences. That what is rational is actual, and what is actual rational, was read by conservatives as a blessing on whatever exists and by radicals as a scandal. But Wirklichkeit is a term of art, and much that exists fails his standard of actuality. That makes it a demand as readily as a consolation. That the owl of Minerva takes flight only with the falling of dusk concedes more. Philosophy comprehends a form of life once it is finished, and cannot instruct the world.

What he actually proposes is neither absolutism nor democracy. The monarch is hereditary. His function is to say yes and dot the i. Laws are made with an assembly of two houses, the lower one reached through corporations and estates rather than by counting heads. Trials are public and by jury. Officials are salaried and appointed on examination. Punishment, he argues, honours the criminal by treating him as rational. The state rests on no contract, because no one chooses whether to belong to one.

The preface also attacks Jakob Friedrich Fries, who had been dismissed from Jena under the Carlsbad Decrees, and quotes him in order to ridicule him. Whether that was a denunciation of a man already down has been argued since Haym. Karl-Heinz Ilting held that the preface was written after the decrees and after the body of the book, and that it is harsher than the course it introduces. The transcripts of the lectures Hegel gave from 1817 to 1825 do show the gap. How far it acquits him is not agreed.

works.t: Lectures on the Philosophy of World History (Vorlesungen über die Philosophie der Weltgeschichte)
p: Hegel gave this course five times in Berlin. It is the most widely read thing under his name. It is also not a book he wrote. Eduard Gans assembled the first edition in 1837 from Hegel’s own manuscript for the introduction and from students’ notebooks for everything else. Hegel’s son Karl reworked it in 1840. The thesis is compact: world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom, from a world in which one is free, through one in which some are, to the modern principle that all are.

Its mechanism is the cunning of reason. Historical agents pursue their passions and interests — Caesar wanted power, not the empire he founded — and the universal is realised through them without their intending it. Great men are those whose private aims happen to meet what the age requires. The scheme carries costs no honest reader can skirt. The course as we have it consigns Africa to a place outside history proper, and treats Asia as the childhood of spirit. That ranking is not incidental to the argument. It has done real damage.

The text has since been dug back towards its sources. Georg Lasson re-edited it from 1917, and Johannes Hoffmeister the introduction in 1955. One single course, that of 1822 and 1823, has now been published from the transcripts and translated in 2011. Reading one year straight is a different experience from reading Gans’s composite. The four realms are Oriental, Greek, Roman and Germanic. The movement runs from east to west. Hegel calls history a slaughter-bench on which the happiness of peoples is sacrificed. He says its periods of happiness are blank pages. He also holds that there is no history proper without a state and written records.

works.t: Lectures on Aesthetics, on the Philosophy of Religion, and on the History of Philosophy
p: None of these are books by Hegel. The society of friends who edited his collected works after 1831 built each course from surviving manuscript fragments and the notebooks of whichever students they could collect. They spliced different years into one continuous text. Modern scholarship has shown how much of the architecture is editorial — above all the reconstruction of the religion lectures year by year, and the critique of Heinrich Gustav Hotho’s heavily shaped Aesthetics. They remain indispensable, and they should be quoted with the transcripts in view.

The Aesthetics divides art into symbolic, classical and romantic. It argues that classical sculpture achieved a balance of meaning and sensuous form which Christian and modern art necessarily broke: the notorious claim that art is, in its highest vocation, a thing of the past. The religion lectures treat Christianity as revealed religion, the same content philosophy grasps conceptually, given in the form of representation. Whether that preserves or dissolves faith split his school within five years. The history of philosophy course made a permanent difference by insisting that earlier systems are stages rather than errors.

Beauty, in the Aesthetics, is the sensuous shining of the Idea. The arts rank by how much matter they need: architecture, sculpture, painting, music, poetry. The religion lectures were delivered four times, in 1821, 1824, 1827 and 1831. Walter Jaeschke’s edition prints the years separately instead of merging them. They treat the death of God as a moment inside the divine life, which is the sentence the school fought over. The history of philosophy follows the order of the categories of the Logic. Thales and Parmenides come first because the Logic begins with being.

legacy: The school broke apart at once, over religion. David Friedrich Strauss, whose Life of Jesus of 1835 treated the gospel narratives as myth, coined the parliamentary metaphor of right, centre and left. Right Hegelians read the master as underwriting Christianity and the Prussian state. The Young Hegelians — Strauss, Bruno Bauer, Feuerbach and briefly Marx — read the same texts as dissolving both. Feuerbach’s inversion, that theology is misread anthropology, set a pattern.

Marx kept the dialectic and threw out the idealism, writing in 1873 that with Hegel it stood on its head and had to be turned right side up. Kierkegaard attacked the System for leaving no room for the existing individual. Rudolf Haym’s Hegel und seine Zeit of 1857 fixed the caricature of a philosopher of Prussian absolutism. Later scholarship has dismantled that charge, not least through Karl-Heinz Ilting’s edition of the lecture transcripts, where he speaks more liberally than he dared print.

The Prussian government eventually tried to answer him from a chair of its own. Schelling was called to Berlin in 1841, reportedly to stamp out the dragon-seed of Hegelian pantheism. His audience included Kierkegaard, Bakunin, Engels and Jacob Burckhardt. The lectures disappointed nearly all of them. Marx had by then written a line-by-line criticism of the Philosophy of Right, in 1843, which stayed unpublished until 1927. Feuerbach’s Essence of Christianity of 1841 did in public what that manuscript could not.

In Britain and America he was first a liberation and then a scandal. Green, Bradley and Royce built idealist systems on him. Russell and Moore founded analytic philosophy on the revolt against them. Popper in 1945 named him an enemy of the open society, a reading few historians now defend. Alexandre Kojève’s Paris seminar of the 1930s put recognition at the centre. It reached Sartre, Lacan and Frantz Fanon.

Every revival since has run on newly available texts. Dilthey’s essay of 1905 and Nohl’s edition of 1907 produced the young Hegel. Georg Lukács published his book on those years in 1948. Benedetto Croce had asked in 1907 what is living and what is dead in Hegel. The question has kept its title. Herbert Marcuse’s Reason and Revolution of 1941 answered the charge that the argument ran towards fascism. J. N. Findlay’s re-examination of 1958 made him readable again for philosophers trained to dismiss him.

One recent argument is unresolved and worth naming as such. Susan Buck-Morss proposed in 2000 that the pages on lordship and bondage were written with the Haitian revolution in view, which Hegel could have followed in the journals he read. Critics answer that he nowhere connects the two. The dispute is about what counts as evidence that a text has a source, and it has not settled.

What survives now is less the system than arguments taken up piecemeal. Recognition has become a working concept in political theory through Charles Taylor and Axel Honneth. Robert Pippin, Terry Pinkard, Robert Brandom and John McDowell have made Hegel a live interlocutor. They read him as a theorist of the sociality of reason, with norms sustained by mutual accountability rather than found in nature. The heavy metaphysics of the Logic has also returned.

The vocabulary was Kant’s and Fichte’s before it was applied to Hegel. It spread after Chalybäus through Marx, who repeated it as Hegel’s method in The Poverty of Philosophy of 1847. Gustav Mueller’s article of 1958 is the standard demolition.

read.first: Begin with the preface and introduction to the Phenomenology alongside a paragraph-by-paragraph commentary. Then read lordship and bondage and the unhappy consciousness in full. After that the Philosophy of Right, the most tractable of the books he actually wrote. Take the Encyclopaedia Logic as the way into the logic, and save the larger Science of Logic for later. Pinkard’s translation of 2018 and Miller’s of 1977 are the usual English Phenomenology. For the Philosophy of Right, use Nisbet’s translation in the edition Allen Wood made in 1991.
read.note: Expect to reread. The sentences are hard because the terms are being redefined as they are used, not because the translation is failing.

hegel.caveat: Four of the works most often quoted as Hegel’s — the lectures on history, aesthetics, religion and the history of philosophy — are posthumous compilations from student notebooks. Their wording, structure and sometimes their emphases belong to their editors. The additions printed through the Encyclopaedia have the same status. The eighteen-volume edition of 1832 to 1845 built those composites. The critical Gesammelte Werke and the separate editions of single courses have been taking them apart since 1968. Where a quotation carries weight, it is worth knowing which year it comes from and whose notebook.

schelling.sub: the idealist who insisted nature has a life of its own
world: Schelling arrived in Jena in 1798 at twenty-three. There Fichte was lecturing, the Schlegel brothers were founding the Athenaeum, and Goethe, who backed his appointment, pursued his own morphology. Natural science was then in a speculative phase: Galvani and Volta on animal electricity, Ritter on electrochemistry, magnetism treated as a key to life. A philosophy making nature productive rather than inert had a scientific audience.

The second half of his career belongs to a different Germany. He moved to Catholic Bavaria, where Montgelas was building a modern administrative state, and spent decades in Munich as an academician. In 1841 Friedrich Wilhelm IV called him to Berlin to counter the pantheism the court saw in the Hegelian school. He came as the state’s answer to a philosophy he had helped make possible.
life: Born in 1775 at Leonberg in Württemberg, son of a Protestant pastor, Schelling entered the Tübingen Stift at fifteen, five years under the normal age. He shared rooms with Hölderlin and Hegel. He was publishing at nineteen and holding a chair at twenty-three. In 1803 he married Caroline Schlegel. Her death in 1809 broke him, and The Ages of the World was drafted three times and abandoned.

Hegel’s jibe in the Phenomenology preface about the night in which all cows are black ended a friendship of twenty years. Schelling published almost no philosophy after 1809, while Hegel’s system conquered Germany. In Berlin in 1841 Kierkegaard, Bakunin and Engels sat in his audience. Kierkegaard was electrified and then bored, and Engels published pamphlets against him within the year. A pirated transcript appeared in 1843, and he soon stopped. He died in Switzerland in 1854.

works.t: Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature (Ideen zu einer Philosophie der Natur)
p: Against Fichte, for whom nature is only the field of resistance posited by the I, Schelling argues that nature is productive in its own right. It is not a finished set of objects but an activity congealing into products. Polarity organises the whole: magnetism, electricity and chemical process are stages of one opposition working itself out. Organic life is where that productivity becomes visible. Extended in On the World Soul of 1798, the programme gave romantic science its charter. It drew from scientists both enthusiasm and the charge of building on analogy.

works.t: System of Transcendental Idealism (System des transscendentalen Idealismus)
p: This is the companion volume. The philosophy of nature runs from the objective up to intelligence. Transcendental philosophy starts from the I and derives nature. He traces consciousness through theoretical and practical stages and ends with art. In the work of art the unconscious productivity of nature and the conscious activity of the artist coincide, so art is the organon of philosophy. Within a year he pushed further. The Presentation of My System of Philosophy of 1801 states the identity philosophy outright, subject and object one in the Absolute.

works.t: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom (Philosophische Untersuchungen über das Wesen der menschlichen Freiheit)
p: The last book he published is also his strangest. Freedom, he argues, is the capacity for good and evil. A system that cannot make evil real has explained it away. To make room for it he distinguishes within God between existence and its dark ground, an ungrounded will that is the condition of personality. The move is drawn from Jakob Böhme. Freedom is then an intelligible deed by which the self chooses its character outside time. The essay opens the way to his late contrast between negative philosophy, which grasps essences, and the positive philosophy beginning from the brute fact that anything exists.

legacy: The philosophy of nature had its most durable afterlife outside Germany, in romantic science and in Coleridge. He carried it into English letters with acknowledgement thin enough to earn him charges of plagiarism. Hegel’s dismissal, and his school’s dominance, left Schelling in the position of a brilliant beginning that somebody else completed. His own long silence did nothing to correct that verdict.

The late work has aged better than the middle. Kierkegaard’s insistence on existence over essence, and Heidegger’s 1936 lecture course on the freedom essay, made Schelling a source for the tradition running into continental philosophy today. Tillich, Habermas and more recently Slavoj Žižek have built on him. He is read now less as a stage between Fichte and Hegel than as idealism’s internal critic.

read.first: Read the freedom essay of 1809 first: it is short, self-contained, and the one text where his central concerns are visible without the apparatus. Follow it with the closing sections of the System of Transcendental Idealism on art.
read.note: Schelling restarted his philosophy so often that there is no single system to master. Treating each phase as a fresh attempt is less frustrating than hunting for consistency.

schopenhauer.sub: the pessimist who named the thing-in-itself Will
world: Schopenhauer was born in 1788 at Danzig, a Baltic trading republic living on grain and timber. When Prussia annexed the city in 1793 his father, a merchant of republican convictions, moved family and business to Hamburg rather than become a Prussian subject. The fortune he left in 1805 was the decisive fact of his son’s life. It produced an income meaning Schopenhauer never needed a salary, a patron, a chair or a readership.

German philosophy in his working years belonged to the universities and, in Prussia, to the state. The University of Berlin, founded in 1810, made philosophy part of the training of civil servants. Fichte, then Hegel, held its chair and its prestige. Schopenhauer thought the arrangement corrupt. His attacks on Hegel aim as much at the professoriate as at idealism.

Two things outside philosophy shaped him. The first was the arrival of Indian scripture in Europe. He read the Upanishads in the Oupnek’hat, Anquetil-Duperron’s Latin version of a Persian translation made for the Mughal prince Dara Shukoh, and kept it by his bed for life. The second was the deflation after 1848, which left German readers with an appetite for a philosophy of disappointment.
life: His father’s death, probably by suicide, released him from a merchant apprenticeship he loathed. He caught up on Greek and Latin. He entered Göttingen in 1809 to read medicine and switched to philosophy under G. E. Schulze, whose advice formed him: read Plato and Kant first. In Berlin from 1811 he heard Fichte and Schleiermacher and disliked both. Jena awarded him a doctorate in absentia in 1813.

At Weimar in 1813-1814 he worked with Goethe on colour. There he met the orientalist Friedrich Majer, who put the Oupnek’hat into his hands. He also quarrelled irreparably with his mother, the novelist Johanna Schopenhauer, and never saw her again. He wrote his main work at Dresden and published it in December 1818, to almost no sales. The printing was eventually pulped.

He habilitated at Berlin in 1820 and scheduled his lectures at the hour of Hegel’s, a provocation that failed completely. He soon gave up teaching for good. Fleeing the cholera of 1831, he settled from 1833 in Frankfurt with a poodle, a flute and an unvarying routine. He won a Norwegian prize in 1839, was refused a Danish one in 1840, and issued a second edition in 1844 to near silence. Fame came with Parerga in 1851, nine years before his death.

works.t: On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason (Über die vierfache Wurzel des Satzes vom zureichenden Grunde)
p: The dissertation argues that the principle that nothing is without a reason is not one principle but four. They operate in four irreducible domains: causes among physical objects, grounds among concepts in inference, the necessary relations of space and time in mathematics, and motives in acting subjects. Confusing them produces a long list of philosophical errors. The cosmological argument applies causal reasoning outside the only region where it means anything.

The book is dry and looks like an academic exercise. But Schopenhauer insisted ever afterwards that nobody could follow his main work without reading it first, and he was right. It fixes the shape of everything later. The world of representation is governed entirely by these forms, so the thing-in-itself cannot be reached along any of them. If it is reachable at all, the route lies elsewhere.

works.t: The World as Will and Representation (Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung)
works.y: vol. I 1818, dated 1819; vol. II added 1844
p: The first volume is built in four books — epistemology, metaphysics of nature, aesthetics, ethics — and turns on a single move. Kant had shown that we know only appearances. Schopenhauer accepts this and claims a way in. One object is known both from outside as body and from inside as willing. The inside view is not another representation. Generalise it and the inner nature of everything is Will: not rational, aiming at nothing, a blind striving objectified in gravity, growth and appetite. The pessimism follows by construction. Willing is lack. Satisfaction ends it for a moment, after which fresh desire or boredom arrives. Two things suspend it: aesthetic contemplation, music first among the arts because it copies the Will rather than any appearance of it, and ascetic denial of the will.

The 1844 second volume is not a revision but fifty supplementary chapters keyed to the first. They hold some of his best writing — on death, on sexual love as the species’ interest working through individuals who believe they are choosing, on the vanity of existence. It also shows the strain. Kant’s argument forbids knowing the thing-in-itself at all, and the supplements concede that Will may be only the nearest description available.

works.t: On the Will in Nature (Über den Willen in der Natur)
p: A short book gathering confirmations of the metaphysics from the empirical sciences of the day: physiology, comparative anatomy, plant life, magnetism, and the instinct of animals that plan nothing. Working naturalists, he argues, keep arriving without noticing at descriptions that require something like blind striving beneath the mechanism they describe. It is the only place where Schopenhauer engages contemporary science at length. Its interest now is methodological. He wanted his central claim treated as a hypothesis about what nature looks like from inside, answerable to evidence, rather than as a deduction from first principles. Some of it has dated badly, the chapter on animal magnetism worst of all.

works.t: The Two Fundamental Problems of Ethics: On the Freedom of the Will; On the Basis of Morality
p: The first essay won the prize of the Norwegian Royal Society. It grants that we feel free before acting and argues that the feeling misleads. Given a character and a motive, one action follows. The sense of openness comes from not knowing our own character in advance. Responsibility attaches to what a person is rather than to what he does.

The second was sent alone to the Danish Royal Society and refused the prize, partly for the rudeness of its remarks about other philosophers. It rejects Kant’s derivation of morality from reason. It grounds morality instead in compassion, Mitleid: the immediate and otherwise inexplicable participation in another’s suffering. Schopenhauer explains that participation as a momentary seeing-through of the illusion that we are separate beings.

Two volumes of side-works and leftovers: essays on the vanity of existence, on suicide, on noise, on university philosophy, together with the popular Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life and, notoriously, an essay on women that is indefensible and was quoted approvingly for a century. Publishers turned the manuscript down. The one who took it printed a small run and paid him nothing.

It made him famous at sixty-three. John Oxenford’s anonymous review in the Westminster Review of 1853, translated into German soon afterwards, presented him to a public that had ignored him for thirty-five years. The irony is exact. The book that carried his system into the world contains almost none of it. Most readers since have entered the philosophy through its offcuts.

legacy: Artists reached him first. Wagner read The World as Will and Representation in 1854 and rebuilt his understanding of music around the claim that it expresses the Will itself. Tristan is unimaginable without it. Nietzsche found the book in Leipzig in 1865 and made it his formation, then inverted it: the same blind force, renamed will to power, affirmed rather than denied. Tolstoy, Hardy, Proust, Mann and Beckett all drew on him.

The philosophical inheritance is quieter. Freud found in him a theory of drives, of repression, and of the intellect as servant of something older than itself. He acknowledged the priority when pressed. Wittgenstein read him early. The ethical and solipsistic passages closing the Tractatus — the willing subject at the limit of the world rather than in it — carry his imprint.

What holds up is the psychology: intellect secondary, motives opaque to their owner, satisfaction structurally unstable. The metaphysics has few defenders, since naming the thing-in-itself is exactly what Kant’s argument was meant to forbid. His engagement with Indian thought matters as the first sustained one in Western philosophy, though in Latin intermediaries. He took chiefly what confirmed him.

In Germany the pessimism became a public quarrel in its own right. Eduard von Hartmann’s Philosophy of the Unconscious of 1869 went through editions Schopenhauer never saw. It set off two decades of argument over whether existence is worth having. That is how the doctrine reached a general readership.

read.first: Read On the Fourfold Root first if you can bear it, then The World as Will and Representation book by book. Keep the 1844 supplements to hand for whichever book you have just finished. Parerga is the easier entry and the one that made his name.
read.note: He is among the best prose stylists in German philosophy. That is a genuine reason to read him, and also a reason to check the arguments rather than the sentences.

schopenhauer.caveat: How far Indian sources shaped the 1818 book rather than confirming conclusions he had already reached is disputed. He met the Upanishads in 1813-1814, and only through a Latin translation of a Persian translation.

comte.sub: the positivist who named sociology and then founded a church
world: Comte came of age in a France that had run through revolution, terror, empire and restoration inside twenty-five years. His lifelong question was how to re-found social order without returning to throne and altar. The École Polytechnique, which he entered in 1814 and left when it was purged in 1816, had made engineers the model of useful knowledge. Industry arrived late and fast. In 1848 came a republic Comte welcomed and then abandoned for Louis-Napoleon.
life: Comte was born at Montpellier in 1798 to a Catholic royalist family. He served as secretary to Henri de Saint-Simon from 1817 until they quarrelled in 1824 over who had written what. He began his private lecture course in 1826, broke down within weeks, spent time in an asylum, and attempted to drown himself in 1827 before resuming. He never held a chair, living on examining work and then on subscriptions raised by admirers including John Stuart Mill. His love for Clotilde de Vaux, who died in 1846, reorganised his ambitions around religion.

works.t: Course of Positive Philosophy (Cours de philosophie positive)
p: The law of three stages holds that every branch of knowledge, and every mind, passes from the theological, which explains events by wills, through the metaphysical, which substitutes abstract essences, to the positive, which abandons causes and seeks only invariable relations among observable phenomena. Comte then ranks the sciences by decreasing generality and increasing complexity — mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology, and last the one still missing, which he named sociology in 1839. Harriet Martineau’s condensed English version of 1853 carried the work to Britain.

works.t: System of Positive Polity (Système de politique positive)
p: Here positivism becomes a cult. Comte proposed a Religion of Humanity with the Great Being, the accumulated achievement of the race, in place of God. It had a priesthood of scientists, sacraments, a thirteen-month calendar of great men, and the motto that love is the principle, order the basis and progress the goal. He coined altruism as its watchword. Émile Littré broke with him, and most scientific followers went too. Mill dismissed the new system as a design for spiritual despotism.

legacy: The word sociology stuck, and so did the programme of treating society as a field of law-governed phenomena. Durkheim took the inheritance seriously enough to argue with it in detail. The religion found real adherents in Brazil, where positivist officers helped make the republic of 1889 and put order and progress on its flag. Twentieth-century logical positivism shares Comte’s hostility to metaphysics and little else. The two are still confused.

read.first: Martineau’s abridgement of the Cours remains the usual way in. Read the opening lecture on the three stages and the lectures introducing sociology.
read.note: The later religious writings repay a look precisely because they embarrass the standard picture of positivism.

comte.caveat: Whether the Religion of Humanity follows from the Cours or betrays it has been disputed since Littré. The answer usually depends on how much weight a reader gives Comte’s own insistence on continuity.

feuerbach.sub: who read theology as anthropology written backwards
world: Hegel died in 1831 and his school split almost at once. The right read the system as underwriting the Prussian state and Lutheran Christianity; the left read the dialectic as a method that would consume them both. The dividing question was the historical truth of the Gospels, opened by Strauss's Life of Jesus in 1835.

The censorship made this a career risk rather than a debate. Prussia policed university appointments, and a man suspected of atheism did not get a chair. Feuerbach never held one after the first, which is why his most influential work was written from a village.
life: Born in 1804 at Landshut, the son of a distinguished jurist. He went to Heidelberg to read theology, moved to Berlin to hear Hegel, and stayed two years, later saying Hegel was his second father and that he had to break with him for that reason. He took a post at Erlangen in 1828.

In 1830 he published, anonymously, Thoughts on Death and Immortality, which denied personal immortality. The authorship was discovered and his academic career ended. He married a woman with a share in a porcelain factory and lived at Bruckberg on its income for twenty-four years, writing. The factory failed in 1859 and he spent his last years poor; Social Democrats organised his support. He died in 1872.

works.t: The Essence of Christianity (Das Wesen des Christentums)
p: God is the human species-essence — reason, will, love — abstracted from actual people, magnified to infinity, and then set over against them as another being. Religion is therefore true as anthropology and false as theology: every doctrine tells us something about ourselves once it is read the right way round. Incarnation says the divine is human. Prayer says the heart's wish is addressed to the heart. The cost is alienation: the richer God is made, the poorer the man who made him, since everything given to God is taken from the species. The remedy is not to abolish religion but to recognise what it has always been about. George Eliot translated it into English in 1854.

works.t: Principles of the Philosophy of the Future (Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft)
p: Speculative philosophy is theology in another idiom: Hegel's absolute spirit is the Christian God rationalised, and the dialectic that begins with thought and derives being from it has the subject and the predicate the wrong way round. Philosophy must begin instead from the sensuous, embodied human being, who is a being with a body, an object outside him, and other people. The programme is what later got called Feuerbach's transformative method — invert the subject and predicate of any speculative sentence and see whether it becomes true.

legacy: Engels described the effect of The Essence of Christianity on his generation as an enthusiasm nothing else matched, and said they all became Feuerbachians on the spot. Marx's Theses on Feuerbach, written in 1845 and printed only in 1888, accept the inversion of Hegel entirely and then turn it against its author: the religious self-alienation Feuerbach describes has a cause in the world that produced it, so the task is to change that world, not to explain the illusion. The eleventh thesis is the most quoted sentence in the tradition, and it is a criticism of him.

Outside Marxism he survives in the projection theory of religion, which reaches Freud and much of the sociology of religion, usually without attribution. Barth, who thought him the most serious opponent Protestant theology had, is the one major theologian to have taken the argument as an argument rather than as an insult.

read.first: The Essence of Christianity, the introduction and the chapters on God as a being of the understanding and on the Incarnation. Then the Principles, which are short.
read.note: The Theses on Feuerbach are three pages and should be read immediately afterwards; they are unintelligible without him and are how most readers meet his name.

feuerbach.caveat: Whether the species-essence he appeals to is itself a residue of the idealism he was rejecting is Marx's charge and is hard to answer on Feuerbach's own terms.

mill.sub: the utilitarian who made room for quality and liberty
world: Mill’s life spans the decades when Britain became the first industrial society and then argued about what to do with itself. Cotton towns, railways and the New Poor Law of 1834 arrived alongside a franchise the Reform Act of 1832 had widened only to the propertied. Chartism answered with the People’s Charter of 1838 and mass petitions in 1839, 1842 and 1848. The Reform Act of 1867 came two years into Mill’s single term in Parliament.

For thirty-five years his employer was the East India Company, which governed a subcontinent from Leadenhall Street. Mill drafted dispatches on Indian affairs without visiting India, and became Examiner of Indian Correspondence in 1856. He wrote the Company’s defence when the Rebellion of 1857 led Parliament to abolish it. The employment marks the philosophy: the liberty he defended was reserved for peoples he judged capable of improvement by discussion.

Intellectually the ground kept moving. The revolutions of 1848 confirmed his republican sympathies and his doubts about their competence. Comte and the Saint-Simonians offered a science of society he half accepted. Darwin’s Origin of Species appeared in the same year as On Liberty, and Mill noted the hypothesis with caution rather than enthusiasm. The suppression of the Morant Bay rising in Jamaica in 1865 set him against Carlyle in a quarrel that cost him friends.
life: James Mill educated his eldest son as a demonstration. Greek at three, Latin at eight, logic at twelve, political economy at thirteen, all at the same desk as his father’s History of British India, with no holidays and no boys of his own age. A year in France in 1820 gave him French and a taste for a less English life. At sixteen he founded a Utilitarian Society. At seventeen he entered the East India Company as a clerk under his father.

In the autumn of 1826, aged twenty, he asked himself whether the achievement of all his objects would make him happy, and answered no. The depression lasted months and lifted, he says, while he read Marmontel’s Mémoires and wept. Wordsworth completed the cure by showing him that feeling could be cultivated. He kept the doctrine, but afterwards read Coleridge, Carlyle and Tocqueville for what his father’s school had left out.

He met Harriet Taylor in 1830. She was married. Their friendship lasted twenty years under public disapproval. They married in 1851 after John Taylor’s death, and she died at Avignon in 1858. Mill credited her with a share in nearly everything he wrote after 1840. He sat as member for Westminster from 1865 to 1868. In 1867 he moved the amendment that would have replaced “man” with “person” in the Reform Bill. It drew seventy-three votes.

works.t: A System of Logic; Principles of Political Economy
p: The two big books of the 1840s made his reputation before any of the famous essays. Against the intuitionists, who held that some truths are known independently of experience, the Logic argues that every genuine inference is inductive, mathematics included. Book III supplies the experimental methods of agreement, difference, residues and concomitant variations. Book VI proposes a logic of the moral sciences. Frege and Russell later destroyed the empiricist account of arithmetic. But the political motive survived: appeals to intuition entrench prejudice as necessary truth.

The Principles was the standard English textbook for forty years, and turns on one distinction. Laws of production have the fixity of physical fact. Laws of distribution are human institutions, alterable by choice. That separation opened classical economics to reform. Successive editions grew friendlier to cooperative production and a chastened socialism.

One very simple principle: power may be used against a member of a civilised community only to prevent harm to others. His own good is never sufficient warrant. Chapter two defends free discussion on grounds independent of tolerance as a sentiment — a silenced opinion may be true, or partly true, and even a false one keeps the truth from decaying into dead dogma. Chapter three defends experiments in living against respectable opinion, a heavier tyranny in England, Mill thought, than any law. The limits strain. He exempts children, and exempts “backward states of society”, where he says despotism is legitimate if it improves them. That is the East India Company official speaking. Critics have pressed harder still on harm itself, which must exclude mere offence and ordinary competitive injury if the principle is to do any work.

Written to rescue the doctrine from the charge that it suits swine, the essay concedes that pleasures differ in kind and appeals to judges competent in both. Those who know the higher and the lower prefer the higher, whatever it costs in contentment. Better, in the phrase everyone remembers, to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. Whether that survives a single standard of utility has been argued ever since.

Chapter four offers what Mill calls a proof, having said that ultimate ends admit of none in the ordinary sense. The sole evidence that a thing is visible is that people see it. The sole evidence that it is desirable is that people desire it. Each person’s happiness is a good to that person, and the general happiness a good to the aggregate. Moore called this a naturalistic fallacy, others a fallacy of composition. Defenders answer that Mill displays grounds rather than deducing a conclusion. But it remains his most attacked page.

works.t: Considerations on Representative Government; The Subjection of Women
p: The Considerations defends representative government where a people is ready for it, then attends to machinery: proportional representation on Thomas Hare’s scheme, open rather than secret voting because a vote is a trust exercised over others, and plural votes for the educated as a stopgap. That last proposal was unpopular then and has aged badly.

The Subjection of Women is the more radical book. The legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and now the chief obstacle to human improvement; nobody can pronounce on women’s nature, since what is observed is a hothouse product; and marriage as the law then stood was the last surviving form of domestic slavery. Written with Helen Taylor at his side, three years after Harriet’s death and out of arguments the two of them had worked through together, it was ridiculed in England and translated rapidly abroad.

Published months after his death and edited by his stepdaughter Helen Taylor, this is a deliberately unliterary account of an education and its correction. It describes James Mill’s experiment in full, records the crisis of 1826 without self-pity, and assigns Harriet Taylor a role so large that generations of readers have suspected chivalry. An earlier draft, more candid about his father and the Taylors, appeared in 1961 and shows that Mill softened rather than invented. The book reads equally well as the classic document of Victorian rationalism and as the case against rearing a child on argument alone.

legacy: On Liberty became the central text of liberal politics in English. The harm principle is still the standard opening move in arguments about censorship, drugs and speech. Its critics have been serious from the start: James Fitzjames Stephen argued in 1873 that society rests on coercion Mill would forbid. Legal moralists such as Patrick Devlin revived the case. The imperial exception has moved from footnote to centre of scholarly discussion since the 1990s.

In ethics he became the reference point for every later utilitarian. Sidgwick built on him, Moore attacked him, and twentieth-century debate over rule and act utilitarianism began by asking which he held, a question still unsettled. The doctrine of higher pleasures is judged either an abandonment of hedonism or the beginning of a better theory of well-being, depending on the commentator.

The Subjection of Women had the slowest and largest afterlife. Almost alone among canonical philosophers before the twentieth century, Mill argued for full legal equality of the sexes and acted on it in Parliament. The book served suffrage campaigns in Britain and America for fifty years. Harriet Taylor’s part in it, long dismissed as uxorious exaggeration, has been reassessed since the 1970s.

It appeared in February 1859, three months after Harriet Taylor’s death, dedicated to her as the inspirer and in part the author of what was best in his writing. Mill said the two of them had gone over it sentence by sentence, and that he would not revise it again.

read.first: Read On Liberty straight through in an evening, then Utilitarianism, then the Autobiography for the life that produced both.
read.note: The prose is lucid, but the qualifications matter. Mill’s worst sentences are usually the ones being quoted at you.

mill.caveat: How much of the later work Harriet Taylor wrote is genuinely unsettled: Mill’s own attributions are generous, the surviving drafts show real collaboration, and scholars disagree about how to weigh them.

kierkegaard.sub: the writer who set the single individual against the system
world: Copenhagen in the 1840s held about 120,000 people inside walls that had not yet come down, in the middle of what Denmark calls its Golden Age: Oehlenschläger in poetry, Thorvaldsen in sculpture, Hans Christian Andersen in the bookshops, Johan Ludvig Heiberg arbitrating taste on Hegelian principles. Everyone of consequence knew everyone else. Kierkegaard could publish in the morning and hear the book discussed by name in the evening. The smallness of the stage explains both the intimacy of his writing and its combativeness.

Church and state were one institution. The Danish People’s Church was established, its clergy salaried officials. Its leading theologian, Hans Lassen Martensen, taught that faith could be comprehended within a speculative system. Absolute monarchy ended in the March days of 1848. A constitution followed in June 1849, with a war over Schleswig alongside. Denmark got its revolution without barricades. Kierkegaard watched with distaste, convinced that changing the form of government does nothing to the problem he cared about.

The press was the other power. In December 1845 the critic P. L. Møller published a sneering review. Kierkegaard replied by inviting abuse from The Corsair, the satirical weekly Møller wrote for under Meïr Aron Goldschmidt’s editorship. It came for months: caricatures of his stoop, his gait, his uneven trouser legs, until schoolboys shouted after him in the street. The affair ended his habit of walking the city talking to everyone. It turned his attention to levelling and to the tyranny of what he called the public.
life: Søren Aabye Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813, youngest of seven children of a wool merchant who had made a fortune and retired early. Michael Pedersen Kierkegaard raised his son in a Moravian pietism heavy with guilt. He confessed something — the sources suggest cursing God as a boy on the Jutland heath — that Kierkegaard called the great earthquake. Five of the seven children died before their father. The inheritance, when it came in 1838, funded a life of writing without employment. He spent it exactly.

He read theology at the University of Copenhagen and defended a dissertation on Socratic irony in 1841. In September 1840 he had proposed to Regine Olsen, then eighteen. Within a year he broke off the engagement, returning her ring and making himself look a scoundrel so that she would be free of him. He spent the winter in Berlin hearing Schelling lecture, was disappointed, and came home to write Either/Or. Regine married Johan Frederik Schlegel in 1847. Kierkegaard wrote about the engagement, always at an angle, for the rest of his life, and left her his estate.

The books came at a rate hard to credit: eighteen months in 1843 and 1844 produced six of them. Pseudonymous works appeared beside signed religious discourses, often on the same day, printed at his own expense. Late in 1854 he attacked the state church in the newspaper Fædrelandet and then in his own broadsheet, spending the last of the money on it. He collapsed in the street in October 1855. He died in hospital on 11 November, forty-two years old.

p: Victor Eremita claims to have found these papers in a secretary desk and prints them without deciding between them. The first volume belongs to A, an aesthete: aphorisms, an essay on Mozart’s Don Giovanni as the musical-erotic, a lecture on rotating one’s crops to stave off boredom, and the long, cold Seducer’s Diary. The second is two enormous letters from Judge William, a married civil servant, arguing that the ethical life chooses itself and so acquires a history, where the aesthete has only moments. The book closes with a Jutland pastor’s sermon on the thought that against God we are always in the wrong. No verdict is offered. The reader is left having to choose, which is the argument.

works.t: Fear and Trembling (Frygt og Bæven); Repetition (Gjentagelsen)
p: Johannes de silentio circles the binding of Isaac through four retellings and three problems. If the ethical is the universal, and Abraham is prepared to kill his son, then either he is a murderer or there is a teleological suspension of the ethical. In that suspension the single individual stands higher than the universal by virtue of a relation to God. The knight of faith differs from the knight of infinite resignation in believing he will have Isaac back in this life, which is absurd. He cannot explain himself, because faith is not a public reason. Constantin Constantius, published the same day, tests the companion category: repetition, which unlike Greek recollection is recovery forward, and which the book cannot demonstrate except through Job and a young man’s broken engagement.

works.t: Philosophical Fragments (Philosophiske Smuler); Concluding Unscientific Postscript
p: Johannes Climacus poses a thought-experiment in the Fragments. If the truth that matters is already in the learner, the teacher is a midwife and Socrates is enough. If it is not, the teacher must supply the condition for receiving it as well as the truth, must enter time to do so. In that case the moment of encounter becomes decisive rather than accidental. Climacus builds the structure of the incarnation without naming it and asks whether such a hypothesis can be thought. It cannot: it is the absolute paradox, which reason meets by colliding with it.

The Postscript is many times longer. It asks how an existing individual can relate to that paradox. Objective approaches, historical or speculative, yield approximation. Approximation is no place to stand for a decision about one’s life. Truth is subjectivity: not that any belief is as good as another, but that here the manner of appropriation belongs to what is believed. The objection to Hegel is that a system of existence is impossible for the one existing inside it. Kierkegaard appended a signed statement acknowledging the pseudonyms and asking that no opinion in them be attributed to him.

Vigilius Haufniensis, the watchman of Copenhagen, writes a psychology of the possibility that precedes sin. Anxiety differs from fear in having no object: it answers to possibility itself, a sympathetic antipathy and antipathetic sympathy before an open future. Kierkegaard’s phrase for it is the dizziness of freedom. Adam, before the prohibition can mean anything to him, is anxious not about a known evil but about being able. The book therefore refuses to explain original sin either as inherited substance or as one first mistake in history. Each person begins it again. Dense and scholastic, it became the most technically influential of his works for later philosophy and psychiatry.

works.t: The Sickness unto Death (Sygdommen til Døden); The Attack upon Christendom
p: Published under Anti-Climacus, a pseudonym standing above the author rather than below him, The Sickness unto Death is the most formally constructed of the books. The self is a relation that relates itself to itself and, in doing so, relates to the power that established it. Despair is any failure in that relation, analysed by permutation, from not knowing one has a self to defiantly willing to be a self of one’s own construction. Despair need not be felt. The comfortable are the likeliest to be in it.

The attack followed five years later, when Martensen eulogised the late Bishop Mynster as a witness to the truth. Articles in Fædrelandet gave way to nine issues of Kierkegaard’s own paper, The Moment, with a tenth unpublished at his death. The charge is not ordinary hypocrisy. It is that official Christianity, by making everyone a Christian at birth and paying its ministers to say so, has abolished the possibility of becoming one. He died refusing communion from a clergyman of that church.

legacy: For fifty years he was a Danish local phenomenon. Georg Brandes’s study of 1877 began the export. German translations followed from 1909. The reception ran through channels he would have found uncomfortable. Karl Barth and dialectical theology took the infinite qualitative distinction between God and man as a weapon against liberal Protestantism; Jaspers and Heidegger took anxiety, possibility and the analysis of the crowd into philosophy; Sartre and Camus made him a founding existentialist, which fits the vocabulary and not the faith.

Adorno’s early book attacked the aesthetic interiority of the position. Wittgenstein called him the most profound thinker of the nineteenth century. Derrida read Fear and Trembling as the exemplary case of a responsibility that cannot be given reasons. The pseudonyms have proved the most durable technical bequest. Scholarship now treats them as a method of indirect communication, an experiment in refusing to hand the reader a doctrine, rather than a screen for opinions privately held.

The texts themselves took a century to settle. His journals and papers were edited and published in stages from 1869, in versions that shaped early readings. The complete Danish critical edition was finished only in 2013. The standard English translations date from the 1930s and then from the Princeton edition completed in 2000. Denmark, having ignored or mocked him, now treats him as a national possession, a fate his own writing anticipated fairly precisely.

read.first: Start with Fear and Trembling, which is short and complete in itself, then the first half of The Sickness unto Death. Come to Either/Or for the writing rather than the argument.
read.note: Read the pseudonym on the title page as a character in the book. Resist converting any of them straight into Kierkegaard’s own view.

kierkegaard.caveat: How far the pseudonymous positions represent his own is genuinely contested. His retrospective account of the authorship as religious from the start was written years afterwards and cannot simply be taken at face value. The account in question is The Point of View for My Work as an Author, written in 1848, withheld during his lifetime, and published by his brother Peter Christian in 1859.

marx.sub: the critic who read capitalism as a historical form
world: The Prussia in which Marx trained treated the press as a police matter. He became editor of the Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in October 1842. He wrote on wood-theft laws and Moselle peasants, and watched the censors tighten until the government ordered the paper closed from April 1843. Expulsion followed him thereafter: from Paris in 1845 at Prussian request, from Brussels in 1848, from Cologne in 1849. He renounced Prussian citizenship in 1845 and was stateless for the rest of his life.

Britain, where he settled in 1849, supplied the evidence. Engels had described Manchester in 1845 as a machine for producing wealth and disease together. The reports of the factory inspectors gave Marx thousands of pages of official testimony against the system that produced them. Chartism had crested and broken in 1848. The Reform Act of 1867 arrived in the year Capital appeared. The British Museum reading room gave him a desk he used for twenty years.

The revolutions of 1848 shaped everything after. Paris in February, Vienna and Berlin in March, then Milan, Prague and Budapest: within eighteen months almost all of it was reversed. The French republic ended with Louis-Napoleon’s coup. Marx’s explanation, worked out in The Eighteenth Brumaire, was that the bourgeoisie preferred order to liberty once the workers appeared as an independent force. The Paris Commune of 1871 reopened the question and made him, for the first time, notorious.
life: Marx was born in Trier in 1818, into a family of rabbis on both sides whose father accepted Lutheran baptism to keep practising law under Prussian rule. He read law at Bonn, then philosophy at Berlin. He fell in with the Young Hegelians of the Doctors’ Club, and took a doctorate from Jena in 1841 on Democritus and Epicurus. Bruno Bauer’s dismissal from Bonn closed the academic career he expected. Journalism took its place.

Paris, from October 1843, was the turning point. He married Jenny von Westphalen that summer and read political economy for the first time. In August 1844 he met Engels again, two years after a cold first encounter in Cologne, and began a collaboration that lasted forty years. Brussels followed, then the Cologne of the Neue Rheinische Zeitung, then London. The family lived for years in two rooms in Dean Street, Soho, in real poverty. Three of their children died young. Engels, working in his father’s Manchester firm, paid the bills.

Income came from journalism and from Engels directly. He was London correspondent of the New-York Daily Tribune from 1852 to 1862, sometimes with Engels ghost-writing. After 1864 the International Working Men’s Association gave him a platform and much committee work. Illness and the deaths of his wife in 1881 and his eldest daughter in 1883 wrecked the last decade. He died in London on 14 March 1883, with about a dozen people at the graveside.

works.t: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844; The German Ideology
p: Neither book was published in his lifetime. Both appeared in Moscow in 1932. The Paris notebooks of 1844 argue that wage labour estranges the worker in four connected ways: from the product, which stands over against him as an alien power; from the act of working, which belongs to another; from species-being, the human capacity to produce freely and by design rather than from need; and from other people, since the product accrues to someone else. Their late arrival split the field. Marcuse and Fromm read them as the humanist key to everything after. Althusser answered in 1965 that an epistemological break separates this Marx from the Marx of Capital.

The German Ideology, written with Engels and abandoned, as Marx put it, to the gnawing criticism of the mice, carries the first full statement of historical materialism. The way a society produces its means of life conditions its law, politics and ideas. Consciousness does not determine life but life consciousness. Recent editorial work has shown that its celebrated opening chapter survives only as unordered sheets, arranged into shape by twentieth-century editors.

works.t: Manifesto of the Communist Party (Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei)
p: The Communist League commissioned it in London late in 1847. Marx wrote the final text from Engels’s draft catechisms. Twenty-three anonymous pages were printed in German in London in February 1848, weeks before the revolutions began. It is not a work of economics. Section one is a history of class antagonism and an astonished tribute to what the bourgeoisie has achieved: the dissolution of fixed relations, a world market, every profession converted into wage labour. Section two lists demands, several of them now unremarkable, including free public education and a progressive income tax. The pamphlet had almost no immediate effect. It was rescued from obscurity by the state trials of the 1850s and the panic after 1871.

Marx filled seven notebooks during the financial crisis of 1857, expecting a revolution and wanting his economics clear before it arrived. He never revised them. They were printed in Moscow in 1939 and 1941 in an edition the war made nearly unobtainable. General readers reached them only after 1953. The methodological introduction, on rising from the abstract to the concrete, is the fullest statement he made of his own procedure. The section later called the fragment on machines argues that as production comes to depend on accumulated social knowledge, direct labour time becomes an increasingly absurd measure of wealth. That passage has carried much of the weight of recent readings of automation.

works.t: Capital, Volume I (Das Kapital, Band I)
p: Published in Hamburg in an edition of a thousand copies, this is the only volume Marx finished. It begins with the commodity and separates use-value from value. It holds that value is determined by the labour time socially necessary to produce a good. The fourth section of chapter one states the doctrine of commodity fetishism. Relations between people take on the appearance of relations between things, so that a price seems a natural property of an object rather than a summary of social arrangements. The point is not that buyers are fooled but that the appearance is produced by the way production is organised.

The engine of the book is surplus value. What the worker sells is not labour but labour-power, whose value is the cost of maintaining and reproducing him. Worked for a full day it yields more value than it costs. The difference is the source of profit. Capital lengthens the working day, then mechanises to cheapen labour-power. The final part replaces the parable of the thrifty founder with enclosure, colonial plunder and the slave trade.

Neither volume is a book Marx wrote. Engels assembled them from manuscripts mostly drafted between 1863 and 1867, choosing among variants, dividing chapters, supplying titles and composing connecting prose. The main text behind volume III predates the publication of volume I. Volume II treats circulation and includes the reproduction schemes that fed later debates on markets and crisis. Volume III presents the transformation of values into prices of production, rent, and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall.

Publication of the original manuscripts in the modern critical edition has shown how much shaping Engels did, particularly in tightening the falling rate of profit into a law. Böhm-Bawerk argued in 1896 that volume III contradicts volume I on value. The transformation problem has been argued over since without settlement. What later states called Marxism-Leninism — dialectical materialism as a philosophy of nature, a fixed schema of historical stages, the party as bearer of science — was built after his death from Engels’s later writings and Soviet codification.

legacy: No nineteenth-century philosopher had a comparable political afterlife. Little of it took the form he envisaged. He expected revolution in the advanced industrial countries. It came in agrarian Russia and then China. The regimes founded there claimed his authority for institutions on which his writings say very little. His late correspondence about the Russian peasant commune suggests he was more open to non-European paths than his followers allowed. Engels reported him saying of certain French disciples that he was not a Marxist.

In the academy the story is quieter and still running. Historical materialism reshaped historiography, from the Annales school to E. P. Thompson. It made class, production and ideology standard categories far outside Marxist circles. The Frankfurt School, Gramsci, Sartre, Althusser and the analytical Marxists of the 1970s each rebuilt the theory around a different centre. G. A. Cohen’s defence of the technological reading in 1978 forced everyone to be more precise about what the doctrine claims.

The economics has fared worst and the diagnosis best. Few economists now defend the labour theory of value as a theory of price. The falling rate of profit is not an established result. He described capitalism as an inherently expansive, crisis-prone system that dissolves settled ways of life, concentrates ownership and turns more of human activity into a commodity. That description has proved durable enough to be quoted by people with no interest in his politics.

The exception is the Critique of the Gotha Programme, written in 1875 and printed by Engels in 1891. It distinguishes a lower and a higher phase of communist society, and supplies the formula about each according to his ability and each according to his needs. It runs to a few pages, and it is very nearly everything he committed to paper about what comes after.

read.first: Begin with the Manifesto for the shape of the argument, then part one and parts three and four of Capital volume I. The 1859 preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy gives historical materialism in two pages.
read.note: The first chapter of Capital is the hardest thing he wrote and no fair sample. Readers who stall should skip to the chapters on the working day and return.

marx.caveat: Much of what is read as Marx was edited into shape by others: Engels for Capital II and III, later editors for The German Ideology. The historical-critical edition still under way keeps revising what he can be said to have held.

brentano.sub: who gave back the mark of the mental, and taught the people who used it
world: Psychology in the 1870s was becoming a laboratory science. Fechner had measured sensation against stimulus, Wundt opened his institute at Leipzig in 1879, and the question was whether mind would be left with any subject matter of its own once the physiologists had finished.

Austria was also the last place in Europe where scholastic philosophy was taught seriously in Catholic faculties, and Brentano knew Aristotle and Aquinas from the inside. The combination — a scholastic training and an empirical programme — is peculiar to him and explains both his question and his answer.
life: Born in 1838 near Boppard into a literary Catholic family; his uncle was Clemens Brentano the poet. He took a doctorate on Aristotle's several senses of being, was ordained priest in 1864, and began teaching at Würzburg.

The Vatican Council's declaration of papal infallibility in 1870 broke him. He was asked by the German bishops to report on it, argued against it, and left the priesthood in 1873. Vienna made him professor in 1874. When he married in 1880 Austrian law still treated an ex-priest as barred, so he resigned the chair, took foreign citizenship, married, and returned as an unsalaried lecturer — which is the position he held for the twenty years in which he taught nearly everyone who mattered. He went blind, moved to Florence and then to Zurich in 1915, and died in 1917.

works.t: Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint (Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkt)
p: The book that returns intentionality to philosophy. Every mental phenomenon, and no physical one, contains an object within itself: what Brentano calls, reviving a scholastic term, the intentional inexistence of an object. A thought is a thought of something, a wish a wish for something, and that directedness is the mark that separates the mental from everything else. He also holds that inner perception, unlike introspective observation, is infallible, and that mental acts are of exactly three kinds: presentations, judgements, and phenomena of love and hate. Only the first two volumes appeared; he revised the doctrine for the rest of his life.

works.t: The Origin of Our Knowledge of Right and Wrong (Vom Ursprung sittlicher Erkenntnis)
p: A lecture to the Vienna Law Society, and the most compact statement of his ethics. Good is what is correctly loved, as true is what is correctly judged — not a definition in terms of feeling, because the correctness is not itself a feeling but something evident in the act, the way the self-evidence of a simple judgement is. G. E. Moore reviewed the English translation and called it a far better discussion of the subject than any he knew, which given Principia Ethica is a striking thing to have said.

legacy: The teaching outran the books. Husserl went to Vienna to hear him and took intentionality as the foundation of phenomenology, while rejecting Brentano's psychologism about logic. Meinong built the theory of objects that Russell attacked. Twardowski carried the method to Lwów and founded the school that produced Tarski and Leśniewski. Stumpf taught the Gestalt psychologists, and Ehrenfels named the Gestalt quality. Masaryk became president of Czechoslovakia. Freud attended his lectures for two years, the only philosophy he formally studied.

So the analytic and phenomenological traditions have a common ancestor, which is easy to forget given what happened next. The concept of intentionality survives in contemporary philosophy of mind as the problem of how a physical state can be about anything — Brentano's thesis, in the form he gave it, is still the standard way of stating what has to be explained.

read.first: Book II chapter 1 of the Psychology, where intentionality is stated, and The Origin of Our Knowledge of Right and Wrong entire.
read.note: Much of what is cited as Brentano comes from posthumous volumes assembled by his students from lectures and dictations, and reflects later revisions he did not publish. Check what is being quoted.

brentano.caveat: His own understanding of intentional inexistence changed substantially after 1874, and he came to hold that only individual things exist. Whether the famous thesis is a claim about a special kind of object or only about a relation of the mind is disputed in his own text.

peirce.sub: the logician who made meaning a matter of practical consequence
world: Peirce grew up inside the Cambridge scientific establishment his father helped run. The quarrel over Darwin’s Origin of Species reached it at once: Asa Gray defended the book, Louis Agassiz refused it. The Civil War then scattered that generation and returned it chastened. The group that met in Cambridge around 1872, remembered as the Metaphysical Club, shared a distrust of convictions held absolutely.

The institution that paid him was not a university but the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey. It employed him for thirty years measuring gravity with pendulums. Academic philosophy in America was only then becoming a profession: Johns Hopkins opened in 1876 on the German model, importing the research seminar and the doctorate. Peirce entered that new world briefly and was expelled from it.
life: Born in Cambridge in 1839 and drilled in mathematics by his father Benjamin, Peirce took a Harvard degree in 1859 and a chemistry degree in 1863. He served the Coast Survey until 1891 and did real science: his Photometric Researches of 1878 was the only book he published in his lifetime. From 1879 he lectured in logic at Johns Hopkins, the one teaching post he ever held.

Hopkins let him go in 1884, the surviving evidence pointing to disapproval of his private life. Nothing academic was offered again. He retreated to a farmhouse near Milford, Pennsylvania, wrote dictionary definitions and reviews for The Nation, and slid into poverty. He was kept afloat by James, who found him lecture fees. He died of cancer in 1914, leaving tens of thousands of unedited manuscript pages.

p: First of six papers in Popular Science Monthly titled “Illustrations of the Logic of Science.” Peirce describes belief and doubt biologically rather than epistemically: belief is a habit one is content to act on, doubt an irritation, inquiry the struggle from the second to the first. He then ranks four methods of settling opinion—tenacity, authority, the a priori taste of metaphysicians, and science—and defends the last because it alone lets something outside our wishes decide. The essay quietly destroys the Cartesian starting point: real doubt must be provoked and cannot be manufactured.

works.t: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
p: The sequel, and the source of the pragmatic maxim. Against the Cartesian grades of clearness Peirce proposes a third: to fix a conception, consider what practical effects its object could conceivably have. That conception of effects is the whole conception. Applied to hardness or to weight, the maxim converts metaphysical disputes into predictions. The paper also gives his definition of truth as the opinion fated to be agreed upon by all who investigate, with the real as whatever that opinion represents—truth as a limit of inquiry rather than a private possession.

works.t: Collected Papers of Charles Sanders Peirce
p: Everything else survives in fragments. From the manuscripts came the theory of signs, with its triad of icon, index and symbol and its insistence that a sign is nothing without an interpretant; abduction, named as a third inference beside deduction and induction, the tentative adoption of a hypothesis that would explain a surprise; and fallibilism. The 1885 paper on the algebra of logic contains a quantifier notation devised independently of Frege. Hartshorne and Weiss arranged the papers by topic rather than date, obscuring the development. The chronological edition begun in 1982 remains unfinished.

legacy: James put pragmatism into circulation with a Berkeley lecture in 1898 that generously credited Peirce. James then turned a criterion of meaning into a theory of truth. Peirce objected, and in 1905 rebaptised his own doctrine “pragmaticism,” a word he judged ugly enough to be safe from kidnappers. Royce took up his theory of interpretation and Dewey his account of inquiry. Peirce himself remained a rumour.

Recovery came slowly. Charles Morris and later semioticians built on the sign theory, historians of logic recognised how much of quantification ran through him, and Putnam revived truth as the outcome of ideal inquiry. The standing misreading treats him as a rough draft of James. What he offered was a scientific realism with fallibilism built in, an architectonic he never finished and never presented whole.

read.first: Read the two 1877-78 essays together, in that order. Then use a chronological selection of the essential writings rather than a topical anthology.
read.note: Peirce rewrote his central terms repeatedly, so date every passage before arguing from it.

peirce.caveat: The bulk of his philosophy exists as unpublished manuscripts whose dating and sequence remain contested. Any account of his late system is therefore a reconstruction.

james.sub: the psychologist who made truth something that happens to an idea
world: James worked at the moment when psychology detached itself from philosophy and acquired instruments. Wundt opened his Leipzig laboratory in 1879. Helmholtz and Fechner had already made sensation measurable. James set up a demonstration room at Harvard in the mid-1870s. Darwin had made mind a product of adaptation, which suited him, and had sharpened the quarrel between science and religion, which he refused to settle.

Harvard was being rebuilt around him. Charles Eliot, president from 1869, installed the elective system and expanded graduate study. James rose through it from physiology to philosophy without becoming a professional academic. His real audience lay outside: the Lowell Institute, the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh, the readers of magazines. He wrote for them, which is why he is still read and why colleagues thought him unrigorous.
life: Born in New York in 1842 to Henry James Sr., a Swedenborgian with money and opinions, he was educated across Europe alongside his brother Henry. He tried painting, joined Agassiz’s Amazon expedition in 1865, and took a Harvard medical degree in 1869. A collapse followed. He later credited his recovery in 1870 to reading Renouvier on free will and deciding to believe in it.

He began teaching physiology at Harvard in 1873 and married Alice Gibbens in 1878. That year he contracted to write a psychology textbook that took twelve years. The Gifford Lectures of 1901-02 were delivered with difficulty. His heart was failing. He died at Chocorua, New Hampshire, in 1910, leaving the papers Ralph Barton Perry gathered in 1912 as Essays in Radical Empiricism.

p: Twelve hundred pages that founded American psychology and then undermined the idea that psychology could be a settled science. Its famous chapter argues that consciousness is not made of discrete ideas but flows: a stream with vague fringes and transitive parts, in which relations are felt as directly as things. Other chapters gave the field habit as the flywheel of society, the James-Lange account of emotion as the perception of bodily change, and a deflationary self made of appropriating thoughts. He condensed it in 1892 as a course text. The long version reads like literature and argues like a naturalist.

The Gifford Lectures, and the fullest application of a policy defended in The Will to Believe of 1897: where an option is live, forced and momentous and evidence cannot decide it, one has the right to believe on other grounds. Varieties sets doctrine aside and studies the documents of conversion, saintliness and mysticism as natural facts, sorting the healthy-minded from the sick soul. Its verdict is empirical and modest: religion is judged by its fruits, and something real seems to reach consciousness through its margins. Critics object that first-person reports are taken too much at their word.

works.t: Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking
p: Eight lectures given at the Lowell Institute and Columbia, pitched at a general audience and paying for it in precision. James takes Peirce’s maxim of meaning and extends it to truth: an idea is true insofar as it works, truth being something that happens to a belief in the course of verification rather than a static copying relation. The talk of cash value invited the charge that he equated truth with convenience, which he spent The Meaning of Truth denying. Behind it lie the radical empiricism essays, where relations are experienced as directly as terms.

legacy: The Principles shaped psychology for a generation and gave literature the phrase stream of consciousness.
