The pragmatism did worse at first: Moore and Russell attacked the truth theory in print, Lovejoy counted thirteen incompatible pragmatisms in 1908, and the emerging analytic school treated the whole thing as amateurish. Peirce, who had supplied the maxim, disowned the use James made of it.

Reputation returned late. Husserl read the Principles closely. Whitehead built on radical empiricism. After 1979 Rorty made James a founder of a post-analytic philosophy he might not have recognised. Putnam recovered the arguments more carefully. In the psychology of religion Varieties never left the syllabus. The ethics of belief remains a live subject largely because of the essay James wrote about it.

read.first: Begin with The Varieties of Religious Experience, which shows the method working on hard material, then read Pragmatism, then selections from the Principles.
read.note: James wrote to persuade an audience in a room, so read him for the argument and not for the epigram.

nietzsche.sub: the genealogist who asked what our values cost us
world: Nietzsche was born in 1844 at Röcken in Prussian Saxony, into a Germany still divided among states. Prussia made it one by war: Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866, France in 1870. By then Nietzsche held a Swiss chair and had given up his Prussian citizenship. So he could not enlist. He went to the front instead as a volunteer medical orderly, moving the wounded in goods wagons.

The service ruined his health. Nursing the wounded, he caught dysentery and diphtheria and was invalided home within a month. The headaches and failing eyesight he had suffered since schooldays never again let him work for long. The Reich proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871 struck him as a cultural disaster dressed as a triumph. Bismarck’s Germany — the founders’ boom, the crash of 1873, the Kulturkampf, a loud nationalist and antisemitic press — confirmed it.

The century’s authority had been shifting from theology to natural science. Nietzsche read Friedrich Albert Lange’s History of Materialism of 1866 and kept going back to it. Lange presented the sciences as knowing appearances only, which suited a reader already holding Schopenhauer. Darwin was being fought over in German by Ernst Haeckel and others. David Friedrich Strauss had made the historical Jesus a public scandal with Das Leben Jesu in 1835. By the 1870s, historical criticism of the Bible was ordinary university work. Nietzsche’s question was not whether Christianity was true. He took that as settled, and asked what its collapse would cost.

Basel, where he taught from 1869, stood outside all of it: a small, rich, patrician city with an unshowy university. Classical philology was then the most exacting discipline in the German-speaking world. It enforced its standards without mercy. His colleagues included the historian Jacob Burckhardt and the church historian Franz Overbeck, who stayed loyal to the end. Wagner’s house at Tribschen was near enough for weekend visits.

From 1878 his books were issued by Ernst Schmeitzner of Chemnitz. Schmeitzner also published antisemitic tracts and a monthly to match. Nietzsche’s letters complain that his own work sat warehoused at an antisemitic address. In 1886, E. W. Fritzsch of Leipzig bought the rights back. After that he paid the printer himself, and Beyond Good and Evil, the Genealogy and the books of 1888 all went to press with C. G. Naumann of Leipzig at Nietzsche’s own cost.

Antisemitism became an organised German politics in exactly these years. Wilhelm Marr popularised the word in 1879. The Berlin historian Heinrich von Treitschke wrote that the Jews were Germany’s misfortune, and a public controversy followed. Adolf Stoecker built a party on the theme. An Antisemites’ Petition was got up in 1880 and 1881, and Bernhard Förster was among its organisers. Förster married Nietzsche’s sister Elisabeth in 1885. Nietzsche’s letters of those years attack antisemites steadily. By Christmas 1887 he was writing to Elisabeth in open disgust at her circle.

He broke down in Turin in the first days of January 1889, just as Georg Brandes’s Copenhagen lectures were carrying his name to a European audience. He never wrote again. His mother Franziska nursed him at Naumburg until her death in 1897. His sister Elisabeth then moved him to Weimar and turned the household into the Nietzsche-Archiv. It was a fixture of Wilhelmine cultural life that received visitors while its subject sat mute upstairs.
life: His father, a Lutheran pastor, died in 1849 when Nietzsche was four, and a baby brother the year after. He grew up in Naumburg among women. From 1858 he boarded at Schulpforta, the most demanding classical school in Prussia. He read theology at Bonn and abandoned it. In 1865 he followed the philologist Friedrich Ritschl to Leipzig, where he found Schopenhauer’s The World as Will and Representation in a secondhand shop.

Ritschl’s recommendation won him the Basel chair of classical philology in 1869, at twenty-four, before he had written a dissertation. Leipzig conferred the doctorate on published articles alone. He surrendered his Prussian citizenship and never took Swiss, remaining stateless for life. In those years he was intimate with Richard and Cosima Wagner. He believed for a while that music drama might do for modern Germany what tragedy had done for Athens.

The belief produced The Birth of Tragedy. It did not survive the first Bayreuth festival of 1876, which he found a fairground of nationalism and celebrity. Illness forced longer leaves each year until Basel pensioned him off in 1879, at thirty-four. He had by then befriended Paul Rée. Rée’s sceptical account of where moral feelings come from pushed him toward the aphoristic naturalism of Human, All Too Human.

For a decade he lived out of trunks, following the weather: summers at Sils-Maria in the Engadine, winters in Genoa, Rapallo, Nice, Venice, finally Turin. In 1882 he met Lou Salomé through Rée. Botched proposals and his sister’s interference destroyed the friendship and left him badly isolated. He published at his own risk. The fourth part of Zarathustra was printed in forty copies for friends.

How he worked followed from what was wrong with him: his eyes took short spells of reading and writing and no more. He composed while walking, for hours a day above Sils-Maria, and wrote into pocket notebooks afterwards. The aphorism was in part a form chosen and in part a form imposed. In 1882 he tried a Malling-Hansen writing ball, an early Danish typewriter, and gave it up as unreliable. Peter Gast, born Heinrich Köselitz, made fair copies of his manuscripts and read his proofs. Much of what reached the printer reached it in another man’s hand.

The money came from Basel, which pensioned him in 1879 at a rate reported as 3,000 Swiss francs a year. It was his income for the rest of his working life. Sales were negligible: Beyond Good and Evil sold about a hundred copies in its first year. Of the forty copies of the fourth Zarathustra, he is reported to have given away only about seven.

1888 alone produced The Case of Wagner, Twilight of the Idols, The Antichrist, Ecce Homo, Nietzsche contra Wagner and a set of Dionysus dithyrambs. Only The Case of Wagner reached readers before he collapsed. He was still correcting proofs and rewriting title pages in December.

1888 was his most productive year and his last. He collapsed in Turin on 3 January 1889 and posted delirious notes signed “Dionysus” and “The Crucified”. The story of the flogged carriage horse comes from later report, not a contemporary witness. Overbeck brought him home. After clinics in Basel and Jena he passed into his mother’s keeping, then his sister’s, and died at Weimar on 25 August 1900.

What caused the collapse is still argued. The tertiary syphilis diagnosed at the Basel and Jena clinics remains the textbook account. But the illness did not run the expected course. Later physicians have proposed a slow-growing tumour behind the right eye, an inherited disease of the small cerebral vessels, and frontotemporal dementia instead.

What he left unpublished is bulkier than what he published. The notebooks run from his student years to December 1888. They hold drafts, plans, copied quotations and finished aphorisms side by side, with nothing marking which is which. Elisabeth came back from Paraguay in 1893, after Förster killed himself there in 1889. She founded an archive at Naumburg in 1894 and moved it to Weimar. Their mother’s death in 1897 left her in sole control of the papers. She edited, withheld and rearranged. She also fabricated. Karl Schlechta’s edition of 1954 to 1956 showed that letters printed as her brother’s had been spliced or re-addressed to her.

works.t: The Birth of Tragedy out of the Spirit of Music (Die Geburt der Tragödie aus dem Geiste der Musik)
p: Greek tragedy, Nietzsche argues, grew from the collision of two impulses: the Apollinian, which makes bounded shining forms, and the Dionysian, which dissolves the individual in music and intoxication. Tragedy holds them together. Its audience finds existence bearable not because it has been explained but because it has been given form. Socrates killed it, with Euripides as his instrument, by demanding that everything be intelligible and that virtue be knowledge. Against the theoretical man, Nietzsche sets the claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon.

The book cites no scholarship and turns in its last third into a manifesto for Wagner as tragedy reborn. The profession answered within months. The young Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff issued a pamphlet accusing him of ignorance and invention, Erwin Rohde defended him, and the argument settled against Nietzsche. Students stopped enrolling, and for a time his lecture room held almost nobody. He never regained a scholarly reputation. His own preface of 1886 calls the book badly written while standing by its question.

The argument runs through the chorus: Nietzsche takes the satyr chorus for the original element of tragedy, with the figures on stage as its vision. Behind the beauty stands the wisdom Silenus gives King Midas: best never to be born, second best to die soon. Art does not refute that wisdom but gives it a bearable form. Looking back in Ecce Homo, he complained that the book smells offensively Hegelian. The question it asks stayed with him — what a culture does with suffering it cannot argue away.

Four essays survive of thirteen planned. The first attacks David Strauss as the model cultural philistine, the man who mistook Prussia’s victory over France for proof of German cultural superiority. The second, On the Uses and Disadvantages of History for Life, is still read. It distinguishes monumental, antiquarian and critical uses of the past. It argues that a culture can be paralysed by knowing too much of it, since a surplus of inherited perspective makes acting impossible.

Nietzsche attacks not historical scholarship, which he practised, but its promotion into a substitute for having a present. The third essay, Schopenhauer as Educator, concerns exemplars rather than doctrines: an educator is someone whose existence proves that a way of living is available. The fourth, Richard Wagner in Bayreuth, praises a composer Nietzsche had privately given up on. It reads in hindsight like a man arguing himself back into a faith.

The second essay names its target as an excess of history without the strength to use it. A culture needs plastic power, the capacity to absorb a past and grow over it. Where that fails, scholarship becomes a way of watching oneself instead of acting. Nietzsche mocks the doctrine, taken from Eduard von Hartmann, that history is a world process moving toward its own justification. The remedy offered is not ignorance but the ability to forget on purpose, which he treats as a condition of doing anything at all.

works.t: On Truth and Lying in an Extra-Moral Sense (Über Wahrheit und Lüge im aussermoralischen Sinne)
p: Nietzsche dictated this essay in 1873 and never published it. It opens with a fable: in some remote corner of the universe, clever animals invented knowing. After a minute the star cooled and the clever animals had to die. Truth, on the account that follows, is a mobile army of metaphors. A nerve stimulus becomes an image, the image becomes a sound, and each step crosses into a wholly different sphere. A concept is made by treating unequal things as equal. Truths are metaphors worn smooth — coins that have lost their faces and now pass as metal.

The piece matters for two reasons. It is his earliest sustained statement of what later gets called perspectivism. It is also a standing warning about the Nachlass. He never returned to it in print. It reached readers only in 1896, in a volume of posthumous writings, and has been quoted since as settled doctrine. Whether an unpublished draft carries the weight of a book is the question his editors have never settled.

This is the book of the break. Nietzsche dedicated it to Voltaire on the centenary of his death. He abandoned continuous exposition for numbered aphorisms, and adopted what he called historical philosophizing: instead of asking what justice or pity is, ask how such feelings could have arisen from unremarkable materials over long stretches of time. He wants a chemistry of moral and religious concepts, on the suspicion that the noblest are compounds of ordinary ingredients.

Metaphysics is treated less as false than as unnecessary. Copies crossed in the post with the libretto of Parsifal in 1878. The friendship with Wagner ended there. Two sequels followed, Assorted Opinions and Maxims and The Wanderer and His Shadow. Readers arriving through Zarathustra tend to skip these books, which hold his most patient psychology and the clearest statement of his method before the genealogy.

The form is doing argumentative work: a numbered aphorism states a case and stops, leaving the reader to test it. Nothing rests on what came before, so a bad section does not bring down a chapter. Later he defended the form directly: the will to a system, he wrote in Twilight of the Idols, is a lack of integrity. The cost is that aphorisms can be quoted against each other, and have been, in every direction.

works.t: Daybreak (Morgenröte) and The Gay Science (Die fröhliche Wissenschaft)
p: Daybreak, subtitled Thoughts on the Prejudices of Morality, opens what Nietzsche later called his campaign against morality. Moral judgements, he argues, rest on mistaken beliefs about causes. The morality of custom trained obedience long before it trained anything resembling conscience. The conclusion is not that we should behave badly, but that morality has never yet been examined by anyone who did not already believe in it.

The Gay Science carries his most quoted passage. In section 125 a madman with a lantern runs into the marketplace crying that God is dead and that we have killed him, and the unbelievers laugh. The announcement is a diagnosis, not a boast. Christian belief has been dissolved by the honesty Christianity itself cultivated. The moral order resting on it has lost its foundation. Hardly anyone has noticed what follows, which is nihilism, the state in which the highest values devalue themselves. Section 341 puts eternal recurrence as a question asked by a demon.

Daybreak takes its epigraph from the Rig Veda: there are so many dawns that have not yet broken. Nietzsche later described it as subterranean work, digging under a morality rather than attacking its front. The Gay Science takes its title from the Provençal gai saber, the troubadours’ art. It is a book of aphorisms with poems at both ends. A fifth book, added in 1887, presses the question the Genealogy would take up, whether the will to truth is itself an article of faith.

Written in short bursts, four parts in under two years, in deliberate pastiche of Luther’s Bible. Zarathustra comes down from his mountain to teach the Übermensch and is misunderstood by everyone he meets. The Übermensch is not a biological superior and not a master race. The word names someone who creates values instead of inheriting them, and who needs no world behind this one to make this one endurable. The three metamorphoses — camel, lion, child — give the sequence: bearing the inherited burden, refusing it, then creating without resentment.

The hardest thought in the book is eternal recurrence, which Zarathustra can barely bring himself to say: that everything returns exactly as it was, endlessly. It works as a test of affirmation rather than a cosmology — whether a life can be willed again entire, nothing subtracted. The book made his name and did him the most damage, since its oracular manner invites quotation and resists argument. Part IV was printed privately in forty copies.

The Prologue sets the terms. Zarathustra offers the crowd the Übermensch, and the crowd asks instead for the last man, who has invented happiness and blinks. A tightrope walker falls and dies, and Zarathustra carries the body away on his back. Will to power appears in the speech On Self-Overcoming, given there as the drive in everything living. Part IV turns comic: Zarathustra collects a set of higher men, finds them insufficient, and catches them worshipping an ass. Plans for further parts survive in the notebooks.

works.t: Beyond Good and Evil (Jenseits von Gut und Böse)
p: Subtitled Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future, this is Nietzsche returning to argument after Zarathustra. The opening part treats the prejudices of philosophers: every great philosophy is an involuntary memoir. The question to ask of a doctrine is not only whether it is true but what kind of life needed it to be. He offers will to power as a psychological hypothesis, that organisms seek not self-preservation but the discharge and expansion of strength.

Section 260 sets master morality against slave morality. In the first, the strong call themselves good and their opposites bad. In the second, the powerless call the strong evil and rename their own weakness virtue. Nietzsche says plainly that both types are mixed in every modern European. The book also holds his most repellent political material, on rank order and the uses of a servile class, which admirers often bracket. It sold barely a hundred copies in its first year.

The book is also his sharpest attack on the theory of knowledge he inherited. Section 16 refuses the immediate certainty of I think, on the ground that the grammar smuggles in a doer behind the deed. Section 17 says a thought comes when it wants, not when I want it. The preface opens by supposing that truth is a woman, and doubts that dogmatic philosophers have understood women. The philosophers he wants are called Versucher, a word holding attempt, experiment and temptation together.

works.t: On the Genealogy of Morality (Zur Genealogie der Moral)
p: His most sustained book: three connected essays sharing a method. The first traces the pair good and bad, coined by an aristocratic class describing itself, being overturned into good and evil by a priestly revaluation born of ressentiment. Ressentiment is the impotent hatred that cannot act and so invents an imaginary revenge. It condemns the strong as wicked and renames its own inability to strike back as virtue. The second derives guilt from the archaic law of debt, and conscience from cruelty turned inward. The third asks why the ascetic ideal has ruled so long, and answers that a will would rather will nothing than not will.

Genealogy is a method, not an insult. Showing that a valuation has a low or violent origin does not by itself refute it, and Nietzsche says so. What the history destroys is the assumption that morality is timeless, self-evident and without alternatives. Once a value is known to have been made, whether to keep it becomes a question one can ask. The first essay’s account of the Jewish priestly revaluation has been read as antisemitism. It is a historical thesis about a revolution he calls both a catastrophe for the strong and the origin of human depth.

He wrote the three essays in a few weeks in the summer of 1887 and subtitled the book A Polemic. The second essay is the strangest. Memory, it argues, was burned into human beings by punishment, since only an animal that can promise is of use to others. Guilt begins as debt, and the German words carry both senses. The third essay turns on science itself. Modern unbelief is not the opposite of the ascetic ideal but its latest form, because it still rests on an unexamined faith that truth is worth having.

works.t: Twilight of the Idols, The Antichrist, Ecce Homo
p: Twilight of the Idols, drafted in about a week and subtitled How to Philosophize with a Hammer, uses the hammer as a tuning fork. It sounds idols to hear whether they are hollow. Its six-paragraph section on how the true world finally became a fable compresses the history of metaphysics from Plato to its self-abolition. Its opening maxims include the line that whoever has a why to live can bear almost any how. It is the best short introduction he wrote.

The Antichrist, finished that September, is a curse on Christianity. It separates Jesus — a psychological type practising a way of life — from Paul, who built a religion of guilt, immortality and revenge. Nietzsche withheld it. It appeared in 1895. Ecce Homo, written in October and November, is an autobiography whose chapters are headed “Why I Am So Wise” and “Why I Write Such Good Books”. Elisabeth suppressed it until 1908 and altered passages about herself and their mother.

Twilight works section by section through what he calls the four great errors. Chief among them is free will, invented, he says, so that men could be found guilty and punished. The Antichrist ends with a Law against Christianity in seven clauses, dated from the first day of a new calendar. Early printings left it out and the critical edition restored it. Ecce Homo reviews his own books one at a time and closes with a chapter headed “Why I Am a Destiny”.

works.t: The Will to Power (Der Wille zur Macht)
p: This is not a book Nietzsche wrote. He did plan a systematic work under the title between 1885 and 1888, and then abandoned the scheme. His last plans replaced it with a Revaluation of All Values, of which The Antichrist is the only finished part. What appeared under the old title was assembled after his collapse by his sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and his former assistant Peter Gast, born Heinrich Köselitz. They picked entries out of the notebooks and arranged them under an outline Nietzsche had discarded: 483 sections in 1901, 1,067 in 1906.

The notes themselves are genuine. The book is an editorial construction. The Colli-Montinari critical edition begun in the 1960s dismantled it by printing the notebooks in the order they were written. The damage lay in the arrangement, which made a private workshop look like a finished system. Elisabeth’s politics decided its shape. She had married the antisemitic agitator Bernhard Förster and founded a racial colony with him in Paraguay. She spent four decades presenting her brother as prophet of a nationalism he had attacked all his working life.

The trouble is not that the notes are worthless. It is that a note is not a claim a man has stood behind. The books he published he had cut, revised and prefaced again. He also filled notebooks with positions he tried once and dropped. Mixed together and numbered, the two look alike on the page. Mazzino Montinari put it flatly: the book does not exist. The critical edition dates every note, so a reader can see which are drafts toward published passages and which were abandoned.

legacy: The Weimar archive controlled the manuscripts, the editions and the image for nearly fifty years. Elisabeth cultivated the German right and received Mussolini’s greetings and Hitler’s visits in the 1930s. She let her brother be enlisted for a movement whose defining commitments — racial nationalism, antisemitism, mass obedience — his books ridicule. The appropriation worked because she supplied the selection, the framing and the endorsement. It needed an editor with a motive.

Recovery came in two stages. Walter Kaufmann’s study of 1950 and his translations rescued Nietzsche for English readers, arguably at the cost of making him tamer than he is. Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari’s critical edition, from 1967, then established what he wrote and when. It ended the standing of The Will to Power as a book of his, though cheap editions of it still circulate under his name.

The reception began before the archive did. Georg Brandes lectured on him at Copenhagen in 1888 and called the position aristocratic radicalism. Nietzsche wrote back that it was the cleverest thing yet said about him. Through the 1890s he was taken up at speed and in every direction: by anarchists, by socialists, by feminists, by novelists looking for permission. A knapsack edition of Zarathustra circulated among German soldiers in the First World War, though the circulation figures usually quoted for it are unreliable.

His influence runs in incompatible directions. Freud said he had avoided reading him to protect his own originality, and conceded the anticipations anyway. Max Weber carried ressentiment into sociology. Mann, Rilke and Musil carried the diagnosis into literature. Heidegger read him as the last metaphysician, while Bataille, Deleuze and Foucault made genealogy the central method of French critical thought. Bernard Williams and Alasdair MacIntyre argued with him rather than about him.

The disagreement about his politics has never closed. Georg Lukács, in The Destruction of Reason of 1954, made him a founder of the irrationalism that ended in fascism. Jürgen Habermas treated him as the point where reason’s self-criticism turned into a rejection of reason. Kaufmann and most Anglophone readers after him answered that the fascist Nietzsche is his sister’s invention. Domenico Losurdo argued in 2002 that the reactionary politics is in the published books and cannot be edited out. That quarrel is about the books, not the compilation, which is why the critical edition did not end it.

In the universities he is now read as an arguer. Arthur Danto’s book of 1965 opened the analytic engagement in English. Alexander Nehamas read the whole authorship as a single work of literary self-creation. Brian Leiter reads him as a naturalist about morality. Maudemarie Clark has worked on whether perspectivism can be stated without collapsing into itself. Philippa Foot asked, in his own terms, what a revaluation would actually require. The Colli-Montinari text is what all of them argue over.

What survives best is the method and the diagnosis. Asking where a value came from, whom it served and what holding it costs is now ordinary practice in history and moral philosophy. What stays contested is the positive half — whether the Übermensch and the revaluation amount to a programme or only a mood, whether perspectivism can state itself without self-refutation, and how far his contempt for equality detaches from the rest.

read.first: Start with On the Genealogy of Morality, his only book built as continuous argument and the fairest test of whether the rest is worth your time. Then Beyond Good and Evil, then The Gay Science. Take Twilight of the Idols as a summary. Take Thus Spoke Zarathustra last, once you know what it is compressing.
read.note: Do not begin with The Will to Power. Treat any edition presenting it as Nietzsche's final book with suspicion. For the notebooks, use the Colli-Montinari numbering, which dates each note and shows what stage of his thinking it belongs to.

nietzsche.caveat: The nature of his final illness is disputed. Syphilis, a slow-growing tumour, an inherited vascular disease and frontotemporal dementia have all been argued from the same thin evidence. Everything he left unpublished passed first through his sister's hands. Quotations from the notebooks are not positions he published, and the difference is marked here where it matters. Some biographical set pieces, the Turin horse among them, rest on later report rather than on a witness. The figures for early sales and for the fourth Zarathustra's distribution come from his own letters and his publishers, and vary between accounts.

dewey.sub: the instrumentalist who made inquiry and democracy one project
world: Dewey arrived in Chicago in 1894, the summer of the Pullman strike, into a city swollen by immigration and short of everything a school system needs. Jane Addams’s Hull House shaped his sense of what institutions could do. The Progressive era treated schooling as the instrument for absorbing an immigrant working class into a democracy. The Laboratory School he founded in 1896 was his answer.

War and the professionalising academy marked the rest. Dewey helped found the American Association of University Professors in 1915 and was its first president, when professors were still dismissed for their politics. He supported American entry into the First World War. His former student Randolph Bourne broke with him publicly. A philosophy of adjusting means to ends, Bourne wrote, had been captured by ends it did not choose.
life: Dewey was born in Burlington, Vermont, in 1859, and took his first degree there. He taught school in Oil City, Pennsylvania, and went to Johns Hopkins for the doctorate he completed in 1884 under the Hegelian George Sylvester Morris. He sat in Peirce’s logic course and was unimpressed. Ten years at Michigan followed, then Chicago, where the Hegelianism gradually turned into a biological account of thinking.

He resigned from Chicago in 1904 after a quarrel with President Harper over his wife Alice’s position, and moved to Columbia. From there he wrote constantly for The New Republic, helped found the American Civil Liberties Union, lectured in Japan, China and Turkey, and in 1937 chaired the commission that heard Trotsky answer the Moscow charges. He died in New York in 1952, aged ninety-two.

p: The book Dewey later said came closest to a full statement of his philosophy, though its title hid that from philosophers. Education is not preparation for a life to be lived afterwards. It is the continuous reconstruction of experience. A curriculum of isolated subject matter cuts the child off from the situations that give any subject a point. The political claim is inseparable: democracy is a mode of associated living, needing schools that produce people able to communicate across divisions of class and occupation. The argument was sketched in the 1899 lectures printed as The School and Society.

Dewey’s metaphysics, and his hardest book. Holmes admired it while calling the writing dreadful. Experience is not a screen between mind and world but the transaction of an organism with its environment. Nature shows up in it as precarious and stable at once. The tradition, he argues, converted its preferred outcomes into antecedent realities, taking the fruits of inquiry for its foundations. The companion volumes press the point: Reconstruction in Philosophy in 1920 and The Quest for Certainty in 1929, which indicts the spectator theory of knowledge for seeking security in contemplation instead of intelligent action.

Written at seventy-nine, this is the systematic statement of instrumentalism. Inquiry is defined as the controlled transformation of an indeterminate situation into a determinate one. Logical forms are held to arise within that operation rather than to govern it from outside. Dewey replaces truth with warranted assertibility, keeping attention on the process and its outcome instead of on a finished correspondence. Formal logicians largely ignored the book, and its account of the proposition satisfied few of them. Its conception of inquiry as situated, communal and self-correcting has worn far better than its logic proper.

legacy: Progressive education carried his name around the world and misused it thoroughly. Schools that dropped subject matter for activity claimed his authority. In 1938 he wrote Experience and Education to say this was not his argument. Hutchins and Adler attacked him for the great books, and Cold War critics for standards. The caricature of Dewey as the enemy of content still circulates.

In philosophy he was eclipsed by the analytic ascendancy and then retrieved. Rorty made him a hero of anti-foundationalism in 1979. Putnam and Bernstein read him more exactly. Social epistemology and deliberative democratic theory now draw on him directly. Art as Experience, the William James Lectures of 1931, quietly became one of the most used books in twentieth-century aesthetics.

read.first: Start with The Quest for Certainty for the critical argument, then Democracy and Education for the constructive one.
read.note: His prose is genuinely difficult, but the difficulty is compression rather than obscurity. It rewards slow reading.

frege.sub: the logician who built the instrument and lost his own system
world: A German academic career ran on a fixed track: doctorate, habilitation, years as an unsalaried Privatdozent living on student fees, then a call to a chair elsewhere. Frege never got the call. He spent his working life at Jena, a small Thuringian university, made extraordinary professor in 1879. In 1896 he was given the honorary title of ordinary professor, without the salary a real chair carried.

Mathematics was then putting analysis on solid ground. Weierstrass had banished the infinitesimal, Dedekind and Cantor were constructing the reals, and the question of what a number is had turned urgent. Logic belonged to the algebraists, who treated inference as a calculus of classes. To them Frege looked like a rival notation. His costly two-dimensional symbolism gave reviewers an excuse to stop reading.

Politics reached him late and badly. Frege belonged to the national-liberal Protestant bourgeoisie. Defeat in 1918, hyperinflation and street violence drove him hard to the right. His diary of spring 1924, published in 1994, records enthusiasm for Ludendorff and Hitler and proposes stripping German Jews of the vote and expelling them. None of that shows in the logic. All of it is on the record.
life: Friedrich Ludwig Gottlob Frege was born at Wismar on the Baltic in 1848, son of a schoolmaster who ran a private girls’ school. He studied at Jena from 1869, took his doctorate at Göttingen in 1873 on the geometrical representation of imaginary forms in the plane, and habilitated at Jena the next year. The physicist Ernst Abbe, of the Zeiss works, was his patron thereafter.

Publication brought him almost nothing. The Begriffsschrift drew a handful of notices, the most visible Schröder’s, which measured it against Boolean algebra and found it redundant. Cantor dismissed the Grundlagen in a careless review. Frege spent the next decade sharpening his semantics in essays rather than pressing on. When the Grundgesetze appeared in 1893, the publisher would take a second volume only if the author paid.

The blow arrived by post. In June 1902 Russell wrote to say the fifth basic law generated a contradiction. Frege, with the second volume at press, added an appendix. It remarks that hardly anything worse can befall a writer than to have a foundation give way once the building is finished. He taught until 1918 and retired to Bad Kleinen. His papers, left to Heinrich Scholz at Münster, were largely destroyed in a 1945 air raid.

works.t: Begriffsschrift, a Formula Language of Pure Thought Modelled on that of Arithmetic
p: Eighty-eight pages, printed in Halle, and the deepest break in the history of logic. Where the syllogism analysed a sentence into subject and predicate, Frege analysed it into function and argument. Cato killed Cato can then be carved three ways, depending on which term is held fixed. On that he laid the quantifier and the bound variable, giving multiple generality—every boy loves some girl—a form that had defeated logicians since Aristotle.

The system is an axiomatic calculus with modus ponens as its only rule, containing the first complete propositional logic and the first workable logic of relations. Its finest move defines the ancestral of a relation, turning mathematical induction from a principle assumed into a theorem proved. Six reviewers took it up—Hoppe, Venn, Tannery, Lasswitz, Michaëlis and Schröder, who measured it against Boole—and none saw what it had done. The notation died. The quantifier reached the world through Peano and Russell.

works.t: The Foundations of Arithmetic (Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik)
p: Frege wrote this one in ordinary German with almost no symbols. It remains his most readable book. The first half demolishes. Numbers are not properties of things, since the same pile is one deck and fifty-two cards; not ideas in a mind, since then your two and mine would differ; not, as Mill held, generalisations from handling pebbles. Against Kant, arithmetic comes out analytic while geometry stays synthetic a priori.

Three principles govern the book, and the second changed philosophy: never ask after the meaning of a word in isolation, only in the context of a sentence. A number statement, Frege argues, says something about a concept. The number belonging to a concept is the extension of the concept equinumerous with it. Equinumerosity is one-to-one correlation defined without using number. Whether such an extension might be Julius Caesar he leaves open.

works.t: On Sense and Reference (Über Sinn und Bedeutung)
p: One of three essays of the early 1890s, with Function and Concept and On Concept and Object, and the one everybody reads. If a = b is true it says of one thing that it is itself, which is trivial. Yet the discovery that the morning star is the evening star was a genuine astronomical result. Frege separates what an expression stands for, its Bedeutung, from how it presents that thing, its Sinn.

The apparatus then extends: a sentence has a sense, the thought it expresses, and a reference, its truth value. So the True and the False are objects. That semantics is compositional and elegant, with one awkwardness, since inside belief reports words shift to denoting their ordinary senses. Whether Bedeutung is best rendered reference, meaning or denotation has been disputed ever since. Truth values as objects remain a minority taste.

works.t: Basic Laws of Arithmetic (Grundgesetze der Arithmetik)
p: Here the programme was executed: the definitions of the Grundlagen rebuilt inside a formal system with gapless proofs, plus a contemptuous polemic in the second volume against formalist accounts of real number. The system draws its power from Basic Law V, which identifies the course-of-values of two functions exactly when those functions agree on every argument. That law turns any concept into an object, and so lets numbers be built from logic alone.

It is also inconsistent. Russell’s letter of June 1902 showed that the concept extension not falling under the concept it is the extension of yields a contradiction. The appendix, written in haste, weakened Law V rather than dropping it. Leśniewski later showed that the repair trivialises the system. Modern work partly vindicates him: drop Law V, take equinumerosity as primitive, and arithmetic follows in second-order logic.

Three late essays—Thought, Negation and Compound Thoughts—published in a yearbook when their author was in his seventies and long out of the argument. Thought is the best of them. Its answer to the question what a thought is comes out uncompromisingly Platonist: thoughts are neither physical things nor episodes in a mind but inhabitants of a third realm, timeless and ownerless.

Two observations carry the case. Two people can think the same thought, impossible if thoughts were private mental events; and a thought does not become true when somebody first entertains it. The essay holds Frege’s sharpest attack on psychologism and a treatment of indexicals—the thought expressed by today is fine needs a different sentence tomorrow—which philosophers of language have mined steadily since.

legacy: Frege was read more widely than the legend of total neglect allows, and understood by very few. Peano corresponded with him. Husserl abandoned psychologism after his 1894 review, though whether the review caused that is disputed. Russell read him in 1901 and introduced him to English speakers in an appendix. Carnap sat in his Jena lectures and kept the notes. Wittgenstein came to see him in 1911 and never stopped arguing with him. He founded no school and left no successors.

What survives is most of modern logic. Every undergraduate course teaches Frege’s quantifier in Peano’s notation. The sense-reference distinction still organises the philosophy of language. The context principle, transmitted through Wittgenstein, is the linguistic turn in a sentence. Michael Dummett’s book of 1973 turned him from a precursor into a contemporary. Neo-logicism now treats the Grundlagen as unfinished business.

Two misreadings recur. The first makes him a philosopher of language who happened to write about numbers. But the semantics was a tool for the foundations of arithmetic, worthless to him without that job. The second modernises Bedeutung into a later notion of reference. As for the man, Dummett recorded his shock on learning what the diaries held. The logic is not less true for them, nor they less real for it.

The last turn is usually left out. In manuscripts of 1924 and 1925, unpublished until 1969, Frege abandoned logicism outright. They are Sources of Knowledge of Mathematics and the Mathematical Natural Sciences, Numbers and Arithmetic, A New Attempt at the Foundations of Arithmetic. He dropped extensions and value-ranges, and proposed grounding number in a geometrical source of knowledge. That would make arithmetic synthetic a priori after all, as Kant had said.

read.first: Begin with The Foundations of Arithmetic, which is short, argumentative and needs no symbolic logic. Then On Sense and Reference and Thought. Come to the Begriffsschrift and the Basic Laws last, in an edition that translates the notation.
read.note: The original two-dimensional symbolism defeats almost everyone. Use a version rendering it in standard symbols rather than concluding that the logic is hard.

frege.caveat: Most of Frege’s Nachlass was destroyed at Münster in 1945. Several unpublished pieces therefore survive only through pre-war transcripts. The dating of some fragments is conjectural.

husserl.sub: the mathematician who tried to make description of consciousness rigorous
world: The German university Husserl entered in the 1880s ran on a fixed ladder: doctorate, Habilitation, then years as an unsalaried Privatdozent living on student fees. Its philosophy chairs belonged to neo-Kantianism — Cohen and Natorp at Marburg, Windelband and Rickert in the southwest — and against them pressed the new experimental psychology. Since Wundt’s Leipzig laboratory of 1879 it had been claiming philosophy’s posts along with its questions. Husserl’s early work sits squarely inside that fight.

War broke the arrangement. His son Wolfgang was killed at Verdun in 1916. His ablest Göttingen student, Adolf Reinach, died in Flanders in 1917. The Kaiserreich collapsed, the inflation of 1923 destroyed academic savings, and a rhetoric of cultural exhaustion became respectable. Husserl never wrote about politics. But his diagnosis of the 1930s — that European science had lost the ground of its own meaning — is unintelligible outside that mood.

Then 1933. The Law for the Restoration of the Professional Civil Service of 7 April, and the Baden decree implementing it, put the seventy-four-year-old emeritus on forced leave. The order was lifted within months. But by 1936 his name had gone from the university roll, and in 1937 he was refused permission to travel to the Descartes congress in Paris. He had been baptised a Lutheran in 1886. The laws counted descent, not confession. He died in Freiburg in April 1938.
life: Born in 1859 at Prossnitz in Moravia to a Jewish cloth merchant, Husserl studied mathematics at Leipzig and Berlin under Weierstrass and took his doctorate at Vienna in 1883. What redirected him was Franz Brentano, whose lectures he attended from 1884. From Brentano came the thesis that mental acts are directed upon objects, and the conviction that philosophy could be pursued with the rigour of a science. Carl Stumpf supervised his Habilitation at Halle in 1887.

Fourteen thin years at Halle followed. The Logical Investigations ended them. Göttingen called him at once, and a movement formed around him — Reinach, Hedwig Conrad-Martius, Roman Ingarden, Alexandre Koyré, with an allied Munich group under Pfänder and Scheler. Ideas I split them in 1913. Most had read the Investigations as a licence for realist description of essences. The transcendental turn looked to them like a relapse into Kant.

Freiburg called him in 1916. Edith Stein served as his assistant until 1918, deciphering his shorthand. Heidegger arrived in 1919, became the designated heir, and took the chair on Husserl’s retirement in 1928. Being and Time carried a dedication to him in friendship and admiration, dropped from the fifth edition of 1941 and restored only after the war. What he left was chiefly some forty thousand pages of Gabelsberger shorthand. The Belgian Franciscan Herman Van Breda took them out of the Reich in 1938 and lodged them at Louvain, where Eugen Fink and Ludwig Landgrebe began transcribing.

The break was philosophical before it was personal. Their attempt to write the Encyclopaedia Britannica article on phenomenology together collapsed over four drafts in 1927 and 1928, Heidegger denying that the reduction was needed at all. Husserl then read Being and Time closely in 1929. He filled the margins of his copy with notes concluding that his assistant had turned transcendental phenomenology into philosophical anthropology.

p: Only the first volume appeared. Husserl set out to ground number in the mental act of collecting: a multiplicity is what is given when consciousness holds several items in one act. Small numbers can be presented authentically, while large ones are handled symbolically. It is a serious book that now reads as a psychology of counting.

Frege reviewed it in 1894 and was merciless. He charged that Husserl had dissolved objective numbers into private mental contents, so that on such a view everything becomes an idea. The tidy story is that the review converted him. Mohanty and Willard have argued from the manuscripts that the retreat from psychologism was already under way and owed more to Bolzano and Lotze. Either way, by 1900 he treated the book’s foundation as a mistake.

The Prolegomena that opens the work is the most destructive thing Husserl wrote. If logical laws are laws of thinking, they are empirical generalisations: vague, merely probable, relative to the species that thinks them. Psychologism therefore entails a relativism it cannot survive, since the psychologist must presuppose the validity of the very laws he is deriving. The argument settled the question for a generation.

The six investigations that follow build the positive apparatus: expression and meaning, ideal species, the founding relations between parts and wholes, a pure grammar of meaning-forms, and in the fifth an analysis of intentional experience without an ego standing behind it. The sixth, on the fulfilment of an empty intention by intuition and on categorial intuition, is the one Heidegger said mattered most to him. Husserl abandoned the recasting he planned and let the 1921 text appear only partly revised, the drafts filling Husserliana XX.

works.t: Ideas for a Pure Phenomenology (Ideen zu einer reinen Phänomenologie), Book One
p: Here the method gets its name. The natural attitude takes the world’s existence for granted. The epochē suspends that commitment — not doubting the world, simply refusing to use its existence as a premise — so that what remains is experience with its objects taken exactly as experienced. Running alongside is the eidetic reduction, which moves from this perception to the invariant structure of perception as such.

The technical core is the noesis–noema pair: every act has its content, the object-as-intended, and phenomenology describes the noema rather than the thing. Whether the noema is an abstract sense on the model of Frege, as Føllesdal argued, or the object itself considered in a certain way, as Gurwitsch and Drummond held, remains the sharpest dispute in Husserl scholarship. Books Two and Three were drafted but withheld, appearing only in 1952.

Invited to the Sorbonne in February 1929, Husserl spoke in the amphitheatre named for Descartes and used the occasion to claim him. The five meditations rebuild the Meditations without the substance Descartes smuggled back in. The ego reached by the reduction is not a small thinking thing but the field in which any object can appear at all. Gabrielle Peiffer and the young Emmanuel Levinas made the French text.

The fifth meditation is the hard one and has generated most of the commentary. Confined to what is genuinely my own, how do I reach another consciousness? The answer is appresentation through pairing. The other’s body is given as a body like mine, and an experiential life is thereby indicated that I can never live through. Critics from Schutz onward have doubted that this escapes the solipsism it was built to defeat.

works.t: The Crisis of European Sciences and Transcendental Phenomenology (Die Krisis der europäischen Wissenschaften)
works.y: lectures 1935; parts I–II published 1936; complete text 1954
p: Barred from publishing in Germany, Husserl lectured in Vienna and Prague in 1935. He printed the first two parts in the Belgrade journal Philosophia in 1936. Walter Biemel assembled the whole from the Nachlass in 1954. The crisis is not a shortage of results but the loss of any account of what the sciences mean for human life.

The historical argument turns on Galileo, at once discoverer and concealer. By substituting a mathematical manifold for the world as perceived, he laid a garb of ideas over the only world anyone inhabits. The substitution was then forgotten. Against it Husserl sets the Lebenswelt, the pre-scientific world of perceived things and practical purposes from which every measurement borrows its sense. The book is also unmistakably Eurocentric, treating philosophy as a European destiny — a claim later readers have found hard to defend.

legacy: Almost every major continental philosopher of the next half-century passed through him. Heidegger recast the method as an inquiry into Being; Stein and Ingarden held to realist description; Schutz carried it into sociology. Merleau-Ponty travelled to Louvain in April 1939, the first foreign scholar to read the unpublished manuscripts. The Crisis materials marked his work permanently.

The misreadings mattered. Sartre’s version, taken from Raymond Aron in 1933 and worked out in The Transcendence of the Ego, jettisoned the transcendental ego. It made phenomenology a doctrine of freedom Husserl would not have recognised. In France the reduction was widely treated as a preliminary to be got past rather than the discipline of the whole enterprise.

What survives is partly technical: the account of intentional content feeds directly into philosophy of mind, and the epistemology of perception has borrowed his vocabulary of horizon and fulfilment. Dummett read the split between him and Frege as the parting of the analytic and continental roads. The Lebenswelt escaped philosophy altogether into sociology and the critique of technocracy. And the archive keeps altering the picture: volumes on time, passive synthesis and intersubjectivity have made the caricature of a Cartesian solitary hard to sustain.

read.first: Start with the Prolegomena to the Logical Investigations, which needs no prior phenomenology and shows the mind that built the rest. Then Ideas I for the method, and the Crisis for the reach.
read.note: His prose is patient to the point of exhaustion and restarts the same analysis many times. So read slowly and expect the argument to accumulate rather than to arrive.

husserl.caveat: Most of what Husserl wrote he never published. Editorial choices in the still-unfinished Husserliana partly determine which Husserl one reads. So judgements about when and how far he became an idealist remain contested.

bergson.sub: the philosopher of lived duration against the clock
world: Third Republic France gave philosophy a public stage and a narrow orthodoxy: neo-Kantian in the university, positivist in temper, with Théodule Ribot importing an experimental psychology that treated mind as measurable function. Bergson’s lectures at the Collège de France after 1900 drew society audiences as well as students. The Church was less pleased: his three main books went onto the Index in 1914.
life: Born in Paris in 1859 to a Polish-Jewish father and English mother, Bergson entered the École normale supérieure alongside Jaurès and Durkheim and took his doctorate in 1889. The Collège de France chair came in 1900, and he later chaired the League of Nations committee on intellectual cooperation and received the Nobel Prize in Literature for 1927. He died in occupied Paris in January 1941.

works.t: Time and Free Will (Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience)
p: The doctoral thesis, and the source of what followed. We think of time on the model of a line, a homogeneous medium in which moments sit side by side, because action and measurement require it. Lived time, durée, is a qualitative interpenetration of states that cannot be divided without being falsified. Freedom is then a fact about acts issuing from the whole self.

An attempt on the mind-body problem by way of the literature on aphasia. Bergson distinguishes habit memory, bodily and repeatable, from pure recollection, stored nowhere and called up as the situation demands. The brain is an organ of selection and action, not a warehouse of images. It is his most disciplined book, and the hardest for later philosophy of mind to dismiss.

The book that made him famous. Against both mechanism and finalism—each of which assumes the end is contained in the beginning—Bergson describes evolution as an élan vital, a surge producing genuinely new forms. The intellect, shaped for solids, takes snapshots and strings them together, an error he calls the cinematographic illusion. Biologists rejected the vital impulse as explanatorily empty, and that verdict stands.

legacy: Around 1910 Bergson was the most celebrated philosopher alive; twenty years later, a byword for the outmoded. The decisive damage came on 6 April 1922, when Einstein answered him in Paris by saying there is no philosophers’ time, only physical and psychological time. Duration and Simultaneity compounded the impression that he had misunderstood relativity; he refused to reprint it. Deleuze rehabilitated him in 1966.

read.first: Read Time and Free Will for the founding distinction, then Matter and Memory, which is the stronger book.
read.note: Bergson writes beautifully, and the prose can carry a reader past arguments that deserve resistance.

bergson.caveat: The report that he queued in 1940 to register as a Jew rather than accept an exemption rests on accounts given after his death and cannot be fully documented.

whitehead.sub: the mathematician who rebuilt metaphysics out of events
world: Whitehead spent his first career inside two upheavals. The foundations of mathematics were in crisis—Cantor, Peano, and in 1901 the paradox his pupil Russell found in set theory. Physics meanwhile was being remade by relativity and quantum theory, which dissolved the enduring bit of matter classical metaphysics had assumed. The First World War took his younger son Eric, shot down in 1918.
life: Born in Kent in 1861, he entered Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1880 and stayed as fellow and lecturer, teaching Russell. He left in 1910 for London, as professor of applied mathematics at Imperial College. In 1924, aged sixty-three and untrained in philosophy, he accepted a chair in it at Harvard. He taught there until 1937 and did the work he is remembered for.

p: Three volumes deriving mathematics from logic, built on a ramified theory of types designed to block the paradoxes. The labour ran to a decade, and Cambridge University Press published at a loss the authors helped cover. A fourth volume on geometry, Whitehead’s responsibility, was never finished. Gödel ended the logicist ambition in 1931, but the book fixed the notation of modern logic.

Whitehead’s philosophy of physics, delivered as the Tarner Lectures. He rejects the bifurcation of nature into the causes science describes and the qualities mind adds. He rebuilds points and instants from overlapping events by extensive abstraction. The Lowell Lectures of 1925, published as Science and the Modern World, carried the argument to a wide audience and named the fallacy of misplaced concreteness.

The Gifford Lectures, expanded into a categoreal scheme of forbidding difficulty. The ultimate constituents of reality are actual occasions: momentary events that arise by prehending everything prior, achieve a determinate character, and perish into the data of what follows. God appears within the scheme, affected by the world, not immune to it. The text was corrupt until the corrected edition of 1978.

legacy: The metaphysics never entered the analytic mainstream his logic helped create. For decades theologians carried it: Hartshorne, then Cobb and the Claremont school, who built process theology on a God who suffers change. Elsewhere the influence is diffuse but real: ecological thought, the Chinese reception of process philosophy, Deleuze and Isabelle Stengers. The fallacy of misplaced concreteness escaped into general use without his name.

read.first: Begin with Science and the Modern World, which states the position in readable form. Approach Process and Reality only with a commentary alongside.
read.note: The technical vocabulary is unavoidable, and each term is defined against the others. Partial reading therefore produces confusion rather than partial understanding.

russell.sub: the logician who made analysis the method of philosophy
world: The Cambridge Russell entered in 1890 was governed by a British Hegelianism. Bradley’s Appearance and Reality appeared in 1893 and argued that relations are contradictory and reality one indivisible whole. McTaggart taught the same lesson at Trinity with more charm. The revolt Russell and Moore began around 1898 was against the metaphysics of their own teachers and, deliberately, against the prose it was written in.

Nineteen fourteen wrecked that world. Cambridge emptied into the army. Conscription came in 1916. The No-Conscription Fellowship, of which Russell was an active member, was prosecuted under the Defence of the Realm Act. Trinity removed him from his lectureship in 1916 after a conviction over a leaflet defending a conscientious objector. In 1918 an article on American troops breaking British strikes earned him six months in Brixton.

After 1919 the subject he had founded moved on without him. The Vienna Circle formed around Moritz Schlick and took the Tractatus, not Principia, as its scripture. Schlick was shot dead in 1936. Hitler scattered the Circle to Britain and America. Russell spent 1938 to 1944 in the United States. He lost a New York appointment in 1940 to a court case over his views on sex, and returned to a Cambridge led by his former student.
life: He was born in Monmouthshire in 1872 into the Whig aristocracy. His grandfather Lord John Russell had twice been prime minister. He lost both parents before he was four and was raised by a strict and pious grandmother. He found Euclid at eleven and later called it the most important event of his life. He went up to Trinity in 1890, read mathematics and then the Moral Sciences, and won a fellowship in 1895.

The turning point was the International Congress of Philosophy in Paris in August 1900, where Peano’s precision struck him as a new instrument. He wrote most of the Principles in a few intoxicated months. In June 1901 he found the paradox that broke his system and Frege’s. The decade with Whitehead on Principia Mathematica cost him his health and, by his own account, most of his mathematical creativity.

War made him a public figure and left him without a post. So for twenty years he lived by journalism and lecture tours. He ran a progressive school at Beacon Hill with his second wife Dora, married four times in all, and inherited an earldom he mostly ignored. Trinity restored his fellowship in 1944. The last quarter-century was campaigning: the Nobel Prize in 1950, the manifesto with Einstein in 1955, nuclear disarmament, a week in Brixton again at eighty-nine, and the tribunal on Vietnam.

works.t: The Principles of Mathematics and Principia Mathematica
p: The Principles announces logicism in English: pure mathematics deals with concepts definable from a very few logical notions, and its propositions follow from a very few logical principles. Russell reached the thesis independently and found Frege late enough to add an appendix, the first serious account of him in English. Much of the book argues with Bradley over whether relations are real. The insistence that they are founds analytic metaphysics.

Principia is the execution, deriving arithmetic by steps so explicit that one plus one equals two arrives hundreds of pages in. The theory of types blocks the paradox by ranking functions so that none takes itself as argument. But the ramified version proved so restrictive that Russell had to add an axiom of reducibility he could never justify. In 1931 Gödel, taking Principia as his target, showed no consistent system of that strength proves every arithmetical truth it can state.

Take the sentence the present King of France is bald. There is no such king, so if the phrase is a name it names nothing and the sentence appears to say nothing. Yet it is plainly meaningful, and its negation seems equally false, which threatens excluded middle. Russell answers that grammar misleads: the F is G asserts three things at once — something is F, at most one thing is F, and whatever is F is G.

So analysed, the denoting phrase disappears. It is an incomplete symbol, meaningless alone and significant only in a whole sentence. The sentence about the king is simply false, its first conjunct failing. Its negation is ambiguous between denying the conjunction and asserting that some king is not bald — what Russell called primary and secondary occurrence, or scope. Meinong’s realm of objects that subsist without existing is no longer needed.

Ramsey called it a paradigm of philosophy. For fifty years it modelled what analysis could do. Strawson attacked it in 1950, arguing that referring is something speakers do rather than sentences, so the sentence is neither true nor false but a failed use. Donnellan added the referential-attributive distinction in 1966. Every later account of descriptions still argues against this one.

works.t: The Problems of Philosophy and Our Knowledge of the External World
p: The first was written in weeks for a shilling series and remains the best short introduction to the subject in English. It begins with a table and separates the sense-data one is directly aware of from the physical object one infers. It works outward through induction, universals and truth. Its lasting doctrine is the division between knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description.

The Lowell Lectures of 1914 turn that into a programme: wherever possible, substitute logical constructions for inferred entities. Rather than posit unobservable objects behind the sense-data, build objects out of actual and possible sense-data, as classes and series. The point becomes a class of overlapping volumes, the instant a class of overlapping events. Russell also declares here that logical analysis is the method proper to philosophy.

works.t: The Philosophy of Logical Atomism and An Inquiry into Meaning and Truth
p: The eight lectures of 1918, given while he awaited prosecution, supply the metaphysics his method assumed and credit it frankly to Wittgenstein. The world consists of facts, not things; facts have constituents; a fully analysed proposition mirrors the structure of the fact that makes it true; and the ultimate constituents are particulars with their properties and relations. Atomism was short-lived even for Russell, but it named the ambition the early movement shared.

The William James Lectures at Harvard, twenty-two years later, return to the question with the metaphysics dropped. Russell builds upward from an object-language learnt by confrontation with what its words apply to, through a hierarchy of languages, to the basic propositions that record perception. His target is the doctrine that truth reduces to coherence among sentences. A belief, he insists, is made true by something outside the system of beliefs.

Grown out of lectures at the Barnes Foundation, written largely from memory in wartime America, and the book that made him financially secure. Its virtue is that it sets philosophers inside their politics and societies rather than treating doctrines as free-floating, and that it is written by someone who can make an argument move. The chapters on Leibniz and the British empiricists are still worth reading.

As history it is unreliable and often careless. Aristotle is handled impatiently. The medieval chapters are thin and unsympathetic. The treatment of Nietzsche is closer to a prosecution than a reading. Throughout, the past divides into allies of liberal reason and enemies of it. It sold enormously, shaped what generations of readers believed philosophy to be, and contributed materially to the Nobel Prize in Literature awarded him in 1950.

legacy: The technical work founded a discipline. Type theory survives in the foundations of computer science and in modern proof assistants. The theory of descriptions defined the philosophy of language for fifty years. Construing disputed entities as logical constructions runs from Carnap’s Aufbau to present-day structuralism about mathematics. His claim that philosophy proceeds by analysing propositions into logical form was for decades the definition of the subject.

His personal influence ran the other way in the end. He recognised Wittgenstein at once in 1911 and secured publication of the Tractatus. Then he found the pupil had taken the movement somewhere he despised. Russell thought the later Cambridge philosophy trivial and said so with mounting bitterness; it thought his atomism a museum piece. His view of that quarrel — that dissolving problems rather than solving them is an abdication — has more defenders now than in 1955.

As a public figure he is remembered more than read: the pacifist imprisoned twice, the campaigner against nuclear weapons, the essayist on marriage and religion. That reputation hides how sharply his views changed, including on pacifism, which he suspended for the Second World War. The History is mistaken for a scholarly authority. It is a brilliant partisan essay by a great logician on subjects where he was often an amateur.

The sharpest instance is 1948. He argued in public that the West should threaten the Soviet Union with atomic war while it still lacked a bomb of its own. It was a position he afterwards denied having held and then, confronted with the record, acknowledged.

read.first: The Problems of Philosophy first, in an afternoon, then On Denoting, which is short and repays being worked through slowly with pencil and paper. The Philosophy of Logical Atomism supplies the metaphysics behind the method.
read.note: Do not begin with Principia Mathematica, which is not a book for reading. Do not take the History of Western Philosophy as an authority on anything but Russell.

legacy: Principia Ethica created metaethics: after Moore the primary question was not what is good but what sort of claim a moral claim is. His argument was promptly turned against his own intuitionism, since if good names no natural property the emotivists could conclude it names nothing and merely voices attitude. Frankena’s paper of 1939 showed the naturalistic fallacy is not clearly a fallacy.

The common-sense papers had a stranger afterlife. Wittgenstein spent his last two years working through them. On Certainty replies that Moore’s truisms are not known at all but are hinges on which knowing turns. Epistemologists still argue about which way the certainty runs. Outside philosophy his largest effect was on the Bloomsbury Group, who took the last chapter of Principia Ethica as a licence for a life of friendship and art. Keynes thought they kept the conclusions and dropped the arguments.
life: George Edward Moore was born at Upper Norwood in south London in 1873, a physician’s son. He went from Dulwich College to Trinity College, Cambridge in 1892 to read classics. Russell, two years ahead, urged him towards the Moral Sciences. He took a first in both. A dissertation on Kant’s ethics won him a prize fellowship from 1898 to 1904, by the end of which he and Russell had turned decisively against idealism.

When the fellowship expired he left Cambridge and lived seven years on a small inherited income, writing without a post. He returned as a lecturer in 1911 and married Dorothy Ely in 1916. He held the chair of Mental Philosophy and Logic from 1925 until 1939, when Wittgenstein succeeded him. Those who knew him remarked on an almost painful honesty in argument. Keynes and Wittgenstein both said they had met nobody with less vanity. He died at Cambridge in 1958.

read.first: Read the two short common-sense papers first, since they are plain and self-contained. Then the first chapter of Principia Ethica, where the whole argument about definition is made.
read.note: Moore’s prose repeats and qualifies to a degree that can seem pedantic. The repetition is the argument, and skimming it removes the point.

moore.sub: the realist who trusted his hands over the argument

p: The central claim is that good is a simple, unanalysable, non-natural quality, as indefinable as yellow. The support is the open question. Whatever natural property is offered as a definition of good—pleasant, desired, conducive to survival—it stays intelligible to ask whether that property is good, which it would not be if the definition held. Moore called the mistake the naturalistic fallacy and charged Bentham, Mill and Spencer with it. Having declared good indefinable, his last chapter states without embarrassment what is good in itself: personal affection and the enjoyment of beautiful objects.

Moore attacks idealism at its narrowest joint, the Berkeleyan formula that to be is to be perceived. His move is to distinguish, within any sensation, the act of awareness from the object one is aware of. The idealist, he argues, runs them together, treating the blue as part of the experiencing rather than what the experiencing is of. Consciousness, he says, is diaphanous: attend to it and one finds only the object. If the distinction holds, the sensed object is not constituted by the sensing, and the idealist inference collapses at its first step.

The first lists propositions Moore claims to know with certainty: that he has a body, that the earth existed long before his birth, that other people have had experiences. It observes that philosophers who deny such things presuppose them in the act of denying. The second, a British Academy lecture, offers the notorious proof. Holding up one hand and then the other, he asserts that here is one hand and here is another, that hands are external objects, and that external objects therefore exist. The point is not naivety but relative certainty: a sceptical premise must be more credible than the ordinary claim it overturns.
works.t: A Defence of Common Sense and Proof of an External World

world: Cambridge in the 1890s was an idealist place. Bradley’s Appearance and Reality of 1893 held that relations are contradictory and reality a single spiritual whole. McTaggart, who befriended the young Moore, argued that time is unreal. The Moral Sciences Tripos was small and clubbable. The Apostles, the university’s secret discussion society, mattered as much as any lecture. In that milieu Moore began simply by asking what a philosopher’s sentences meant.

The century that followed left him strikingly untouched. He edited Mind from 1921 to 1947, through the Depression, the rise of Nazism and a second war. Almost none of it appears in his philosophy. He was not indifferent—he lectured in America from 1940 partly because his sons were safer there—but wrote no political philosophy. His effect on the wider culture came through one book on ethics and the people who read it young.

wittgenstein.sub: the engineer who twice redrew the limits of language
world: Vienna before 1914 lived beyond its political means and at the height of its cultural ones: Klimt painting, Mahler at the Opera, Freud consulting, Loos stripping ornament from buildings and Karl Kraus prosecuting the corruption of the German language week by week. That last preoccupation, the suspicion that public confusion is at bottom linguistic, was in the Viennese air long before Wittgenstein made it a method.

War took him into the Austro-Hungarian artillery: a river gunboat, then observation posts in Galicia during the Brusilov offensive of 1916, and finally the Italian front. In Galicia he repeatedly volunteered for the most exposed positions and was decorated. He finished the Tractatus on leave in the summer of 1918. He was captured in November when the front collapsed, and spent nine months in Italian camps. From captivity he sent the text to Russell.

In the 1920s the Vienna Circle formed around Moritz Schlick and made the Tractatus its founding document, reading its silence about ethics as dismissal rather than reverence—a misreading Wittgenstein resented and never corrected. Schlick was murdered on the university steps in 1936 by a former student. The Anschluss of 1938 put Wittgenstein’s siblings under the racial laws. The family bought an exemption from Berlin. The Circle itself dispersed to Britain and America.
life: Ludwig Wittgenstein was born in Vienna in 1889, youngest of eight children in a household of enormous wealth and severe unhappiness. Three of his brothers killed themselves. He studied mechanical engineering in Berlin and aeronautics at Manchester from 1908, patenting a propeller with jet-driven tips. Questions about the foundations of mathematics took him to Frege at Jena in 1911. Frege sent him to Russell, who within a term decided the young Austrian would do the next work in logic.

After a solitary year in a hut at Skjolden in Norway he enlisted in 1914. He wrote the Tractatus in the war and in captivity, and came home in 1919 convinced philosophy was finished. He gave his entire inherited fortune to his siblings. He spent six years in remote village schools in Lower Austria. There he compiled a spelling dictionary for elementary pupils, the only other book published in his lifetime. After a boy collapsed under his hand in 1926 he resigned.

He worked as a monastery gardener, then designed an austere house for his sister in Vienna. Conversations with Schlick and Frank Ramsey drew him back to Cambridge in 1929. There he submitted the Tractatus as his doctoral dissertation to Russell and Moore, and by 1930 he was dismantling it in lectures. He held Moore’s chair from 1939 and hated the profession. He spent much of the war as a hospital porter, resigned in 1947, and died of cancer at Cambridge in April 1951.

p: Seven numbered propositions with decimal commentary, about eighty pages, and no arguments in the usual sense, only pronouncements arranged so that each supports the one above it. The core is the picture theory: a proposition is a picture of a possible state of affairs. It can depict because it shares a logical form with what it depicts. Names go proxy for objects. Every complex proposition is a truth-function of elementary ones.

From this follows the limit. What can be pictured can be said clearly. What cannot—logical form, ethics, aesthetics, the existence of the world—shows itself and cannot be stated. Since the book’s own sentences attempt exactly that, its penultimate proposition calls them nonsense: the reader who has understood throws away the ladder after climbing it. The last proposition prescribes silence. Whether that self-destruction is a fatal flaw, an ethical gesture or genuine therapy is now the main fault line in the scholarship.

Two sets of notes dictated to students at Cambridge and circulated in typescript for two decades before publication. The later philosophy was therefore known by hearsay long before anyone could buy it. The Blue Book asks what the meaning of a word is. It redirects attention from objects to methods of use. It introduces the language-game as a device: describe a small, complete, primitive practice of communication and see what meaning amounts to inside it.

The Brown Book carries this further, building a sequence of imagined languages of rising complexity. It is the closest thing in the corpus to a systematic exposition. Wittgenstein began rewriting it in German, abandoned the attempt and called the result worthless. That revision fed directly into the Investigations. Read now, the two are the best bridge between the early and the late work.

It opens by quoting Augustine on learning to speak—words name objects, sentences combine names—and spends its length showing how little that explains. The alternative is not a rival theory but a changed question: ask how a word is used, in what practice, to what end. Meaning is use. The practices are language-games. The activities called language share no defining feature but a family resemblance.

Two long stretches carry the weight. The discussion of rule-following observes that no rule contains its own application, since any action can be brought into accord with it under some interpretation. It concludes that grasping a rule is mastering a technique inside a shared practice. The private language argument then denies there could be a language whose words name sensations knowable only to the speaker. Without a public criterion nothing distinguishes using the word correctly from believing one has.

The method throughout is therapeutic. Philosophical problems arise when language idles, when a word is taken outside the practice that gave it work. The aim is relief rather than doctrine. Whether this succeeds, and whether the book contains arguments or only reminders, is still disputed. Its influence is not: it made ordinary language philosophy possible and forced every later theory of meaning to answer it.

works.t: Remarks on the Foundations of Mathematics
p: Wittgenstein thought the philosophy of mathematics his central business. These remarks apply the later method to it. A proof is not the discovery of a truth about abstract objects but the establishment of a new rule, a change in what counts as making sense. Necessity is grammatical. The treatment of contradiction is deliberately unalarmed, since an inconsistency matters only where it causes trouble in practice.

The book met the worst reception of anything published under his name. Georg Kreisel reviewed it as a surprisingly insignificant product of a sparkling mind.
