Alan Turing had objected in person, in the 1939 lectures, that a contradiction in the calculus used to build a bridge will drop the bridge. The editors were also criticised for heavy cutting and for imposing an order the manuscripts lacked. A much enlarged edition followed in 1978.

The last work, written in the final eighteen months and continued to within two days of his death. It was prompted by Moore’s claims to know that here is a hand and that the earth existed long before his birth. Wittgenstein sides with Moore against the sceptic. He rejects Moore’s way of putting it. Such propositions are not known, because doubting them is not an available move: they are hinges on which inquiry turns.

The result is a picture of knowledge resting on a groundless but not arbitrary practice, learnt as one learns to act rather than proved. Whether this makes him a relativist about world-pictures, or supplies the strongest answer to scepticism available, is genuinely contested. Both readings have serious defenders. The remarks are unpolished and unrevised. They are still among the most influential things he wrote.

legacy: Few philosophers have founded two movements, and none by refuting himself. The Tractatus gave the Vienna Circle its verification principle and its scorn for metaphysics, neither of which Wittgenstein held. The Investigations gave post-war Oxford and Cambridge the conviction that philosophical problems are confusions in the use of words. It shaped Anscombe and a generation of students who imitated his manner better than his thought. It ran alongside the independent Oxford work of Ryle and Austin. Kripke’s book of 1982 recast the rule-following passages as a sceptical paradox about meaning.

The texts themselves are contested ground. He published one book of philosophy and a school dictionary in his lifetime. He left some twenty thousand pages of manuscript to three literary executors. Over four decades they issued edited volumes assembled from notebooks that often had no settled order. Critics object to silent conflation of sources, to omissions, and to titles the author never chose. The Bergen electronic edition finally made the manuscripts themselves available.

What survives is less a doctrine than a set of pressures. Meaning as use, family resemblance, forms of life and the private language argument are common property well outside philosophy, in linguistics, anthropology and theology. He is also the most misappropriated of modern philosophers, invoked for relativism, quietism, mysticism and behaviourism. All of these he would have refused. The most durable inheritance may be the least quotable: look at how an expression works before theorising about what it must mean.

The undoing continues. The fourth edition of 2009, edited by P. M. S. Hacker and Joachim Schulte, numbered the remarks the executors had printed as Part II. It retitled the whole of it Philosophy of Psychology—A Fragment, on the ground that Wittgenstein never settled its place in the book. That decision has itself been argued against in print.

read.first: Start with the first hundred sections of the Philosophical Investigations, which are self-contained and need no background. Then the Blue Book, and only then the Tractatus with a commentary beside it.
read.note: Nothing he wrote can be skimmed. The numbered remarks are compressed to the point of obscurity, and repay slow re-reading far more than secondary literature does.

wittgenstein.caveat: Everything except the Tractatus and a school spelling dictionary is posthumous and editorially constructed. The titles, divisions and ordering of the later books are therefore the executors’ decisions rather than the author’s.

carnap.sub: the builder who kept rebuilding empiricism from the ground up
world: Vienna from 1919 to 1934 belonged to the Social Democrats, who taxed the rich for housing blocks, clinics and adult-education institutes. The circle forming around Moritz Schlick from 1924 saw itself as part of that work. Its 1929 manifesto, The Scientific Conception of the World, was drafted by Hans Hahn, Otto Neurath and Carnap. It was a programme for a rational society as much as a statement about logic.

Austrian democracy died in the civil war of February 1934. The clerical dictatorship that followed shut the Circle's public arm, the Ernst Mach Society. On 22 June 1936 a former student shot Schlick on a university staircase. A Catholic-nationalist weekly defended the killer and called the victim's philosophy a Jewish corruption, though Schlick was not a Jew. The members scattered to America, where loyalty investigations would soon make a left-wing past a liability.
life: Born in 1891 at Ronsdorf in the Wuppertal, Carnap read physics, mathematics and philosophy at Jena. There he sat in Frege's thinly attended lectures on the concept-script, and grasped their importance long before the profession did. His 1922 dissertation on space pulled apart three questions — formal, physical and intuitive — that Kantians and physicists had been running together. Schlick brought him to Vienna in 1926.

A chair at the German University in Prague followed in 1931. Carnap sailed for America in December 1935 and settled at Chicago, where Charles Morris had made room for him. 'Testability and Meaning' (1936-37) loosened the movement's central demand. It traded verification for degrees of confirmation, and admitted dispositional terms by partial definitions. He moved to UCLA in 1954, in Reichenbach's place. He died at Santa Monica in 1970.

works.t: The Logical Structure of the World (Der logische Aufbau der Welt)
p: Carnap set out to show that every concept science uses can be constructed, by explicit definition, from one primitive relation: remembered similarity between total momentary experiences. The construction climbs from the private to the physical to the social, in the logic of Principia Mathematica. The disclaimer matters as much as the system. Choosing a basis is not a claim about what is ultimately real, and a physicalist basis would serve. Nelson Goodman showed in 1951 that the definitions do not go through as stated.

works.t: The Logical Syntax of Language (Logische Syntax der Sprache)
p: The most ambitious book the movement produced. Philosophy here has no subject matter of its own. It is the logical syntax of the language of science. Disputes about things dissolve once restated in the formal mode as disputes about sentences. Carnap builds two artificial languages and states the principle of tolerance: in logic there are no morals, and anyone may construct the language he likes provided he sets out its rules. Gödel's incompleteness results, absorbed early, cost the programme much of what it promised.

works.t: Meaning and Necessity, with 'Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology'
p: Tarski's work on truth convinced Carnap that semantics could be done as rigorously as syntax. The book replaces Frege's sense and reference with a method of extension and intension, defines logical truth by state-descriptions, and gives modal logic an interpretation. The essay makes his most durable move. Questions about numbers or physical objects asked inside a linguistic framework have determinate answers. The external question whether such entities really exist is a practical choice of language, settled by convenience rather than discovery.

legacy: Quine, who had studied with him in Prague in 1933, took apart the analytic-synthetic distinction in 1951, and with it the ground his frameworks stood on. Carnap answered that a distinction drawn by explicit rules in a constructed language needs no prior account of synonymy in ordinary speech. Few were persuaded. Logical empiricism became the position everyone had refuted without reading.

That verdict has been reopened since the 1990s. Historians working from the German texts found no phenomenalist foundationalism in the Aufbau, and a deeper Kantian inheritance than the textbooks allowed. The internal-external distinction has returned in metaontology, where deflationists deploy it against heavyweight metaphysics. What survives most quietly is the method: explication, the replacement of a vague concept by a precise one.

read.first: Start with 'Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology', ten pages that show the mature Carnap thinking, then the opening chapters of Meaning and Necessity.
read.note: The Aufbau is a technical document and rewards a commentary more than a first solo reading.

carnap.caveat: How much of the Aufbau is empiricist reduction and how much a neo-Kantian account of objectivity remains genuinely disputed among historians.

popper.sub: the theorist who made refutation the engine of knowledge
world: The Vienna of Popper's youth was a capital without an empire: two million people governing a small, cold and hungry republic, and politically at war with itself. He was briefly a communist at seventeen. He left after police shot young demonstrators in 1919 at a protest he had helped bring out. What stayed with him was the discovery that he had taken a theory on authority and let it explain away every fact against it.

Otto Glöckel's school reform gave him his training and his first employment. The civil war of 1934 and the approach of the Anschluss sent him looking for work abroad. He spent the war at the other end of the world, in Christchurch, writing his political books as what he called his war effort. In 1946 the London School of Economics, itself just back from wartime exile in Cambridge, brought him to England.
life: Popper was born in Vienna in 1902 to a lawyer with a large library. His parents were of Jewish descent and had been baptised Lutheran. He left school early, apprenticed briefly to a cabinetmaker, qualified as a primary teacher and took a doctorate in 1928 under the psychologist Karl Bühler. Logik der Forschung appeared at the end of 1934 in the series Schlick and Philipp Frank edited, so the Circle published the book attacking it.

He taught for nine years at Canterbury University College in New Zealand, reached the LSE in 1946, and held its chair of logic and scientific method from 1949. On his first Cambridge visit that October he and Wittgenstein quarrelled over a poker, an incident retold more often than either man's arguments. Knighted in 1965, he taught Imre Lakatos, Paul Feyerabend and John Watkins. He died at Croydon in 1994.

works.t: The Logic of Scientific Discovery (Logik der Forschung)
p: The argument is narrower than the slogan. A theory is empirical if the class of its potential falsifiers is not empty: there are basic statements, singular reports of observable events, that it forbids. Falsifiability is a matter of logical form, and marks off science rather than sense, since Popper thought metaphysics meaningful and often fruitful. No number of instances verifies a universal statement, while one counter-instance contradicts it.

Popper knew the difficulties. Basic statements are themselves accepted by decision. No hypothesis is tested alone, so failure can always be blamed on an auxiliary assumption. His ban on ad hoc rescue is a methodological convention rather than a result. Strictly, statistical hypotheses forbid nothing. Kuhn's normal science, Lakatos's protected hard core and Laudan's argument of 1983 that no single criterion divides science from the rest have left demarcation open.

works.t: The Open Society and Its Enemies
p: Written in New Zealand from a poor library and published in two volumes after several rejections. Its target is historicism, the doctrine that history obeys discoverable laws of development, which Popper attacked separately in The Poverty of Historicism (Economica, 1944-45; as a book, 1957). If the future is fixed, reform becomes obstruction and violence becomes midwifery. Against Plato, Hegel and Marx he sets piecemeal engineering and institutions that let a government be removed without bloodshed. Specialists have shown the readings to be tendentious. The political argument has outlived the exegesis.

The most readable statement of the position, and the book most people mean when they cite Popper. The opening essay recounts how, as a young man, he compared Einstein's risky prediction about starlight with the way Marxism and Adler's psychology accommodated every outcome. He drew the demarcation from that contrast. Later essays argue that observation is never theory-free and that inquiry begins from problems. Objective Knowledge (1972) added a World 3 of objective contents, which even sympathetic readers found the most obscure part of the system.

legacy: Working scientists took to falsifiability faster than philosophers did. It survives in textbooks and grant applications as a rule of hygiene. Within philosophy of science the confrontation with Kuhn, staged in London in 1965 and printed as Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge, went badly for the strict version. Lakatos's rescue conceded that good theories are defended for long stretches against apparent refutation.

The political books had the wider life. The Open Society became a text of Cold War liberalism and was reprinted across eastern Europe after 1989. The paradox of tolerance, buried in a footnote, is now quoted constantly without its qualification that suppression is a last resort. What endures best is the temper rather than the doctrine, the demand that a claim specify what would count against it.

read.first: Begin with Conjectures and Refutations, chapter one, then the autobiography Unended Quest.
read.note: Read the early chapters of The Logic of Scientific Discovery before repeating anything about falsification. The book is more careful than its reputation.

ryle.sub: the Oxford analyst who exorcised the ghost in the machine
world: Oxford emptied in 1939. Its philosophers went into the Welsh Guards, the Intelligence Corps and the Special Operations Executive. They came back in 1945 with a taste for evidence and plain talk, and no patience left for system-building. Ryle ran the faculty that resulted, helped establish the graduate B.Phil., edited Mind from 1947 for a quarter of a century, and placed his pupils in chairs across the English-speaking world.
life: Born at Brighton in 1900, the son of a doctor with philosophical interests, Ryle read classics and then the new Modern Greats at Queen's College. He was elected to a tutorship at Christ Church in 1925. He served through the war in the Welsh Guards and in intelligence work, ending as a major. In 1945 he succeeded R. G. Collingwood as Waynflete Professor of Metaphysical Philosophy. He held the chair until 1968.

p: Ryle's target is what he calls the official doctrine, the dogma of the Ghost in the Machine: mind as an inner theatre running alongside the body. His charge is not falsehood but category mistake, of the kind made by a visitor shown the colleges and libraries who then asks to see the University. Mental terms mostly ascribe dispositions and capacities displayed in what people do. Knowing how is not knowing that: if intelligent action required first rehearsing a proposition, the rehearsing would itself have to be done intelligently, and the regress never stops.

Eight short Cambridge lectures on cases where two good arguments leave no room for each other, fatalism against deliberation, or the physicist's account of a table against the table one sets. The conflict, Ryle argues, is manufactured by treating two kinds of discourse as rival answers to one question. The book shows his method at its most economical and its most vulnerable.

legacy: The Concept of Mind was widely read as logical behaviourism and refuted under that description. Ryle thought that a misreading, since his dispositions never reduced to bodily movement. The functionalism that displaced him kept the case against the inner theatre while restoring inner states as causes. The knowing-how distinction proved most durable, seeding work on skill and tacit knowledge. It was challenged in 2001 by Jason Stanley and Timothy Williamson, who argued that knowing how is a species of propositional knowledge.

read.first: The Concept of Mind, chapters one and two, which contain the whole argument.
read.note: The wit is doing philosophical work; where a joke lands, an analysis is usually being proposed.

austin.sub: the anatomist of what saying something does
world: Austin spent the war in the Intelligence Corps, running the section that assembled terrain and defence intelligence for the Normandy landings. He ended a lieutenant-colonel. Colleagues thought the experience visible afterwards in his patience with detail and his distrust of a clever theory unsupported by the record. His Saturday morning meetings in Oxford through the 1950s ran the same way, on a shared body of examples rather than a doctrine.
life: Born at Lancaster in 1911 and schooled at Shrewsbury, Austin took a first in classics at Balliol and was elected to All Souls in 1933. He became White's Professor of Moral Philosophy in 1952 and gave the William James Lectures at Harvard in 1955. He published very little and died of cancer in 1960 at forty-eight. Everything he is now read for was assembled from his lecture notes by J. O. Urmson and G. J. Warnock.

works.t: How to Do Things with Words
p: Austin begins with utterances that plainly report nothing — 'I promise', 'I name this ship', the words said at a wedding. He shows they are assessed not as true or false but as happy or unhappy, under conditions whose failure yields a misfire or an abuse. Then he dismantles his own distinction, since statements have felicity conditions too. What replaces it is a theory of three things done at once: the locutionary act of saying something, the illocutionary act performed in saying it, and the perlocutionary effect it brings about.

A demolition of the sense-datum theory, aimed principally at Ayer's The Foundations of Empirical Knowledge. Austin denies that there is one thing called perceiving material objects, or one argument from illusion. The cases lumped together, sticks in water, mirages, double vision, dreams, are different, and most are not illusions at all. It works better as demolition than as construction. Its refusal to say what perception is has left readers divided about what it settled.

The clearest statement of the method. Austin proposes to study excuses because the distinctions there are fine, unnoticed and consequential, and because ordinary usage has been tested by generations of practical need. His defence of that starting point is careful: the common stock of words embodies the distinctions men have found worth drawing, which makes it the first word rather than the last.

legacy: Speech act theory left Oxford and became a discipline. John Searle systematised it. Paul Grice's work on implicature grew alongside it. It now underwrites much of linguistic pragmatics and arguments in the law of contract and defamation. Derrida's reading of Austin, and Searle's furious reply, turned a small quarrel into a long one between traditions. Feminist philosophers, notably Rae Langton, have used the illocutionary category to argue that some speech constitutes harm rather than merely causing it.

read.first: How to Do Things with Words, read straight through so the collapse of the performative-constative distinction lands.
read.note: Remember that the text is a transcript of lectures, and that Austin never signed off on it.

austin.caveat: All three books are editors' reconstructions from notes. The wording is Austin's, but the shape of the argument is partly his editors'.

quine.sub: the empiricist who made philosophy continuous with science
world: American philosophy in the 1930s was still pragmatist, genteel and thinly professional. The emigration changed it: Carnap to Chicago, Reichenbach to Los Angeles, Hempel, Feigl, Tarski and Gödel elsewhere. They brought a technical standard the younger Americans could meet and then exceed. Quine was among the few who had gone to Europe first and knew what was arriving.

After 1945 the Servicemen's Readjustment Act put more than two million veterans through American colleges. Philosophy departments grew into a journal-driven profession that prized technique. The Cold War pressed the same way. Quine, a political conservative who had spent the war in naval intelligence, was untroubled by it. His teacher Carnap, whose Vienna project had been openly socialist, watched that side of logical empiricism quietly drop away in America.
life: Born at Akron, Ohio, in 1908, Quine read mathematics at Oberlin, where a tutor pointed him to Principia Mathematica. He finished a Harvard doctorate under Whitehead in two years. A travelling fellowship in 1932-33 took him to Vienna for Schlick's circle, to Prague to sit with Carnap over the typescript of the Logical Syntax, and to Warsaw for Tarski and Leśniewski.

He was a Junior Fellow, then a member of the Harvard faculty for the rest of his life, interrupted by four years in the Navy decoding German submarine signals. 'Two Dogmas' was read to a philosophical meeting in December 1950 and printed the next year. Word and Object, nine years in the writing, appeared in 1960. He travelled to well over a hundred countries, wrote a spare and mannered prose, and died in Boston in 2000.

p: The most consequential twenty pages of twentieth-century analytic philosophy. The first dogma is the analytic-synthetic distinction. Every attempt to explain analyticity leans on synonymy, definition or semantic rule, each of which needs analyticity to explain it. So the circle never opens. The second is reductionism, the belief that each statement has its own confirming experiences. In their place Quine offers holism, in which our statements face the tribunal of experience not one by one but as a corporate body. It is a field whose edges touch observation, and whose interior, logic included, is revisable if the price is right.

Quine constructs the thought-experiment of radical translation: a field linguist facing a language with no bilingual to help him has only observable behaviour and the stimulations prompting assent. A rabbit runs past and the native says 'Gavagai'. Stimulus meaning fixes the whole sentence. It does not fix whether the term picks out a rabbit, an undetached rabbit part or a stage in a rabbit history, since any choice can be compensated for elsewhere in the manual. Rival manuals may fit all possible behaviour and still conflict. There is nothing further to be right about.

The title essay carries indeterminacy home. Reference in our own language is no more determinate than in the jungle, since a proxy function can reinterpret every term while leaving all sentences true. What a theory is about can be specified only relative to a background theory taken at face value. That is the mature form of the slogan that to be is to be the value of a bound variable. 'Epistemology Naturalized' concludes that the search for foundations should give way to a chapter of empirical psychology.

legacy: Quine's holism ended the positivist programme and made naturalism the default setting of American philosophy: no first philosophy above the sciences, ontology answered by asking what our best theories quantify over. Davidson built a theory of interpretation on the translation argument, while Putnam, Kripke and later Boghossian pushed back on the analytic-synthetic case. He also gave the web of belief its name, in a primer written with J. S. Ullian in 1970.

Indeterminacy has worn least well. Chomsky replied that behavioural dispositions are the wrong evidence base for a science of language. Few philosophers of mind now grant the premise. What survives is the picture rather than the theses: belief as a network under adjustment, meaning as a matter of degree, and the refusal to let philosophy claim a vantage point outside the sciences it comments on.

read.first: Read 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' in From a Logical Point of View, then chapter two of Word and Object.
read.note: His prose is compressed and unusually beautiful. Go slowly, and expect an argument to turn on a single sentence.

ayer.sub: the man who imported Vienna to Britain and later unbuilt it
world: British philosophy in the early 1930s was still working its way out of idealism and the Cook Wilson tradition at Oxford. The Vienna Circle was scarcely read in English. A short book that dismissed metaphysics and theology outright arrived in 1936, in a decade already impatient with grand systems. It was written in a prose that a general reader could follow without training.
life: Ayer was born in London in 1910 to a Swiss father and a Dutch-Jewish mother, and went from Eton to Christ Church. Ryle, his tutor, sent him to Vienna after graduation. He attended the Circle's meetings through the winter of 1932-33 and wrote Language, Truth and Logic at twenty-four. The war took him into the Welsh Guards and then intelligence work. He was Grote Professor at University College London from 1946, Wykeham Professor of Logic at Oxford from 1959, and a broadcaster and public figure until his death in 1989.

p: The verification principle in its English form: a statement has literal meaning only if it is analytic or empirically verifiable. Metaphysics and theology are not false but senseless. Ethical judgements express and seek to arouse feeling, so that calling an act wrong adds nothing factual to naming it. The book's own status was the standing objection, since the principle is neither analytic nor verifiable and so condemns itself. The 1946 introduction offered a weakened criterion, which Alonzo Church showed in 1949 to admit any statement at all.

The later Ayer, patient where the young one was peremptory. He works through perception, memory, other minds and the past, taking the sceptic's challenge seriously in each case and asking what would count as an answer. He arrives at a qualified defence of ordinary claims to know. It is the better book and much the less read.

legacy: Language, Truth and Logic did more than any other book to make positivism a public position in Britain. Much of what educated readers still assume about meaning and metaphysics comes from it at second hand. Its influence outran its defensibility. Austin took it apart in the lectures published as Sense and Sensibilia. Ayer, interviewed by Bryan Magee in the 1970s, said the book's main defect was that nearly all of it was false. He remained glad to have written it.

read.first: Language, Truth and Logic, with the 1946 introduction read first so the retreat is visible.
read.note: Treat it as a historical document by a very young man, not as a statement of a live position.

sellars.sub: who named the Myth of the Given and put Kant back into analytic philosophy
world: American philosophy after 1945 was logical empiricism transplanted. Carnap was at Chicago, Reichenbach at UCLA, Feigl at Minnesota, and the programme was to build knowledge on a foundation of what is given in experience and to treat theoretical talk as a device for organising it.

Two pressures were already on that programme from inside. Quine's 'Two Dogmas' of 1951 removed the analytic-synthetic distinction, and the philosophy of science was becoming historical. Sellars applied the third pressure, on the foundation itself, and did it in a vocabulary — Kant, Hegel, the scholastics — that his colleagues mostly did not read.
life: Born in Ann Arbor in 1912, the son of the philosopher Roy Wood Sellars, a critical realist and a principal author of the first Humanist Manifesto. He went to Michigan, then Buffalo, then Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, where he read Kant closely and never finished the doctorate.

He taught at Iowa, Minnesota and Yale, and from 1963 at Pittsburgh, where he built one of the strongest departments in the country and stayed until his death in 1989. With Feigl he founded Philosophical Studies, in part because the existing journals would not print what he wanted to publish. He is famous for being hard to read, and he knew it.

works.t: Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind
p: The attack on the Given. Empiricism assumes there are episodes — sensings, given-nesses — that are both non-inferential and capable of justifying beliefs, and Sellars argues that nothing can be both: to be aware of something as a such-and-such is already to have the concept, and concepts come with a whole language. In the sentence everyone quotes, in characterising an episode as knowing we are not giving an empirical description of it but placing it in the space of reasons, of justifying and being able to justify what one says. He then tells the myth of Jones, who teaches his community to speak of inner thoughts and impressions on the model of overt speech — showing how a theoretical vocabulary could be introduced for the mental without the mental having been given first. Rorty called it the beginning of the end of foundationalism; Brandom's edition made it teachable.

works.t: Philosophy and the Scientific Image of Man
p: Two pictures compete for the title of how things are: the manifest image, in which the world contains persons, colours and reasons, and the scientific image, in which it contains particles and fields. Sellars refuses the easy resolutions. The scientific image is the measure of what there is — in the dimension of describing and explaining the world, science is the measure of all things — but the manifest image is not thereby false, because it is the home of the normative, and persons and their commitments cannot simply be deleted. The task he sets is a stereoscopic fusion of the two, and he does not claim to have achieved it.

legacy: Rorty took the attack on the Given, joined it to Quine's attack on analyticity, and wrote Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature, which is where most readers first met Sellars' name. His Pittsburgh students and colleagues — Brandom, McDowell — built inferentialism and the arguments of Mind and World out of the same materials; the phrase 'the space of reasons' is now used by people with no idea whose it is.

The splitting of his inheritance is itself well known: right Sellarsians take the scientific image seriously and get eliminativism and the Churchlands; left Sellarsians take the space of reasons seriously and get Pittsburgh Hegelianism. That both sides can claim him is a fair measure of how far he got with the fusion.

read.first: Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind, in Brandom's edition with the study guide. Then 'Philosophy and the Scientific Image of Man', which is easier.
read.note: He is genuinely difficult, and the difficulty is not decoration: the argument is cumulative and the terminology is his own. Read the secondary guide alongside rather than after.

sellars.caveat: Whether the two images can be fused, or whether the scientific image simply displaces the manifest one, is the question his own followers split over. He did not answer it.

davidson.sub: who built a theory of meaning out of a theory of truth
world: Quine had left the field in a particular state. Meanings as entities were gone, the analytic-synthetic distinction was gone, and translation was indeterminate — so a theory of meaning, if there was to be one, could not help itself to meanings. Tarski, meanwhile, had shown in 1933 how to define truth for a formal language without circularity.

Action theory was in a comparable state. The orthodoxy, following Wittgenstein and Anscombe, held that reasons cannot be causes because a reason and the action it explains are not logically independent. Davidson's first famous paper is the reply.
life: Born in Springfield, Massachusetts in 1917. He read classics at Harvard, wrote a dissertation on Plato's Philebus, and spent the war in the Navy teaching pilots to recognise aircraft. He then spent a decade working on decision theory with Patrick Suppes, running experiments, before publishing the papers he is known for.

He taught at Stanford, Princeton, Rockefeller, Chicago and from 1981 at Berkeley. He wrote no monographs: the work is some forty papers, later collected into volumes, each of which says something the others depend on. He flew planes, built a house, played piano, and was by all accounts formidably unhurried. He died in 2003.

p: Reasons are causes. The standing objection — that a reason and its action are connected logically rather than causally, so the relation cannot be causal — fails, Davidson argues, because the logical connection holds between descriptions, and causation holds between events however described. The paper also poses the problem it does not solve: a reason may cause an action in the wrong way, as when a climber's wish to let go so unnerves him that his hand opens, and it is still not an action done for that reason. Deviant causal chains have occupied action theory ever since.

The proposal is to take a Tarski-style truth theory for a natural language and use it as the theory of meaning. To know what a sentence means is to know the conditions under which it is true. A finite theory yields a T-sentence for each of infinitely many sentences, which explains how a finite creature understands a language it has never heard the whole of. No meanings are quantified over anywhere. The programme launched decades of work on how to fit natural-language constructions — adverbs, indirect speech, moods — into that form; Davidson's own treatment of adverbs by quantifying over events is standard.

works.t: On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme
p: An attack on the relativism that says different cultures or theories carve the world into incommensurable schemes. The idea requires a distinction between an organising scheme and uninterpreted content, and Davidson argues the distinction cannot be made out: to recognise something as a language at all we must be able to interpret it, and interpretation proceeds by charity, assigning beliefs that are largely true by our lights. Massive disagreement is therefore not something we could ever have evidence of. Rorty made the paper a weapon; Kuhn and Feyerabend were the intended targets.

Anomalous monism, which is an attempt to hold three plausible things at once: mental events cause physical ones, causation requires strict laws, and there are no strict psychophysical laws. Davidson's resolution is that every mental event is a physical event — token identity — while mental descriptions form no lawlike system, because attributing attitudes is governed by norms of rationality that physics knows nothing of. The position has been attacked ever since for making the mental causally idle, a charge he denied.

legacy: Truth-conditional semantics is the framework most work in the philosophy of language and much formal semantics still operates in, whether or not Davidson's specific claims are accepted. Event semantics for adverbs is textbook. Anomalous monism is the standard entry point for non-reductive physicalism and for the epiphenomenalism objection to it. Radical interpretation and the principle of charity are common property.

His method — forty interlocking papers, no book, each moving one piece — has itself been influential, and made him hard to summarise. The unified picture he gestured at, in which meaning, belief and action are worked out together and cannot be done separately, is more often admired than adopted.

read.first: 'Actions, Reasons, and Causes' and 'Truth and Meaning'. Then 'On the Very Idea of a Conceptual Scheme'.
read.note: The two collections, Essays on Actions and Events and Inquiries into Truth and Interpretation, are the primary texts. The papers cross-refer heavily, so read them in the collections rather than singly.

davidson.caveat: Whether anomalous monism leaves mental properties any causal work is the oldest live objection to it, and his replies are not generally regarded as conclusive.

anscombe.sub: the philosopher who made intention a subject and revived the virtues
world: Postwar British moral philosophy had narrowed to the analysis of moral language, emotivism giving way to prescriptivism, with little to say about what a person does or why. Anscombe wrote against that from a Catholic position formed early. She had opposed the bombing of civilians in a pamphlet of 1939. In 1956 she spoke in Convocation against Oxford's honorary degree for Harry Truman, on the ground that he had ordered the deliberate killing of the innocent.
life: Born in Limerick in 1919, Anscombe read classics at St Hugh's, was received into the Roman Catholic Church as an undergraduate, and married the philosopher Peter Geach in 1941. They had seven children. A research fellowship took her to Cambridge in 1942, where she attended Wittgenstein's classes and became one of his closest students and, later, a literary executor. She held the Cambridge chair of philosophy from 1970 to 1986 and died in 2001.

p: A hundred pages that created a subject. Anscombe asks what marks an action off from a mere happening. She answers that a particular sense of the question 'why?' applies to it, the sense asking for the agent's reason rather than a cause. One movement falls under many descriptions — moving an arm, working a pump, poisoning a household — and which are intentional depends on where that question gets an answer. An agent also knows what he is doing without observing it, a practical knowledge she calls the cause of what it understands.

Three theses, stated flatly. Moral philosophy should be set aside until we have an adequate philosophy of psychology; the notions of moral obligation and duty should be jettisoned as survivals of a law conception of ethics whose lawgiver has been abandoned; and the English moral philosophers from Sidgwick on differ only trivially, since all allow that consequences might justify anything. The essay coined 'consequentialism' as a term of reproach and pointed back to Aristotle.

works.t: Philosophical Investigations, translated from Ludwig Wittgenstein
p: Anscombe's English is the form in which the Investigations entered the world. Its phrasings, language-game, form of life, family resemblance, became a generation's vocabulary. She edited or co-edited most of the other posthumous volumes as well. A revised version by P. M. S. Hacker and Joachim Schulte appeared in 2009, correcting details while keeping her renderings where they had become canonical.

legacy: 'Modern Moral Philosophy' is the founding document of the revival of virtue ethics, taken up by Philippa Foot, Alasdair MacIntyre and Rosalind Hursthouse. None of them, though, accepted her view that obligation without a divine lawgiver is incoherent. Intention shaped everything since written on action. Donald Davidson called it the most important treatment of the subject since Aristotle, and then argued for the causal account of reasons she had denied.

read.first: 'Modern Moral Philosophy' first, since it is short and shows the temper, then Intention slowly.
read.note: She writes compressed, unaccommodating prose on purpose. Nothing in Intention can be skimmed.

murdoch.sub: who put attention where the will had been
world: Oxford after 1945 was doing linguistic philosophy, and its moral philosophy was mostly meta-ethics: Ayer's emotivism, Hare's prescriptivism, the shared assumption that a moral judgement expresses a choice and that value is not part of the world. Murdoch thought this described a fictional person.

She also had something almost nobody else in Oxford had: continental philosophy read in the original and at first hand. She met Sartre in Brussels in 1945, wrote the first book in English on him, and read Weil, Heidegger and the phenomenologists while her colleagues were reading Austin. Her generation of Oxford women — Anscombe, Foot, Midgley, Murdoch — had come up when the men were at the war, which Midgley thought was why they were free to do something different.
life: Born in Dublin in 1919 and raised in London. She read classics at Somerville, joined the Communist Party as an undergraduate and left it, and spent the war in the Treasury and then with UNRRA in Belgium and Austria, working with displaced persons.

A postgraduate year at Cambridge put her near Wittgenstein's circle, though she met him only once. She was elected to a fellowship at St Anne's, Oxford, in 1948 and taught there for fifteen years. From 1954 she published twenty-six novels, several of which are among the best English novels of the century, alongside the philosophy; she married John Bayley in 1956. She developed Alzheimer's disease in the 1990s and died in 1999.

p: The central text. Moral philosophy has taken the moral life to consist of choices made by a will in a value-neutral world, so that between decisions nothing morally significant happens. Murdoch's example of M and her daughter-in-law D — a mother who, over years and without any outward act, comes to see a girl she had thought vulgar as refreshingly simple — is designed to show that the work is done before the choice, in how the person is seen. The moral task is therefore attention: the just and loving gaze directed upon an individual reality, which requires unselfing, since the obstacle is the fat relentless ego. Good, not right, is the central concept, and she takes the Platonic sun seriously as a metaphor for a reality we can approach and never possess.

The first of the three essays and the one that does the demolition. Behaviourism in psychology, existentialism in ethics and the linguistic method in philosophy converge, she argues, on a single picture: the inner life is either unreal or morally inert, and what matters is the observable choice. Against this she insists that the vocabulary in which we describe a person is already moral work, that we can be better or worse at it, and that this is where the difficulty of goodness actually lies.

works.t: Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals
p: Her Gifford Lectures worked up into a long, digressive book covering Plato, Kant, Schopenhauer, Derrida, Buddhism and the ontological proof. The argument she cares about is that a metaphysical picture is not optional for ethics: how we take reality to be settles what moral attention could be attending to. It is the fullest statement of her position and by common consent the hardest to extract an argument from.

legacy: The Sovereignty of Good is now read as one of the books that ended the meta-ethical consensus, alongside Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' and Foot's early papers. Attention, taken from Weil and given a philosophical job, is a standard term in contemporary moral psychology; so is the claim that moral difficulty is often perceptual rather than volitional. Charles Taylor, Cora Diamond, John McDowell and the moral-perception literature all work downstream of her.

She has no school, partly because she gave no arguments in the form that invites development and partly because the novels absorbed most of the attention. Her standing has risen steadily since the 1990s, and she is now routinely named with Anscombe, Foot and Midgley as one of the four who turned Anglophone ethics back towards the good.

read.first: The Sovereignty of Good entire — it is a hundred pages. Read 'The Idea of Perfection' first even though the essays are often taught in the other order.
read.note: Her Platonism is meant, not decorative. Readers who take the sun and the cave as rhetoric end up puzzled about what the good is supposed to be.

murdoch.caveat: Whether her moral realism amounts to a defensible metaphysics or a way of speaking is the standing objection, and Metaphysics as a Guide to Morals does not obviously settle it.

foot.sub: who found the content moral language was supposed not to have
world: The orthodoxy she attacked was Hume's fact-value gap in its mid-century form: Stevenson and Ayer on emotivism, Hare on prescriptivism, and the shared view that no description entails an evaluation, so that anything at all could in principle be a person's ultimate moral concern.

What made that hard to hold in 1958 was the recent past. Anscombe had just tried to stop Oxford giving Truman an honorary degree, and the question of whether the camps were wrong or merely disapproved of was not academic. The Oxford women who reopened virtue ethics — Anscombe, Foot, Murdoch, Midgley — all say in one way or another that emotivism could not survive the war.
life: Born Philippa Bosanquet in 1920, a granddaughter of the American president Grover Cleveland, raised in Yorkshire and educated by governesses. She read PPE at Somerville, worked as an economist in wartime Whitehall, and returned to Oxford, where she was a fellow of Somerville from 1947 to 1969 and later Griffin Professor at UCLA.

She shared a house with Anscombe, a friendship and argument that lasted decades and survived deep disagreement. Her marriage to the historian M. R. D. Foot ended in divorce. She helped found Oxfam. She continued to publish into her eighties, and her one full-length book appeared when she was seventy-eight. She died on her ninetieth birthday in 2010.

p: The frontal attack on the fact-value gap. If evaluation were wholly independent of description, anything could serve as a moral consideration, and Foot's method is to show that it cannot: try to treat clasping and unclasping your hands as a reason for action and the attempt collapses, because moral concepts have content. Whether something injures a person is a matter of fact, and injury is not a neutral description that we then choose to disapprove of. The paper is usually paired with 'Moral Arguments' of the same period, and together they open the line of argument the next forty years of virtue ethics develops.

works.t: The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of Double Effect
p: The paper that invented the trolley problem, in a footnote's worth of space and for a purpose almost nobody remembers. Foot is examining whether the distinction between what is intended and what is merely foreseen can carry the moral weight the doctrine of double effect puts on it, and the runaway tram is one case among several designed to isolate that distinction from the confounding factor of killing versus letting die. The industry the example later supported — variants, surveys, brain scans — detaches it from the argument it was built for, which she found more irritating than flattering.

Her one book, and the mature statement. Moral evaluation of human beings is the same kind of judgement as calling an oak sound or a wolf defective: it measures an individual against what its species needs to live the life characteristic of it. Such judgements are factual and species-relative, not projections of attitude, and goodness in a person is therefore a natural, not a supernatural or a subjective, property. This also lets her retract in print the view she had held for decades, that moral reasons are hypothetical and bind only those who happen to want what morality serves — on the new account, practical rationality and human goodness cannot come apart.

legacy: With Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' and Murdoch's Sovereignty of Good, her early papers are why virtue ethics is one of the three standard positions in normative ethics rather than a historical curiosity. Ethical naturalism in its contemporary form — Michael Thompson, Rosalind Hursthouse, Alasdair MacIntyre on one side of it — is largely the development of Natural Goodness.

The trolley is her most famous legacy and the one she liked least. Thomson's variants made it a method; experimental philosophy and moral psychology made it an instrument; it is now in undergraduate lectures, popular books and self-driving-car policy papers, usually with no mention of double effect and often with none of Foot. The retraction of 1995 is itself worth noting as a piece of intellectual conduct: a philosopher stating plainly, after thirty-five years, that her best-known argument had been wrong.

read.first: 'Moral Beliefs', then Natural Goodness, which is short and argued in order. The trolley paper last, and read the whole paper rather than the example.
read.note: Virtues and Vices collects the early papers. The 1995 retraction is in 'Does Moral Subjectivism Rest on a Mistake?' and matters for reading anything she wrote before it.

foot.caveat: Whether facts about what a species needs can by themselves yield reasons for a particular person to act is the standing objection to Aristotelian naturalism, and Natural Goodness answers it briefly.

kuhn.sub: the physicist who made scientific change a historical problem
world: The bomb changed the standing of physics in American life. The Manhattan Project had ended a war, its builders became national assets, and federal money followed. So did an anxious public question about what science was. James Bryant Conant, Harvard’s president and a chemist who had helped run the wartime research effort, answered it pedagogically. His general education programme taught science to non-scientists through historical case studies. Kuhn was assigned to teach in it.

Sputnik, launched in October 1957, brought a second wave of federal spending, and a little of it reached the humanities. History and philosophy of science acquired programmes, chairs and journals. Kuhn held posts in three universities that built them. The philosophy he wrote into was still largely logical empiricist. That Structure appeared in the positivists’ own International Encyclopedia of Unified Science looks stranger than it was. Charles Morris commissioned it, and Carnap wrote welcoming the manuscript.
life: Born in Cincinnati in 1922, Kuhn took a Harvard physics degree in 1943. He spent the rest of the war on radar countermeasures. He returned for a doctorate in solid-state physics, finished it in 1949, and never practised the subject again. The turn had already come: preparing course material in 1947, he tried to read Aristotle’s physics as failed Newton and could not. On its own terms the system was coherent, and asking different questions.

A junior fellowship and an assistant professorship at Harvard ended without tenure. In 1956 Kuhn moved to Berkeley to teach history of science and drafted Structure there. He finished it at the Center for Advanced Study in the Behavioral Sciences. Princeton took him in 1964, MIT in 1979. He disliked controversy and was bad at it. He gave much of his last thirty years to revising the position rather than defending it.

p: Written out of the Harvard course, the book does two things at once. It explains the technical astronomy—spheres, epicycles, the equant—clearly enough that a reader can see what Copernicus actually changed. It also embeds the heliocentric proposal in cosmology, theology and the physics of motion, none of which could absorb a moving earth without breaking. Copernicus emerges as a conservative repairing an inherited system. His own model is no more accurate than Ptolemy’s. The interest lies in everything else that had to give way before the new astronomy could be believed.

The book describes a cycle. Normal science is work inside a paradigm—an achievement concrete enough to define legitimate problems and the shape of acceptable solutions—and it is puzzle-solving, not testing, because the framework is not on trial. Anomalies that resist repeated attack accumulate into crisis; rivals appear; a community transfers allegiance. Kuhn called competing paradigms incommensurable: terms shift sense across the divide, standards of judgement shift with them, and no neutral observation language stands outside to adjudicate. He denied this made theory choice irrational, and persuaded few critics. The 1969 Postscript admitted that “paradigm” had been used too loosely—Margaret Masterman counted more than twenty senses—and split it into the disciplinary matrix a community shares and the exemplars through which its members learn to see one problem as like another.

Twenty years of papers, and the best correction to the caricature. The title essay was given at a 1959 conference on identifying scientific talent. It argues that research needs convergent and divergent thinking together, and that deep training in orthodoxy is the condition of fruitful heresy rather than its enemy. Other pieces separate discovery from invention, rework the simultaneous discovery of energy conservation, and set out how history and philosophy of science differ as enterprises even when they share their material.

legacy: Structure became one of the most cited academic books ever written. It was read, almost at once, in ways its author rejected. The 1965 London colloquium that pitted him against Popper produced Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge. In it Lakatos accused him of making revolutions a matter of mob psychology, and Feyerabend welcomed an ally who had not volunteered. Sociologists then pushed the theory-ladenness of observation further than Kuhn would go.

Outside the academy the book supplied a phrase. “Paradigm shift” passed into management prose and advertising, where it means little more than a change of mind. Kuhn made no secret of his irritation. What survives in the discipline is less quotable. Philosophy of science now argues from real historical cases as a matter of course. Normal science, anomaly and crisis remain the standard vocabulary for what scientists do between revolutions.

read.first: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions straight through, then the 1969 Postscript, then The Copernican Revolution as the worked example the argument was abstracted from.
read.note: Read the Postscript as a correction Kuhn thought necessary rather than an optional appendix. Treat The Essential Tension as his own guard against the relativist reading.

kuhn.caveat: What incommensurability amounts to—a thesis about meaning, about standards of appraisal, or about translation—remains disputed. Kuhn’s successive restatements did not settle it.

lakatos.sub: the defender of rationality who appraised research programmes
world: The Hungarian rising of October 1956 and its suppression by Soviet armour a fortnight later scattered some two hundred thousand people westward, Lakatos among them. He arrived in a Britain where the London School of Economics under Popper housed the most combative philosophy of science in Europe. The Cold War gave the question of what makes a belief rationally held a seriousness it had lacked for a generation. Lakatos, who had believed a great deal on authority, felt it personally.
life: Born Imre Lipschitz in Debrecen in 1922, he survived the war in hiding under a changed name while his mother and grandmother were murdered at Auschwitz. He joined the Communist Party and worked in the Ministry of Education. He was then imprisoned by the regime he served, spending 1950 to 1953 in the Recsk labour camp. He fled in 1956, took a Cambridge doctorate under R. B. Braithwaite, and joined the LSE in 1960. He died suddenly in February 1974, aged fifty-one.

p: A classroom dialogue, with the real history in the footnotes. It follows Euler’s formula relating the vertices, edges and faces of a polyhedron through a century of proposed proofs and awkward solids that broke them. Mathematics, Lakatos argues, does not grow by deduction from fixed definitions. A counterexample forces the concepts themselves to be reworked, and a term like “polyhedron” is stretched and narrowed under argumentative pressure.

works.t: Falsification and the Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes
p: Popper said a theory is scientific if it can be refuted. The history said no important theory was ever abandoned on its first refutation. Lakatos moved appraisal from the single theory to the research programme. A programme has a hard core its practitioners decide to hold immune, and a protective belt of auxiliary hypotheses that absorbs anomalies. A programme is progressive when its modifications predict novel facts that are then found, degenerating when it only patches failures afterwards.

legacy: Hard core and protective belt entered ordinary scientific and economic argument. They outlived the detailed methodology, which few now defend intact: a degenerating programme can revive, so the advice never quite says what to do next. Lakatos wanted a middle path between Popper’s rigour and what he took to be Kuhn’s irrationalism. The attempt remains the clearest statement of what such a path would have to supply.

read.first: Proofs and Refutations for the pleasure of it, then the 1970 methodology essay for the position he is remembered by.
read.note: The dialogue needs no mathematics beyond counting faces. The essay is where the argument with Popper and Kuhn is actually conducted.

lakatos.caveat: Lakatos’s conduct as a young communist in Hungary, including his part in the death of a fellow activist in 1944, is documented but contested in its details. He never discussed it publicly.

feyerabend.sub: the anarchist of method who argued from real history
world: Berkeley in the 1960s supplied the setting and much of the provocation. Feyerabend taught there through the Free Speech Movement of 1964, the anti-war protests, and the arrival under new admissions policies of students whose inheritance the standard curriculum ignored. Teaching them, he later wrote, made him doubt his right to replace their traditions with his own. The era’s wider question—whether expertise deserved the authority the postwar state had given it—runs straight into his own.
life: Born in Vienna in 1924, Feyerabend was conscripted into the Wehrmacht and shot in the spine during the retreat of 1945. The injury left him in pain and walking with a stick for the rest of his life. He studied under Victor Kraft in Vienna, went to London intending to work with Wittgenstein, who died first, and studied instead with Popper at the LSE. Bristol followed in 1955, then Berkeley from 1958 until 1990. He died of a brain tumour in 1994.

p: Conceived as half of a debate with Lakatos, who died before writing his reply, the book argues from cases rather than principle. Galileo won not by obeying methodological rules but by breaking them, using ad hoc hypotheses, propaganda, and a telescope whose reliability he could not yet demonstrate. That the only rule surviving the historical record is “anything goes” is offered as diagnosis rather than advice. It carries counter-induction with it: pursuing hypotheses that contradict well-confirmed facts, since those facts may be artefacts of the theory under challenge.

Part reply to reviewers, part political argument. Science is one tradition among several, Feyerabend maintains, and in a democracy its results should be subject to lay control as other public institutions are. Laymen can and should judge experts. The book is combative to the point of self-damage, and its polemical sections cost the substantive ones a hearing.

Written as he was dying and published posthumously, this short memoir gives the war, the wound, the singing lessons, the four marriages and the late happiness with Grazia Borrini in a flat, unsparing voice. It shows the provocateur as genuinely uncertain rather than merely mischievous. It has changed how the earlier books are read.

legacy: Feyerabend was long treated as the reductio of the historical turn, the man who showed where Kuhn’s premises led if taken seriously. That reading is receding. His case studies survive scrutiny better than his slogans, his insistence on the proliferation of rival theories is now conventional, and his question about the standing of science has become unavoidable wherever expertise and democratic consent collide.

read.first: Against Method, with attention to the Galileo chapters where the historical argument is actually made.
read.note: Take the slogans as deliberate provocation and hold him to the cases instead. Killing Time is the best short introduction to the man behind them.

rawls.sub: the philosopher who asked what we would choose without knowing who we are
world: Political philosophy had been pronounced dead. Peter Laslett said so in print in 1956, and the diagnosis was widely shared. The positivists had classified value judgements as expressions of attitude. Anglophone political theory had retreated into conceptual analysis and the history of doctrines. Outside the seminar room the country was arguing about nothing else. The civil rights movement made the justice of basic institutions a practical question, the Vietnam draft made the obligations of citizens one, and Harvard was occupied by its students in 1969.

What followed A Theory of Justice in 1971 was not the consensus its reviewers predicted but an argument about the welfare state that has not ended. The postwar settlement was breaking. Inflation, the oil shock of 1973 and rising public spending gave the political right an opening it took. Rawls’s defence of redistribution arrived just as redistribution stopped being taken for granted. Nozick replied in 1974, Hayek’s influence grew, and Rawls’s terms were soon used mostly against his conclusions.
life: Rawls was born in Baltimore in 1921. Two younger brothers died of illnesses caught from him. He stammered for the rest of his life. At Princeton he wrote a senior thesis on sin and faith and considered ordination. He then served in the Pacific infantry—New Guinea, the Philippines, occupied Japan—saw the ruins of Hiroshima, lost his Christian belief, and left the army in 1946 as a private. He condemned the atomic bombings in print half a century later.

A Princeton doctorate in 1950 and a Fulbright year at Oxford, where Hart and Berlin were teaching, were followed by Cornell, MIT and then Harvard, where he stayed. The 1958 article “Justice as Fairness” holds the germ. The book took thirteen years. Rawls shunned publicity, taught with unusual care, and left an extraordinary number of students who became first-rate philosophers themselves. A stroke in 1995 slowed the late revisions without stopping them. He died in 2002.

p: The device is a thought experiment. Parties choosing principles for their society do so in an original position, behind a veil of ignorance hiding their class, talents, race, sex, generation and conception of the good. Nobody can rig the terms in his own favour, so whatever is chosen is fair. Rawls argues that rational parties, unable to gamble on odds they cannot know, would take the maximin route and select two principles: an equal scheme of basic liberties for all, and inequalities attached to positions open under fair equality of opportunity and working to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged—the difference principle. The priority rules matter as much: liberty cannot be traded for prosperity, nor opportunity for gains to the worst off. The method throughout is reflective equilibrium, the mutual adjustment of principles and considered judgements until the two sit together.

Rawls came to think his first book had presented justice as fairness as a comprehensive doctrine, resting on a Kantian account of the person that free citizens could reasonably reject. The new problem was narrower and harder: how a just and stable society is possible when its members hold irreconcilable but reasonable views of the good life. The answer is an overlapping consensus, in which a political conception is affirmed from within many comprehensive doctrines for their own reasons. It is supported by a duty of public reason. Critics on both flanks called it a retreat.

The extension to international justice disappointed many followers. Rawls applies a second original position to representatives of peoples rather than individuals. He produces principles of non-intervention, treaty-keeping, human rights and assistance to burdened societies—but no global difference principle, and a place at the table for decent hierarchical societies that are not liberal democracies. Cosmopolitans argued that his own premises demanded more, since birthplace is as morally arbitrary as talent. He answered that the aim was toleration between peoples, not a world state.

legacy: A Theory of Justice restored normative political philosophy as a going enterprise. The shape of the subsequent argument is the shape of the objections to it. Nozick attacked the idea of a patterned distribution; Hart pressed on the priority of liberty; Sandel and MacIntyre denied that a self could be specified prior to its ends; Susan Moller Okin asked why the family escaped the basic structure; G. A. Cohen argued that Rawls had conceded too much to incentives.

The apparatus outlived the conclusions. The veil of ignorance is now a standard tool of practical argument, invoked in medical ethics, tax policy and constitutional design by people who have never read the book. Charles Mills and others press the sharpest recent objection: that a theory built for a well-ordered society has little to say about societies deformed by historical injustice. Rawls remains the figure Anglophone political philosophy is organised around, by agreement or refusal.

read.first: A Theory of Justice, though not cover to cover on a first pass. Part One states the argument, and Part Three develops the account of stability.
read.note: Justice as Fairness: A Restatement, published in 2001, is Rawls’s own shorter and later version, and the kinder point of entry.

putnam.sub: who kept changing his mind in public, and was usually right to
world: Post-war American philosophy was professionalising fast, and Putnam moved through most of its centres of gravity in turn: mathematical logic and Hilbert's tenth problem, the philosophy of physics, then the new computational picture of the mind, then the realism debate his own arguments had reopened.

He was also political in a way his colleagues mostly were not. He was in the Communist Party in the 1950s, an organiser of the campus anti-Vietnam movement at Harvard, and a member of the Progressive Labor Party into the early 1970s, which cost him more than it gained him.
life: Born in Chicago in 1926 and raised partly in France; his father translated Spanish literature and wrote for the Daily Worker. He took his doctorate under Reichenbach at UCLA, taught at Northwestern, Princeton and MIT, and was at Harvard from 1965 until retirement.

With Martin Davis and Julia Robinson he did the work that led to the negative solution of Hilbert's tenth problem, a theorem in mathematics rather than philosophy. In later life he returned to the Judaism of his grandparents, learned Hebrew in his forties, had a bar mitzvah at sixty-eight, and wrote on Jewish philosophy. He died in 2016.

p: Functionalism, in the version that made it the orthodoxy. Pain is not a brain state, because octopuses and possibly machines can be in pain and are not made the way we are; it is a functional state, defined by its causal role between inputs, other states and outputs. The model is the Turing machine: the same program can run on different hardware. Putnam later became the position's most determined critic, arguing in the 1980s that computational states are too easily realised to individuate mental ones and that meaning is not in the head anyway.

Twin Earth. A planet exactly like ours except that its clear drinkable liquid is XYZ rather than H2O; an Earthling and his twin in 1750, neither knowing any chemistry, are in the same psychological state, yet 'water' in one mouth refers to H2O and in the other to XYZ. So meanings just ain't in the head: reference is fixed by the world and by a division of linguistic labour, in which most speakers defer to experts for terms like 'elm' or 'gold'. Semantic externalism starts here, and takes the philosophy of mind with it.

The turn against metaphysical realism. The brain-in-a-vat argument is here: a brain that had always been in a vat could not, by its own causal theory of reference, truly say that it was one, since its word 'vat' would refer to vats in the image. The model-theoretic argument runs deeper — that for any theory, even an ideal one, there are many ways of mapping its terms onto the world, so reference cannot be fixed from outside all schemes. What replaces metaphysical realism is internal realism, on which truth is idealised rational acceptability. He abandoned that too, in the 1990s, for a direct realism he traced to James and Austin.

legacy: Three of his positions are standard equipment: functionalism, which he later rejected; semantic externalism, which he did not; and the indispensability argument for mathematical realism, which he formulated with Quine and also later softened. Twin Earth is one of the two or three most productive thought experiments of the century.

The changes of mind are part of the record and he insisted on it — a philosopher, he said, who never changes his mind is not thinking. Critics took the succession of positions as instability; the more common view now is that each shift was forced by an argument he had himself found, which is a harder discipline than consistency.

read.first: 'The Meaning of "Meaning"' — the Twin Earth sections at least — then Reason, Truth and History, chapters 1 and 3.
read.note: Because he changed position repeatedly, always date what you are quoting. The three volumes of Philosophical Papers and the late collections are the primary sources.

putnam.caveat: Internal realism was abandoned by its author, and how much of the model-theoretic argument survives that abandonment is disputed among people who take it seriously.

nozick.sub: the libertarian who argued from rights to the minimal state
world: The argument about the welfare state that followed Rawls found its sharpest reply in 1974, a year of oil shock, stagflation and the visible exhaustion of the postwar settlement. The great expansion of American social programmes was a decade old and already contested. The campus left that Nozick had watched at Columbia and Harvard supplied the ideas he had once shared. His book gave philosophically serious form to a position previously left to economists and pamphleteers, exactly as the political weather changed.
life: Born in Brooklyn in 1938 to a Russian Jewish immigrant family, Nozick studied at Columbia under Sidney Morgenbesser. He took a Princeton doctorate in 1963 under Carl Hempel. He arrived at libertarianism reluctantly, having been a campus socialist. By his own account he was argued into it. Harvard made him a full professor at thirty. He wrote fast and moved on, refusing to spend a career defending one book. He taught a different course almost every year. He died of stomach cancer in 2002.

p: The book opens by asserting that individuals have rights no person or group may violate. It asks what room this leaves for a state. Part one derives a minimal state from anarchy by an invisible-hand story: protective associations compete, one becomes dominant, and it compensates those it disarms, so the state arises without rights being violated. Part two attacks patterned theories of justice, Rawls’s included. On the entitlement theory a distribution is just if it arose justly, by original acquisition or voluntary transfer, with rectification for past wrongs. The Wilt Chamberlain argument makes this concrete: begin from any distribution you consider just, let a million people each pay a quarter to watch him play, and the pattern is gone through nothing but free choices. Preserving a pattern therefore requires continuous interference with free exchange.

A deliberate change of manner. Nozick rejects philosophy as coercive argument—proofs designed to force assent—and offers explanations of how things might possibly be instead. The book contains a tracking analysis of knowledge in counterfactual terms, a closest-continuer theory of personal identity, and an account of the value of life. The experience machine, from the earlier book, shares that temper: most people would not plug into a device delivering perfect simulated pleasure. Pleasure is therefore not all we want.

legacy: Anarchy, State, and Utopia won the National Book Award and became the canonical statement of philosophical libertarianism. Nozick declined that role, calling the position of his first book seriously inadequate in The Examined Life in 1989 while denying he had abandoned it. Philosophers still press the weak point: the theory of just original acquisition, on which everything rests, is the least developed part of the argument.

read.first: Anarchy, State, and Utopia, part two first if time is short—that is where Rawls is answered and the entitlement theory stated.
read.note: Read it alongside A Theory of Justice rather than alone. The book is written as a reply and loses half its force without its target.

kripke.sub: the logician who separated necessity from the a priori
world: American analytic philosophy in the 1960s was confident, well funded and technically ambitious, with logic at its centre. Quine’s scepticism about necessity and essence set the agenda everyone had to answer. Quine held that quantified modal logic committed one to an unrespectable Aristotelian essentialism. The discipline had largely accepted that meanings, not things, carried whatever necessity there was. Harvard, Princeton and the Rockefeller University formed a circuit along which the new modal semantics travelled by lecture and transcript.
life: Born in 1940 and raised in Omaha, where his father led a Conservative congregation, Kripke was a prodigy of the kind that makes other prodigies uncomfortable. While still at school he published a completeness proof for modal logic in a leading journal. He took a Harvard mathematics degree in 1962 and was teaching graduate logic at MIT before he had one. Rockefeller and then Princeton followed, and from 2003 the CUNY Graduate Center. He published little and circulated much, and died in 2022.

p: The technical foundation. Kripke supplies a model theory in which necessity is truth at all worlds accessible from a given one. He shows that varying the accessibility relation—reflexive, transitive, symmetric—yields the familiar competing systems as distinct logics rather than rival guesses. Possible-world semantics gave modal talk a mathematically respectable interpretation. It made Quine’s objection look like a preference rather than a result.

Three lectures given at Princeton in January 1970 without notes and printed from the transcript. Kripke attacks the description theory on which a name abbreviates a description: Aristotle might never have taught Alexander and would still have been Aristotle. Names are rigid designators, picking out the same individual in every world where it exists. Their reference is fixed by an initial baptism and carried along a causal-historical chain of use. From this he prises metaphysical necessity apart from the epistemic notion of the a priori. That water is H2O, if true, is necessarily true, yet was discovered by experiment.

works.t: Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language
p: Kripke reads the Philosophical Investigations as centring on a sceptical paradox: nothing in a speaker’s past use or mental history determines that he meant addition rather than a deviant function agreeing with it on every case computed so far. The sceptical solution appeals not to a fact about the individual but to a community’s practice of correction. Whether this is Wittgenstein’s argument is disputed. The position is filed under “Kripkenstein” to sidestep the question.

legacy: Kripke made essentialism respectable again after decades of positivist hostility. The necessary a posteriori reopened metaphysics as a subject with its own questions rather than a residue of semantics. The causal theory of reference reshaped philosophy of language. It travelled into philosophy of mind and science, where Putnam developed a parallel argument about natural kinds. Descriptivists have mounted sophisticated replies, but the distinctions themselves are now part of the equipment.

read.first: Naming and Necessity, which reads as spoken argument and needs no formal logic.
read.note: Take the three lectures one at a time. The informal delivery hides how much is being conceded and taken back.

macintyre.sub: the critic who read modern morality as the wreckage of a tradition
world: Two events of 1956, the Soviet crushing of the Hungarian rising and the Suez expedition, broke the British left in two and produced the New Left. In it MacIntyre spent his twenties and thirties arguing over whether Marxism could supply a morality. It could not, he decided, because it had inherited the same broken vocabulary as everyone else. He moved to the United States around 1970. The country was conducting its public arguments—over Vietnam, abortion and welfare—in exactly the interminable register his diagnosis predicted.
life: Born in Glasgow in 1929 and raised partly within the Gaelic-speaking world of his family, MacIntyre studied classics in London and philosophy at Manchester. He published a book on Marxism at twenty-four. He passed through the Communist Party, the New Left and several Trotskyist groups, and through Anglicanism and a period of unbelief. He then entered the Roman Catholic Church in the early 1980s, and took up Aquinas as the tradition in which his argument could be completed. He taught at Essex, Brandeis, Boston, Vanderbilt, Duke and above all Notre Dame. He died in 2025.

p: The opening asks the reader to imagine the natural sciences destroyed and later reassembled from fragments, so that people use the terms correctly by habit while the framework that made them intelligible is gone. That, MacIntyre argues, is the state of our moral language. Deprived of Aristotle’s teleology—an account of what human beings are for—moral claims lose their footing, and disagreement becomes interminable. That is why emotivism correctly describes what moral talk has become rather than what it always was. The reconstruction proceeds through practices with goods internal to them, the narrative unity of a single life, and the traditions that carry both.

The sequel answers the obvious objection: if morality needs a tradition, and traditions conflict, what settles anything? MacIntyre traces four rival accounts of justice and practical reason—Aristotelian, Augustinian, Scottish Enlightenment, liberal—and argues that rationality is itself tradition-constituted, with no neutral standpoint available. Traditions can nonetheless be compared, by whether each resolves the crises generated by its own standards.

A late correction of his own work. MacIntyre says After Virtue had wrongly assumed an Aristotelian ethics could dispense with biology. Here he starts from human vulnerability, disability and animal dependence. He argues that the virtues of acknowledged dependence—giving and receiving care without accounting—matter as much as the virtues of independent practical reasoning.

legacy: After Virtue made virtue ethics a live option alongside consequentialism and Kantian theory. It gave communitarian critics of Rawls their sharpest formulation, though MacIntyre disliked the label. The historical narrative has been attacked as too clean, since the Enlightenment it condemns was less unified than the argument requires. The book’s closing hope for another and very different St Benedict has been taken up as a programme for withdrawal. What has held is the claim that moral concepts have histories.

read.first: After Virtue, reading the first three chapters slowly. The diagnosis has to land before the reconstruction makes sense.
read.note: Resist reading the closing paragraph as a call to retreat. Take Dependent Rational Animals afterwards for the author’s own revisions.

lewis-david.sub: who took possible worlds literally, and built a system on the bill
world: Modal logic had been given a formal semantics by Kripke and others around 1960, in which necessity is truth at all accessible worlds.
