That made possible worlds indispensable to the technical work and left everyone with a question about what they were supposed to be: a way of speaking, a set of sentences, an abstract object.

Metaphysics itself was returning. Quine's austerity had kept it marginal for a generation, and by the late 1960s systematic metaphysical theorising was respectable again, with the constraint that it be argued for the way anything else is — by weighing what a theory buys against what it costs.
life: Born in Oberlin, Ohio in 1941 to two academics. A year at Oxford as an undergraduate, hearing Ryle, turned him to philosophy; he took his doctorate at Harvard under Quine. He taught at UCLA and from 1970 at Princeton, where he stayed.

He visited Australia almost every year for decades, to the point where Australian philosophy and his own are hard to separate; the phrase 'Australian materialism' names a shared project. He bred and studied cats, kept a model railway, and answered letters from students at length. He had a kidney transplant from his wife Stephanie and died of diabetes-related complications in 2001, at sixty.

p: A semantics for 'if it had been the case that A, it would have been that C' in terms of comparative similarity between worlds: the counterfactual is true if some world where A and C holds is more similar to ours than any world where A and not-C. It is short, formally clean, and it made counterfactuals a usable tool, which in turn made possible the counterfactual analyses of causation, of dispositions and of knowledge that occupied the next thirty years. Lewis's own analysis of causation, in the same year, defines it by chains of counterfactual dependence between events.

Modal realism, defended without flinching. Other possible worlds exist, concretely, in the same sense ours does; they are spatiotemporally and causally isolated from us and from each other; 'actual' is indexical, meaning this world, the way 'here' means this place. Lewis does not claim the view is intuitive — he records the incredulous stare as the standard response and says it is not an argument — but that the theoretical benefits are enormous and no rival delivers them at lower cost. Counterparts rather than identity across worlds; a world for every way a world could be. The book is the most thoroughgoing piece of speculative metaphysics of the century and is also very funny.

His dissertation, answering Quine's scepticism about conventions of language. A convention is a regularity in solving a recurring coordination problem, sustained because everyone expects everyone else to conform and prefers to conform given that — no agreement, explicit or tacit, required. Doing it needs an account of common knowledge, which he supplies, and the book is cited in game theory and economics as often as in philosophy.

The programme behind the system: everything there is supervenes on the arrangement of local qualities across spacetime, one little thing after another, with no necessary connections between distinct existences. Laws of nature are the theorems of the best deductive system balancing simplicity and strength; chance, causation and dispositions are then built from that base. He named the programme after Hume and allowed that quantum entanglement might refute it — a statement of what would make him wrong that is rarer in metaphysics than it should be.

legacy: The apparatus is everywhere: closest-world semantics for counterfactuals, counterpart theory, the best-system account of laws, natural properties as a primitive that does theoretical work across ontology, and the papers on convention, on knowing what it is like, and on elusive knowledge. A large share of analytic metaphysics since 1980 consists of arguing with him about one of these.

Modal realism itself has almost no adherents, which Lewis expected. Its function has been to set the price: any competing account of modality is now expected to say what it buys and what it costs, in his terms, and most of the ersatz theories were designed to get his benefits without his ontology. He is the standing example of the view that in philosophy one should follow the argument and pay the bill, however strange the destination.

read.first: 'Causation' (1973) and the first chapter of On the Plurality of Worlds, where the case for modal realism is laid out in fifty pages.
read.note: The five volumes of Philosophical Papers are where most of the work is. His prose is plain and the arguments are explicit, which makes him far easier to read than his reputation for difficulty suggests.

lewis-david.caveat: Almost nobody accepts modal realism, and the epistemological objection — that we could have no causal contact with the other worlds and so no knowledge of them — is widely thought decisive. Lewis's reply, that modal knowledge is not causal to begin with, is the point at which the debate usually stops.

heidegger.sub: the thinker who reopened the question of Being and compromised himself with the Reich
world: Heidegger came out of Catholic provincial Baden into a university system under visible strain. The theology faculty that first funded him assumed a settled scholastic order. The philosophy he moved to was ruled by neo-Kantian epistemology, which he found bloodless. After 1918 the German academy filled with returning soldiers and ruined bourgeois families, and with a widespread sense that the inherited apparatus of liberal scholarship had failed. His Marburg lecture courses drew crowds because they promised to start over.

Weimar never won the loyalty of the professoriate. Inflation, then the slump after 1929, produced a milieu in which talk of decline, rootedness and national renewal passed as ordinary conversation rather than extremism. Heidegger’s enthusiasm in 1933 was his own, but it was not eccentric: much of the German university welcomed the regime, and thousands of academics signed declarations of support that year.

After 1945 the French occupation authorities governed Freiburg. A denazification committee, to which Karl Jaspers submitted a damning report, found against him. He was barred from teaching from 1946 until the ban was lifted in 1949, and lectured again as emeritus only from 1951. The reckoning proved slow and repeatedly reopened — by Farias in 1987, by Hugo Ott’s archival work in 1988, and most seriously by the Black Notebooks from 2014. It reopened because each round produced material the previous defence had assumed did not exist.
life: Born in Messkirch in 1889, son of the sexton of the Catholic church, Heidegger reached higher education on church scholarships. He entered a Jesuit novitiate and left within weeks on grounds of health. He read theology at Freiburg from 1909 and switched to philosophy. He took his doctorate in 1913 on judgment in psychologism, and habilitated in 1915 on a treatise on categories then ascribed to Duns Scotus. Marriage to Elfride Petri in 1917 and the war’s end closed his Catholic career.

From 1919 he was Husserl’s assistant, and from 1923 professor at Marburg. His students there included Gadamer, Karl Löwith, Leo Strauss and Hannah Arendt, with whom he began an affair in 1924. He published almost nothing for a decade. Being and Time, written under pressure to secure a chair, appeared in 1927 and made him the most discussed philosopher in Germany. Freiburg gave him Husserl’s chair the following year.

He joined the National Socialist party on 1 May 1933, ten days after his election as rector of Freiburg on 21 April. He remained a member until 1945. As rector he imposed the Führer principle on the university constitution, spoke for the regime, and wrote assessments of colleagues that damaged them. He resigned in April 1934 after clashes with party officials, and never apologised publicly. The 1966 Spiegel interview, released at his death in 1976, offered explanation without contrition. His later decades went into lecture courses and the hut at Todtnauberg, with Hölderlin displacing Aristotle as the central text.

p: The question is why the tradition since Plato has treated Being as though it were a kind of entity. The strategy is to approach it through the one being that has any understanding of Being. Dasein names us, the word chosen because subject, mind and person all carry Cartesian freight. Dasein is not a thinker facing objects but being-in-the-world, absorbed in dealings that come before contemplation. A hammer in use is ready-to-hand, transparent, part of a web of purposes. Only when it breaks does it appear as a present-at-hand object with properties — precisely the mode philosophy mistook for the primary one.

We are thrown, finding ourselves already in a situation, a body, a language and a history we did not pick. Mostly we live as das Man, doing what one does. Anxiety, in which the world goes flat and nothing in particular threatens, strips that away. Being-toward-death completes the analysis: death is mine, cannot be delegated and cannot be outrun. Holding it in view is what lets a life be owned rather than drifted through. Only the first two divisions were published. The section that was to turn from time back to Being was withheld.

works.t: Kant and the Problem of Metaphysics (Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik)
p: Written straight after the Davos disputation with Ernst Cassirer, this reads the Critique of Pure Reason not as epistemology but as an aborted ontology of human finitude. On that reading the transcendental imagination is its hidden root, and Kant’s retreat from it in the second edition a failure of nerve. Cassirer, and most Kant scholars since, called it violent interpretation. Heidegger did not really disagree, holding that reading a philosopher means pressing him toward what he did not manage to say.

works.t: The Self-Assertion of the German University (Die Selbstbehauptung der deutschen Universität)
p: The rectoral address is the hardest document in the corpus to place. It binds the university to labour service, military service and knowledge service, invokes the beginning of Greek science, and speaks of a German historical mission in language deliberately continuous with the regime’s. Defenders note that it praises no racial doctrine and cites no party programme. The fact remains that the man delivering it had joined the party three weeks earlier and used the office to enforce its policies.

works.t: Introduction to Metaphysics (Einführung in die Metaphysik)
p: The course opens with the question why there is something rather than nothing, works through Greek usage of physis and logos, and ends in a diagnosis of Europe caught between American and Soviet technics. Printing it in 1953, Heidegger kept the phrase about the inner truth and greatness of the movement. He glossed it in a parenthesis as the encounter of planetary technology with modern man. Whether that parenthesis stood in the 1935 manuscript has been argued ever since. Habermas made the passage a public scandal that year.

works.t: The Origin of the Work of Art (Der Ursprung des Kunstwerkes)
p: Art is not the expression of an artist’s feeling but a way in which truth happens. A Greek temple does not depict a world. Standing there, it opens one, gathering the paths and relations in which a people lives, while the rock beneath it shows itself as sheltering and closed — earth. Truth is the strife of world and earth held still in the work. Reading Van Gogh’s shoes as a peasant woman’s drew a famous rebuke from Meyer Schapiro in 1968, who argued the shoes were the painter’s own.

Addressed to Jean Beaufret while Heidegger was banned from teaching, the letter repudiates Sartre’s existentialism. It denies that Being and Time was ever a philosophy of the human subject. It announces the turn: the question is not what man makes of Being but how Being addresses man, with language as its house and thinking a kind of listening rather than a producing. It is the clearest statement of the later work, and it says nothing whatever about the preceding twelve years.

works.t: The Question Concerning Technology (Die Frage nach der Technik)
works.y: lecture 1953, from the Bremen lectures of 1949
p: Technology is not a stock of tools but a way things are disclosed. Under Gestell, enframing, everything shows up as standing-reserve, on call for use: the Rhine becomes a supplier of water power, a forest a stock of timber, and in the end people become human resources. The danger is not machinery but that this becomes the only way anything can appear. He closes with Hölderlin’s line that where danger is, the saving power also grows — a hope the argument does not quite earn.

legacy: The influence is hard to overstate and runs largely through people who rejected his politics. Gadamer built hermeneutics from the analysis of understanding; Arendt, Levinas, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty, Derrida and Foucault worked with or against him; Bultmann took the existential analytic into New Testament theology. In analytic philosophy Hubert Dreyfus turned the ready-to-hand against the representational assumptions of artificial intelligence research, an argument that has aged well.

Then there is the record: party membership from 1933 to 1945, a rectorship exercised in the regime’s service, denunciations of colleagues, and silence about the camps broken chiefly by a 1949 remark comparing mechanised agriculture to the manufacture of corpses in gas chambers. The Black Notebooks compounded it. Their passages on world Jewry and calculation are not asides but sit inside the philosophical argument about the history of Being.

How far this contaminates the work is unresolved and probably will stay so. One camp holds that the notebooks expose a metaphysical antisemitism lodged in the structure of the thought. Another holds that the analyses of tools, mood, death and technology stand or fall on their own evidence, as the mathematics of a scoundrel would. What is no longer available is the claim that the politics was an eccentric episode with no bearing on the philosophy.

The Spiegel interview is itself part of the record rather than a comment on it. Heidegger told his interviewers that the rectorship had been an attempt to shield the university, that he had withdrawn from politics after 1934, and that the Husserl dedication was dropped at the publisher’s insistence. Hugo Ott’s archival work established that the first two claims will not stand. Heidegger had stipulated that the text appear only after his death.

read.first: Read Division One of Being and Time on being-in-the-world and equipment before anything else, then The Question Concerning Technology for the later manner. Keep a translators’ glossary at hand.
read.note: His German coins terms and mines etymologies constantly, so expect the first reading to be slow. Take the Black Notebooks controversy alongside the philosophy rather than after it.

heidegger.caveat: Heidegger controlled his own complete edition and barred critical apparatus from it. Lecture texts therefore sometimes carry later revisions that cannot be checked against the manuscripts — the 1935 parenthesis on the movement being the notorious case.

horkheimer.sub: the director who made critical theory a working programme
world: The Institute for Social Research opened in Frankfurt in 1923, endowed by Felix Weil out of a fortune made in the Argentine grain trade: private money for Marxist scholarship inside a German university. Around it the Weimar Republic staggered from the defeated revolution of 1918-19 through hyperinflation into slump. Within weeks of the Nazi seizure of power in 1933 the Institute was closed. Its endowment had gone abroad already. In 1934 it reopened at Columbia University in New York.
life: Born in 1895 near Stuttgart to a Jewish textile manufacturer who expected him to take over the mills, Horkheimer went to Frankfurt instead. He habilitated under Hans Cornelius in 1925 and took charge of the Institute in 1930. His inaugural lecture set the terms: philosophy would pose the questions, and economists, psychologists and sociologists would test them. He edited the Institute’s journal through exile in Geneva, New York and Los Angeles. He brought it home to Frankfurt in 1950, and died in 1973.

works.t: Traditional and Critical Theory (Traditionelle und kritische Theorie)
p: The essay that named a school. Traditional theory, traced from Descartes through modern natural science, treats knowledge as the ordering of facts by a subject who stands outside what he studies. Critical theory refuses that vantage point. It knows that its own concepts, funding and questions are products of the society it examines. It judges that society against the freedom the society advertises. Whom that leaves to act, after the defeat of the German workers’ movement, Horkheimer never said.

Written with Adorno in Californian exile and printed in Amsterdam, the book argues that enlightenment and myth are entangled from the start. Reason that frees us by mastering nature ends by mastering people, and shrinks to the calculation of means. The chapters on Odysseus, on Sade, on the culture industry and on antisemitism are linked essays rather than a system. Critics have pressed the obvious question of how a critique this total can still be uttered, and from where.

Delivered at Columbia and published in English, this restates the same argument for an American audience. Horkheimer separates objective reason, which asked what ends are worth pursuing, from subjective or instrumental reason, which asks only whether means fit ends already given. Positivism and pragmatism are his chief examples of the second. The book is plainer than its companion and thinner. It names the loss with precision and says almost nothing about how objective reason might be recovered.

legacy: Horkheimer’s durable achievement is institutional as much as intellectual. He built a programme joining philosophy to empirical research and psychoanalysis. He got most of its people out of Germany alive. In old age he grew cautious, blocking reprints of his radical essays until pirated copies circulated among students and an authorised collection followed in 1968. Habermas founded the second generation by rejecting his teacher’s conclusion that reason is instrumental all the way down.

read.first: Start with the 1937 essay, which is short and states the whole programme. Then Eclipse of Reason, and only then Dialectic of Enlightenment.
read.note: Read him for the argument rather than the sentences. The style is heavy without being difficult.

horkheimer.caveat: The division of labour with Adorno in Dialectic of Enlightenment cannot be settled chapter by chapter. Both men insisted the book was dictated jointly.

benjamin.sub: the critic who read modernity from its discarded objects
world: Benjamin’s adult life ran the whole arc of the German catastrophe. He was a student when the war came, a freelance in Berlin when the revolution of 1918-19 failed and inflation ruined rentier families like his own, and a Jewish writer without a university post when the Nazis took power in 1933. He left for Paris that year and lived on small Institute stipends. After the German invasion he fled south. Stopped at the Spanish border town of Portbou in September 1940 and told he would be sent back, he took his own life.
life: Born in Berlin in 1892 to a prosperous assimilated Jewish family, Benjamin never got the academic career he wanted. His habilitation study of German baroque mourning-plays was effectively refused at Frankfurt in 1925. He withdrew it, publishing it as a book in 1928. He lived thereafter by reviewing, radio talks and translation. He was pulled between Gershom Scholem’s summons to Jerusalem and Bertolt Brecht’s materialism, with Adorno as both patron and critic. Almost everything he wrote is short, occasional or unfinished.

p: Sixty short pieces named after shop signs, filling stations, stamp shops and cellars. It is Benjamin’s first attempt to do philosophy through the surfaces of a city rather than through arguments. Its montage form—one thought per fragment, no connecting tissue—is the method he used for the rest of his life. Contemporaries read it as avant-garde whimsy. Later readers found a serious claim in it, that the truth of a period sits in its trivial objects.

works.t: The Work of Art in the Age of Its Technological Reproducibility (Das Kunstwerk im Zeitalter seiner technischen Reproduzierbarkeit)
p: Photography and film do not merely copy artworks. They dissolve the aura, the here-and-now uniqueness that bound art to ritual. What replaces it can be exhibited, cut and distributed, and so becomes available to politics—either to a communism that politicises art or to a fascism that aestheticises war. Benjamin revised the text repeatedly. Adorno objected that it overrated film’s emancipatory pull. It founded much of modern media theory nonetheless.

works.t: The Arcades Project (Das Passagen-Werk) and On the Concept of History
p: For thirteen years Benjamin gathered quotations and notes on the iron-and-glass shopping arcades of Paris, intending a prehistory of the nineteenth century assembled entirely from citation. He left roughly a thousand pages of files with Georges Bataille at the Bibliothèque Nationale. They were printed only in 1982, so what we call the book is an editorial construction. The eighteen theses On the Concept of History distil the method: history is wreckage rather than progress. Klee’s Angelus Novus is blown backwards into the future while the wreckage piles up.

legacy: Adorno and Scholem edited the first substantial German selection in 1955. Hannah Arendt’s Illuminations of 1968 delivered him to English readers. Since then he has been claimed by Marxists and by theologians, by film and media studies, by art history and by urban theory, each finding a different Benjamin in the fragments. That plasticity follows directly from the fact that he finished almost nothing and settled almost nothing.

read.first: Read One-Way Street first for the voice, then the work of art essay, then the theses on history, which run to eight pages and repay a dozen readings.
read.note: Resist systematising him. The fragments are not chips off a lost whole.

benjamin.caveat: A manuscript he was reportedly carrying at Portbou has never been found. The Arcades Project as printed reflects editorial decisions Benjamin never made.

marcuse.sub: the Freudian Marxist the New Left took as its own
world: Marcuse watched the German revolution of 1918-19 collapse from inside it, sitting on a soldiers’ council in Berlin. From its defeat he drew a lifelong scepticism about the organised left. Exile carried him to Geneva, then in 1934 to New York with the Institute, and during the war into American government service as an analyst of Nazi Germany. The postwar United States he wrote about was the opposite of Weimar: employed, comfortable, saturated with advertising, and on his reading more effectively closed to opposition than a police state.
life: Born in Berlin in 1898 to a prosperous Jewish family, Marcuse took a doctorate at Freiburg in 1922. He returned there in 1928 to study with Heidegger and Husserl. He left when his Hegel habilitation found no support and a German career became impossible. He joined the Institute in 1933. Unlike Horkheimer and Adorno he stayed in America after the war, teaching at Brandeis from 1954 and at San Diego from 1965. At San Diego his politics drew death threats and public demands for his dismissal. He died in 1979.

p: Freud’s verdict was that repression is the permanent price of culture. Against it Marcuse distinguishes the basic repression any social life requires from the surplus repression imposed by a particular order of domination. Modern industry, he argues, has made much of that surplus technically unnecessary. What enforces it is the performance principle, the historical shape the reality principle takes under competitive labour. He then sketches a non-repressive civilisation under the signs of Orpheus and Narcissus. Freudian orthodoxy rejected the reading.

Affluent society does not need to repress opposition because it absorbs it. It generates false needs and satisfies them, converts dissent into another consumer option, and flattens language until no vocabulary survives in which a different society could be described. Freedom of choice among goods coexists with unfreedom about ends. The pessimism is nearly total. The hope is placed at the margins, among outcasts and outsiders. The book closes by quoting Benjamin’s line that it is only for the sake of the hopeless that hope is given to us.

Where the means of being heard are distributed as unequally as the wealth, Marcuse argues, tolerating every opinion equally is not neutral. It lends the prestige of impartiality to views that money and institutions already amplify. He therefore proposes a liberating tolerance that would withdraw it from movements of the right and extend it to those of the left. The essay drew immediate charges of authoritarianism, which a postscript did not quiet. It remains the most contested thing he wrote.

legacy: For a few years around 1968 Marcuse was the most famous living philosopher in the world, invoked by students in Berlin, Paris and California. It was a role he had not sought, and one he defended only with reservations. He refused to bless every tactic taken in his name. Angela Davis was his student. Academic philosophy then largely dropped him. His reputation has recovered only partly: One-Dimensional Man reads differently in an economy built on attention, and his tolerance essay keeps returning to the centre of public argument.

read.first: Begin with One-Dimensional Man, then read Repressive Tolerance in the volume where it first appeared, alongside its two dissenting co-authors.
read.note: He writes far more plainly than his Frankfurt colleagues. That makes it easier to see where the argument is asserted rather than shown.

adorno.sub: the dialectician who refused to complete a system
world: Frankfurt in the 1920s was a wealthy commercial city with a young university and an intense musical life. Adorno moved between its concert halls and its seminar rooms for years without deciding which was his profession. That world ended in 1933. The wartime exile that followed, in Los Angeles from 1941, was extraordinary and miserable at once. Horkheimer, Brecht, Schoenberg and Thomas Mann lived within a few miles, while the surrounding film and radio industries supplied the material for his most influential thesis.

He returned to Frankfurt in 1949. The Institute reopened there in 1951 with Adorno soon at its head, insisting on the radio and in print that the country had not worked through its past. The students who took up that insistence in the late 1960s then turned it against him. After the shooting of Benno Ohnesorg in June 1967 the movement demanded action rather than theory. Activists occupied the Institute in January 1969 and Adorno called the police. A lecture that April was broken up.
life: Born in Frankfurt in 1903 as Theodor Ludwig Wiesengrund, son of a Jewish wine merchant and a Catholic singer, he went to Vienna in 1925 to study composition with Alban Berg. He spent the rest of his life half inside music. He came back without a career as a composer. He completed a habilitation on Kierkegaard’s aesthetics in 1931, and published it, by grim coincidence, in 1933.

In New York from 1938 he worked on Paul Lazarsfeld’s Princeton Radio Research Project, an unhappy collaboration that gave him data on how popular music is heard. After the return to Germany he taught, broadcast, and wrote on Beethoven, Mahler and Schoenberg. He died of a heart attack in Switzerland in August 1969, at sixty-five, with Aesthetic Theory unfinished.

p: Adorno’s share of the joint book with Horkheimer includes the excursus on Odysseus and the chapter on the culture industry. The two coined that term in preference to mass culture precisely to insist that the culture in question is not made by the masses. Film, radio and popular song are produced industrially to a standard, sold as leisure, and work to reconcile people to the week that made the leisure necessary. Pseudo-individuation supplies the appearance of variety. It is the most quoted and most contested thing either man wrote.

works.t: Minima Moralia: Reflections from Damaged Life
p: A hundred and fifty-three numbered fragments, written for Horkheimer’s fiftieth birthday. Adorno takes as his material the small change of private existence in exile—gifts, doors, hotel rooms, tact—and reads each as evidence about the society that shaped it. Its best-known sentence, that there is no right life in the wrong one, is a claim about the impossibility of ethical privacy under general wrong. It is the most readable of his books and the one most often mistaken for pessimism about manners.

Co-authored with Else Frenkel-Brunswik, Daniel Levinson and R. Nevitt Sanford for the American Jewish Committee, this is Adorno at his least aphoristic: interviews, projective tests and attitude scales given to some two thousand Americans in search of the character structure that makes a person susceptible to fascist appeals. The resulting F-scale measured conventionalism, submission to authority and a taste for stereotype. Methodologically it was attacked at once, for acquiescence bias and for fixing the interpretation in advance. Its question has outlived every objection to its instruments.

The nearest thing to a systematic statement by a philosopher opposed to systems. The target is identity thinking, the habit by which a concept is taken to exhaust its object, so that whatever in the particular fails to fit is discarded as inessential. Against it Adorno asks that thought keep faith with the non-identical, and that concepts be arranged in constellations, grouped around an object to illuminate it from several sides rather than subsuming it. Here he also revisited his 1951 remark that to write a poem after Auschwitz is barbaric. He granted that perennial suffering has as much right to expression as a tortured man has to scream, and that it may therefore have been wrong to say it.

Left unfinished and assembled for publication by Gretel Adorno and Rolf Tiedemann, the book has no chapters and no argumentative sequence. Adorno meant to write it without a first term, so that no part would be foundational. Art matters, on his account, because the successful work is autonomous, obeying its own formal laws rather than the market’s. In that autonomy it registers the society it refuses. Modernist dissonance is thus social truth rather than private difficulty. Sympathetic readers concede that the prose is close to impassable.

legacy: The sharpest critique came from inside the house: Habermas argued that a theory declaring reason wholly instrumental cannot account for the rationality of its own claims. He built the second generation on that objection. Cultural studies from the 1970s inverted the culture industry thesis by showing audiences using mass culture against its makers’ intentions. His writings on jazz, which mistook a music he barely knew for a symptom, are now generally treated as an embarrassment.

What survives is the vocabulary. Identity thinking, the constellation, the culture industry and the non-identical are working terms in aesthetics, sociology and criticism. Aesthetic Theory remains a standing challenge to any account of art as communication. His most quoted sentence is almost always cited without the qualification he later added, and often as a prohibition he never issued—a fate that would not have surprised a man who wrote against summary.

read.first: Start with Minima Moralia, read in short stretches, then the culture industry chapter, and only then attempt Negative Dialectics.
read.note: His sentences are built to resist paraphrase, which is part of the argument rather than an obstacle to it.

adorno.caveat: Aesthetic Theory is a reconstruction from drafts. Its order of presentation is the editors’ rather than Adorno’s.

sartre.sub: the philosopher who made freedom something nobody can refuse
world: France fell in six weeks in May and June 1940. Roughly one and a half million French soldiers went into German captivity. Sartre was one of them. Under the Occupation the press was licensed, paper was rationed, and a play could not reach a stage in Paris without passing the German censor. The Liberation brought the épuration. Courts tried writers for what they had published, and Robert Brasillach was shot in February 1945.

After 1945 the Left Bank became an industry. Sartre, Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty founded Les Temps modernes in October of that year. The cafés of Saint-Germain-des-Prés filled with reporters looking for existentialists. The Communist Party took over a quarter of the vote and claimed the Resistance as its own, so every intellectual quarrel became a Cold War position. Soviet tanks in Budapest in 1956 broke Sartre's alignment with the party. The Algerian war broke his relations with the state, and the OAS bombed his flat twice in 1961 and 1962.
life: Born in Paris in 1905, Sartre lost his naval-officer father before he was two. He grew up in the household of his maternal grandfather Charles Schweitzer, a teacher of German and a relation of Albert Schweitzer. He entered the École Normale Supérieure, failed the agrégation in 1928, and passed first the following year with Beauvoir placed second. He taught at Le Havre, spent 1933–34 in Berlin reading Husserl, and published La Nausée in 1938.

Captured in June 1940 and released in the spring of 1941, he returned to Paris, started a short-lived resistance group called Socialisme et Liberté, and finished L'Être et le néant. Fame arrived with the Liberation and never left. He moved steadily toward Marxism without joining the party. He refused the Nobel Prize in 1964 on the ground that a writer must not let himself be turned into an institution. He sold banned Maoist papers on the street in 1970, and died in 1980. Tens of thousands followed the coffin.

p: Gallimard took the manuscript, retitled it, and published the diary of Antoine Roquentin, a historian stalled in the port town of Bouville. What Roquentin suffers is not depression but a collapse of the ordinary sense that things have to be as they are. The famous scene under a chestnut tree in the public garden turns a root into pure existence. Nothing about it is necessary or justified, and Roquentin finds himself, like it, de trop. The book is philosophy done as fiction rather than a novel with a doctrine attached. That is why it survives the doctrine. Its weakness is the ending, where art is offered as a way out on rather little argument.

works.t: Being and Nothingness (L'Être et le néant)
p: Subtitled an essay in phenomenological ontology, the book divides being into the in-itself, which is massively what it is, and the for-itself, consciousness, which is never simply what it is. Consciousness is a kind of hole in being. That non-coincidence is freedom. From it Sartre derives bad faith, the flight from freedom into a fixed nature: the waiter who plays at being a waiter, the woman who lets her hand be held while pretending not to notice. The chapter on the Look argues that another's gaze makes me an object, so conflict is the original meaning of being-for-others. Merleau-Ponty and later critics pressed the charge that the two regions are too cleanly split and the lived body too thin.

works.t: Existentialism Is a Humanism (L'existentialisme est un humanisme)
p: Delivered to a packed hall in October 1945, this is the short text that carried the doctrine to the public. Sartre states the thesis precisely. For a manufactured object like a paper knife the essence precedes the existence, because the artisan works from a concept. For human beings, with no maker and no blueprint, existence precedes essence, meaning that a person first exists, turns up in the world, and only afterwards defines what he is. From there come anguish, abandonment and despair, and the case of the student torn between his mother and the Free French, where no rule decides. Sartre later regretted publishing it. Philosophers have always found it cruder than the treatise it summarises.

works.t: Critique of Dialectical Reason (Critique de la raison dialectique)
p: The attempt to make existentialism and Marxism fit was written at speed and under amphetamines. It opens with the essay Search for a Method and the claim that Marxism is the unsurpassable philosophy of the age which has nonetheless stopped thinking. Scarcity is the starting fact. Human projects congeal into the practico-inert, the world of machines, institutions and past labour that turns action back against the actor. Sartre then distinguishes the series, a crowd of separate people defined by an outside, from the group in fusion that forms in an event such as the storming of the Bastille. He asks how such a group hardens into an institution. The book is difficult, was little read, and remains the most serious effort to give Marxism an account of the individual.

legacy: For fifteen years after the Liberation Sartre was the model of what a philosopher could be in public. The reaction was correspondingly sharp. Lévi-Strauss closed The Savage Mind in 1962 with an attack on the Critique. The structuralist generation treated him as a man of the previous century trying to think this one. By 1970 his politics had outrun his readership, and the Flaubert study consumed his last working years without being finished.

What has lasted is not the system but the analyses. Bad faith, the Look, and the insistence that freedom is always situated rather than abstract have passed into moral psychology, social theory and ordinary speech. Anglophone philosophy, which long dismissed him, has read him seriously again since the 1990s. His record on the Soviet Union and on revolutionary violence remains the standing charge against him. It is a fair one.

read.first: Begin with Nausea, then the sections of Being and Nothingness on bad faith and the Look, which stand alone.
read.note: The 1946 lecture is the easiest entry and the least reliable guide to what he actually held.

sartre.caveat: The second volume of the Critique was left unfinished and published only after his death. So his final account of history is a reconstruction from drafts.

beauvoir.caveat: How much she and Sartre owed each other is still argued. The surviving letters and diaries are edited selections rather than a complete record.
legacy: The immediate reception was hostile and personal: François Mauriac and others reviewed the author rather than the argument. The Index followed in 1956. Second-wave feminism then made the book foundational, with Betty Friedan, Kate Millett and Shulamith Firestone all working in its wake. Later feminists pushed back: Luce Irigaray on her acceptance of a male norm of transcendence, and others on the near absence of race and colonialism from the analysis. Judith Butler's 1986 essay, by contrast, took the sentence about becoming a woman as the origin of the sex-gender distinction.

For decades she was read as Sartre's able disciple. She encouraged that reading herself. Scholarship since the 1990s, much of it by Margaret Simons and her collaborators, has established the opposite case from the diaries and the chronology. The problem of the Other and the reciprocity of freedoms are worked out in her hands first. She Came to Stay precedes the treatise it is supposed to illustrate. She is now taught as a philosopher in her own right, which is where the evidence puts her.
life: Beauvoir was born in Paris in 1908, into a devout bourgeois family whose money was going. She lost her faith at about fourteen. She decided early that she would live by writing. She read philosophy at the Sorbonne. She passed the agrégation in 1929 as the youngest candidate ever to do so. She placed second to Sartre, after a jury debate about which of them was the real philosopher. She taught at Marseille, Rouen and Paris.

Her first novel, She Came to Stay (1943), came out of the three-cornered affair with her pupil Olga Kosakiewicz. It takes its epigraph from Hegel on each consciousness seeking the death of the other. It works out a problem about the reality of other minds that Being and Nothingness would take up the same year. She edited Les Temps modernes, won the Goncourt in 1954, published four volumes of memoirs, and died in 1986, buried beside Sartre at Montparnasse.

read.first: Read the introduction to The Second Sex in the 2009 complete translation, then The Ethics of Ambiguity entire.
read.note: Avoid the abridged 1953 English text, which quietly removes names and arguments she thought essential.

beauvoir.sub: the existentialist who showed that women are made, not born

p: Written to answer the charge that existentialism could ground no morality, this is the ethics Sartre promised at the end of Being and Nothingness and never delivered. Ambiguity names the condition of being at once a thing in the world and a freedom that exceeds it. Beauvoir refuses to resolve it in either direction. The central argument is that my freedom is empty unless it takes hold in a world made by others. Willing my own freedom thus commits me to willing theirs. Oppression is therefore wrong on existentialist grounds and not merely disliked. A gallery of failures — the sub-man, the serious man, the nihilist, the adventurer — carries much of the analysis. She later spoke of the book with impatience. It remains the best worked-out ethics the movement produced.
works.t: The Ethics of Ambiguity (Pour une morale de l'ambiguïté)

p: The first volume assembles what biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism have said about women, and finds each explanation partial. The second describes a life from girlhood to old age as it is actually lived under those conditions. The organising claim is that woman has been constituted as the Other, the term defined by contrast with a male norm that presents itself as simply human. From this follows the sentence about not being born but becoming a woman: femininity is a situation produced and enforced, not a nature. Twenty-two thousand copies sold in the first week. The 1953 English version by H. M. Parshley cut roughly a tenth of the text, including much of the history. A complete translation appeared only in 2009.

Beauvoir's Goncourt-winning novel follows a circle of Paris intellectuals from the Liberation into the Cold War. It argues through fiction the questions her essays argue directly: what a writer owes to a party, whether to publish evidence of the Soviet camps when it will serve the right, how private happiness survives political defeat. The characters are close enough to Sartre, Camus and Koestler that readers treated the book as a roman à clef. She denied that. The label obscured the philosophical work the novel does. The psychiatrist Anne Dubreuilh, whose affair with an American writer draws on Beauvoir's own with Nelson Algren, carries the strongest sections. It is the fullest portrait anyone left of that milieu from inside.

Published in America as The Coming of Age, this long book applies the method of The Second Sex to a subject almost nobody was treating philosophically. Beauvoir surveys the biology and ethnography of ageing, then the lived experience of a body and a social position one does not recognise as one's own. Her sharpest point is that old age is the one condition in which a person is made Other to himself, and that a society reveals its real values in how it treats those it has stopped needing. The indictment of French institutional neglect is documentary and angry. It was less read than her feminist work and has been rediscovered by philosophers of disability and care.

world: The France that The Second Sex addressed had given women the vote only in 1944. The ordinance was applied for the first time in the municipal elections of 1945. Married women still worked under legal disabilities inherited from the Napoleonic Code. A wife needed her husband's consent to take a job until 1965. Contraception remained illegal until the Neuwirth law of 1967, and abortion until the Veil law of 1975. Beauvoir wrote into that legal order, not after it.

Her intellectual world was the same Occupation and Cold War as Sartre's. It treated her differently. She lost her teaching post in 1943 after a pupil's mother complained about her conduct. The Catholic press received her 1949 book as an obscenity. The Vatican placed it, together with The Mandarins, on the Index of Prohibited Books in 1956. During the Algerian war she and the lawyer Gisèle Halimi campaigned publicly over the torture and rape of the FLN militant Djamila Boupacha. In 1971 she signed the manifesto of women declaring they had had abortions.

merleau-ponty.sub: the philosopher who made the perceiving body the subject
world: Merleau-Ponty belonged to the École Normale generation of 1926, alongside Beauvoir and just behind Sartre. He came of philosophical age as French thought discovered Hegel, Husserl and Heidegger almost at once. He served as an infantry officer in 1939–40, joined the small Resistance group Socialisme et Liberté, and wrote both his major books in occupied Paris. After the Liberation he co-founded Les Temps modernes and ran its political line.
life: Born at Rochefort-sur-Mer in 1908, he passed the agrégation in 1930 and taught in provincial lycées. In 1939 he became the first foreign scholar admitted to Husserl’s unpublished manuscripts at Louvain. The late Husserl of the life-world marked all his later work. In 1952 he took the chair of philosophy at the Collège de France, its youngest holder. The Korean War and the Soviet camps then broke him with Sartre. He left the journal and set out the quarrel in Adventures of the Dialectic in 1955. A stroke killed him in May 1961.

works.t: The Structure of Behaviour (La Structure du comportement)
p: A patient dismantling of reflex theory using the psychologists’ own material, chiefly Gestalt research and neurological case studies. Behaviour cannot be resolved into stimulus and response, he argues, because organisms respond to forms and whole situations — a finding that rules out mechanism without licensing a mind bolted on top.

works.t: Phenomenology of Perception (Phénoménologie de la perception)
p: Empiricism builds perception out of sensations. Intellectualism has a mind interpreting them. Both assume a world of bare data nobody ever encounters. What we actually meet is a field already organised into figures, distances and possibilities for action. What meets it is the lived body — the standpoint from which there are objects at all, not an object among them.

The evidence is clinical and ordinary by turns: the phantom limb, the brain-injured patient Schneider, the hand that reaches a pocket without being located first. Perception is perspectival and never complete, so ambiguity is the condition of having a world rather than a defect to be cleared away.

works.t: The Visible and the Invisible (Le Visible et l’invisible)
p: Edited posthumously by Claude Lefort from a partial draft and working notes, the book reworks the earlier position in a vocabulary of flesh, chiasm and reversibility. It takes the hand that touches while being touched as the model for a perceiver made of the same stuff as what it perceives.

legacy: For a long stretch after 1961 he was the overshadowed third of the French existential generation, read less than Sartre and displaced by structuralism. That has reversed. Embodied and enactive cognitive science treats the Phenomenology of Perception as a founding text. His account of motor intentionality and the body schema reached robotics and the theory of skill by way of Dreyfus, Varela and Alva Noë. His political writing, cautious about revolutionary violence where Sartre was not, has worn better than most of that milieu.

read.first: The Phenomenology of Perception is the essential book. Its preface and the chapters on the body can be read on their own before the whole.
read.note: He argues through case material rather than theses, so watch for the philosophical claim being made by the example rather than stated after it.

merleau-ponty.caveat: The Visible and the Invisible is a fragment assembled by an editor. So any account of the late ontology of the flesh rests on notes their author had not settled.

weil.sub: who took her own arguments as far as her body would carry them
world: France between the wars: the Popular Front, the factory occupations of 1936, and a left divided over the Soviet Union. Weil belonged to the small anti-Stalinist left that said early and loudly that the USSR was a new bureaucratic class society; Trotsky stayed at her parents' flat and argued with her about it.

Then the collapse. The occupation of 1940, the Vichy statutes that stripped her of her teaching post for being Jewish, exile to Marseille and New York, and the Free French in London. Almost everything she is read for was written in the last four years, much of it in notebooks she did not prepare for publication.
life: Born in Paris in 1909 to an assimilated Jewish family, brother of the mathematician André Weil. She placed first in the entrance examination to the École Normale Supérieure the year Simone de Beauvoir placed second, studied under Alain, and taught philosophy in provincial girls' lycées, where she gave much of her salary away and was repeatedly moved on for political activity.

In 1934 she took a year's leave and worked on assembly lines at Alsthom and Renault, which she said taught her what affliction was and left her marked. She went to Spain in 1936 with an anarchist column, was invalided out after stepping into cooking oil, and had, between 1935 and 1938, three religious experiences that turned her towards Christianity — without ever accepting baptism, on the ground that the Church's anathema sit excluded too much of the world. In London in 1943 she worked for the Free French and restricted her food to what she believed was rationed in occupied France. She died at Ashford in August 1943, aged thirty-four; the inquest said suicide by starvation, which her friends disputed.

p: Written for the Free French as advice on the reconstruction of France, and unlike anything a government has been handed before or since. It begins by reversing the usual order: obligations are prior to rights, since a right means nothing until someone is obliged to honour it, and it is the obligation that is unconditional. It then lists the needs of the soul — order, liberty, obedience, responsibility, equality, hierarchy, honour, punishment, truth — each paired with its opposite, on the ground that the soul needs both. Déracinement, uprootedness, is the modern disease, and money, education and nationalism are its agents. De Gaulle is reported to have thought the author mad.

works.t: Gravity and Grace (La Pesanteur et la grâce)
p: Not a book she wrote: Gustave Thibon selected and arranged passages from the notebooks she left with him. Gravity is the force by which the soul moves to fill itself — every natural movement of the self is downward, and grace is the only exception. Décréation is the consent to being nothing, which she distinguishes sharply from destruction. Affliction, malheur, is not suffering but the thing that destroys the person suffering, and cannot be willed or borrowed. Attention, the faculty of waiting without grasping, is both the whole of prayer and the whole of study, which is why she thought geometry homework had a spiritual use.

works.t: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force
p: Written as the German army entered Paris. Force is what turns a person into a thing, and its perfection is the corpse; but the argument is that force also possesses whoever uses it, so the victor is as much its object as the victim. The Iliad is the only poem she knows that sees this and refuses to take a side. It is a reading of Homer and a diagnosis of 1940 at once, and it has stayed the most widely read thing she wrote.

legacy: Camus, who edited her posthumous volumes at Gallimard, called her the only great spirit of the age and went to her parents' flat before collecting the Nobel Prize. Eliot introduced The Need for Roots in English. Iris Murdoch took attention from her and made it the central term of her moral philosophy, which is how the concept entered Anglophone ethics. Anscombe, Bataille, Miłosz and Susan Sontag all wrote about her, mostly with the mixture of awe and unease she seems to produce.

She is not a philosopher's philosopher: there is no system, most of the work is fragmentary, and the life keeps getting in the way of the reading. What has proved durable are a handful of concepts — attention, affliction, uprootedness, force — and the priority of obligation over rights, which has had a second career in recent political philosophy.

read.first: The Iliad, or the Poem of Force, then Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies. Gravity and Grace after those, in short sittings.
read.note: Remember that Gravity and Grace is an editor's book. Read the Notebooks themselves if a passage matters to your argument, since Thibon's arrangement makes her sound more systematic than she is.

weil.caveat: Her remarks on Judaism and on the Old Testament are hostile and have been called antisemitic by serious readers; they are not incidental to the work and cannot be edited out of an account of it.

camus.sub: the moralist who refused despair and the excuses of history
world: Colonial Algeria held around a million Europeans among nine million Muslims who were French subjects without the rights of citizens. Camus grew up on the poor European side of that arrangement, in the Belcourt quarter of Algiers. He reported in 1939 on famine in Kabylia in terms that got his newspaper suppressed. On 8 May 1945, as Europe celebrated, French forces put down a rising at Sétif and Guelma. The scale of the killings is still disputed, and certainly ran into thousands. War proper began in November 1954.

In France he lived the Occupation as an editor of the clandestine paper Combat. He lived the Liberation as a public argument with François Mauriac over whether the purge should serve justice or mercy. Then came the Cold War, a Communist Party that dominated the intellectual left, and the slow forcing of the Soviet camps into public view through the Kravchenko trial of 1949 and David Rousset's campaign the same year. The break with Sartre in 1952 happened inside that argument, not beside it.
life: Born in 1913 at Mondovi in eastern Algeria, Camus lost his father at the Marne the next year. He was raised in near-poverty by an illiterate, partly deaf mother and a severe grandmother. A primary teacher, Louis Germain, got him to the lycée. He never forgot it, and wrote to Germain after the Nobel. Tuberculosis at seventeen ended his football and closed the academic career the agrégation would have opened. He took a degree in philosophy at Algiers with a dissertation on Plotinus and Augustine. He joined the Communist Party about 1935 and left within two years.

He crossed to France in 1940 and worked for Paris-Soir. He published The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus in 1942, while stranded by the Allied landings in North Africa. Editing Combat made him a moral voice at thirty-one. The Rebel cost him Sartre's friendship in 1952. His appeal for a civil truce in Algiers in 1956 was shouted down from both sides, and he said little publicly afterwards. The Nobel came in 1957, at forty-four. He was killed in a car crash at Villeblevin on 4 January 1960 with an unused train ticket in his pocket.

works.t: The Myth of Sisyphus (Le Mythe de Sisyphe)
p: The essay opens by declaring suicide the one genuinely serious philosophical problem and spends the rest of its length answering no. The absurd, Camus insists, is not a property of the world and not a mood in us. It is the confrontation between a human demand for meaning and a universe that returns silence. Remove either term and the absurd disappears. That is why he rejects both suicide and what he calls philosophical suicide, the leap that Kierkegaard, Chestov and Jaspers make into a God who restores sense. What remains is revolt, freedom and passion, illustrated by the actor, the conqueror and Sisyphus. His consciousness of a pointless task is exactly his victory. Wartime censorship forced the removal of the chapter on Kafka, restored in later editions.

Meursault reports his mother's funeral, a swim, a film, and then a killing on a beach in the same flat perfect tense. The flatness is the argument. The first part shows a man who will not say more than he feels. The second shows a court that convicts him less for the shooting than for not having wept at the funeral, because a society needs its members to perform the meanings it assigns. Sartre's 1943 essay remains the best short account of how the style produces the effect. Modern criticism has pressed hard on the fact that the murdered man is only ever “the Arab”. Edward Said read the book as a colonial document, and Kamel Daoud answered it in 2013 with a novel narrated by the dead man's brother.

An epidemic seals the Algerian city of Oran. Camus uses it to move from the solitary absurd of 1942 to something shared. Dr Rieux, who narrates without saying so until the end, works because a doctor works; Tarrou wants to be a saint without God; Rambert tries to escape and stays; Father Paneloux preaches the plague as punishment and then watches a child die. The book was read at once as an allegory of the Occupation. Roland Barthes objected in 1955 that a bacillus is morally innocent in a way the Germans were not, so the analogy dissolves history into fate. Camus replied that the target was any force that turns people into abstractions. Both are partly right. The novel outlives the quarrel.

The long sequel to Sisyphus asks how the absurd man is to act. It answers that the slave who refuses an order thereby affirms a value he holds in common with others: I rebel, therefore we are. That affirmation carries a limit. The book traces two centuries of thought — Sade, the romantics, Ivan Karamazov, Nietzsche, the surrealists, then Hegel, Marx and 1793 — in which rebellion forgets the limit, hands itself to history, and licenses murder in the name of a future. Francis Jeanson demolished it in Les Temps modernes in 1952 as sentimental and historically illiterate. Camus answered the editor rather than the reviewer. Sartre's reply ended the friendship in public.

legacy: The quarrel with Sartre defined Camus's reputation for twenty years and cost him the argument at the time, since anti-communism was then the unserious position on the Paris left. The books were widely translated regardless. The anti-totalitarian turn of the 1970s, driven by Solzhenitsyn's publication in French, made The Rebel look prophetic. His silence on Algeria after 1956 still divides readers. So does the Stockholm remark that he believed in justice but would defend his mother before justice, routinely quoted in a cruder form than he used.

He denied being an existentialist as early as 1945, noting that he and Sartre were surprised to find their names always coupled. The denial is philosophically accurate: he had no ontology, no theory of consciousness, and no interest in building one. What survives is the definition of the absurd as a relation rather than a property, the argument that revolt sets its own limits, and a body of fiction that keeps the philosophy in the situations where it applies. He is read more now than at his death.

read.first: Take The Myth of Sisyphus and The Stranger together, in that order, since they were written as a pair.
read.note: Read The Rebel only after them. It is the hardest of his books, and the one most often summarised by people who have not finished it.

camus.caveat: The First Man, the autobiographical novel recovered from the wreck of the car, was published in 1994 from an unrevised draft. It cannot be read as a finished statement.

gadamer.sub: the hermeneutician who defended tradition as the condition of understanding
world: Gadamer’s working life spanned the whole German century: born in Marburg in 1900, a student under Weimar, a professor under the Reich, rector of Leipzig under Soviet occupation in 1946, and finally a Heidelberg professor in the Federal Republic. He joined no party, but he stayed, signed the 1933 professors’ declaration of loyalty, attended a political re-education course in 1935, and took the Leipzig chair in 1938 in a faculty emptied by dismissals. Whether that was prudence or complicity is still argued.
life: He came to philosophy through classical philology at Marburg under Natorp and Hartmann, took his doctorate at twenty-two, and survived a bout of polio that left him lame. Heidegger’s arrival in 1923 was decisive. It was Heidegger who pressed him to qualify as a classicist first. He published his major book at sixty, succeeded Jaspers at Heidelberg in 1949, and went on lecturing into his late nineties, dying in 2002 at 102.

p: The habilitation thesis reads the Philebus as a dramatic conversation rather than a store of doctrine. Plato’s arguments, it argues, cannot be lifted out of the exchange that carries them. The move is small and consequential: dialogue is not the packaging of a philosophy but its form. Understanding it means entering the conversation.

The title is a provocation: method, as the human sciences borrowed it from the natural ones, is not how truth is reached in art, history and text. What the Enlightenment dismissed as prejudice is the stock of pre-judgements handed down by tradition. Without it nothing could be understood at all. The task is to bring those pre-judgements into play and let the text contest them.

Understanding is therefore a fusion of horizons, in which the interpreter’s situation and the work’s meet and both shift. So recovering an author’s intention untouched is not merely hard but incoherent. Gadamer adds effective history: a work reaches us already shaped by its reception. The whole rests on his claim that being which can be understood is language.

legacy: Hermeneutics after him became a general philosophical position rather than a technique of biblical and legal exegesis, with effects in literary theory, jurisprudence and the philosophy of the social sciences. Habermas pressed the sharpest objection: tradition transmits domination as readily as insight, and a critique of ideology needs a standpoint outside it. Gadamer replied that there is no such standpoint, and that critique is a move within the conversation. The persistent misreading casts him as a conservative urging deference to tradition, when the claim is descriptive — prejudice is where understanding starts, not where it should stop.

read.first: Part Two of Truth and Method, on prejudice, horizon and effective history, is the argument in its most portable form. The shorter essays are a gentler way in.
read.note: He writes long, courteous, digressive sentences, and assumes a reader at home in Greek philosophy. So the classical examples repay looking up.

levinas.sub: the survivor who put the claim of the other before ontology
world: Born in 1906 into the Jewish world of Kaunas, in a Lithuania then under Russian rule, Levinas grew up between Hebrew, Yiddish and the Russian novel. He came to Strasbourg in 1923, took French citizenship around 1930, and was mobilised in 1939 as an interpreter. Captured in 1940, he spent five years in a German prisoner-of-war camp in a segregated Jewish labour detachment, protected only by the French uniform. Maurice Blanchot helped hide his wife and daughter; his parents and both brothers were murdered in Lithuania in 1941.
life: He studied at Freiburg in 1928–29 with Husserl and heard Heidegger. His 1930 thesis on Husserl’s theory of intuition, with his co-translation of the Cartesian Meditations, effectively introduced phenomenology to France. The post-war lectures published as Time and the Other already contain the programme. He ran a Jewish teachers’ college in Paris for decades and studied Talmud with the teacher known as Chouchani. He reached a university chair only at Poitiers in 1964, then Nanterre and the Sorbonne.

p: Western philosophy, on this account, has been a reduction of the other to the same: to know is to grasp, to bring under a concept, to fold into a totality — and Heidegger’s priority of Being over beings is the last and most sophisticated version. Against it Levinas sets the face of the other person, which is not a phenomenon I constitute but a summons preceding any argument, commanding before reasoning begins that I not kill.

Hence ethics as first philosophy: the relation to the other is not derived from ontology but conditions it. Responsibility here is unchosen and asymmetrical, mine rather than reciprocal, and not cancelled if the other fails to return it. Derrida objected in 1964 that the book must borrow the language of Greek ontology to say any of this. Levinas partly conceded the point.

works.t: Otherwise than Being, or Beyond Essence (Autrement qu’être ou au-delà de l’essence)
p: The second major book answers Derrida by writing differently — dense and incantatory, working through substitution, hostage, proximity, and the saying that always exceeds the said. Its dedication, to the memory of those closest among the millions murdered by National Socialism, is the one place where the biography surfaces directly.

legacy: He shaped Derrida, Ricoeur and Jean-Luc Marion. He gave later moral philosophy, care ethics and a good deal of theology a vocabulary of alterity and the face. Critics press two charges: that the asymmetry of responsibility makes justice between third parties hard to reach, a problem he took up but arguably never solved, and that some of his remarks on non-European cultures sit awkwardly with the universality of the claim. What endures is the reversal — the argument that the first philosophical fact is not what exists but that someone is facing me.

read.first: Begin with the short lectures of Time and the Other, then Section III of Totality and Infinity on the face. Leave Otherwise than Being until the vocabulary is familiar.
read.note: The prose is deliberately not argumentative in the usual sense. Readers who demand premises and conclusions on every page will find the later book impassable.

arendt.sub: the theorist of action, plurality and the public world
world: Arendt’s formative political experience was the speed of 1933. Within months the German-Jewish middle class to which she belonged had lost its livelihood and its legal standing. She was briefly held by the Gestapo for collecting antisemitic material for a Zionist organisation, and left for Paris. Statelessness was for eighteen years her own status. She later described it as the condition of having no right to have rights. In 1940 she was interned at Gurs in southern France, escaped, and reached New York in 1941.

The America she wrote in was a Cold War country. There the destruction of European Jewry had only begun to be publicly reckoned with. That reckoning acquired a stage in 1961, when Israeli agents brought Adolf Eichmann from Argentina and tried him in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion’s government designed the proceedings as national instruction, with more than a hundred survivor witnesses whose testimony often had no bearing on the charges. Arendt went as a reporter. She was convinced that a court exists to judge a defendant rather than to teach a history.
life: Born in 1906 and raised in Königsberg, she studied at Marburg with Heidegger. She had an affair with him at eighteen, and never quite stopped arguing with his Nazism. She then took her doctorate at Heidelberg in 1929 under Karl Jaspers, on the concept of love in Augustine. Jaspers remained the friendship of her life. In Paris she worked for Youth Aliyah and married Heinrich Blücher, a former communist and no academic.

In America she wrote for the German-language Aufbau, edited at Schocken Books and directed Jewish Cultural Reconstruction, salvaging looted Jewish libraries. All of that came before any university employed her. Teaching came late and irregularly: Berkeley, Chicago, a visiting appointment at Princeton in 1959, finally the New School. She resisted being called a philosopher, on the ground that philosophy since Plato had been hostile to the plurality politics requires. She died in New York in 1975.

p: Three books in one: on nineteenth-century antisemitism, on imperialism and the return of colonial administration to Europe, and on totalitarian rule itself. The claim that made it famous is that Nazism and Stalinism constitute a form of government genuinely new, not tyranny intensified. Its instruments are total ideology, terror applied to the innocent rather than the guilty, and the atomisation of a mass society in which people have no ties to shelter them. Historians contest much of the first two volumes and the equation of the two regimes. The third is still read as political theory of the first rank.

Arendt divides the active life into labour, which serves biological necessity and leaves nothing behind; work, which fabricates the durable world of objects; and action, which occurs only among plural people and discloses who, rather than what, the actor is. Action is unpredictable and irreversible, which is why promising and forgiving matter politically. Her diagnosis of modernity is that the third has collapsed into the first two, reducing politics to the administration of a national household. Against Heidegger’s being-toward-death she sets natality: because people are born, beginnings keep entering the world.

A comparison that runs against both national mythologies. The French Revolution, on Arendt’s account, was wrecked because it took up the social question, the sheer misery of the poor, and let compassion license terror. The American Revolution, on her account, succeeded because it concerned itself with founding a durable structure of public freedom. She is drawn throughout to the council forms that appear spontaneously in revolutions and are always suppressed. Critics find her indifference to poverty as a political matter hard to accept, and her account of the American founding markedly idealised.

works.t: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
p: Arendt covered the trial for The New Yorker. The man in the glass booth struck her not as a demonic antisemite but as a careerist fluent in cliché and incapable of thinking from another’s standpoint. The subtitle’s phrase named that. Many readers took it as diminishing his guilt, which she denied. Far more damaging were the pages arguing that the Jewish councils had cooperated in registering and delivering their own communities. Gershom Scholem accused her of lacking love for the Jewish people. Friendships ended permanently, and whole books were written to refute her. The quarrel over both the phrase and the councils has never been settled.

Her return, at the end, to the contemplative faculties she had spent decades bracketing. It is also an attempt to follow through the question the trial left her with: whether the activity of thinking can prevent wrongdoing. Two parts were drafted, Thinking and Willing. The third, Judging, where she meant to derive a political faculty of judgement from Kant’s aesthetics, was never written. A sheet bearing the title and two epigraphs was found in her typewriter. What she would have argued has to be reconstructed from her Kant lectures. Reasonable readers reconstruct it differently.

legacy: Arendt fits no school. That delayed her absorption and then made her useful to everyone: republicans and participatory democrats drawing on the council tradition, theorists of statelessness taking up her account of the rightless, and commentators who apply the word totalitarian to regimes she would have said it did not fit. Sustained academic attention arrived largely after her death. Interest rises whenever refugee crises or authoritarian politics make her vocabulary feel immediate.

The Eichmann quarrel has never been laid to rest. Defenders read the book as a study of thoughtlessness inside a bureaucratic role. Opponents hold that she misjudged the man. They hold that her pages on the Jewish councils were both careless with the evidence and cruel to the survivors who had to read them. Later archival work on Eichmann’s own writings from Argentina reopened rather than settled the question of what he was.

read.first: Read The Human Condition for the framework and Eichmann in Jerusalem for the argument that made her notorious, ideally alongside one serious critic of it.
read.note: She defines her terms idiosyncratically and expects the definitions to be held. Skimming produces confident misreadings.

arendt.caveat: The third part of The Life of the Mind was never written. Her account of judgement therefore exists only in lecture notes and fragments.

habermas.sub: the rationalist who located reason in speech itself
world: Habermas was fifteen when the war ended. The Nuremberg trials and the newsreels from the camps arrived as a personal shock in a Rhineland household that had been unremarkably conformist. The Federal Republic he grew up in rebuilt itself at speed while declining to examine what it was rebuilding from. That silence set the shape of his public life. In 1953 he attacked Heidegger in the press for reissuing a wartime lecture course without a word about its politics.

Two later conflicts mattered as much. In 1967 he warned the radicalising student movement that its provocations risked what he called left fascism, a phrase he partly withdrew and never lived down. Then in 1986 came the Historikerstreit, the historians’ quarrel over whether the Holocaust could be explained as a response to Bolshevik terror and folded into a usable national story. Reunification and the building of the European Union kept him in the newspapers for decades after that.
life: Born in Düsseldorf in 1929 and raised in Gummersbach, he was born with a cleft palate. Operations left his speech difficult — an experience he later connected, without making much of it, to an interest in what it takes to be understood. He studied at Göttingen, Zurich and Bonn, took a doctorate on Schelling in 1954, and supported himself by journalism.

Adorno hired him as an assistant at the Institute in 1956. Horkheimer, who thought him politically exposed, obstructed his habilitation, so he completed it at Marburg under the socialist jurist Wolfgang Abendroth. Chairs at Heidelberg in 1961 and Frankfurt in 1964 followed, then twelve years directing a Max Planck institute at Starnberg, then Frankfurt again. He wrote for the newspapers until very late in life. He died in 2026.

works.t: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (Strukturwandel der Öffentlichkeit)
p: His habilitation, and still his most widely read book outside philosophy. It traces the emergence in eighteenth-century Britain, France and Germany of a bourgeois public sphere — coffee houses, salons, moral weeklies, a periodical press — in which private people reasoned about public matters. In principle they set rank aside and let the better argument decide. Habermas then charts its hollowing out, as commercial mass media and public relations turn a reasoning public into a consuming one. Later historians disputed the idealisation of a narrow, male, propertied forum. Feminist critics named the counter-publics it left out.

works.t: Knowledge and Human Interests (Erkenntnis und Interesse)
p: Against positivism’s picture of a single disinterested method, Habermas argues that inquiry is constituted by three knowledge-guiding interests: a technical interest in prediction and control, grounding the empirical sciences; a practical interest in mutual understanding, grounding the interpretive ones; and an emancipatory interest in freedom from unnecessary constraint, grounding critique. Psychoanalysis is his model of a discipline whose success consists in a patient coming to recognise an account of himself as true. He later judged the foundations mistaken and rebuilt the project on a theory of language.

works.t: The Theory of Communicative Action (Theorie des kommunikativen Handelns)
p: Two volumes, and the decisive break with Horkheimer and Adorno. Instrumental rationality, oriented to success and the control of things, is only one form of reason. Communicative rationality, oriented to reaching understanding, is another, and it is built into ordinary speech. Anyone who asserts something in earnest undertakes to defend it with reasons. The counterfactual standard of an unconstrained discussion — the ideal speech situation he had developed in the early 1970s — is presupposed whenever we argue at all. Modern pathology is then the colonisation of the lifeworld by money and administrative power.

works.t: Between Facts and Norms (Faktizität und Geltung)
p: The legal and political payoff of the communicative theory. Law mediates between the coercive facticity of an enforced order and the claim that its norms deserve assent. A constitution is legitimate to the extent that citizens can regard themselves as the authors of the laws they obey. Private and public autonomy are therefore co-original, neither derivable from the other. He models this as a two-track system in which informal opinion-formation in the public sphere feeds the formal circuits of parliament and courts. That picture anchored the deliberative turn in democratic theory.

legacy: The Historikerstreit went largely his way. The Federal Republic’s official memory came to look much as he argued it should. Constitutional patriotism — loyalty to institutions and principles rather than to a nation — entered German political language. He did the same work in miniature many times over. That is why he was widely treated as the republic’s public conscience even by people who had never opened the books.

Academically his effect is largest in political and legal theory, where deliberative democracy is now a standing position, and in discourse ethics, which supplies a procedure to fields from bioethics to constitutional law. His exchange with Rawls in 1995 is a model of disagreement conducted well. The objections are equally established: that his public sphere was a narrow one, that the ideal speech situation asks too much of ordinary argument, and that his quarrel with Foucault left each side describing the other rather than meeting it.

read.first: Begin with The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere, which is a genuine work of history and readable as such. Then take the communicative theory through a good summary before the two volumes.
read.note: His technical vocabulary is unusually stable across forty years, so the effort of learning it once pays across the whole body of work.

deleuze.sub: the philosopher who put difference before identity
world: Deleuze was fifteen when the Germans took Paris. The Occupation reached his family directly: his elder brother Georges was arrested for resistance activity and died in transport to a camp. The philosophy faculty he entered afterwards was ruled by what the students called the three H's: Hegel, Husserl and Heidegger. Jean Hyppolite's Hegel was at the centre, and the Communist Party held much of the intellectual ground. Deleuze never joined it and never wrote as a phenomenologist, taking his bearings instead from the history of science and from authors the syllabus ignored.
