May 1968 changed his working life. The government answered the revolt by founding an experimental university at Vincennes, where degrees were for years not fully recognised. Deleuze taught there from 1969 until the campus was demolished in 1980 and moved to Saint-Denis. Around him the Lacanian school was splitting, anti-psychiatry was at its height, and Félix Guattari was running an unorthodox clinic at La Borde. In the 1980s American departments imported these Paris arguments as “French theory”. Deleuze arrived late in that traffic, and largely through art, architecture and film schools.
life: Deleuze was born in Paris in 1925 to a conservative middle-class family. He studied at the Sorbonne under Ferdinand Alquié, Jean Hyppolite and Georges Canguilhem, and passed the agrégation in 1948. He then spent well over a decade teaching in lycées and provincial faculties. He published a book on Hume at twenty-eight and then a run of monographs on Nietzsche, Kant, Proust, Bergson and Spinoza. Chronic lung disease dogged him from the 1960s and cost him a lung.

The year 1968 brought both doctoral theses, Difference and Repetition and the Spinoza book. The following year he met Guattari, a militant psychoanalyst with no academic post. Their collaboration produced four books over twenty years and a manner of writing neither could have managed alone. Deleuze taught at Vincennes and Saint-Denis until 1987, gave few interviews, travelled little, and wrote on cinema, Leibniz and Francis Bacon in his last decade. Unable to breathe or write, he took his own life on 4 November 1995.

works.t: Nietzsche and Philosophy (Nietzsche et la philosophie)
p: The most consequential of the early monographs reads Nietzsche as a systematic philosopher of forces rather than a stylist of aphorisms. Deleuze distinguishes active from reactive force and affirmation from negation. He argues that the dialectic is the philosophy of the reactive, since it can only reach the positive by way of the negative. The eternal return is read as a selective test: what returns is difference, never the same. The book effectively rescued Nietzsche in France from his fascist reception. It set the pattern for the others — Hume in 1953, Bergson in 1966, Spinoza in 1968 — which together build a counter-canon of thinkers the mainstream had marginalised. Deleuze described the method as taking an author from behind and giving him a monstrous child that was nonetheless his own.

His principal thesis argues that philosophy has always made difference secondary, treating a thing as different from something under an identical concept, and that repetition has been reduced to resemblance under a general law. Deleuze wants difference in itself and repetition as the return of the singular. The book dismantles what he calls the dogmatic image of thought, the assumption that thinking is naturally oriented to truth and begins with recognition. Genuine thought, he says, begins with an encounter that forces it. Alongside this runs an ontology of the virtual. Ideas are problems with a differential structure that get actualised in divergent ways. Intensity is what drives the actualisation. It is a difficult book by design, and the most rigorous statement of his metaphysics.

works.t: The Logic of Sense (Logique du sens)
p: Organised as thirty-four series rather than chapters, this is Deleuze's book on meaning, built from the Stoics and Lewis Carroll. The Stoic distinction between bodies with their causes and incorporeal effects at the surface gives him the event. To be cut is not a property of a body but something that happens at its surface and is expressed in language. Sense, accordingly, is neither a word nor a thing but the expressed of a proposition. It comes with paradoxes that cannot be cleaned up. The closing sections turn to Melanie Klein and to Antonin Artaud, where the surface breaks down. It is the last book before Guattari, and the one analytic readers of Frege and Carroll can most easily engage.

works.t: Capitalism and Schizophrenia: Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus
p: Anti-Oedipus, written with Guattari and published into the aftermath of 1968, attacks psychoanalysis for confining desire within the family triangle and for defining it by lack. Desire, they argue, is productive: it makes connections. Oedipus is a device for shrinking a social field to a nursery. A speculative universal history follows, in which coding, overcoding and the decoding characteristic of capitalism organise societies. A Thousand Plateaus, eight years later, replaces chapters with plateaus meant to be read in any order. It offers its best-known image: the rhizome, with no root and no hierarchy, against the tree of ordered knowledge. Its concepts — assemblage, deterritorialisation, smooth and striated space, the war machine — travelled further than any of his other work, sometimes as slogans.

legacy: Foucault's remark in a 1970 review that the century might one day be called Deleuzian was meant partly in jest, and has been quoted ever since in earnest. The Anglophone boom came in the 1990s. It came as much through architecture, geography, film studies and art criticism as through philosophy departments. Alan Sokal and Jean Bricmont attacked his use of mathematical vocabulary in 1997 as decorative. Alain Badiou, more interestingly, argued the same year that this apparent philosopher of multiplicity is really a thinker of the One, a reading his followers contest.

What holds up is the ontology of the virtual, the account of difference without a prior identity, and the critique of a psychoanalysis that reads every social conflict back into the family. The theory of affect that runs through contemporary aesthetics and cultural studies is largely his. The standing complaint is fair too: the prose resists paraphrase, the vocabulary invites imitation, and “rhizomatic” has been used to mean almost nothing at all.

read.first: Start with Nietzsche and Philosophy, which is lucid. Then take the first two chapters of Difference and Repetition slowly.
read.note: A Thousand Plateaus is written to be entered anywhere, but it makes far more sense once the earlier metaphysics is in place.

deleuze.caveat: How the labour was divided in the books with Guattari is not settled. Both men insisted the question was badly posed.

foucault.sub: the historian of how our categories were built
world: Foucault grew up in Poitiers under the Occupation, the son of a surgeon. In 1946 he entered the École Normale Supérieure, into a milieu where the Communist Party was close to compulsory for a serious young intellectual. He joined in 1950 at Louis Althusser's urging and left three years later. The philosophy on offer was Hegelian and phenomenological. The alternative he took up came from the French history of science, Gaston Bachelard and Georges Canguilhem, which treated concepts as things with histories and ruptures.

The middle of his career runs through two upheavals. In 1966 The Order of Things sold like a novel and made structuralism a public event. Two years later the May revolt reorganised the universities and produced Vincennes, where Foucault built the philosophy department. Elected to the Collège de France in 1970, he was obliged to lecture publicly each year on new research. Those courses became a second body of work.

Prisons then dominated his politics. With others he founded a group in 1971 to gather and publish information from inside French prisons. It was a time of mutinies and of a penal system still using long solitary confinement. The later 1970s brought the anti-totalitarian turn, the reception of Solzhenitsyn, his controversial reporting from revolutionary Iran in 1978 and 1979, and a growing American audience at Berkeley that he plainly enjoyed.
life: Refusing the medical career his father wanted, Foucault took degrees in philosophy and psychology and worked in a psychiatric hospital as an observer. As a student he suffered severe depressions, which he later connected to the criminal and clinical status of homosexuality in the France of his youth. His doctorate, defended in 1961, was already a large and strange book about madness.

He spent the later 1950s abroad, running French cultural institutes at Uppsala, Warsaw and Hamburg. He taught at Clermont-Ferrand from 1960 to 1966 and then in Tunisia, where the student revolt of 1968 reached him before the Paris one did. He returned to a chair at Vincennes, then to the Collège de France, where he held a chair he named the History of Systems of Thought.

In his last decade he lectured in California, revised the sexuality project completely, and lived with Daniel Defert, who had co-founded the prison group. He died in Paris on 25 June 1984 of an AIDS-related illness, one of the first public figures in France to do so. His lecture courses have been published steadily since 1997. The fourth volume of the sexuality history appeared in 2018.

works.t: History of Madness (Histoire de la folie à l'âge classique)
p: The doctoral thesis argues that madness was not discovered by medicine but constituted, over the classical age, as unreason: something to be excluded rather than heard. Its hinge is the “great confinement” that begins with the founding of the Hôpital Général in Paris in 1656. That foundation shut up the poor, the idle, the venereal and the mad together under a single administrative category. The liberations of Pinel and Tuke at the end of the eighteenth century are read not as humanity arriving but as the substitution of moral supervision and guilt for chains. Historians objected hard. H. C. Erik Midelfort showed the ship of fools was largely literary and the confinement figures shakier than claimed. Andrew Scull and Roy Porter disputed the periodisation. Much of the Anglophone quarrel was conducted against a heavily abridged 1965 translation. The full text appeared in English only in 2006.

The philosophical objection came a decade before the historians’. In 1963 Derrida argued in Cogito and the History of Madness that a history of madness written from madness’s own side is impossible, since the language of any such history is already the language of reason. Foucault answered only in 1972, in an appendix to the second French edition. The two were estranged for most of the following decade.

works.t: The Birth of the Clinic (Naissance de la clinique)
p: Subtitled an archaeology of medical perception, this short book asks how doctors came to see what they now see. Around 1800, Foucault argues, medicine stopped classifying diseases as species in a table and began locating them in tissue. He ties that shift to the reorganisation of hospitals and teaching after the Revolution and to Bichat's pathological anatomy. The corpse becomes the instrument of knowledge. The “medical gaze” is not a passive look but a trained practice that constitutes its object. The claim that matters philosophically is that perception itself has a history, structured by institutions. Critics have found the break too clean and the debt to Canguilhem understated. The book nonetheless gave medical history a vocabulary it still uses.

works.t: The Order of Things (Les Mots et les choses)
p: Foucault's bestseller proposes that every period has an episteme, a set of unstated rules fixing what can count as knowledge at all — not opinions people hold but the ground on which their opinions become possible. Three follow one another: Renaissance knowledge organised by resemblance, classical knowledge by representation and the ordered table, and modern knowledge from around 1800 by depth, history and finitude. In that last shift general grammar, natural history and the analysis of wealth become philology, biology and economics. Man appears as both the object of knowledge and its condition. Hence the famous closing image of man as a face drawn in sand, about to be erased. The opening reading of Velázquez's Las Meninas is the most-read pages he wrote. He rejected the structuralist label the book earned him.

works.t: The Archaeology of Knowledge (L'Archéologie du savoir)
p: Written to explain and correct the three histories that preceded it, this is Foucault's only methodological book. He sets out to describe discourse without appealing to the usual unities of intellectual history — the author, the oeuvre, the tradition, influence, the slow maturation of an idea. In their place he puts the statement, the minimal unit of what actually got said, the discursive formation that groups statements by rules of dispersion, and the archive, the system governing what can be said in a period. The book is dry, self-critical, and openly unstable. Foucault soon stopped calling his work archaeology. It matters because it states plainly that he is describing conditions of possibility rather than explaining beliefs by causes. That is what most misreadings get wrong.

The book opens with the public torture of the regicide Damiens in 1757. Three pages later it turns to a prison timetable drawn up eighty years afterwards, then asks what happened in between. Foucault's answer is that punishment was not softened but redirected, from the body of the condemned to the soul of the delinquent. The prison, on that answer, belongs to a wider technique — discipline — also at work in barracks, schools, workshops and hospitals. Discipline works through the partitioning of space, the timetable, hierarchical observation, normalising judgement and the examination. It produces docile and useful bodies. Bentham's panopticon supplies the diagram: a visibility so arranged that the inmate takes over his own surveillance. The last part argues that the prison's evident failure to reduce crime is not a defect, since it manufactures a manageable delinquency the police can use. This is genealogy rather than archaeology: history written to make a present arrangement look strange.

works.t: The History of Sexuality (Histoire de la sexualité)
p: The first volume attacks the repressive hypothesis, the story in which the Victorians silenced sex and we have been liberating it since. On the contrary, Foucault argues, the nineteenth century generated an enormous machinery for making people speak about sex — confession, medicine, psychiatry, pedagogy, demography — and installed sexuality as the truth of the self. Power here is productive: it does not merely forbid, it constitutes the homosexual, the hysteric, the masturbating child as kinds of person. The volume closes with biopower, the modern state's business of managing populations, birth rates and health, of making live rather than threatening death. Eight years and a complete change of plan produced volumes two and three in 1984, on Greek and Roman practice. There the question becomes how one forms oneself as an ethical subject through the care of the self rather than by obeying a code. The fourth volume, on the Christian fathers, was published in 2018 despite his objection to posthumous publication.

legacy: No twentieth-century philosopher has been taken up more widely outside philosophy. Criminology, the history of medicine, sociology of the professions, geography and education all use his vocabulary. Edward Said built Orientalism on the discourse analysis. Queer theory in Eve Sedgwick's and Judith Butler's hands starts from the first volume on sexuality. Panopticism became the standard idiom for describing surveillance, often applied far beyond anything he claimed.

The objections are serious and have not gone away. Historians continue to find the archival base thinner than the conclusions. Lawrence Stone argued so in a public exchange with him in 1982 and 1983, and specialists on confinement and on the prison have argued it in detail. Jürgen Habermas pressed a different charge: if knowledge and power produce each other all the way down, the critic has no ground to stand on. Foucault's writing, by that charge, is normative while denying itself norms. His late answers to that are suggestive rather than complete.

What survives best is the method he called a history of the present: taking a category that feels natural — madness, delinquency, sexuality, the self — and showing when and by what practices it was assembled. The Collège de France lectures have shifted the picture since 1997. The courses on governmentality and on liberalism especially are now more used by political theorists than the books. “Foucauldian” also names a mood in much writing that owes him nothing but suspicion.

read.first: Read Discipline and Punish first, whole. Then take the first volume of The History of Sexuality, which is short and states the method.
read.note: Use the complete History of Madness rather than the old abridgement. Treat the lecture courses as working drafts rather than settled doctrine.

foucault.caveat: The historical evidence in the early books is genuinely contested. The fourth sexuality volume was published against his stated wish. The lecture courses are transcripts he never revised for print.

derrida.sub: the reader who showed that texts undo their own hierarchies
world: Derrida was born in 1930 at El Biar outside Algiers into a Sephardic Jewish family that had held French citizenship since the Crémieux decree of 1870. Vichy repealed that decree in October 1940 and imposed quotas on Jewish pupils. In 1942 the twelve-year-old was sent home from his lycée on the first day of term. He spent about a year outside the French school system. The war of independence broke out in 1954. He served his military obligation from 1957 to 1959 teaching soldiers' children near Algiers rather than fighting. After 1962 the family, like almost the whole European population, left for France.

Paris took him in at the moment structuralism was becoming the dominant idiom of the human sciences. He made his name by pressing it from inside. In October 1966 he crossed to a conference at Johns Hopkins convened to introduce structuralism to America. He delivered a paper that announced its limits instead. The American reception of “French theory” effectively dates from that room. Through the 1970s and 1980s he taught regularly in the United States while French institutions kept him at arm's length. The transatlantic asymmetry shaped how he was read on both sides.
life: After the lycée in Algiers, where he had wanted to be a professional footballer, Derrida went to Paris in 1949 and boarded at Louis-le-Grand. He failed the entrance to the École Normale Supérieure once and the agrégation once, and passed both at the second attempt. His early work was on Husserl: a 1954 dissertation on the problem of genesis, then a translation of The Origin of Geometry in 1962. That translation's introduction ran longer than the text and won a prize.

In 1967 he published three books at once and became a figure overnight. He taught at the École Normale for twenty years without a chair, took the state doctorate only in 1980, and moved to the École des Hautes Études in 1984. Arrested in Prague in 1981 on a planted drugs charge after teaching a clandestine seminar, he was freed following French government pressure. He helped found an international college of philosophy in 1983, taught for years at Irvine, and died of pancreatic cancer in October 2004.

p: The book names the target: logocentrism, the long habit of treating the spoken word as the natural home of meaning and writing as a derivative, dangerous copy. Derrida traces the pattern from Plato to Saussure, who defines language as a system of differences and then excludes writing from it. He argues that everything blamed on writing — absence of the speaker, repeatability, drift of context — is a condition of language as such. The second half is a sustained reading of Rousseau on the “dangerous supplement”. There writing, education and masturbation all turn out to be additions that are needed only because the origin they supplement was already incomplete. The sentence usually rendered “there is nothing outside the text” belongs to this reading. It claims that there is no access to meaning from outside every context, not that reality is unreal.

works.t: Writing and Difference (L'Écriture et la différence)
p: Eleven essays written between 1959 and 1966 show the method being applied rather than stated. The piece on Foucault argues that a history of madness written in the language of reason cannot occupy the outside it claims, and that Foucault's reading of a passage in Descartes will not carry the weight put on it. Foucault waited nine years to reply, and the friendship did not recover. “Violence and Metaphysics” presses Emmanuel Levinas on whether the wholly other can be spoken of at all without the ontological language he rejects. It visibly changed Levinas's later work. The closing lecture, given at Johns Hopkins, uses Lévi-Strauss to show that a structure always presupposes a centre it cannot itself contain. For most readers this is the best way in.

works.t: Speech and Phenomena (La Voix et le phénomène)
p: Derrida said this was the book he valued most. It is the most conventionally argued. He takes a single distinction from the first of Husserl's Logical Investigations, between expression and mere indication. He shows that the attempt to find a sphere of pure self-presence in silent inner life fails on Husserl's own account of time. Retention already introduces a trace of what is no longer present, so self-presence is never complete. Hearing oneself speak had seemed the one place where sign and meaning coincide. It turns out to be an effect rather than a foundation. The argument was extended in a lecture of January 1968 on différance, a coinage whose altered vowel is inaudible in French and visible only in writing. The word names at once differing and deferring.

This book was delivered as lectures in California in 1993, when the collapse of the Soviet bloc had made the end of Marxism a settled opinion. It insists that one inherits from Marx whether or not one chooses to. Its guiding figure is the ghost, taken from the opening of Hamlet and of the Communist Manifesto: something neither present nor absent that returns and makes claims. Derrida offers a list of ten afflictions of the new world order — unemployment, homelessness, the arms trade, foreign debt — against Francis Fukuyama's triumphalism. He calls for a “New International” without party or state. Marxist readers, collected in a 1999 volume of replies, largely found it evasive about political economy. It remains his most direct political book.

legacy: In America deconstruction was absorbed first by literary departments, above all at Yale. There it hardened into a technique and then a caricature: the claim that texts mean anything, that truth is a fiction, that rigour is optional. What Derrida actually did is narrower and harder — read a text closely enough to find the point where its governing opposition depends on the term it subordinates. John Searle's 1977 exchange with him over Austin produced heat and little agreement. In 1992 nineteen philosophers, Quine and Ruth Barcan Marcus among them, wrote to The Times opposing an honorary degree at Cambridge. The university put it to a ballot. It passed by 336 votes to 204.

The Paul de Man affair of 1987 did more lasting damage. Nearly two hundred wartime articles de Man had written for a collaborationist Belgian paper came to light, one of them plainly antisemitic. Derrida's long response was widely judged to have used subtle reading to soften a plain fact. Readers who had never trusted him took it as proof. His standing now rests on the readings themselves and on the later work on law, hospitality, forgiveness and the gift. That later work has been taken up in legal theory, theology and postcolonial criticism more readily than in philosophy departments.

read.first: Begin with Writing and Difference, taking “Violence and Metaphysics” and the Johns Hopkins lecture first, then move to Of Grammatology.
read.note: He is answering particular texts very closely. Read him next to the Rousseau, Husserl or Saussure he is reading, and the difficulty halves.

derrida.caveat: Whether the later work on ethics, justice and religion follows from the early arguments or marks a change of direction is still disputed among his readers.

laozi.sub: the doubted author of a layered book about the unnameable Way
world: The Zhou kings had lost real power long before any part of the Daodejing reached its present shape. In 771 BCE the dynasty abandoned its western capital and re-established itself at Luoyang. From then on the king was a ritual centre with no army worth the name. His former vassals fought, swallowed one another and swore covenants among themselves. By the fourth and third centuries BCE, where most scholars now place the compilation of the text, a handful of large bureaucratic war-states were conscripting peasants by the tens of thousands and taxing them to pay for it.

Those states competed for advisers as hard as they competed for territory. Qi funded the Jixia academy. Qin, Wei and Chu hired persuaders, drafters and diviners. A man with a doctrine could carry it from court to court. The Daodejing belongs to that market. Much of it is addressed to a ruler and tells him to tax less, campaign less and leave his people alone. Its praise of the small state with few people reads as a direct rebuke of the age that produced it. The archives and scribal offices in which the legendary Laozi supposedly served were real institutions, even if his post in them was not.
life: Everything traditional about Laozi comes from a short and visibly uncertain notice in Sima Qian’s Records of the Grand Historian, written around 100 BCE, at least three centuries after the supposed events. It makes him Li Er, a keeper of the Zhou archives, an older contemporary whom Confucius consulted about ritual and who rebuked him for his pride. Seeing the Zhou decline, he rode west. The keeper of the pass asked him for a book. He wrote some five thousand characters on the Way and its power and disappeared. Sima Qian then names two other men he might have been, and admits he does not know.

Modern scholarship treats the figure as largely legendary. Laozi means simply the Old Master, which is a title rather than a name. The received book is manifestly composite: rhymed aphorisms, ruler’s counsel and cosmological fragments assembled from a stock of circulating sayings. What the excavated manuscripts do show is that some version existed well before the Han. The safe statement is that the text is Warring States material of uncertain authorship, and that the biography attached to it grew backwards from the book.

works.t: The Classic of the Way and Its Power (Daodejing / Tao Te Ching)
works.y: compiled fourth to third century BCE; received text established third century CE
p: Eighty-one short chapters in two parts, about five thousand characters, heavily rhymed and built on paradox. The dao is prior to naming, so the first line withdraws its own subject: a way that can be spoken is not the constant way. Two moves carry the argument. The first is wu wei, acting without forcing, paired with ziran, the self-so, the way things go when unbullied. Water is the standing example, since it takes the low place and wears away stone. The second is the argument from emptiness — thirty spokes converge on a hub, and it is the hole that makes the wheel useful. The politics follow: a ruler who legislates and campaigns manufactures the disorder he then punishes. The obscurity is real. The text tolerates readings from quietism to statecraft.

Three bundles of bamboo slips from a tomb near Jingmen in Hubei carry roughly two-fifths of the received text, in a different order and with no division into the familiar chapters. They matter for two reasons. They prove that substantial parts of the book circulated by about 300 BCE, which sets a floor under the dating. And in one famous passage the Guodian wording lacks the sharp attack on Confucian benevolence and rightness found in the received chapter 19, telling the ruler instead to discard artifice and greed. That single variant unsettles the picture of Daoism and Confucianism as fixed rival camps from the start.

Two silk copies from a Han tomb near Changsha give something close to the whole text a century and a half before the earliest surviving commentaries. Both put the de section first and the dao section second, reversing the received order. Both differ from it in wording throughout, usually in ways that clarify grammar rather than doctrine. Together with the Beida bamboo copy acquired in 2009, they show a text still fluid in the early empire and only fixed later, chiefly through the recensions carrying the commentaries of Heshang Gong and of Wang Bi.

legacy: Early Han court thought absorbed the book as Huang-Lao doctrine, a programme of light government credited to the Yellow Emperor and the Old Master. Emperor Wen’s reign was later remembered as its application. The interpretive turn came with Wang Bi, who died in 249 at twenty-three and whose commentary made the dao an argument about original non-being. His recension and his reading dominated for over a millennium and founded the tradition of Mysterious Learning. Religious Daoism took a different road, deifying Laozi as the Most High Lord Lao and reading the text as revelation in the second-century Xiang’er commentary of the Celestial Masters.

Outside China the Daodejing became the most translated Chinese book and one of the most translated books of any kind, with hundreds of English versions since James Legge in 1891. Most of them are paraphrases of paraphrases. The popular Western reading — a gentle mysticism of flow and balance — quietly drops both the manuscript problems and the hard political counsel about keeping subjects ignorant and content. Serious study since 1973 has been reorganised around the excavated texts, which is now the first thing a reader should ask a translation to acknowledge.

read.first: Read a translation made after the Mawangdui and Guodian finds, with facing notes on variants. Read it twice: once straight through for the rhythm, once slowly against the commentary.
read.note: Any version that presents a single seamless sage speaking is hiding the state of the evidence from you.

laozi.caveat: Whether Laozi existed at all is genuinely unsettled. The book bearing his name is a compilation whose earliest recoverable form, at Guodian, is neither complete nor in the received order.

confucius.sub: the teacher who made character rather than birth the basis of nobility
world: Confucius was born in 551 BCE into the late Spring and Autumn period, when the Zhou order survived as etiquette and almost nothing else. The king at Luoyang performed the sacrifices. The fighting and the taxing were done by states such as Jin, Chu, Qi and his own small Lu. Hegemons enforced order among them when they could. Lu was distinctive for its careful preservation of Zhou ritual forms. That gave Confucius both his subject matter and his sense of loss. It was also badly governed. Three collateral branches of the ducal house, the Ji, Meng and Shu, had divided the state’s lands and troops between them and reduced the duke to a figurehead. Their own stewards sometimes usurped them in turn.

Underneath this ran a change that made his career possible. War and administration had outgrown the hereditary aristocracy. A class of educated men of modest rank—the shi—were needed as scribes, ritual specialists, envoys and officers. They could be hired, and they could move between states. Confucius took that emerging professional class and gave it an ethic. He argued that the qualities of a gentleman were learnable rather than inherited. His constant complaint was that ritual was being usurped, that the Ji family danced eight rows of dancers in their courtyard when only the king might. That complaint is not fussiness about protocol. It is the observation that the forms sustaining political order were being emptied out.
life: He was born in Zou, in Lu, to a family of low aristocratic rank and no money. His father died when he was young. He said of himself that he was fond of learning, and that at fifteen he set his heart upon it. He held minor posts in Lu, keeping granaries and livestock. The tradition that he rose to be minister of crime, and resigned when the duke accepted a gift of dancing girls from Qi, is reported in sources centuries later. It cannot be verified. In his fifties he left Lu with a group of students. He spent something like fourteen years travelling through Wei, Song, Chen and Cai, seeking a ruler who would employ his programme. None did.

He returned to Lu around 484 and taught until his death in 479. The disciples are better attested than the master’s offices: Yan Hui, whom he mourned bitterly and who died young; the blunt and brave Zilu, killed in a coup in Wei in 480; the diplomat and merchant Zigong; Zengzi, to whom later tradition traced a line of transmission. Confucius wrote no book. What he left was a school, and that school’s memory of his conversation. His students and their students assembled it over the following century and more.

works.y: compiled from the fifth to the second century BCE
p: Twenty short books of remarks, exchanges and fragments, with no argument running from one end to the other. It is not a book Confucius wrote. It is a layered compilation by disciples and later disciples. Philologists since the Qing have argued that the middle books are earlier, and that parts of the last five are late accretions. Three recensions circulated in the Han. A partial copy on bamboo slips excavated at Dingzhou in 1973 differs from the received text. What holds it together is a vocabulary. Ren, humaneness, is the disposition to treat others as bearing the same claims as oneself, first at home and then outward. Li, ritual propriety, is the whole repertoire of learned form—ceremony, deference, dress, funerals, manners—treated not as decoration but as the discipline through which a person is shaped. The two are inseparable: form without feeling is hollow, feeling without form is unusable.

works.t: The doctrine of the rectification of names (zhengming)
p: Asked what he would do first if given charge of a state, the Confucius of book 13 answers that he would rectify names. His grounds are that when names are not correct, speech does not fit, affairs are not completed, ritual and music do not flourish, and punishments miss their mark. The claim is that political terms carry normative content. A ruler who does not rule as a ruler should is not properly called one. Calling him so corrupts the language in which the fault could be described. Some scholars doubt this passage is early. Their reason is that its chained reasoning is unlike the surrounding material and its concerns look later. Taken as an argument it is powerful. It is the ancestor of a long Chinese tradition of political criticism conducted through the assessment of titles and precedents.

works.t: The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) and the classical curriculum
works.y: attributed to him; the chronicle covers 722 to 481 BCE
p: Later tradition credited Confucius with editing the Odes, the Documents and the Rites, with writing the appendices to the Changes, and with composing the Spring and Autumn Annals, the terse court chronicle of Lu. In that chronicle every choice of word was read as a hidden verdict on the conduct of rulers. Almost none of this survives modern scrutiny. The Annals is a state record he could not have authored in its entirety. The appendices to the Changes are demonstrably later. The Odes were not cut by him from three thousand poems to three hundred. What is true, and important, is that his school taught from these texts and that its curriculum turned them into the classics of the empire.

legacy: The school was attacked before it was established. Mozi condemned its funerals and its graded affection within a generation or two. The Warring States saw Mencius and Xunzi develop it in opposite directions. Qin, following Legalist advisers, is said to have burned its books in 213 BCE. The rehabilitation came under the Han. Emperor Wu established court erudites for the Five Classics in 136 BCE. Dong Zhongshu wove Confucian ethics into a cosmology of resonance between ruler and Heaven. From there the texts became the material of official examination, formalised under the Tang and reshaped by Zhu Xi. His Four Books—a canon that promoted the Analects and the Mengzi above the older classics—governed the examinations from 1313 until their abolition in 1905.

Jesuit missionaries in the seventeenth century latinised the name Kong Fuzi into Confucius. They presented him to Europe as a rational moralist without theology, a portrait that pleased Leibniz and Voltaire and irritated Rome. Chinese reformers of the May Fourth generation attacked the same tradition as the ideology of the family despot and the eunuch bureaucracy. Both readings flatten a body of thought that is chiefly about the formation of persons through practice. The negative formulation of the golden rule—do not impose on others what you do not want yourself—stands in the Analects centuries before its Western parallels. Virtue ethicists now read the book alongside Aristotle rather than as a curiosity.

read.first: Read the Analects in a translation that keeps ren and li untranslated or consistently rendered, with book and section numbers and a short introduction on the text’s layers.
read.note: It reads as disconnected until you notice that the same handful of questions recurs, put to different students who need different answers.

confucius.caveat: Confucius wrote nothing that survives. The Analects is a compilation assembled by later disciples over a century or more. Its layers are not all equally close to him.

buddha.sub: the teacher who diagnosed suffering and prescribed a path out of it
world: The Ganges plain in the fifth century BCE was in the middle of its second urbanisation. Iron tools had opened the wet eastern forests to rice agriculture. Surpluses fed towns such as Rajagaha, Savatthi, Vesali and Kosambi. Punch-marked silver coins, guilds and long-distance caravans appeared together. Politically the region had consolidated into a set of large kingdoms and a few surviving clan oligarchies, of which the Buddha’s own Sakya was one. Magadha under Bimbisara and then Ajatasattu was swallowing its neighbours and would eventually control the whole plain. Kosala under Pasenadi was its chief rival. Both kings appear in the canon as patrons.

Religiously the plain was contested. Brahmanical authority rested on the Vedic sacrifice, an expensive apparatus of offerings and fees that only the wealthy could commission and only Brahmins could perform. Against it stood the shramana movements. These were wandering renouncers who rejected the sacrifice, the ritual expertise and often the caste order. They lived on alms from precisely the new merchant and urban wealth that the old system did not serve. Their range was wide—the strict asceticism and non-injury of Mahavira’s Jains, the fatalism of the Ajivikas, the frank materialism of Ajita, the evasive scepticism of Sanjaya. The Buddha’s middle way is stated against these positions and cannot be read apart from them.
life: Siddhattha Gotama was born to a leading family of the Sakya, at Lumbini near the modern Nepal border, and grew up at Kapilavatthu. The familiar story—the sheltered palace, the four sights of an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a renouncer, the night departure leaving wife and infant son—is scripture rather than biography. It was elaborated over centuries into the form most readers meet. The canon itself preserves a plainer account: he left home while young and healthy, against his parents’ wishes, to seek an end to ageing and death. He trained under two meditation teachers, Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta, found their attainments insufficient, practised severe austerity with five companions, and abandoned it.

The awakening is placed at Uruvela, later Bodh Gaya. The first teaching is placed in the deer park at Isipatana near Varanasi, to the five ascetics who had left him. Forty-five years of teaching followed, in a circuit of the middle Ganges towns. It was structured by the annual rains retreat and supported by lay patrons such as the merchant Anathapindika. The canon records a monastic order that admitted women after some resistance, a schism attempted by his cousin Devadatta, and a death from illness at Kusinara in his eightieth year. His dates are the unresolved problem. The traditional 563 to 483 BCE was long standard, while most current scholarship favours a range roughly a century later, around 480 to 400.

works.y: oral transmission from the fifth or fourth century BCE; written down in Sri Lanka c. 29 BCE
p: The Buddha wrote nothing. There is no first-hand document of any kind. What exists is a collection in three baskets—monastic discipline, discourses, and the later systematic Abhidhamma. Reciters who specialised in one division each preserved it for centuries. It was committed to writing in Sri Lanka under King Vattagamani, by tradition at the Aluvihara, around the middle of the first century BCE. Oral transmission of this kind is not casual: the texts are built for it, with numbered lists, formulaic repetition and stock passages that make deviation audible. But it is not stenography either. The canon plainly contains material of different ages. The strongest control is comparative. Chinese translations of the parallel Agamas, preserved by other schools, and Gandhari manuscript fragments from the first centuries CE agree with the Pali often enough to establish an early common core. They disagree often enough to forbid treating any single version as the master text.

works.y: traditionally the first teaching; text as transmitted
p: The discourse that sets the wheel of dhamma turning opens by rejecting two extremes, indulgence in pleasure and the mortification of the body, both of which the speaker had tried. Between them lies the eightfold path: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. The four noble truths are then set out in a form borrowed from medicine—symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment. There is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness that runs through birth, ageing, sickness, loss and even pleasure because pleasure ends; it arises from craving; with the ending of craving it ends; and there is a practice that ends it. The structure is what makes the teaching distinctive. It is not a description of the world’s badness but a causal claim with a therapeutic conclusion. It stakes everything on the second truth being true.

works.t: The teaching of non-self and dependent origination
p: The second discourse to the five ascetics takes each of the five aggregates that compose a person—body, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness—and argues that none can be the self, because each is impermanent, each leads to suffering, and no one can command it to be otherwise. There is no additional sixth thing left over. This is anatta. It is grounded in the wider principle of dependent origination: whatever arises does so conditioned by something else, so nothing stands unchanging underneath. The result is a person without a substantial soul but with real continuity. That is why the canon can deny the self and still speak of memory and moral responsibility. Hume reached a comparable bundle view two millennia later by a different route. The Buddha also refused a set of speculative questions—whether the world is eternal, what becomes of the awakened after death—on the ground that answering them does not remove the arrow.

legacy: Within two centuries the order had spread across northern India. It split, first over discipline and then over doctrine, into the schools whose Abhidhamma systems dominated Buddhist philosophy for a millennium. Ashoka’s patronage in the third century BCE gave it inscriptions, endowments and missions, including the one to Sri Lanka that preserved the Pali texts. His edicts are the earliest datable evidence for the tradition’s spread. Mahayana movements from around the turn of the era added new sutras and a new ideal. Buddhism travelled the Central Asian trade routes into China, then Korea, Japan and Tibet, and by sea into Southeast Asia, while receding in India itself.

Europe met the texts seriously only in the nineteenth century, and misread them twice over. The first misreading was pessimism, in Schopenhauer’s appropriation. The second, in the Pali Text Society’s Victorian framing after 1881, was a rational ethical philosophy purified of ritual, gods and rebirth, which the canon does not support. Both readings still circulate. Philosophically the durable contributions are the analysis of the person without a substrate, the causal treatment of suffering, and the refusal of metaphysical questions that make no practical difference—positions now argued over in journals of philosophy of mind rather than only in monasteries.

read.first: Begin with an anthology of discourses from the middle-length and connected collections, in a modern translation with introductions, rather than with a general book about Buddhism.
read.note: The repetitions are not padding but the mechanics of an oral text. They stop being tiresome once you read them as designed.

buddha.caveat: Nothing was written in his lifetime, the earliest manuscripts postdate him by centuries, and his dates are disputed by nearly a hundred years between the traditional 563 to 483 BCE and the revised range of roughly 480 to 400.

mozi.sub: the first consequentialist, and Confucianism’s earliest serious critic
world: Mozi worked in the opening decades of the Warring States. The old chariot aristocracy was giving way to mass infantry, crossbows and long sieges. States were absorbing one another outright rather than merely humbling one another. Warfare on that scale was paid for by peasants who also paid for the ritual apparatus of the courts: three years of mourning for a parent, lavish burials, orchestras of bell and chime. Mozi’s arguments are directed at that arithmetic. He also worked in a period when the artisan trades—carpentry, fortification, mechanics—were producing knowledge that no court school had systematised.
life: Mo Di lived roughly from 470 to 391 BCE, though the dates are inferred rather than recorded. Almost nothing personal survives. Later sources suggest an artisan or low-status background. The tradition that he was trained in Confucian learning before rejecting it is plausible but not documented. What is clear is that he founded something no other early Chinese thinker did: a disciplined organisation under a grandmaster. Its members lived austerely, could be assigned to serve in office, and were dispatched to help defend cities under attack. In the book’s story he walks ten days to Chu to talk a king out of invading Song, then out-argues the engineer Gongshu Ban in a mock siege on a belt buckle. It is told as illustration rather than as record.

works.y: compiled fourth to third century BCE
p: Fifty-three of an original seventy-one chapters survive. The ten central doctrines appear in triplicate—three overlapping versions each—which scholars read as evidence of three later Mohist sub-schools transmitting the teaching separately. The prose is repetitive, explicit and argued, a genuine novelty after the aphorism. Its method is stated: a doctrine is tested against the precedent of the sage kings, against what people actually see and hear, and above all against its results in practice for the wealth, order and population of the state. Jian ai, impartial concern, follows from that test rather than from sentiment. Partiality is the root of aggression, so we should care for others’ parents as for our own. Elaborate funerals and court music fail the same test, since they consume what the living need.

works.t: The Dialectical Chapters, or Mohist Canons (Mojing)
p: Six chapters of terse canons with explanations, produced by the later Mohists rather than by Mozi himself. They contain definitions of terms such as cause, duration and sameness, an analysis of disputation in which of two contradictory claims exactly one must win, geometrical and mechanical propositions covering levers and balances, and a set of optical observations including the inverted image formed by a pinhole. It is the only sustained attempt at logic and natural science in classical China. The text was catastrophically garbled in transmission. Its recovery depended on the philological reconstruction of Sun Yirang in 1894 and, in English, of A. C. Graham a century later.

legacy: Mohism was Confucianism’s chief rival for two centuries: Mencius complained that the doctrines of Yang Zhu and Mo Di filled the world. It then vanished almost completely after the Qin unification, its organisation gone and its book preserved chiefly by inclusion in the Daoist canon. Qing evidential scholars recovered it. The twentieth century read it twice over: as China’s indigenous utilitarianism and proto-science, and, less charitably, as a joyless austerity that could not survive contact with ordinary family feeling. Both readings understate how much of it is simply argument, offered where others offered precedent.

read.first: Read a selection built around the core doctrinal triads on impartial care, against offensive warfare, and moderation in expenditure, with the Canons kept for later.
read.note: The style is flat and hammering by design. It is what argument looked like when someone first tried to make positions answerable to evidence.

mozi.caveat: His dates are reconstructed. Nothing biographical about him is securely attested. The book is a school compilation in which the technical chapters are demonstrably by later hands.

mencius.sub: the Confucian who held that human nature already tends toward the good
world: By the middle of the fourth century BCE the Warring States had contracted to seven serious contenders. Government had become a technical business of registers, granaries, conscription and law. Qin, under the reforms attributed to Shang Yang from the 350s, had gone furthest: hereditary privilege replaced by ranks earned in battle, the population organised into mutually liable groups, agriculture and war declared the only worthy occupations. The results were visible in the field. Other states copied what they could. Mencius travelled among rulers who wanted to know how to enlarge their territories. They were told, to their evident irritation, that they should begin by reducing taxes.

Intellectually the age was crowded. Qi maintained the Jixia academy at Linzi, where stipended scholars of every persuasion argued in public. Mohists preached impartial concern and the audit of consequences. Followers of Yang Zhu argued that one should not give a hair from one’s body to benefit the world. Logicians pressed puzzles about names. Mencius names Yang and Mo as the two errors he must refute, egoism and impartialism. He positions his own account of the moral emotions between them. The Confucian school in this period was one competitor among many, and by no means the strongest.
life: Meng Ke came from Zou, a small state near Confucius’s Lu, probably around 372 BCE. He died around 289. The tradition that he studied under a follower of Zisi, Confucius’s grandson, is late and unverifiable. It does correctly place him in a transmission that ran through the master’s family school. The famous story of his mother moving house three times—away from a cemetery, away from a market, finally beside a school—comes from Han collections written more than a century after his death. It belongs to legend.

His career followed the pattern of the itinerant persuader. He spent time at the court of King Xuan of Qi, where he seems to have held an honorary position. He visited King Hui of Liang, the small state of Teng, and others, arguing for a humane government that would win the empire without fighting for it. No ruler adopted the programme. He withdrew from public life in old age. With disciples including Wan Zhang and Gongsun Chou, he produced the record of his conversations that carries his name.

works.y: compiled late fourth to early third century BCE
p: Seven books, each divided in two, and a different kind of text from the Analects: the exchanges run to a page or more, opponents answer back, and the arguments have structure. The audience is largely royal. Confronted by King Hui, who asks what profit his state can expect from the visit, Mencius answers that the king should speak of humaneness and rightness and not of profit. He then explains why a state that begins from advantage disintegrates into competing advantages. Zhao Qi’s commentary around 200 CE fixed the seven-book text and dismissed four further “outer” books as spurious. Those are lost. The surviving material is generally accepted as an early record of his teaching.

works.t: The debate on human nature with Gaozi
p: Gaozi holds that human nature is like swirling water, indifferent to east and west, and that morality is imposed on it as cups are carved from a willow. Mencius replies that water indifferent to direction is not indifferent to height: it goes down, as human nature goes toward good. The positive argument is the child at the well. Anyone who suddenly saw an infant about to fall in would feel alarm and compassion—not to gain the parents’ favour, not for a reputation, but immediately. That reaction is evidence of a sprout already present. Four such sprouts—compassion, shame, deference, and the sense of right and wrong—grow into humaneness, rightness, propriety and wisdom if they are nourished. They wither if they are not. Ox Mountain is bare, he adds, but it was not always bare; it was grazed.

works.t: The political chapters and the Mandate of Heaven
p: The economic proposals are concrete: fixed and light taxation, a state that keeps its people from starving before it teaches them, and the well-field scheme in which eight families farm their own plots and work a ninth in common for the lord. His schematic history of it was probably never practice. It nevertheless shaped land reform arguments for two thousand years. The political conclusion is far bolder. Heaven’s mandate is conditional on the ruler’s treatment of the people. The people are the most valuable element in a state, the altars of soil and grain next, and the ruler least. Asked whether the founder of the Zhou committed regicide in killing the last Shang king, Mencius answers that he had heard of the execution of a mere fellow, not the murder of a sovereign.

legacy: Xunzi took the opposite view within the same school, holding that human nature is bad and that virtue is the deliberate achievement of ritual training. The argument between the two positions ran for two millennia without resolution. For much of the early imperial period Mencius was a secondary figure. His elevation came with the Song. Zhu Xi placed the Mengzi among the Four Books in 1190. From 1313 the examinations rested on that canon, which made his account of the sprouts something close to official psychology. Not everyone welcomed it. The founder of the Ming had the passage on tyrannicide removed from the examination text in 1395, which is the most eloquent testimony to its force.

Korean and Japanese Confucianism inherited the same canon and the same argument. Wang Yangming later pushed the innate knowledge of the good much further than Mencius had. Modern Western readers have found in him the nearest classical Chinese analogue to moral sentimentalism. Comparisons with Hutcheson and Hume are now standard. He differs from both, though, in treating the moral emotions as needing cultivation rather than merely as given. The four sprouts remain one of the few genuinely testable claims in classical ethics. Developmental psychologists have taken an interest in them.

read.first: Read book 2A, then book 6A, then the opening exchanges with King Hui, before going through the whole in a translation with the section numbers marked.
read.note: He argues by analogy far more than by definition. The analogies repay the same scrutiny his opponents give them.

mencius.caveat: The four outer books rejected by Zhao Qi are lost. The biographical traditions about his mother and his teachers are Han-era additions rather than evidence.

zhuangzi.sub: the sceptic who wrote in parables and refused a fixed standpoint
world: The late fourth century BCE was the high season of the persuader. Rulers of Qi, Wei, Chu and Qin maintained scholars, strategists and diplomats. A man with a well-turned argument could rise from nothing to a chancellorship. The Jixia academy in Qi paid stipends to teachers of every school. The schools themselves were hardening into camps with doctrines to defend. Zhuangzi’s Song lay between the great powers and was eventually destroyed by them, in 286 BCE, near the traditional date of his death. Much of the book’s scorn for public usefulness is written from that vantage: conspicuous talent got men employed, and employment in that period got them killed.

His immediate philosophical neighbours were the disputers. Hui Shi and Gongsun Long pressed paradoxes about names, sameness and difference. The Mohist dialecticians were building a theory of how disputes are decided. Confucians and Mohists shouted at each other about ritual and impartial care, each taking the other’s affirmations as denials. That environment supplies both the material and the target of the Inner Chapters. Their central question is not which school is right, but what it would take for any of them to establish that it was.
life: Sima Qian gives him a short notice: Zhuang Zhou of Meng, in Song, who held a minor post at the lacquer garden, was a contemporary of King Hui of Liang and King Xuan of Qi, and wrote more than a hundred thousand words, mostly parables. That is close to everything documentary. The traditional dates of roughly 369 to 286 BCE are inferences from the rulers he is said to have overlapped with.

The rest is anecdote, told in the book about its own supposed author. Envoys from Chu offer him the chancellorship. He asks whether a sacred tortoise, dead three thousand years and honoured in a temple, would not rather be alive and dragging its tail in the mud. He tells them to go away. He argues with his friend Hui Shi on a bridge over the Hao about whether one can know that the fish are happy. His wife dies, and he is found drumming on a tub and singing, having reflected that she has gone back into the great transformation. These are literary set pieces, and it is a mistake to read them as memoir. They are the book showing what its own doctrine looks like when lived.

works.y: fourth to second century BCE; received text edited c. 300 CE
p: The received book has thirty-three chapters, in three groups: Inner (1 to 7), Outer (8 to 22) and Miscellaneous (23 to 33). It reached that form through Guo Xiang. Around 300 CE he cut a text the Han catalogue records as fifty-two chapters down to what he considered genuine, discarding material he thought fantastic. Only the Inner Chapters are usually treated as plausibly the work of Zhuang Zhou himself. The rest is by later hands of several kinds. A. C. Graham separated out a Primitivist writer hostile to civilisation, a Yangist strand concerned with preserving life, and a Syncretist editor who tried to fit Daoism to statecraft. This matters for interpretation, because some of the best-known positions attributed to Zhuangzi—the frank primitivism, the political programme—belong to strata he did not write.

works.t: On the Equality of Things (Qiwulun), chapter 2
p: The hardest and most important chapter in the book. Its argument begins from the observation that every affirmation is made from somewhere: what is this from where I stand is that from where you stand. The disputes between Confucians and Mohists consist of each affirming what the other denies. Zhuangzi then closes the obvious exit. If you and I argue and you win, are you right? Suppose we call in a third party—he must agree with one of us, or with neither. In each case he cannot settle it without already having taken a side. The regress is genuine and it is not answered. What follows is not the doctrine that all views are equally true, which would be one more fixed position, but a loosening of insistence. The sage uses the ordinary distinctions and does not lean on them. The butterfly dream closes the chapter without resolving it.

Cook Ding has cut up oxen for nineteen years and his blade is as sharp as the day it was ground, because he no longer looks but works where the spaces already are. He slows only at the difficult joints. The wheelwright tells a duke that his craft cannot be put into words, and that the books the duke is reading are therefore the dregs of dead men. A cicada catcher holds his pole as still as a tree stump. The point is epistemological, not sentimental. These figures know how to act with an accuracy that no articulated rule reproduces. Their mastery grew through practice into responsiveness—which is what wu wei looks like when it is not being preached. The same chapters supply the counter-image of uselessness, the gnarled tree that no carpenter will fell and that lives out its span.

legacy: Guo Xiang’s edition and commentary carried the book into the Mysterious Learning of the third and fourth centuries, where it was read alongside the Daodejing and the Changes. It gave the poets and eccentrics of the period—the circle remembered as the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove—their vocabulary of withdrawal. When Buddhism arrived, its translators borrowed Zhuangzi’s terms. Chan inherited both his distrust of doctrinal formulation and his taste for the deflating story. Chinese landscape painting and poetry drew on him for a thousand years.

In modern philosophy the argument has been over what kind of sceptic he is. Some read him as a relativist, some as a therapeutic sceptic who suspends judgement without asserting that no judgement is true, some as a mystic for whom the regress opens onto something beyond argument. The comparisons pressed hardest are with Pyrrho, with the later Wittgenstein, and with Nietzsche on perspective. What deserves emphasis is that the text does not merely recommend flexibility but supplies a real argument for it. Its literary form—jokes, invented conversations, an unreliable narrator—is itself the refusal to occupy the position of the man who has settled the question.

read.first: Read the Inner Chapters first and entire, in a translation that marks the division and explains it. Leave the Outer and Miscellaneous chapters for a second pass.
read.note: Chapter 2 will not yield on a first reading. The parables around it are how the book teaches you to read it.

zhuangzi.caveat: Only the seven Inner Chapters are generally regarded as plausibly by Zhuang Zhou. The received text is Guo Xiang’s reduction of a longer Han-era book. The biographical anecdotes come from the book itself.

nagarjuna.sub: the Buddhist dialectician who emptied even emptiness
world: The India of the second century CE was politically divided and commercially rich. The Kushans ruled the north-west and much of the Ganges plain from Purushapura and Mathura, minting gold, patronising Buddhist establishments and connecting India to the silk routes. The Satavahanas held the Deccan. The ports of the western and eastern coasts traded with Rome. Buddhist monasticism prospered on that wealth. The great stupa complexes of Amaravati and, later, Nagarjunakonda in the Krishna valley were built and rebuilt by donations from merchants, guilds and royal women. Monasteries had libraries, endowments and the leisure for scholastic argument.

That argument had a specific shape. The Abhidharma schools, above all the Sarvastivada, had spent centuries analysing experience into lists of dharmas, the ultimate constituents into which persons and objects decompose. The person was empty, but the constituents were held to possess svabhava, intrinsic nature. Meanwhile the Perfection of Wisdom sutras were circulating, declaring in an oracular register that all things are empty and that there is nothing to attain. Nāgārjuna’s work stands exactly between the two: it takes the sutras’ claim and supplies the argument that the scholastics’ method demanded.
life: There is almost no biography. The traditional lives—a Chinese one associated with Kumārajīva around 405, and much later Tibetan accounts—make him a South Indian Brahmin who mastered the Vedas as a boy, entered the order, retrieved the Perfection of Wisdom sutras from the underwater realm of the nāgas, practised alchemy, advised a king, and lived several hundred years. Some of these accounts place him at Nālandā, which did not yet exist. They are hagiography. The tradition itself preserves variants that contradict one another.

What can be said with reasonable confidence is that a South Indian author wrote the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā in the second or early third century CE, that he addressed a work of advice to a king who was probably a Sātavāhana, and that his Sanskrit is that of a trained scholastic arguing with named Abhidharma positions. The complication is that there is more than one Nāgārjuna. Tantric works from the seventh and eighth centuries, medical and alchemical texts, and a large Chinese commentary all circulate under the name. The tradition merged them into a single very long-lived sage.

works.t: Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā)
p: Twenty-seven chapters of compressed verse, each taking a category the schools treated as fundamental—causation, motion, the senses, fire and fuel, time, the self, the Buddha, nirvana—and showing that it cannot be given a coherent account if its terms are supposed to have intrinsic nature. The characteristic instrument is the tetralemma: a thing does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause. Since these exhaust the options, nothing arises in the way the analysis requires. The conclusion is śūnyatā, emptiness, which Nāgārjuna identifies with dependent origination itself and calls the middle way. Chapter 24 answers the obvious objection, that if everything is empty the four noble truths collapse. He replies that the objector has it backwards, since only what is empty can arise, change and cease. The most radical claim follows in chapter 25, where nirvana and the round of rebirth are said to have not the slightest difference between them.

A short work in verse with the author’s own prose commentary, devoted to a single objection: if all things lack intrinsic nature, the sentence asserting this lacks intrinsic nature too, and therefore cannot refute anything. Nāgārjuna’s reply is that he has no thesis of his own to defend. His statement is like a magically produced man who stops another magically produced man—empty, and effective for exactly that reason, since it works by removing a supposition rather than by asserting a fact. Whether this reply succeeds is still argued. It is the pivot on which readings of him as a nihilist, a sceptic, or a therapist of concepts turn. The work also engages the Nyāya theory of the means of knowledge, denying that any such instrument can be self-certifying.

Beyond the two works above, a small group is widely though not universally accepted: the Sixty Verses on Reasoning, the Seventy Verses on Emptiness, the Precious Garland and the verse Letter to a Friend, the last two being counsel to a king on governing well and generously. Those two show a practical and political side rarely mentioned. Beyond that the attributions weaken sharply. The vast Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom survives only in Kumārajīva’s Chinese and is generally doubted. Devotional hymns are contested. The tantric and alchemical works are certainly by later men of the same name. No consensus list exists. Any strong claim about what Nāgārjuna thought should be checked against which texts it rests on.

legacy: Madhyamaka became a school in the hands of his commentators. Buddhapālita, Bhāviveka and Candrakīrti disagreed over whether the emptiness argument may be stated as a formal proof or only as a reduction of the opponent’s position. Tibetan doxographers later hardened that dispute into the division between Svātantrika and Prāsaṅgika. Candrakīrti’s commentary is also the reason the Sanskrit verses survive at all, since they are preserved embedded in it. Kumārajīva’s translations carried the system to China as the Three Treatise school and from there to Japan. In Tibet it became the philosophical foundation of every major order. Tsongkhapa’s reading of it remains authoritative for the Geluk.

Western scholarship spent a century deciding what kind of position this is. Stcherbatsky read it as an absolutism behind the negations, Murti in 1955 as a Kantian critique of reason, others as plain nihilism. That charge Nāgārjuna himself anticipated and rejected, warning that emptiness misgrasped destroys the one who grasps it, like a snake seized at the wrong end. The reading now dominant, advanced in different forms by Ruegg, Garfield and others, takes the two truths seriously: conventional truth is not a lie but the only place where anything functions, and the ultimate truth is that nothing possesses the independence our concepts assign it. Comparisons with Pyrrhonism and with Wittgenstein are common and productive, and generally overstate the resemblance.

read.first: Read the Fundamental Verses with a translation that carries a full commentary on the facing page. Read chapter 24 on the two truths before attempting chapter 1.
read.note: The verses are notes for an argument rather than the argument itself. Without a commentary they will look like a string of denials.

nagarjuna.caveat: His biography is legend almost in its entirety. His dates are approximate. The attribution of several works bearing his name—including at least one very large one—is disputed or rejected.

shankara.sub: the non-dualist who read the Upanishads as a single argument
world: The India in which Śaṅkara wrote was the post-Gupta world of regional powers — Pallavas, Chālukyas, Rāṣṭrakūṭas — whose temple endowments and land grants funded a professional class of scholars and commentators. Two opponents shaped his work. Mīmāṃsā, systematised by Kumārila and Prabhākara shortly before him, held that the Veda is authoritative precisely as a body of ritual injunctions, so that a statement about what merely is could have no religious force. Buddhist scholasticism, in its Yogācāra and Madhyamaka forms, was still institutionally strong and philosophically formidable. Śaṅkara had to show that the Upanishads assert something, and that what they assert is not the Buddhists’ emptiness.
life: Tradition places his birth at Kālaṭi in Kerala and his death at thirty-two, and gives the dates 788 to 820. But those dates are late and contested. Many scholars now argue for the first half of the eighth century or earlier. He is said to have studied under Govinda, in a line running back to Gauḍapāda, to have taken sannyasa as a boy, to have travelled the subcontinent debating rival teachers, and to have founded the four monastic seats that still claim him. The hagiographies telling this are centuries later and frankly miraculous. The harder problem is the corpus: more than three hundred works circulate under his name. Only a handful are securely his.

p: His largest and most certainly authentic work, and the text against which every other attribution is tested. Its opening section on superimposition is the philosophical heart: we habitually confuse the self with the body, mind and their attributes, as one mistakes a rope for a snake or silver for mother-of-pearl. This beginningless confusion is ignorance rather than error about a particular fact. The body of the commentary then works through the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Jain and Buddhist alternatives and refutes each. It defends a Brahman that is without qualities at the ultimate level and describable with qualities at the level of worship.

works.t: Commentaries on the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita
p: The commentaries on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Chāndogya are securely his, as are several on the shorter Upanishads and the one on the Gita. Their strategy is consistent and pointed. The great sayings — that thou art, I am Brahman — are read as statements of identity between ātman and Brahman, not as instructions to meditate or to sacrifice, which answers Mīmāṃsā on its own ground. Māyā names the status of the world that follows: not a hallucination, but real at the empirical level and not at the ultimate. Liberation is therefore recognition of what was always the case rather than an achievement.

The only independent, non-commentarial work that scholars generally accept as his, and the best entry to his thought because it is not tied to another author’s sequence. It has a prose part staging an exchange between teacher and pupil, and a longer metrical part. Its subject is how the identity of self and Brahman can be conveyed at all, given that the pupil’s ignorance is what needs removing. Its authenticity, argued at length by Sengaku Mayeda, is one of the firmer results of twentieth-century philology on this corpus.

legacy: His immediate pupils Sureśvara and Padmapāda founded the lines that became the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa schools. Advaita went on to dominate Vedanta scholastically — which is why Rāmānuja in the twelfth century and Madhva in the thirteenth built their theistic Vedantas as refutations of him. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Vivekananda and the neo-Vedantins presented Advaita to Western audiences as the essence of Hinduism itself, a claim Śaṅkara never made and that flattens a plural tradition. Deussen and, through him, Schopenhauer read him as an Indian Kant. The resemblance to Kant’s two standpoints is real, but the arguments are not the same.

read.first: Start with A Thousand Teachings in Mayeda’s translation, then read the preamble on superimposition from the Brahma Sutra commentary.
read.note: Much that is sold under his name is by later Advaitins, so check any short devotional work against the accepted list before treating it as his.

shankara.caveat: His dates are disputed by at least half a century. The traditional life is hagiography. Of the hundreds of works ascribed to him, only a small number are securely authentic. His dates are contested rather than merely approximate. The years 788–820, long printed in reference works, are the traditional hagiographic ones. Nakamura’s argument for c. 700–750 is now the more widely held view. This timeline uses the earlier dating.

zhu-xi.sub: who made Confucianism a metaphysics, and the metaphysics an examination syllabus
world: The Southern Song had lost the north to the Jin in 1127 and governed from Hangzhou under permanent military threat. A defeated dynasty asks what went wrong, and one answer was that Buddhism and Daoism had hollowed out the Chinese tradition from within.

They had done so partly by being better at metaphysics. Confucian texts said how to behave and said little about what there is, while Buddhism offered a complete account of mind and reality. The Northern Song thinkers — the Cheng brothers, Zhou Dunyi, Zhang Zai — had begun building an answer. Zhu Xi's work is the completion of theirs, and the printing press made its spread possible.
life: Born in 1130 in Fujian, the son of an official who had opposed peace with the Jin and lost his post for it. He passed the highest examination at eighteen, unusually young, and then spent most of his life avoiding office: of some fifty years of official appointment he served about nine, most of it in minor local posts, preferring temple sinecures that paid a stipend and required nothing.

He taught instead, restoring the White Deer Grotto Academy in 1179 and turning it into the model for private academies for centuries. He wrote constantly and argued constantly; the correspondence with Lu Xiangshan over whether moral knowledge requires study or only the recovery of the mind is one of the great philosophical exchanges. In 1196 his teaching was proscribed as false learning and his followers were purged. He died in 1200 under the ban, and thousands came to the funeral in defiance of it.

works.t: Collected Commentaries on the Four Books (Sishu zhangju jizhu)
p: Zhu Xi selected the Analects, the Mencius, the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean out of the classical corpus, called them the Four Books, and wrote the commentary that says what they mean. The selection is itself the argument: it puts a short, teachable canon about self-cultivation at the centre where the older Five Classics had been. From 1313 to 1905 this book, with his commentary, was the examination syllabus of the Chinese state. It is hard to name a text that has been studied by more people for longer.

Compiled with Lü Zuqian: six hundred and twenty-two passages from the four Northern Song masters, arranged by topic, with the metaphysics first and the practical matters after. It is a philosophical anthology built to be taught, and it defined which predecessors counted. The Korean and Japanese Neo-Confucian schools learned the tradition from this book.

works.t: Classified Conversations of Master Zhu (Zhuzi yulei)
p: A hundred and forty chapters of his students' notes, which is where the system is stated most plainly. Everything is li, pattern or principle, together with qi, the psycho-physical stuff that makes it this particular thing; the two are never found apart but are not the same. Human nature is li in a person and is therefore good, and evil is turbidity in the qi, which practice can clarify. The programme that follows is the investigation of things: examine the pattern in particular things, one after another, and the coherence of the whole eventually opens.

legacy: Rehabilitated within a generation of his death and canonised soon after, his reading became the state orthodoxy in 1313 and stayed so for nearly six hundred years, which makes him the most institutionally successful philosopher in history. Korea's Chosŏn dynasty adopted it as official doctrine and produced in Yi Hwang and Yi I a tradition of extraordinary technical refinement; in Japan it became the Tokugawa orthodoxy.

Orthodoxy invites attack. Wang Yangming in the sixteenth century, having tried to investigate the pattern in a bamboo for seven days and made himself ill, concluded that principle is in the mind and not in things. Qing evidential scholars said the whole system was Buddhism in Confucian clothes. Twentieth-century reformers blamed it for everything they wanted to change. What is not disputed is the scale: for most of the last millennium, to be educated in East Asia meant to be educated in Zhu Xi.

read.first: Reflections on Things at Hand in Wing-tsit Chan's translation, which is annotated for readers coming from outside the tradition. Then selections from the Classified Conversations.
read.note: The commentary on the Four Books is best approached through a translation that prints the classic and the commentary together, so that it is clear which claims are Zhu Xi's.

zhu-xi.caveat: Whether li and qi are two principles or two aspects of one thing was disputed in his lifetime and remains so; his own formulations differ, and the Korean debates over the priority of the two ran for centuries on the strength of that ambiguity.
